Discussion  In this work, we introduced HistoEncoder, a FM for PCa DP. FMs hold significant promise to contribute to precision cancer medicine. Whereas pre-training a FM takes considerable computational resources, the model can then be fine-tuned to a multitude of specific tasks. 60 ,  61 ,  62  Importantly, fine-tuning often requires orders of magnitude less data and resources than pre-training. 6 ,  63 ,  64   We pre-trained HistoEncoder with 48 million tile images extracted from prostate tissue images and showed how the model could distinguish malignant and benign tissues, Gleason grades, as well as stromal and epithelial tissues without any annotated information on tissue types being available during training. In this study, we demonstrated how pre-training with domain-specific images yielded substantially better performance than using natural images for prostate histopathology tasks. In line with our findings, recent FMs trained on tissue images have had excellent performance in DP downstream tasks such as cancer detection and survival prediction. These models have, however, not challenged existing cancer-specific clinical prediction models to the extent that we address PCa.  Here, we demonstrated extending and applying HistoEncoder in two clinically relevant tasks. First, we created a classifier which achieved high performance in predicting the presence of PCa. We observed significantly better prediction accuracy, and compute and data efficiency with HistoEncoder models trained with tissue images compared to identical models trained with natural images, also in unsupervised cancer grading task. We also benchmarked HistoEncoder against four recent large pan-tissue H&E FMs, and observed that all performed at a consistently high level in Gleason grading. These results are compatible with the recent benchmarking effort by Akebli et al., who explored tissue image pathology FMs as a basis for PCa detection. It is important to note, however, that HistoEncoder models are much smaller in terms of model parameters and thus, much faster to execute than the leading pan-tissue models such as H-Optimus-1. This gives HistoEncoder models an advantage in resource efficiency and ability to perform a multitude of clinical analysis tasks in limited hardware settings. Second, we used HistoEncoder to summarize the distribution of histological patterns in each patient's tissue and evaluated these histological cluster fractions as predictors of PCa-specific mortality. In internal nested cross-validation, the image features alone achieved discrimination of a similar magnitude to conventional Gleason grading, showing that the self-supervisedly learnt representations capture prognosis-associated morphology. However, the confidence intervals were wide, the image-feature model did not outperform Gleason grading, and adding image features to Gleason grade did not improve discrimination. The prognostic information captured by the cluster fractions therefore appears to overlap substantially with that represented by Gleason grade in this cohort.  Previously, Pinckaers et al. developed a CNN model trained on BCR outcomes in a case–control setting.  65   A biomarker derived from this ImageNet-pre-trained ResNet50-D model demonstrated significant predictivity in a multivariable model including pre-operative PSA, ISUP Gleason grade, pathological stage, and surgical margin status. In an external validation cohort, however, the conventional ISUP Gleason grade outperformed the biomarker. This highlights the challenge of developing generalizable models for real-world clinical applications.  A widely acknowledged challenge is heterogeneity in the histopathological ground truth across institutions and time periods, reflecting evolving grading recommendations, including known controversies between the 2019 ISUP and GUPS consensus statements for reporting PCa. Our datasets, as datasets in many previous publications, span different institutions and diagnostic eras, and the annotations or slide labels were not retrospectively rereviewed or harmonized. Annotation heterogeneity matters for grade-based downstream evaluation. However, it is less directly relevant to the self-supervised objective because Gleason, IDC-P, and cribriform labels are not used as pre-training targets. For these reasons, the main interest of the field and how the FM should be utilized is not to repeat Gleason grading with AI. Rather, finding new, potentially prognostic or predictive, features with the help of AI is the key objective in cancer diagnostics and treatment decision making. This reinforces the need for harmonized and well-curated cohorts that include long-term survival data.  We provide HistoEncoder as an easy-to-use Python package containing both the models pre-trained with prostate tissue images, as well as a standalone software tool to extract features and cluster tissue tile images. HistoEncoder can thus be extended to specific tasks involving any histopathological images.  As proof of concept, we were able to address clinical questions with HistoEncoder using limited data and computing resources from a single laptop computer. This exemplifies the utility of such FMs in lowering the barrier to creating clinical software tools. The prostate-s and prostate-m encoder models were able to compress information from large tissue areas into a feature vector, which was subsequently combined with other data modalities. If the other data modalities, such as spatial transcriptomics data  48   or TMA spot labels, contain information for small tissue regions, feature vectors can be directly extracted for these regions with HistoEncoder models.  Taken together, our results demonstrate how HistofaEncoder can provide clinically relevant insights from tissue images. FMs such as HistoEncoder enable the rapid development of computational methods for precision cancer medicine, even with limited domain-specific data. Here, we showed that HistoEncoder performs at the same level as much more resource-intensive pan-cancer models in PCa detection, aligning with a previous study. An exciting direction would be to explore the utility of FMs in the analysis of multiple clinically relevant modalities and as part of multimodal predictor and interpreter models. Future multimodal models are likely to allow for leveraging tissue imaging on a large scale in conjunction with other clinical and molecular profiling data, leading to improved tools for cancer diagnosis, prognosis and treatment.  As it has been empirically demonstrated 21 ,  66  that larger datasets and higher capacity SSL-pre-trained models will produce better performance, training on larger pathology datasets should be a priority. On the other hand, HistoEncoder provides clearly less resource-demanding FM for prostate-specific tasks such as domain-specific feature extraction, and performs on par with recently introduced pan-tissue FMs H-Optimus-1, Virchow2, UNI2, and CONCH that are trained with massive amounts of multiorgan pathology image data. HistoEncoder is thus a low-compute alternative to pan-tissue FMs, and easy to adopt to prostate-specific tasks. We envision combining HistoEncoder-derived features with electronic health record information to further increase its performance in clinically meaningful tasks. evidence_text: Calibration-Aware Patient-Level Prediction of Source-Defined MSIMUT Status in Colorectal Cancer from Whole-Slide Histopathology Images Using Foundation-Model Embeddings. Background/Objectives: Microsatellite instability (MSI) is clinically important in colorectal cancer, but definitive assessment requires molecular or immunohistochemical testing. This study developed a leakage-safe, calibration-aware patient-level framework for predicting a source-defined MSIMUT category from hematoxylin-and-eosin whole-slide-derived patches using fixed Phikon foundation-model embeddings. Methods: The TCGA-derived colorectal cohort comprised 360 patients, including 65 source-defined positive and 295 MSS cases, represented by 192,312 pre-extracted patches. Patch embeddings were aggregated using mean, max, and mean-plus-max pooling, and downstream classifiers were evaluated under patient-level cross-validation with calibration, threshold, decision-curve, clinicopathological, source-provenance, and patch-count sensitivity analyses. Results: In the primary random patient-level evaluation, logistic regression with mean-plus-max pooling achieved a mean ROC-AUC of 0.915 and PR-AUC of 0.809. Fully nested Platt calibration yielded pooled out-of-sample ROC-AUC 0.913, PR-AUC 0.796, Brier score 0.073, calibration slope 1.037, and calibration-in-the-large 0.023. Within the internally cross-validated mean-plus-max framework, an exploratory sensitivity ≥ 0.95 operating point yielded sensitivity 0.969, specificity 0.393, and negative predictive value 0.983. Provenance reconstruction identified source-partition-dependent patch-count structure. In a source-TRAIN to source-TEST holdout, mean-plus-max ROC-AUC decreased to 0.788, while patch count alone was near chance in source-TEST (ROC-AUC 0.517) and explicit patch-count addition did not improve discrimination. Conclusions: These findings support the methodological feasibility of fixed foundation-model embeddings for internal MSI-related pre-screening research, while showing that apparent performance is sensitive to source structure. Independent multicenter validation with clinically adjudicated MSI-H/dMMR endpoints remains necessary before clinical application. 1. Introduction Microsatellite instability (MSI) is a molecular phenotype resulting from deficient DNA mismatch repair and the consequent accumulation of insertion and deletion errors within repetitive genomic regions [ 1 , 2 ]. In colorectal cancer, MSI is associated with a distinct hypermutated tumor biology and has important implications for prognostic assessment, therapeutic stratification, and response to immune checkpoint blockade [ 1 , 3 ]. Although MSI is defined at the molecular level, MSI-high tumors may also exhibit recognizable histomorphological and immune-related characteristics on routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained sections, including prominent lymphocytic infiltration, mucinous differentiation, architectural heterogeneity, and variation in the tumor microenvironment [ 1 , 3 , 4 ]. This relationship between molecular status and tissue morphology makes MSI a particularly relevant target for computational pathology, in which routinely acquired histological images can be analyzed as high-dimensional biomedical data. In current clinical practice, MSI or mismatch repair status is generally assessed using polymerase chain reaction-based microsatellite testing or immunohistochemistry for the mismatch repair proteins MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2 [ 1 , 3 ]. These established approaches remain essential for definitive biomarker assessment but require testing beyond routine morphological examination. By contrast, H&E-stained slides are already generated as part of standard histopathological workflows and may contain image-level correlates of the underlying molecular phenotype. Computational analysis of these routinely available images has therefore been investigated as a potential pre-screening approach for identifying patients who may benefit from prioritized confirmatory testing [ 4 , 5 ]. Such methods should not be considered replacements for validated molecular or immunohistochemical assays, but rather as complementary strategies that may support prioritization within existing diagnostic pathways. The digitization of histopathological slides has enabled artificial intelligence methods to extract clinically relevant information from whole-slide images. Landmark work by Kather et al. demonstrated that deep learning could predict MSI directly from H&E-stained histological images of gastrointestinal cancers, establishing an important proof of concept for image-based molecular biomarker inference [ 5 ]. Subsequent studies and reviews have expanded this evidence base and further demonstrated the potential of computational pathology for MSI prediction [ 4 , 6 , 7 ]. However, the published literature also shows substantial heterogeneity in cohort composition, class prevalence, image preprocessing, model architecture, validation design, reference standards, and clinical framing [ 4 , 6 , 7 ]. The central question has therefore progressed beyond whether MSI-associated information is present in histomorphology to how this information should be represented, validated, and interpreted to support reliable, transparently evaluated, and potentially transferable patient-level inference. Methodological rigor is particularly important in whole-slide image analysis because individual patients may contribute multiple slides and thousands of correlated image patches. If these observations are partitioned without preserving patient-level independence, related samples may occur in both the training and evaluation sets, creating information leakage and producing optimistically biased performance estimates [ 8 ]. Moreover, discrimination alone does not fully characterize the potential relevance of a biomarker prediction model. Although the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) summarizes the ability of a model to rank positive and negative cases, it does not establish whether predicted probabilities are appropriately calibrated, whether operating thresholds suitable for a proposed use can be identified, or whether model-guided action may offer net benefit relative to default strategies [ 9 , 10 , 11 ]. Evaluation should therefore extend to class-imbalance-sensitive metrics, uncertainty estimation, probability calibration, threshold-dependent performance, and decision-analytic assessment. Robustness to variation in the amount of available tissue information is also relevant because whole-slide images may differ substantially in tissue area and patch burden. Accordingly, an unresolved methodological need is a patient-level framework that combines strict leakage control with calibration, operating-point analysis, decision curve evaluation, and representation-robustness assessment. Task-specific end-to-end deep-learning pipelines can require substantial computational resources, extensive model optimization, and careful management of cohort-dependent effects [ 6 , 7 , 8 ]. Pathology foundation models provide a modular alternative by learning transferable representations from large and heterogeneous histopathology collections [ 12 , 13 , 14 ]. In an embedding-based workflow, image patches are processed using a fixed pretrained encoder, after which the resulting feature vectors can be aggregated into slide- or patient-level representations for downstream prediction. This separation of representation learning from task-specific classification reduces the need for repeated end-to-end retraining and allows the effects of representation design, classifier selection, calibration, and robustness to be examined within a common feature space. Within such a framework, deterministic mean and max pooling provide a transparent means of testing whether pretrained embeddings retain sufficient globally distributed and locally salient information without introducing an additional trainable attention mechanism. The resulting representations can then be evaluated using comparatively simple downstream models, improving analytical traceability and facilitating representation-level interpretation. Nevertheless, latent embedding dimensions should not be assumed to correspond directly to specific microscopic structures, and an embedding-based workflow does not eliminate the computational burden of patch extraction and foundation-model inference. Against this background, the present study developed and internally evaluated a calibration-aware, leakage-safe, and decision-support-oriented framework for patient-level prediction of the source-defined MSIMUT category using a publicly available TCGA-linked colorectal cancer patch archive derived from routine H&E-stained whole-slide images [ 15 , 16 ]. The source repository defines MSIMUT as microsatellite unstable or highly mutated; accordingly, this category was treated as the positive analytical endpoint and was not assumed to be equivalent to a uniformly assay-confirmed MSI-H/dMMR outcome. The verified cohort comprised 360 patients, and patch-level features were extracted using the fixed Phikon pathology foundation model [ 17 ]. Mean pooling, max pooling, and their concatenation were evaluated for constructing patient-level representations, and multiple downstream classifiers were compared under strict patient-level separation. Evaluation extended beyond conventional discrimination analysis by incorporating repeated patient-level validation, bootstrap-based uncertainty estimation, leakage-safe nested probability calibration, threshold-based screening assessment, decision curve analysis, pooling-strategy comparison, patch-burden sensitivity analysis, and representation-level interpretability. The objective was to determine whether fixed Phikon-derived histopathology embeddings could support informative patient-level prediction that remained stable across alternative internal patient-level partitions, without end-to-end retraining, while explicitly characterizing probability behavior, operating-point trade-offs, potential decision-analytic relevance, and representation robustness. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Study Design, Data Source, and Cohort Assembly This retrospective computational pathology study investigated patient-level prediction of microsatellite instability-related status using a publicly available colorectal histopathology patch dataset derived from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained whole-slide images. The patient was prespecified as the fundamental analytical unit because individual cases could contribute multiple correlated image-derived observations. Maintaining patient-level independence was intended to preserve the clinical interpretation of the prediction task and to reduce the risk of information leakage and optimistically biased performance estimates [ 6 , 8 ]. Accordingly, patient-level separation was maintained throughout representation construction and model evaluation. The overall study workflow is summarized in Figure 1 . Additional internal sensitivity analyses were designed to examine potential site- and clinicopathological confounding within this cohort, but they were not considered substitutes for independent multicenter validation across different institutions, staining protocols, scanners, specimen-processing workflows, or patient populations. Source Patch Dataset and Patch-Level Feature Extraction Image analysis was based on a publicly available colorectal histopathology patch collection published by Kather et al. Provenance reconstruction showed that the upstream resource had been distributed in predefined TRAIN and TEST partitions with class-specific patch-count structures shaped by upstream dataset construction. The source TRAIN partition contained 46,704 MSIMUT and 46,704 MSS patches; according to the source documentation, this patch-level balance reflected random reduction of the more numerous MSS training patches [ 16 ]. The reconstructed source TEST partition contained 28,335 MSIMUT and 70,569 MSS patches. These counts refer to image files reconstructed from the available source filename manifest and matched to the 360-patient analytical cohort. At the patient level, these partitions comprised 260 TRAIN patients (39 MSIMUT and 221 MSS) and 100 TEST patients (26 MSIMUT and 74 MSS), with no patient overlap. Because the pooled derivative archive combined patients originating from these differently structured source partitions, absolute patient-level patch burden could encode upstream dataset-construction characteristics in addition to the amount of available tissue. This possibility was therefore examined explicitly through source-partition-specific patch-count analyses and a reconstructed source-holdout sensitivity analysis described below. The archive was supplied as a colorectal-only image collection, and no additional filtering by TCGA project, tissue-source site, or other source-related metadata was applied before patient-level representation construction. Because the analysis used pre-extracted patches rather than reprocessing the original whole-slide images, the original tiling stride and overlap configuration could not be determined from the available source documentation. The source repository defines MSIMUT as microsatellite unstable or highly mutated [ 16 ]. In the present analysis, this source-defined category constituted the positive class, whereas MSS constituted the negative class. TCGA case identifiers embedded in the patch filenames were extracted programmatically and used to associate each patch with its source patient and to establish the patient-level identifier framework subsequently used for linkage to TCGA/GDC metadata. This procedure reconstructed 360 non-overlapping patient groups, comprising 65 patients in the source-defined positive category and 295 patients in the MSS category. No patient identifier occurred in both categories. Each patch was retained only as an intermediate image-derived observation, whereas the patient was preserved as the indivisible analytical unit throughout downstream dataset partitioning, model development, and performance evaluation; patches originating from the same patient were never distributed across training and test subsets. Patch-level features were extracted using the original Phikon pathology foundation model, loaded through the Transformers interface using the model identifier owkin/phikon [ 17 ]. Each patch was opened in RGB format and processed using the corresponding AutoImageProcessor. The encoder was maintained in evaluation mode, and feature extraction was performed without gradient computation, task-specific fine-tuning, or end-to-end retraining. The reconstructed patient identifiers were retained unchanged across downstream analyses and provided the linkage key for the source-related metadata analyses described separately below. Counts reported here refer to image files reconstructed from the available source filename manifest and matched to the analytical cohort. These reconstructed source partitions were not used to define the primary five-fold cross-validation and were examined as a provenance-based sensitivity analysis. A source-holdout evaluation was then performed by fitting the prespecified logistic-regression pipeline exclusively on the 260 source-TRAIN patients and applying the fitted pipeline once to the untouched 100 source-TEST patients. Models were not refitted during bootstrap resampling. Because both partitions originated from the same upstream TCGA-derived resource rather than from independent institutions or acquisition domains, this analysis was interpreted as a source-structured internal holdout and not as independent external validation. 2.3. Patient-Level Representation Construction For each patient i , let z i j ∈ R 768 denote the embedding of the j -th patch, where j = 1 , … , n i and n i is the number of patches associated with that patient. The complete set of patch embeddings for patient i was represented by the matrix Z i ∈ R n i × 768 , with z i j corresponding to its j -th row. Because the number of available patches varied among patients, these variable-sized embedding matrices could not be used directly by the downstream classifiers, which required one fixed-length feature vector per patient. Each patient’s embedding matrix was therefore aggregated independently using deterministic and label-free pooling operations. Two complementary pooling operations were applied along the patch dimension. Mean pooling generated a 768-dimensional vector by averaging each embedding dimension across all patches belonging to the patient: (1) μ i = 1 n i ∑ j = 1 n i z ij Max pooling generated a second 768-dimensional vector by retaining the largest observed activation in each embedding dimension: (2) m i , k = max 1 ≤ j ≤ n i z ij , k ,   k = 1 , … , 768 Mean pooling summarized the overall latent activation profile across the patient’s available tissue patches, whereas max pooling retained the strongest patch-level activation observed within each latent dimension. The two operations were treated as complementary because target-associated information could plausibly be broadly distributed across the available patches or concentrated within a smaller subset. The principal patient-level representation was constructed by concatenating the mean-pooled vector followed by the max-pooled vector: (3) x i = μ i   ∥   m i ∈ R 1536 where ∥ denotes vector concatenation. This procedure produced a 360 × 1536 patient-level feature matrix, with one row per patient. The first 768 dimensions corresponded to mean-pooled features, and the remaining 768 dimensions corresponded to max-pooled features. Mean-only and max-only matrices, each of size 360 × 768 , were also retained for the pooling-strategy comparison described in Section 2.7 . The mean-plus-max representation was used as the principal input for candidate classifier comparison and subsequent model evaluation. The notebook implementation confirms that patient-specific embedding matrices were pooled using mean(axis = 0) and max(axis = 0) and concatenated in mean-then-max order to generate the 360 × 1536 matrix. No global feature scaling was applied during representation construction. For scale-sensitive classifiers, feature standardization was performed within the model pipeline using parameters estimated exclusively from the training portion of each validation fold, as detailed in Section 2.4 . Because the representation dimension exceeded the number of patients, with p = 1536 and n = 360, model-specific complexity control and strict patient-level validation were applied at the classifier stage to limit optimistic performance estimation. The aggregation procedure contained no trainable parameters and did not use class-label information to determine patch contributions. Unlike attention-based multiple-instance learning approaches, in which instance contributions are estimated through learned attention weights, no patch-level attention scores or learned instance weights were estimated in the present framework [ 20 , 21 , 22 ]. This deterministic design provided a reproducible bridge between variable-sized patient patch collections and fixed-length patient-level representations while allowing globally averaged and maximal embedding information to be evaluated both jointly and separately. 2.4. Candidate Classifiers and Patient-Level Validation Five downstream classifiers were evaluated using the same 1536-dimensional mean-plus-max patient representation: logistic regression, a linear support vector machine (linear SVM), a multilayer perceptron (MLP), random forest, and gradient boosting. These algorithms were selected to span linear, neural-network-based, and tree-based modelling approaches with different levels of complexity. Candidate comparison was treated as an empirical model-selection step because the relative performance of linear and nonlinear downstream learners may depend on the encoder, aggregation strategy, cohort, and validation design [ 23 , 24 , 25 ]. Fixed model configurations were applied consistently across all validation folds. Logistic regression was implemented using median imputation and feature standardization within each training fold, the lbfgs solver, L2 regularization with C = 1.0, a convergence tolerance of 1 × 10 −4 , a maximum of 5000 iterations, balanced class weights, and a random seed of 42. The Linear SVM used median imputation, feature standardization, a linear kernel, probabilistic output estimation, balanced class weights, and the same random seed. Random forest was configured with 500 decision trees, a random seed of 42, and parallel processing across the available CPU cores. Gradient boosting was preceded by median imputation and was fitted using a random seed of 42. The MLP comprised two hidden layers with 128 and 64 neurons, respectively, rectified linear unit activation, the Adam optimizer, an L2 penalty parameter of 1 × 10 −4 , an initial learning rate of 1 × 10 −3 , a maximum of 300 iterations, and a random seed of 42. Median imputation and feature standardization were also included in the MLP pipeline. Parameters not explicitly specified were retained at the defaults of the recorded software environment. Preprocessing operations were incorporated within the corresponding model pipelines. Consequently, median values and standardization parameters were estimated exclusively from the training patients in each fold and were subsequently applied to the held-out test patients. No preprocessing parameter was estimated from the complete cohort before cross-validation. Standardization was applied to logistic regression, the Linear SVM, and the MLP, whereas the tree-based models were fitted without feature scaling. No feature selection, dimensionality reduction, or data-driven hyperparameter search was performed during candidate classifier comparison. Primary internal validation was performed using stratified five-fold cross-validation with shuffling and a fixed random seed of 42. Patient-level identifiers, rather than image patches, were assigned to the folds. Each fold contained 288 training patients and 72 held-out test patients. The class distribution was preserved across folds, with each test fold containing 13 patients from the source-defined positive category and 59 MSS patients. Every patient therefore contributed to the held-out test set exactly once, and no patient or patch derived from that patient could occur simultaneously in the training and test partitions of the same fold. For each classifier and fold, the probability assigned to the positive category was obtained for every held-out patient. Threshold-independent performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) and the area under the precision–recall curve (PR-AUC). Because the cohort was class imbalanced, PR-AUC was considered an important complementary measure to ROC-AUC. At the conventional probability threshold of 0.50, accuracy, balanced accuracy, precision, sensitivity, F1 score, Matthews correlation coefficient, and confusion-matrix counts were calculated. The Brier score was additionally reported to quantify the overall accuracy of the predicted probabilities. Candidate-model performance was summarized as the mean and standard deviation across the five held-out folds. The classifier with the highest mean ROC-AUC, with PR-AUC considered as a secondary discrimination criterion, was designated as the primary model and carried forward to the repeated-validation, uncertainty, calibration, threshold, and decision-analytic evaluations described in the subsequent sections. To quantify potential optimism arising from selection of the primary analytical pipeline within the same cohort, an additional nested pipeline-selection sensitivity analysis was performed. The original five outer patient-level test folds were kept completely untouched. Within each corresponding outer-training set, five-fold stratified inner cross-validation was used to compare the same five prespecified analytical pipelines and fixed model configurations used in the primary classifier comparison. Candidate selection was based on mean inner ROC-AUC, with mean inner PR-AUC used as a prespecified tie-breaker. The selected pipeline was then refitted on the complete outer-training set and evaluated once on the corresponding untouched outer-test fold. No outer-test observation contributed to pipeline selection. Before performing the nested analysis, the exact candidate configurations were required to reproduce the original fixed-fold classifier results within a predefined numerical tolerance. This nested analysis was intended to quantify pipeline-selection sensitivity and potential selection optimism rather than to establish intrinsic superiority of an algorithm family. An additional sensitivity analysis was performed to examine whether the primary logistic-regression result depended strongly on the specified regularization strength or class weighting. Using the original fixed five patient-level folds, L2-regularized logistic regression was evaluated at C values of 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, and 100 with both balanced and unweighted class objectives. The solver (lbfgs), convergence tolerance (1 × 10 −4 ), maximum number of iterations (5000), random seed (42), median imputation, and within-training-fold standardization were otherwise held fixed. This analysis was prespecified as a sensitivity analysis and was not used to retrospectively optimize or replace the primary C = 1 balanced logistic-regression pipeline. Convergence warnings were recorded for each evaluated configuration. 2.5. Repeated Validation, Bootstrap Uncertainty Estimation, and Calibration To assess whether the performance of the selected primary logistic regression model depended on a single cross-validation partition, the complete model pipeline was additionally evaluated using repeated stratified five-fold patient-level cross-validation. The five-fold procedure was repeated 10 times using a fixed random seed of 42, yielding 50 held-out evaluations. In every split, 288 patients were used for model training, and 72 patients were reserved for testing. Stratification preserved the source-defined positive/MSS class distribution, and all preprocessing and model-fitting operations were performed using only the training portion of each split. Each patient appeared in a held-out test fold once per repeat and therefore received 10 out-of-sample probability estimates generated under different repeated partitions. Fold-level performance metrics were first averaged across the five folds within each repeat, after which the mean and standard deviation were calculated across the 10 repeat-level estimates. This two-stage summarization avoided treating the 50-fold-level results as statistically independent observations. For patient-level uncertainty estimation, the 10 out-of-sample probabilities generated for each patient were averaged to obtain one patient-specific probability estimate. Point estimates of ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, accuracy, balanced accuracy, precision, sensitivity, F1 score, Matthews correlation coefficient, and Brier score were calculated from these patient-averaged probabilities. Threshold-dependent metrics at this stage used the default probability threshold of 0.50. A nonparametric bootstrap analysis was then performed using a NumPy random-number generator initialized with a fixed seed of 42. The 360 patient-level outcome–probability pairs were resampled with replacement, with each bootstrap sample containing 360 observations. Samples containing only one outcome class were discarded because discrimination metrics could not be calculated, and resampling continued until 2000 valid bootstrap samples had been obtained. Performance metrics were recalculated for every valid resample, and two-sided 95% confidence intervals were defined by the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the corresponding empirical bootstrap distributions [ 26 ]. The prediction model was not refitted during this procedure; the bootstrap analysis therefore quantified uncertainty in the performance estimates derived from the fixed patient-averaged out-of-sample predictions. Probability calibration was assessed using a fully nested procedure within each of the original five outer patient-level folds. For each outer fold, five-fold inner cross-validation was performed using only the corresponding outer-training patients to generate out-of-fold base-model decision scores. Three candidate probability strategies—uncalibrated probabilities, Platt scaling, and isotonic regression—were compared using the Brier score [ 27 ] calculated exclusively from cross-fitted outer-training predictions, consistent with standard supervised probability-calibration approaches [ 28 , 29 , 30 ]. The calibration strategy with the lowest inner cross-validated Brier score was selected without access to the outer-test outcomes. The selected calibration mapping was then fitted using the outer-training out-of-fold scores and applied once to the untouched outer-test base-model scores. Thus, no outer-test observation was used for calibration-method selection or calibrator fitting. Platt scaling was implemented as an unweighted logistic mapping of the common base-model decision scores, whereas isotonic regression was implemented as an unweighted monotonic nonparametric mapping. A same-score audit was additionally performed to verify preservation of ROC ranking under Platt scaling. Because Platt scaling is strictly monotonic, its fold-specific ROC-AUC was required to equal the ROC-AUC of the corresponding uncalibrated outer-test scores. Isotonic regression was evaluated separately because its piecewise-constant mapping can introduce ties and therefore can alter rank-based discrimination metrics. Calibration was characterized using the Brier score, a joint calibration intercept and slope estimated from logistic recalibration, and calibration-in-the-large (CITL). CITL was treated separately from the jointly estimated calibration intercept; ideal calibration corresponds to a joint calibration intercept of 0, a calibration slope of 1, and a CITL of 0. CITL was estimated as the intercept from an intercept-only logistic calibration model with the logit-transformed predicted probability entered as an offset, corresponding to a calibration slope fixed at 1. The nested-selected out-of-sample probabilities were carried forward to the threshold and decision-curve analyses. 2.6. Threshold-Based Screening and Decision Curve Analysis Threshold-based analyses were repeated using the nested-selected Platt-calibrated out-of-sample probabilities generated by the procedure described in Section 2.5 . For each evaluated threshold, patients with predicted probabilities greater than or equal to the threshold were classified as positive, whereas those with probabilities below the threshold were classified as negative. Operating-point performance was quantified using accuracy, balanced accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, F1 score, Matthews correlation coefficient, and the numbers of true-positive, true-negative, false-positive, and false-negative classifications. The primary balanced operating point was identified using the Youden index: (4) J = S e n s i t i v i t y + S p e c i f i c i t y − 1 The observed probability threshold maximizing the Youden index was designated as the exploratory Youden threshold. To examine screening-oriented operating conditions, additional thresholds targeting sensitivities of at least 0.90 and 0.95 were evaluated. Candidate thresholds consisted of the unique nested-Platt-calibrated out-of-sample probabilities and were examined in descending order. For each sensitivity target, the highest probability threshold satisfying the prespecified requirement was selected, thereby retaining the greatest achievable specificity among the observed thresholds meeting that target. Because these operating points were derived and evaluated using the same internally generated out-of-sample probability set, they were interpreted as exploratory cohort-specific thresholds rather than externally validated clinical cutoffs. Uncertainty in threshold-dependent performance was quantified using patient-level stratified bootstrap resampling. For each fixed operating threshold, the patient-level outcome–probability pairs were resampled with replacement, and the corresponding sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, classification metrics, and confusion-matrix-derived quantities were recalculated. Two-sided 95% bootstrap confidence intervals were defined by the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resulting empirical distributions. Threshold selection itself was not repeated within each bootstrap sample; these intervals therefore quantify uncertainty conditional on the internally derived operating thresholds. Decision curve analysis was repeated using the nested-selected Platt-calibrated probabilities to assess potential decision-analytic value within a clinically focused low-threshold range [ 10 , 11 ]. Threshold probabilities from 0.01 to 0.30 were evaluated at increments of 0.005. The false-positive term was weighted by the odds associated with the selected threshold probability, thereby incorporating the relative consequences of unnecessary confirmatory assessment and missed source-defined positive cases. The calibrated model was compared with test-all and test-none reference strategies. For the test-all strategy, in which every patient was prioritized for confirmatory assessment, net benefit was calculated as: (6) NB all p t = π − 1 − π p t 1 − p t where π denotes the observed source-defined positive-class prevalence. For the test-none strategy, in which no patient was prioritized for confirmatory assessment, net benefit was defined as: (7) N B n o n e p t = 0 At each threshold probability, model net benefit was compared with the better of the two default strategies. Uncertainty in incremental net benefit was assessed using paired patient-level stratified bootstrap resampling, thereby preserving direct comparison between the model and the corresponding default strategy within each resample. Two-sided 95% bootstrap intervals were obtained from the empirical distribution of the paired net-benefit difference. The number of confirmatory assessments performed or avoided per 100 patients and the number of source-defined positive cases missed per 100 patients were additionally summarized to provide an interpretable description of the internal testing-burden trade-off. Because calibration, operating-threshold derivation, and decision-curve evaluation were performed within the same retrospective TCGA-derived cohort, these analyses were considered exploratory internal assessments. They do not establish prospective clinical utility, cost-effectiveness, safety of rule-out decisions, or transportability to other clinical settings. Independent multicenter validation with prespecified calibration and operating thresholds would be required before the model could inform confirmatory testing or patient-care decisions. For application to a previously unseen patient, the intended inference pathway would require a single frozen version of the complete analytical pipeline. Histopathology patches would first be encoded using the same fixed Phikon feature extractor and aggregated into the prespecified mean-plus-max patient representation. The imputation and standardization parameters learned from the development data would then be applied without refitting, followed by the frozen logistic-regression model to generate a base decision score. A prespecified Platt calibration mapping, fitted only from development data, would transform this score into a calibrated probability. That probability would then be compared with a prespecified operating threshold chosen according to the intended clinical use; patients at or above the threshold would be prioritized for confirmatory MSI-related assessment, whereas those below the threshold would not be considered model-positive. The present cross-validation analysis was designed for internal performance estimation and therefore did not generate or validate a deployment-ready single final model, calibrator, or clinical threshold. Before prospective use, these components would need to be refitted or frozen using the complete development set according to a prespecified protocol and then evaluated without modification in an independent external cohort. 2.7. Pooling Comparison, Patch-Burden and Patch-Count Sensitivity, and Interpretability To determine whether patient-level predictive information was primarily retained in averaged or maximal embedding activations, three pooling representations were compared: mean-only pooling, max-only pooling, and their concatenated mean-plus-max representation. Mean-only and max-only pooling each produced a 768-dimensional feature vector per patient, whereas mean-plus-max pooling produced the principal 1536-dimensional representation described in Section 2.3 . Each representation was evaluated using the same fixed five-fold patient-level partitions and the same primary logistic regression pipeline described in Section 2.4 . All preprocessing and model-fitting operations were performed exclusively within the training portion of each fold, and balanced class weights were applied consistently across the three representations. No additional feature selection, dimensionality reduction, calibration, or hyperparameter optimization was performed for this comparison. Fold-level ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, accuracy, balanced accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, negative predictive value, F1 score, Matthews correlation coefficient, and Brier score were calculated, with threshold-dependent metrics evaluated at the default probability threshold of 0.50. Performance was summarized as the mean and standard deviation across the five folds. Because the classifier configuration and patient partitions were held constant, differences in performance reflected changes in the pooling representation rather than changes in the downstream modeling procedure. Patch burden sensitivity analysis was conducted to assess whether the performance of the principal mean-plus-max representation depended on the availability of the complete patch collection for each patient. Patch embeddings were randomly subsampled without replacement at fractions of 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of each patient’s available patches. For patient i and subsampling fraction f , the number of retained patches was defined as: (8) n i , f = max 1 f ⋅ n i where n i denotes the total number of available patches for patient i , and ⋅ denotes the ceiling function. Mean-pooled and max-pooled vectors were recalculated from the retained patches and concatenated to reconstruct a 1536-dimensional patient representation. Subsampling was repeated 10 times for each fraction using fixed and reproducible random seeds. At the 100% reference condition, all available patches were retained; consequently, the reconstructed representations were identical across repetitions. Each reconstructed dataset was evaluated using the same fixed five-fold patient-level partitions and the same primary logistic regression pipeline used in the main analysis. All preprocessing and classifier-fitting steps were confined to the corresponding training fold. For each patch fraction and repetition, performance was first averaged across the five folds. The mean and standard deviation were then calculated across the 10 repeat-level estimates. This two-stage procedure avoided treating the 50-fold–repeat evaluations within each patch fraction as statistically independent. The analysis assessed robustness to reduced patch availability within the existing patch archive and was not intended to reproduce variability arising from alternative tissue sampling, slide preparation, scanning systems, or external clinical sites. To distinguish robustness to proportional reductions in patch availability from potential confounding by absolute patch count, an additional fixed-N sensitivity analysis was performed. Patients were randomly subsampled without replacement to fixed patch counts of N = 6, 25, 50, 100, and 200, with 10 independent repetitions at each N. For a given fixed-N condition, only patients with at least N available patches were eligible. The original patient-level fold assignments were retained after restriction to the eligible cohort. Mean-only, max-only, and mean-plus-max representations were reconstructed from the sampled patches and evaluated using the same logistic-regression pipeline as in the primary analysis. To separate the effect of fixed patch number from changes in cohort composition at higher N values, an all-patch comparator was recalculated using exactly the same eligible patients and the same restricted fold assignments for each N. Patch-count dependence was additionally examined in two complementary analyses. First, class-specific patch-count distributions and a patch-count-only prediction model were evaluated to quantify the extent to which patch burden itself was associated with the source-defined outcome. Second, because max pooling may increase with the number of opportunities to observe extreme latent activations, each of the 768 max-pooled embedding dimensions was residualized with respect to log1p-transformed patient patch count within each outer-training fold only. Both linear and quadratic patch-count adjustment specifications were evaluated. The relationship estimated from the outer-training patients was then applied unchanged to the corresponding held-out patients. The resulting residualized max representation was evaluated alone and after concatenation with the original mean-pooled representation using the same primary logistic-regression pipeline. This analysis was designed as a sensitivity analysis of patch-count-associated representation variation and was not used to replace or retrospectively optimize the primary model. As an additional audit of the residualization procedure, out-of-fold patch-count decoding was performed to test whether multivariable patch-count information remained recoverable from the raw or residualized max-pooled representations. Using the same five patient-level outer folds, ridge regression models were trained to predict log1p-transformed patient patch count from the raw max-pooled representation, the linearly residualized max-pooled representation, and the quadratically residualized max-pooled representation. For the residualized analyses, the patch-count adjustment was fitted only within the corresponding outer-training fold before decoding models were trained. The resulting out-of-fold predictions were evaluated using R 2 , Spearman correlation, and mean absolute error. This analysis was used only to assess residual patch-count information in the representations and was not used for outcome prediction or model selection. Representation-level interpretability was assessed using SHapley Additive exPlanations generated with a linear SHAP explainer. The analysis used the principal 1536-dimensional mean-plus-max representation and followed the same five fixed patient-level folds used for primary model evaluation. Within each fold, the preprocessing steps and primary logistic regression configuration described in Section 2.4 were fitted exclusively using the 288 outer training patients. The transformed outer-training matrix was subsequently provided to the linear explainer as the candidate background dataset. Because the number of training patients exceeded the masker’s default maximum background size, the SHAP Independent masker selected 100 training patients without replacement using its deterministic default random state of 0. SHAP values were then calculated only for patients in the corresponding held-out outer test fold. This procedure produced one out-of-sample SHAP vector for each of the 360 patients and prevented held-out patients from contributing to preprocessing, classifier fitting, or selection of the background distribution used to explain their predictions. The Independent masker generated interventional feature attributions for the fitted linear classifier; correlations among the latent embedding dimensions were not explicitly incorporated into the attribution procedure. The first 768 dimensions of the representation were labeled as mean-pooled features, and the remaining 768 dimensions were labeled as max-pooled features. Global feature importance was defined as the mean absolute SHAP value across all out-of-sample patients. Importance was summarized separately for the mean-pooled and max-pooled halves of the representation. The 20 dimensions with the highest global mean absolute SHAP values were additionally examined to characterize the relative representation of mean-pooled and max-pooled components among the most influential latent dimensions. SHAP values were used solely for post-hoc interpretation and did not influence representation construction, feature selection, classifier selection, model fitting, calibration, or performance estimation. Because the explained variables were latent foundation-model embedding dimensions rather than directly labeled histopathological attributes, the SHAP analysis was interpreted strictly at the representation level. A high SHAP importance value indicated greater reliance of the linear classifier on a particular pooled embedding dimension but did not identify a specific patch, tissue region, cell type, or recognizable microscopic structure. The analysis therefore did not provide spatial localization, direct morphological attribution, mechanistic biological interpretation, or evidence of causal relationships. 2.8. Clinicopathological and Site-Related Sensitivity Analyses TCGA case identifiers reconstructed from the image archive were linked to publicly available GDC metadata to investigate whether clinicopathological or site-related factors could account for part of the observed predictive signal. All 360 cases were matched to GDC records and originated from TCGA-COAD or TCGA-READ. Available variables included age, AJCC pathologic stage, tissue or organ of origin, primary diagnosis, project identifier, and tissue-source-site (TSS) code. Sex/gender and a uniform clinical molecular MSI-test result were not included in the analyzable metadata extract used for the present sensitivity analyses; these variables therefore could not be incorporated into the sensitivity models. Separately, GDC-derived MSIsensor2 annotations were retrieved for a secondary concordance and endpoint-sensitivity analysis; these bioinformatics-derived molecular annotations were not treated as equivalent to a clinically adjudicated PCR-, immunohistochemistry-, or sequencing-confirmed MSI-H/dMMR reference standard. Associations between the source-defined outcome and available clinicopathological variables were evaluated using the Mann–Whitney U test for age and permutation-based chi-square tests for categorical variables. To quantify the extent to which these variables alone could discriminate the source-defined classes, a clinical-only logistic-regression model was evaluated under the same fixed five patient-level folds. A second sensitivity model combined the 1536-dimensional image representation with age, project identifier, broad pathologic stage, tissue or organ of origin, and primary diagnosis. Numeric variables were imputed and standardized within each training fold, and categorical variables were imputed and one-hot encoded using training data only. Potential site effects were further investigated using TSS code. A TSS-only model was evaluated under the fixed folds, and an additional TSS-group-isolated validation used grouped cross-validation so that all patients from a given TSS were confined entirely to either the training or test portion of a fold. These analyses were intended to assess sensitivity to clinicopathological and source-site structure within the available TCGA cohort and were not interpreted as external validation. 2.9. Cohort, Patch-Level Data, and Patient-Level Representation The final verified cohort comprised 360 patients. Of these, 65 patients belonged to the source-defined positive category designated as MSIMUT in the original repository, whereas 295 patients belonged to the MSS category. The source-defined positive class therefore accounted for 18.1% of the cohort, resulting in an imbalanced binary outcome distribution. The same cohort and source-defined class assignments were used in all subsequent analyses. The colorectal histopathology archive contained 192,312 JPEG patches linked to the included patients. Patch availability varied substantially across patients, with a mean of 534.2 patches per patient (standard deviation, 699.9), a median of 291.5 patches (interquartile range, 119.8–592.3), and a range of 6 to 4305 patches. The patches served as intermediate inputs for feature extraction, whereas model development and performance evaluation were conducted at the patient level. Each retained patch was encoded as a 768-dimensional vector using the fixed Phikon pathology foundation model. The number of patch embeddings available for an individual patient corresponded to that patient’s patch count. All available embeddings for each patient were used to construct the primary representation, without imposing a common patch-count requirement across patients. Deterministic pooling converted each patient’s variable-length set of patch embeddings into fixed-length representations. Mean pooling produced a 360 × 768 matrix, and max pooling produced a second 360 × 768 matrix. Concatenation of the mean-pooled and max-pooled vectors yielded the primary 360 × 1536 analytical matrix, corresponding to one 1536-dimensional feature vector for each of the 360 patients. An overview of the cohort and analytical representation is provided in Table 1 . Detailed cohort composition and patch-count characteristics are reported in Supplementary Table S1 . 3.2. Candidate Classifier Comparison and Primary Model Selection Five candidate classifiers were evaluated using the same 1536-dimensional mean-plus-max patient-level representation and the same fixed five-fold patient-level partitions. Logistic regression achieved the numerically highest mean discrimination, with a ROC-AUC of 0.915 ± 0.035 and a PR-AUC of 0.809 ± 0.035. At the default probability threshold of 0.50, it yielded an accuracy of 0.908, balanced accuracy of 0.836, precision of 0.760, sensitivity of 0.723, specificity of 0.949, F1 score of 0.737, Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.685, and Brier score of 0.076. Linear support vector machine and MLP produced discrimination estimates close to those of logistic regression. Their mean ROC-AUC values were both approximately 0.911, and their mean PR-AUC values were 0.798 and 0.803, respectively. Linear support vector machine achieved the highest precision among the evaluated implementations, at 0.799, together with a specificity of 0.966, but its sensitivity was lower at 0.569. MLP achieved a sensitivity of 0.646 and specificity of 0.946, with a Brier score of 0.084 compared with 0.077 for Linear support vector machine and 0.076 for logistic regression. The two tree-based implementations showed less favorable positive-class recovery at the default threshold. Random forest achieved a mean ROC-AUC of 0.886 and PR-AUC of 0.696, but its sensitivity was 0.092 and its specificity was 1.000. Gradient boosting achieved a mean ROC-AUC of 0.826 and PR-AUC of 0.609, with sensitivity of 0.292 and specificity of 0.969. Consequently, their overall accuracies of 0.836 and 0.847 were driven largely by correct classification of the majority MSS class and did not reflect balanced recovery of both outcome groups. These threshold-dependent findings apply specifically to the fixed model implementations and the default threshold of 0.50 used in the comparison. Logistic regression and linear support vector machine incorporated balanced class weights, whereas the evaluated MLP, random forest, and gradient boosting implementations used unweighted objectives. No classifier-specific threshold optimization, post-hoc calibration, hyperparameter search, or harmonized imbalance treatment was performed at this stage. The results therefore should not be interpreted as demonstrating intrinsic inferiority of the corresponding algorithm families. According to the predefined ranking procedure, which prioritized mean ROC-AUC and subsequently mean PR-AUC, logistic regression ranked first among the five candidate implementations. It additionally achieved the lowest Brier score and the highest Matthews correlation coefficient. Differences in discrimination among logistic regression, linear support vector machine, and MLP were numerically modest, and no formal pairwise statistical superiority test was performed. Nevertheless, logistic regression provided the most favorable combined profile of discrimination, positive-class recovery, classification balance, probability accuracy, and model parsimony within the prespecified comparison and was therefore selected as the primary model for repeated validation, uncertainty estimation, calibration, threshold analysis, decision curve analysis, robustness assessment, and representation-level interpretability. The nested pipeline-selection sensitivity analysis reproduced the original fixed-fold results for all five candidate pipelines before nested selection was undertaken. Logistic regression was subsequently selected within the outer-training data in all five outer folds. The nested-selected pipeline therefore achieved the same mean outer-fold ROC-AUC of 0.915 ± 0.035 and PR-AUC of 0.809 ± 0.035 as the fixed logistic-regression reference evaluated on the same untouched outer-test folds. The corresponding pooled out-of-sample ROC-AUC and PR-AUC were 0.915 and 0.802, respectively, for both approaches. Accordingly, the observed paired differences between the nested-selected and fixed logistic-regression predictions were 0.000 for both ROC-AUC and PR-AUC. These findings indicate that, within this internal sensitivity analysis, the original selection of logistic regression was reproduced independently within every outer-training set; however, the comparison remains internal to the same cohort and should not be interpreted as evidence of intrinsic algorithm-family superiority. Detailed fold-level results are provided in Supplementary Table S14 . Regularization-sensitivity analysis showed that discrimination was relatively stable across the more strongly regularized C = 0.01–1 range. With balanced class weights, mean ROC-AUC values were 0.923, 0.917, and 0.915 at C = 0.01, 0.1, and 1, respectively, with corresponding mean PR-AUC values of 0.822, 0.812, and 0.809. Performance decreased with weaker regularization, with mean ROC-AUC values of 0.903 and 0.892 at C = 10 and 100, respectively. At C = 1, removing class weighting produced the same mean ROC-AUC of 0.915 and a similar PR-AUC of 0.805 compared with 0.809 for the balanced configuration. No convergence warnings occurred across any of the evaluated regularization or class-weight settings. Because this was a sensitivity analysis rather than a hyperparameter-selection procedure, the original balanced C = 1 configuration was retained as the primary model. Threshold-Based Screening Performance and Decision Curve Results Threshold-based analyses were repeated using the nested-selected Platt-calibrated out-of-sample probabilities from the internally cross-validated mean-plus-max primary pipeline described in Section 2.5 . At the exploratory Youden operating point, the selected probability threshold was 0.2474. This threshold yielded an accuracy of 0.878, balanced accuracy of 0.865, sensitivity of 0.846, specificity of 0.885, positive predictive value of 0.618, negative predictive value of 0.963, F1 score of 0.714, and Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.652. The corresponding confusion matrix comprised 55 true-positive, 261 true-negative, 34 false-positive, and 10 false-negative classifications. Overall, 89 patients were assigned to the positive-prediction group and 271 to the negative-prediction group. At the screening-oriented operating point targeting sensitivity of at least 0.90, the highest-specificity threshold satisfying the target was 0.1327. Sensitivity was 0.908 and specificity was 0.786, with a positive predictive value of 0.484, negative predictive value of 0.975, accuracy of 0.808, balanced accuracy of 0.847, F1 score of 0.631, and Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.564. Of the 65 source-defined positive patients, 59 were classified as positive and 6 were missed. Among the 295 MSS patients, 63 were classified as positive. Overall, 122 patients were assigned to the positive-prediction group and 238 to the negative-prediction group. For the operating point targeting sensitivity of at least 0.95, the selected threshold was 0.0219. Sensitivity reached 0.969 and negative predictive value reached 0.983, whereas specificity decreased to 0.393 and positive predictive value to 0.260. This threshold yielded an accuracy of 0.497, balanced accuracy of 0.681, F1 score of 0.410, and Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.297. It identified 63 of the 65 source-defined positive patients, while 179 MSS patients were classified as positive. Overall, 242 patients were assigned to the positive-prediction group and 118 to the negative-prediction group. These operating points illustrate the expected trade-off between positive-class detection and confirmatory-testing burden. Relative to testing all patients, the sensitivity ≥ 0.90 operating point would have reduced the number of confirmatory assessments by approximately 66.1 per 100 patients while missing approximately 1.67 source-defined positive patients per 100. At the sensitivity ≥ 0.95 operating point, approximately 32.8 confirmatory assessments per 100 patients would have been avoided, while approximately 0.56 source-defined positive patients per 100 would have been missed. These calculations quantify an internal triage trade-off only and do not establish that confirmatory testing can safely be withheld. Because the operating points were derived and evaluated using the same internally generated out-of-sample probability set from the random patient-level mean-plus-max framework, they should be regarded as exploratory cohort-specific thresholds rather than source-holdout-tested, patch-count-neutral, or clinically validated cutoffs. Decision curve analysis was repeated using the nested-Platt probabilities over a clinically focused threshold-probability range of 0.01 to 0.30. Model net benefit was compared with both test-all and test-none strategies, and uncertainty was assessed using patient-level stratified bootstrap resampling. The observed model net benefit exceeded both default strategies at several low thresholds; however, the lower 2.5th percentile of the paired bootstrap difference relative to the better default strategy remained above zero only from approximately 0.055 through 0.30. The exploratory sensitivity ≥0.95 operating threshold of 0.0219 was therefore below the range in which bootstrap-supported superiority over the better default strategy was observed. For example, at a threshold probability of 0.10, model net benefit was 0.141 compared with 0.090 for the test-all strategy, and the paired bootstrap difference relative to the better default strategy was 0.051 with a 95% interval of 0.037 to 0.064. At a threshold probability of 0.15, model net benefit was 0.134 compared with 0.036 for test-all, with a corresponding difference of 0.098 and a 95% interval of 0.082 to 0.113. These results indicate potential internal decision-analytic value within the evaluated low-threshold range. However, they do not establish prospective clinical utility, cost-effectiveness, safety of rule-out decisions, or transportability to other clinical settings. Reconstructed Source-Partition Holdout Analysis The original source-defined TRAIN/TEST partition of the upstream Kather dataset was successfully reconstructed for all 360 patients and all 192,312 analyzed patches, with no patient overlap between the two partitions. The source-documented random reduction of the larger MSS training-patch set provides a direct mechanism for the class-dependent patch-count structure observed in source-TRAIN. This partition therefore provided a provenance-defined holdout that was distinct from the random patient-level folds used in the primary cross-validation analysis. When the prespecified logistic-regression pipeline was fitted exclusively on source-TRAIN and evaluated once on the untouched source-TEST cohort, the mean-only representation achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.794 (95% CI, 0.671–0.898), PR-AUC of 0.668 (95% CI, 0.511–0.843), and Brier score of 0.174 (95% CI, 0.111–0.243). Thus, discrimination remained above chance under the reconstructed source holdout, but performance was attenuated relative to the original random-fold evaluation, and the numerical ordering of the pooling representations differed from that observed in the primary analysis. Both confidence intervals included zero, providing no clear evidence of a pairwise ROC-AUC difference among these representations in the source-holdout cohort. Accordingly, the numerically higher mean-only performance in source-TEST should not be interpreted as demonstrating superiority over the combined representation. Patch-count discrimination was strongly dependent on the reconstructed source partition. Raw patient patch count yielded a ROC-AUC of 0.918 and PR-AUC of 0.815 within source-TRAIN but only a ROC-AUC of 0.517 and PR-AUC of 0.330 within source-TEST. The near-chance ROC-AUC in source-TEST contrasts with the stronger patch-count association observed in the pooled cohort and demonstrates that patch burden was not a stable discriminator across the predefined source partition. The count-only logistic-regression model yielded a ROC-AUC of 0.5169 and PR-AUC of 0.3301. Mean-only performance changed less across validation schemes, from ROC-AUC 0.820 in the primary fixed-fold analysis to 0.794 in source-TEST, whereas mean-plus-max performance decreased from 0.915 to 0.788. At the same time, image-derived representations retained moderate discriminatory information in the untouched source-TEST cohort despite the loss of patch-count discrimination and the lack of improvement after explicit patch-count addition. Because both source partitions originated from the same upstream TCGA-derived resource, these findings represent a source-structured internal robustness analysis rather than independent external validation. 3.7.
