This attenuation indicates that source-site structure may contribute to the apparent predictive performance and should not be ignored; however, substantial discrimination remained under TSS-isolated internal validation. These internal sensitivity analyses reduce, but do not eliminate, concern regarding clinicopathological and site-related confounding. Detailed clinicopathological association, clinical-comparison, and TSS sensitivity results are provided in Supplementary Tables S16–S18 . 4. Discussion 4.1. Principal Findings This study developed a calibration-aware, patient-level framework for predicting the source-defined positive category from colorectal histopathology using fixed pathology foundation-model embeddings. Its principal contribution was not the introduction of another end-to-end image architecture, but the integration of leakage-safe patient-level modeling, uncertainty estimation, calibration assessment, threshold-dependent evaluation, decision curve analysis, representation testing, and interpretability within a single reproducible workflow. Within the internally evaluated cohort, this approach demonstrated that pretrained histopathology embeddings could support informative patient-level prediction without retraining the image encoder. Logistic regression provided the most favorable combined profile among the five prespecified classifier implementations, achieving a primary ROC-AUC of 0.915. Its selection reflected the predefined ranking procedure, probability quality, positive-class recovery, and model parsimony rather than formal statistical superiority over Linear SVM or MLP, which showed similar discrimination. Repeated cross-validation and bootstrap analyses indicated that performance was not narrowly dependent on a single random patient-level partition. However, the reconstructed source-partition analysis provided a more stringent provenance-based test: when the prespecified logistic-regression pipeline was trained on the reconstructed source-TRAIN cohort and evaluated on the untouched source-TEST cohort, ROC-AUC decreased from 0.915 in the primary random-fold analysis to 0.788 for the mean-plus-max representation. By contrast, the mean-only representation changed from 0.820 in the primary fixed-fold analysis to 0.794 in source-TEST. This pattern indicates that the magnitude of discrimination observed under random patient-level cross-validation, especially the apparent increment associated with adding max pooling, was partly sensitive to upstream source structure. The more source-robust internal discrimination observed here was therefore closer to approximately 0.79–0.82 than to the primary random-fold mean-plus-max estimate. Nevertheless, above-chance discrimination was retained in the source-defined holdout, supporting the presence of predictive information within the fixed embedding representation while arguing against interpreting the primary cross-validation estimate as source-independent performance. This substantially attenuated source-holdout performance was therefore treated as a central interpretive limitation of the framework rather than as a secondary sensitivity finding. The nested calibration analysis materially changed the interpretation of probability performance. When calibration-method selection was nested entirely within the outer-training data, Platt scaling was selected in all five folds. The uncalibrated predictions showed a calibration slope below 1 (0.403) with a CITL of 0.040. Because the primary logistic-regression model used a balanced-class objective and was evaluated within the present development cohort, these probability-scale characteristics were interpreted descriptively rather than attributed to a single source of calibration error. After leakage-safe nested Platt calibration, the calibration slope was 1.037 and CITL was 0.023, with the pooled Brier score improving from 0.076 to 0.073. The same-score audit further confirmed that Platt scaling preserved fold-specific ROC-AUC exactly, whereas isotonic regression could alter rank-based metrics through the introduction of tied probabilities. These results address the optimism inherent in the original post-hoc calibration comparison but remain internal estimates requiring external reassessment. The clinicopathological sensitivity analyses also qualify interpretation of the image-derived signal. Age, broad pathologic stage, tissue or organ of origin, project membership, and primary diagnosis were associated with the source-defined outcome, confirming that clinically relevant covariate structure is present within the cohort. Nevertheless, the clinical-only model discriminated substantially less well than the image model, and addition of the audited clinical variables produced essentially no incremental improvement over image-only prediction. TSS-group-isolated validation produced lower performance than the original fixed-fold analysis but retained substantial discrimination. The reconstructed source-holdout analysis showed a further attenuation of the primary mean-plus-max ROC-AUC from 0.915 under random patient-level cross-validation to 0.788 when training and testing followed the original source partition. Considered together, these analyses indicate that clinicopathological, site-related, and broader source-provenance structure can influence apparent model performance. At the same time, the persistence of above-chance discrimination under both TSS-isolated and source-holdout evaluation suggests that these measured source effects do not fully account for the predictive signal. Residual confounding by unmeasured morphological, specimen-related, preprocessing-related, or center-specific technical factors nevertheless cannot be excluded. Threshold analysis also showed that no single operating point was uniformly optimal. Lowering the threshold reduced missed source-defined positive cases but substantially increased the number of MSS patients prioritized for confirmatory assessment. At the sensitivity ≥ 0.95 operating point, 2 source-defined positive patients were missed, while 179 MSS patients were classified as positive. Decision curve analysis showed bootstrap-supported internal net-benefit superiority over the better default strategy only from approximately 0.055 through 0.30; the sensitivity ≥ 0.95 threshold of 0.0219 fell below this range. Moreover, these threshold and decision-curve analyses were derived from internally cross-validated mean-plus-max predictions and were not repeated in the reconstructed source-holdout setting. Together, these results support further investigation of the model as a candidate prioritization or pre-screening framework, but they do not justify withholding confirmatory testing or adopting the derived thresholds as clinical cutoffs. The representation analyses indicated that aggregation design was an important component of model performance. Within the original fixed-fold cross-validation analysis, mean-plus-max pooling provided the most favorable overall numerical profile, whereas max-only pooling outperformed mean-only pooling. This ordering was not preserved under the reconstructed source holdout: mean-only pooling yielded a numerically higher ROC-AUC than mean-plus-max and max-only pooling, although paired bootstrap confidence intervals for the representation-level ROC-AUC differences included zero. The change in numerical ordering across validation schemes indicates that the apparent advantage of a particular pooling strategy was partition dependent and should not be interpreted as evidence of intrinsic representation superiority. The predominance of max-pooled dimensions among the highest-ranked SHAP features is therefore not sufficient to support a morphological multiple-instance-learning interpretation. Because raw max-pooled embeddings strongly encoded patch count, highly ranked max-pooled SHAP dimensions may also capture patch-burden or source-preprocessing proxies. Within the primary fixed-fold analysis, the combined representation performed more favorably than max pooling alone, consistent with additional information being retained by the mean-pooled component. However, the lack of the same numerical ordering in the source-holdout analysis indicates that the relative value of the pooling components was not invariant to dataset partitioning. Because the explanations remained confined to latent dimensions, they cannot establish that the model detected specific tumor regions, lymphocytic infiltration, mucinous morphology, or other recognizable MSI-associated histopathological patterns. The patch-count analyses showed that interpretation of the max-pooled component requires additional caution. In the pooled cohort, source-defined positive patients had substantially more available patches than MSS patients, and patch count alone showed appreciable discrimination. The upstream source documentation indicates that the source TRAIN partition was patch-balanced by random reduction of the more numerous MSS training patches [ 16 ], providing a concrete provenance mechanism for at least part of the class-dependent patch-count structure. Because the probability of observing an extreme latent activation can increase with the number of available patches, part of the apparent advantage of max pooling may therefore reflect patch-burden or preprocessing structure rather than histopathological information alone. Consistent with this concern, performance was attenuated when a common fixed number of patches was imposed across eligible patients. Raw max-pooled embeddings also strongly encoded patch count in the out-of-fold decoding audit. After fold-contained residualization, useful multivariable patch-count decoding was substantially attenuated by R 2 and mean absolute error, although a small inverse rank association remained. In the original random patient-level folds, the mean-plus-residualized-max representations still outperformed mean-only pooling; however, the source-holdout analysis did not confirm a transportable incremental advantage of max-containing representations over mean-only pooling. These findings indicate that patch burden contributed substantially to the raw max-pooled signal and that residualized random-fold performance should be interpreted cautiously rather than as proof that patch-count effects were fully removed. The reconstructed source-partition analysis further showed that the pooled patch-count association was not stable across the original source structure. Patch-count discrimination was strong in source-TRAIN but approached chance level in source-TEST, consistent with the class-dependent patch-sampling history of the upstream training partition. Explicitly adding log1p-transformed patch count to the image-derived representations did not materially improve source-TEST discrimination. At the same time, image-derived representations retained moderate discrimination in source-TEST despite the loss of patch-count discrimination. These results argue against absolute patch burden alone explaining the source-holdout predictions, while also showing that the magnitude and pooling-specific pattern of performance under random patient-level cross-validation were sensitive to upstream source structure. Residual confounding by other source-associated technical, specimen-related, preprocessing-related, or morphological factors therefore remains possible. In the separate proportional patch-subsampling analysis, performance also remained comparatively stable when patient representations were reconstructed from reduced patch fractions, without a monotonic benefit from increasing patch availability. This finding suggests that the model was not critically dependent on exhaustive patch enumeration within the existing archive and may have implications for computational efficiency. It does not, however, demonstrate robustness to differences in specimen sampling, staining, scanning, institutional practice, or external patch-generation pipelines. Taken together, the findings support the methodological feasibility of a calibration-aware, embedding-based patient-level prediction framework while also demonstrating that validation design materially affects the estimated magnitude of performance. Random patient-level cross-validation yielded strong discrimination, whereas the reconstructed source holdout produced more moderate discrimination and revealed sensitivity to upstream dataset structure. Accordingly, the primary ROC-AUC of 0.915 should be interpreted as an estimate of performance under internal random patient-level partitioning rather than as evidence of source-independent generalizability. The source-holdout findings strengthen the rationale for independent multicenter validation rather than substituting for it. External multicenter validation, prospective workflow assessment, and spatially resolved pathological interpretation remain necessary before the framework can be considered for clinical integration. 4.2. Comparison with Previous MSI Prediction Studies As outlined in the Introduction, Kather et al. first established the feasibility of inferring MSI-related information directly from routine H&E-stained gastrointestinal cancer histology [ 5 ]. Subsequent studies extended this concept through larger colorectal cancer cohorts, alternative deep-learning architectures, and multi-cohort validation designs [ 33 ]. Systematic reviews and meta-analytic evidence have since confirmed that histology-based MSI-H/dMMR prediction can achieve strong discrimination, while also documenting substantial heterogeneity related to cohort composition, reference standards, image processing, model design, and validation setting [ 4 , 34 ]. In particular, the lower and more variable specificity observed across external validation settings reinforces that favorable internal discrimination does not by itself establish clinical transportability. Earlier MSI-prediction pipelines relied on task-specific convolutional training, patch-level classification, or trainable weakly supervised slide-level aggregation. The present study addressed a related but distinct question: whether a fixed pathology foundation model already encoded sufficient task-relevant information for patient-level prediction using deterministic pooling and comparatively simple downstream classifiers. Recent foundation-model benchmarks similarly suggest that performance depends not only on encoder capacity, but also on pretraining data, aggregation design, downstream adaptation, and validation strategy [ 23 , 24 , 35 ]. Consequently, neither increasing encoder scale nor using a more complex slide-level learner should be assumed to provide consistent improvements across cohorts and tasks. The predictive performance observed in the present study lies within the broad range reported for histology-based MSI prediction, but direct numerical ranking against previous models would be inappropriate. Published studies differ in cancer-site composition, specimen type, MSI prevalence, molecular reference standard, tissue selection, preprocessing, and whether testing was performed internally or on genuinely independent cohorts [ 5 , 23 , 33 , 34 ]. More importantly, many previous investigations used PCR-, immunohistochemistry-, or sequencing-confirmed MSI-H/dMMR outcomes, whereas the current analysis used the source repository’s MSIMUT category, defined as microsatellite unstable or highly mutated, as the positive class. The available source metadata do not permit the highly mutated component to be assigned to a more specific molecular subgroup. The analytical target should therefore not be treated as equivalent to a strictly assay-confirmed MSI-H endpoint. Because the patch archive was derived from a TCGA-linked resource also represented in earlier MSI studies, the present analysis constitutes an internally validated methodological investigation rather than an independent external replication [ 5 , 16 ]. More clinically advanced studies have evaluated whether histology-based models can function as high-sensitivity pre-screening systems. MSIntuit was blindly validated in an independent consecutive cohort and designed to identify patients for whom standard MSI testing could potentially be avoided while maintaining very high sensitivity [ 36 ]. This operational logic is conceptually aligned with the sensitivity ≥ 0.95 operating point examined in Section 3.4 of the present study. However, the distinction in evidentiary strength is important: the MSIntuit thresholds were evaluated in an independent cohort and across different scanners, whereas the operating points reported here were derived and assessed internally and remain exploratory. A subsequent multicentre blinded evaluation involving more than 1200 patients further illustrates the level of external evidence required to assess cross-site transportability and realistic workflow performance [ 37 ]. The contribution of the present study therefore lies less in claiming higher discrimination than in characterizing dimensions of model behavior that have not been reported consistently across the MSI literature. The framework evaluated PR-AUC and probability accuracy alongside ROC-AUC, quantified calibration intercept, calibration slope, and calibration-in-the-large, compared calibration strategies within a leakage-safe nested procedure, examined prespecified sensitivity targets, and estimated decision-analytic net benefit. It also treated pooling strategy and patch availability as explicit methodological variables. These analyses provide a more complete account of internal model behavior than discrimination metrics alone, but they do not place the model at the same evidentiary level as externally validated or prospectively specified clinical systems. The pooling and interpretability findings provide an additional point of comparison with trainable attention-based and multiple-instance-learning approaches. Rather than learning slide-level attention weights, the present framework compared deterministic mean, max, and mean-plus-max representations. The predominance of max-pooled dimensions among the highest-ranked SHAP features was compatible with predictive information being concentrated within a subset of patches, while the stronger overall performance of the combined representation within the random patient-level folds suggested that more distributed information remained complementary; however, this ordering was not preserved under the reconstructed source holdout. Because the analysis did not localize or pathologically annotate influential regions, it complements rather than replaces heatmap-based, attention-based, or pathologist-validated spatial interpretation used in previous studies. Overall, the present study does not demonstrate superiority over previously published end-to-end, weakly supervised, foundation-model-based, or clinically validated MSI systems. Instead, it shows that fixed pathology foundation-model embeddings, deterministic patient-level pooling, and a parsimonious linear classifier can support informative internal prediction when accompanied by explicit evaluation of uncertainty, calibration, operating thresholds, decision-analytic value, and representation robustness. The study is therefore positioned as a methodological complement to prior MSI-prediction research and as a foundation for subsequent external multicentre and prospective validation. 4.3. Methodological and Translational Implications The first methodological implication is that the analytical unit should correspond to the intended clinical unit of prediction. In patch-rich computational pathology datasets, the apparent number of image samples can obscure the fact that the effective number of independent observations is determined by patients. Maintaining patient-level separation throughout representation construction, model fitting, calibration, and evaluation was therefore essential to prevent correlated tissue fragments from producing optimistic estimates. Within this constraint, the combination of a fixed encoder, deterministic pooling, and a comparatively simple downstream classifier provided a modular framework in which representation, aggregation, and prediction could be examined separately. This modular design has implications for reproducibility and model maintenance. Keeping the Phikon encoder fixed avoids repeated task-specific image-model training and allows downstream components to be audited, recalibrated, or replaced without retraining the complete image-processing pipeline. Related work in computational pathology has also illustrated the broader value of modular representation-transfer strategies, including the transfer of information from multimodal training frameworks to models operating on a single histopathology modality [ 21 ]. Recent pathology foundation-model benchmarks indicate that downstream performance depends not only on encoder capacity, but also on representation quality, aggregation strategy, task adaptation, and validation design [ 24 , 35 ]. In the present cohort, the favorable performance of logistic regression indicated that task-relevant information was accessible to a linear downstream classifier within the fixed Phikon-derived representation space. This finding should not be interpreted as evidence that simple classifiers will be optimal across other datasets, encoders, aggregation strategies, or clinical endpoints. Rather, it supports evaluating representation quality and aggregation design before increasing downstream model complexity. An embedding-based workflow should nevertheless not be regarded as computationally cost-free. Whole-slide tiling, patch storage, and foundation-model inference may still impose substantial processing and infrastructure requirements. The principal efficiency advantage lies in avoiding repeated end-to-end task-specific training rather than eliminating whole-slide processing costs. Similarly, the stability observed under reduced patch fractions supports further investigation of predefined patch budgets, adaptive sampling, or sequential stopping strategies, but the present study did not measure execution time, storage requirements, energy consumption, or prospective turnaround time. The patch-burden findings therefore indicate the feasibility of resource-aware investigation rather than a demonstrated operational efficiency benefit. A further translational implication is that discrimination must be complemented by evaluation of probability behavior and intended clinical action. Calibration analysis showed that informative rankings may coexist with probabilities requiring adjustment, while threshold analysis demonstrated that the relative consequences of missed positive cases and unnecessary confirmatory assessments vary substantially across operating points. Calibration and threshold selection should therefore be repeated in the intended deployment population, accounting for disease prevalence, clinical consequences, and workflow-specific tolerance for false-positive and false-negative results. The source-defined positive prevalence was 18.1% in the present cohort and may differ materially from that of future screening populations, with corresponding effects on predictive values and testing burden. Decision curve analysis can support this assessment but does not replace prospective workflow evaluation, health-economic analysis, or direct measurement of clinical outcomes [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 38 ]. The most plausible translational role for the framework is not autonomous MSI diagnosis, but candidate pre-screening and prioritization of confirmatory testing. An H&E-based probability estimate could potentially help identify cases for earlier molecular or immunohistochemical assessment, whereas a high-sensitivity operating point could be investigated within a rule-out-oriented workflow. If validated prospectively, such an approach might reduce avoidable testing, shorten diagnostic pathways, and, particularly in tissue-limited specimens, contribute to tissue stewardship by preserving tumor material for other clinically indicated molecular or targeted biomarker analyses. These potential benefits were not measured in the present study. Moreover, because the modeled endpoint was the source-defined MSIMUT category rather than a uniformly assay-confirmed MSI-H/dMMR outcome, the current framework cannot support withholding or replacing established PCR- or immunohistochemistry-based testing [ 36 , 37 , 38 ]. Representation-level interpretability provides only a partial basis for translational transparency. The SHAP analysis characterized reliance on latent mean- and max-pooled dimensions but did not identify the tissue structures responsible for individual predictions. For the max-pooled component, the patch producing the maximum value in a specific embedding dimension is mathematically traceable through dimension-wise argmax tracking, provided that patch-level embeddings and provenance mappings are retained. This could support future spatially resolved analyses, but it would identify dimension-specific source patches rather than, by itself, establish a single causal or pathologically meaningful region for the patient-level prediction. Future studies should combine such tracing with patient-level attribution, spatial visualization, pathologist review, and validation against recognizable histopathological patterns. Clinical translation would additionally require external multicenter validation, locked preprocessing and calibration procedures, slide-quality control, assessment across scanners and staining protocols, evaluation of uncertain or non-evaluable cases, fairness analysis, and model-version governance. The present findings therefore support a transparent methodology for evaluating foundation-model embeddings in patient-level biomarker prediction, rather than a deployment-ready diagnostic system. Leakage control, modular representation design, probability calibration, operating-point analysis, decision-analytic assessment, and patch-burden testing address complementary requirements that should be considered before an embedding-based computational pathology model progresses toward prospective clinical evaluation. 4.4. Strengths and Limitations This study has several methodological strengths. First, the patient was maintained as the analytical and validation unit throughout the complete workflow. Patch-level embeddings derived from the same patient were not divided between training and testing subsets, reducing the risk of optimistic performance estimates caused by correlated tissue fragments. A single verified patient manifest, outcome vector, representation matrix, and set of validation partitions were retained across classifier comparison, repeated validation, calibration, threshold analysis, pooling comparison, patch subsampling, and interpretability assessment. This consistency strengthened the internal traceability of the computational workflow. Second, model evaluation extended beyond a single cross-validation estimate or discrimination metric. The primary five-fold analysis was complemented by repeated patient-level cross-validation, bootstrap uncertainty estimation, leakage-safe nested probability calibration, sensitivity-targeted operating-point analysis, and decision curve analysis with bootstrap-based uncertainty assessment. Additional sensitivity analyses examined clinicopathological and tissue-source-site structure within the cohort. Reporting ROC-AUC together with PR-AUC, Matthews correlation coefficient, Brier score, calibration parameters, predictive values, and confusion-matrix counts provided a broader characterization of model behavior under class imbalance. Pooling comparison and patch-burden experiments additionally evaluated assumptions concerning representation design and image availability, while SHAP analysis was explicitly restricted to representation-level interpretation. The use of a fixed encoder, deterministic pooling procedures, controlled random seeds, training-fold-contained preprocessing, and programmatically retained intermediate outputs further supported reproducibility and auditing. Several limitations nevertheless constrain the interpretation of the findings. Most importantly, all analyses were based on a single retrospective TCGA-derived cohort, and no independent external dataset was available. Patient-level internal validation reduces information leakage but cannot reproduce the domain shifts encountered across independent institutions, patient populations, specimen-processing protocols, staining conditions, scanners, or digital-pathology systems. Two complementary source-structure assessments were included: TSS-group-isolated validation based on TCGA/GDC metadata and a reconstructed holdout based on the original upstream TRAIN/TEST partition. Both analyses remained internal to the same TCGA-derived source resource. The attenuation from a primary mean-plus-max ROC-AUC of 0.915 under random patient-level cross-validation to 0.788 under the reconstructed source holdout demonstrates that internal random-fold estimates were sensitive to source partitioning and should not be interpreted as evidence of transportability. Neither the TSS-isolated analysis nor the reconstructed source holdout constitutes independent external multicenter validation. The present results therefore characterize performance across multiple internal validation structures within the available source cohort rather than demonstrating transportability across clinical settings. Performance, calibration, fairness, and operating characteristics across independent patient populations, laboratories, staining workflows, scanners, and acquisition systems remain unknown. The outcome definition also requires caution. The positive class remained the source repository’s MSIMUT category, formally defined as microsatellite unstable or highly mutated, rather than a uniformly clinically adjudicated PCR-, immunohistochemistry-, or sequencing-confirmed MSI-H/dMMR endpoint. GDC-derived MSIsensor2 status was available for all 360 cases. Among the 351 patients with an unambiguous GDC-derived MSI or MSS designation, agreement with the source archive label was 98.9%, with a Cohen’s κ of 0.959. Existing image-based out-of-sample predictions also retained strong discrimination when evaluated against this secondary GDC-derived endpoint. However, the GDC-derived MSIsensor2 annotation represents a bioinformatics-derived molecular annotation rather than a uniform clinical reference assay. The high concordance therefore supports consistency of the source labels but does not convert the primary outcome into a clinically adjudicated MSI-H/dMMR endpoint. Accordingly, the model should continue to be interpreted as predicting the source-defined archive label. Detailed MSIsensor2 concordance and secondary-endpoint performance results are provided in Supplementary Table S19 . The study also depended on a previously processed JPEG patch archive rather than direct reconstruction from the original whole-slide repository. Although the derivative dataset title refers to TCGA colon adenocarcinoma, linkage of all 360 patient identifiers to GDC metadata confirmed that the analytical cohort contained both TCGA-COAD and TCGA-READ cases, supporting its description as a colorectal cohort. Nevertheless, the derivative archive was accessed through a community-hosted repository without a persistent dataset DOI or a peer-reviewed data descriptor. The complete upstream case-selection pathway used to create the derivative archive—including the initial number of TCGA cases considered, case-level exclusion criteria, the number of originating whole-slide images, and all preprocessing decisions—could not be reconstructed fully. Upstream tissue detection, patch selection, stain normalization, slide-quality control, tiling stride, and overlap therefore could not be independently modified or completely audited. These provenance limitations remain relevant despite successful patient-level linkage to the original TCGA case identifiers. The sample size was modest relative to the 1536-dimensional patient representation, and only 65 patients belonged to the source-defined positive class. Regularization, patient-level cross-validation, and repeated resampling reduced but did not eliminate risks related to high dimensionality and class imbalance. Regularization-sensitivity analysis further showed that discrimination remained similar across C = 0.01–1 but declined under substantially weaker regularization at C = 10–100, while no convergence warnings were observed across the evaluated configurations. Moreover, the candidate classifiers represented prespecified fixed implementations rather than an exhaustive or independently optimized comparison. Logistic regression and Linear SVM used class weighting, whereas the evaluated MLP, random forest, and gradient boosting implementations used unweighted objectives. Because imbalance handling was not harmonized across all candidate implementations, the classifier comparison should be interpreted as a comparison of the prespecified analytical pipelines rather than as an intrinsic ranking of the underlying algorithm families. The primary classifier was selected from five prespecified implementations using internal cross-validation within the same cohort. To examine potential classifier-selection optimism directly, a nested pipeline-selection sensitivity analysis restricted pipeline selection entirely to each outer-training set. Logistic regression was selected in all five outer folds, and the resulting nested-selected outer-test predictions were identical to those of the fixed logistic-regression reference, yielding no observed difference in ROC-AUC or PR-AUC. This finding supports the internal reproducibility of the original pipeline choice. Nevertheless, because both the original comparison and the nested sensitivity analysis were performed within the same cohort, model-selection uncertainty cannot be considered eliminated, and the results should not be interpreted as demonstrating intrinsic superiority of logistic regression over other algorithm families. Calibration and decision-oriented analyses remained internal, although the principal source of calibration-method selection optimism identified in the original analysis was addressed through the fully nested calibration procedure. Calibration-method selection was repeated within a fully nested procedure in which uncalibrated probabilities, Platt scaling, and isotonic regression were compared using cross-fitted predictions generated exclusively from the corresponding outer-training data. Outer-test observations were not used for calibrator selection or fitting, and Platt scaling was selected in all five outer folds. The resulting nested-Platt probabilities showed substantially improved calibration, with a pooled calibration slope of 1.037 and calibration-in-the-large of 0.023. Nevertheless, calibration performance remains specific to the present development cohort and requires reassessment in an independent population. Similarly, the Youden and high-sensitivity operating thresholds were derived and evaluated from internally generated out-of-sample probabilities and remain exploratory cohort-specific operating points. Decision-curve analysis was supplemented by paired bootstrap uncertainty assessment, but its results likewise do not establish prospective clinical utility. The bootstrap procedures resampled patient-level outcome–prediction pairs without repeating the complete sequence of representation construction, model fitting, calibration selection, and threshold derivation and therefore quantify uncertainty conditional on the generated predictions rather than all sources of model-development uncertainty. Interpretability remained confined to latent embedding dimensions. SHAP values characterized relative reliance on the mean- and max-pooled components but did not identify specific histopathological structures, cell populations, or causal biological mechanisms. The predominance of max-pooled dimensions among the top SHAP-ranked features should be interpreted cautiously because raw max-pooled embeddings strongly encoded patch count; these dimensions may therefore partly reflect patch-burden or source-preprocessing proxies. The interventional masker did not explicitly model correlations among embedding dimensions, and attribution magnitudes may differ under correlation-aware explanation methods. Dimension-wise max-pooling provenance could potentially permit tracing individual maximal activations back to source patches, but such tracing was not performed or validated through pathologist review. The original proportional patch-subsampling experiment represented repeated reductions within each patient’s existing archive and therefore assessed robustness to reduced patch availability, but it did not equalize absolute patch counts across patients and should not be interpreted as a control for patch-count confounding. Fixed-N, fold-contained patch-count-adjustment, source-holdout, and explicit patch-count-addition analyses demonstrated that absolute patch burden and upstream patch-generation history contributed to the raw max-pooled signal. Patch count itself may reflect a mixture of tissue area, tumor extent, source-image characteristics, and upstream patch-generation or tissue-selection processes; consequently, neither fixed-N subsampling nor statistical residualization can determine which biological or technical mechanism generated the observed patch-count difference. Metadata linkage allowed several potentially relevant clinicopathological and site-related factors to be examined, including age, pathologic stage, tissue or organ of origin, primary diagnosis, TCGA project membership, and tissue-source-site code. These variables showed measurable associations with the source-defined outcome. A clinical-only model nevertheless discriminated less well than the image-only model, whereas combining the audited clinical variables with the image representation produced essentially no incremental discrimination over the image-only pipeline. In addition, discrimination was attenuated but remained substantial when all patients sharing the same TSS were isolated between training and testing. These findings indicate that the measured clinical and site variables do not fully account for the image-model discrimination; however, they do not exclude residual confounding by unmeasured morphological, technical, or clinical factors. Important covariate limitations therefore remain. Sex/gender and a uniform clinical molecular MSI-test result were not included in the analyzable metadata extract used for the present sensitivity analyses, and the study did not incorporate pathologist-adjudicated histological subtype, detailed tumor-cell content, treatment information, complete pathology-report variables, or center-specific staining and scanner characteristics. Prospective turnaround time, computational cost, storage requirements, energy consumption, cost-effectiveness, tissue preservation, workflow acceptability, and effects on patient management were also not evaluated. A further reproducibility limitation is that the commit-specific revision of the Phikon encoder used during the original embedding-generation run was not pinned or retained; consequently, bitwise regeneration of the patch embeddings directly from the source images cannot be guaranteed across different hardware and software environments. This limitation is partly mitigated by the public release of the exact patient-specific embedding arrays used as fixed inputs for all downstream analyses. Collectively, these limitations indicate that the framework should be regarded as a transparent internally validated methodological investigation rather than a clinically validated or deployment-ready MSI decision-support system. 4.5. Future Directions The immediate priority for future research is independent multicenter validation using a prespecified and frozen version of the complete analytical pipeline. The pathology foundation-model revision, preprocessing procedures, pooling strategy, classifier parameters, calibration mapping, and operating thresholds should be locked before external evaluation. Direct transportability should first be assessed without site-specific refitting or retrospective threshold optimization. If discrimination or calibration deteriorates, recalibration or domain-adaptation strategies should be evaluated in a separately designed development phase and tested in data that were not used to select the adaptation procedure. Performance should be reported by institution, scanner, staining protocol, specimen type, and clinically relevant patient subgroup to distinguish genuine generalizability from average performance that conceals site-specific failure [ 35 , 37 , 38 , 39 ]. Where transfer of raw whole-slide images is restricted by data-governance, infrastructure, or privacy constraints, distributed validation and federated-learning strategies could be investigated. The modular separation between fixed embedding extraction and a lightweight downstream classifier may facilitate such designs. However, latent embeddings should not be assumed to be inherently anonymous or privacy preserving. Any distributed implementation would require explicit evaluation of information leakage, secure aggregation, institutional governance, and reproducibility across local computational environments. Future validation should also use clinically adjudicated reference standards. Cohorts with PCR-, immunohistochemistry-, or sequencing-confirmed MSI-H/dMMR status would determine whether the source-defined MSIMUT signal identified in the present study transfers to a more narrowly defined clinical endpoint. When multiple assays are available, discordant results should be reviewed explicitly rather than collapsed automatically into a binary label. Consecutive or population-based cohorts would additionally permit calibration, predictive values, testing burden, and operating thresholds to be evaluated under prevalence conditions that more closely reflect the intended clinical setting. Robustness assessment should extend beyond random patch reduction within a single preprocessed archive. Relevant evaluations include alternative tissue blocks and slide sections from the same patient, biopsy versus resection material, variable tumor content, staining perturbations, scanner platforms, tissue-detection procedures, and external patch-generation pipelines. The modular framework also permits controlled comparison of Phikon with alternative pathology foundation-model encoders. Such comparisons should use identical patient partitions, pooling strategies, downstream classifiers, calibration procedures, and evaluation metrics to separate encoder-related differences from variation introduced elsewhere in the pipeline. Encoder selection should be completed within development data rather than through retrospective comparison on the final external test cohort. Resource-aware processing should be evaluated concurrently with these robustness experiments. Predefined patch budgets, adaptive tissue sampling, uncertainty-guided patch selection, and sequential stopping criteria could be compared with exhaustive patch processing. These analyses should measure not only predictive performance but also inference time, storage requirements, computational cost, energy consumption, and diagnostic turnaround time. This would establish whether the observed internal tolerance to reduced patch fractions can produce a reproducible operational benefit. Spatially resolved interpretability represents another important research direction. Dimension-wise provenance tracking could identify the source patches responsible for individual max-pooled activations, after which these patches could be mapped back to their originating slide locations. Patient-level attribution would then need to be integrated with spatial visualization and independent pathologist assessment. Such studies could examine whether influential regions correspond reproducibly to immune-rich areas, mucinous differentiation, glandular irregularity, architectural heterogeneity, or other recognizable histopathological patterns. Attribution stability across tissue perturbations, agreement among pathologists, and comparison with correlation-aware explanation methods would be required before latent feature importance could support morphological or biological interpretation. Prospective studies should evaluate a clearly prespecified clinical role rather than generic deployment. A plausible initial setting would be model-assisted prioritization of confirmatory MSI testing, with molecular or immunohistochemical assessment remaining the reference procedure. A rule-out-oriented strategy would require externally validated sensitivity, a fixed operating threshold, and predefined management of uncertain, low-quality, and non-evaluable slides. Prospective outcomes should include missed positive cases, additional testing generated by false-positive predictions, turnaround time, tissue consumption, costs, workflow acceptability, and effects on clinical decisions. Retrospective threshold and decision-curve analyses can inform the design of such studies but cannot replace direct workflow evaluation [ 10 , 11 , 36 , 37 , 38 ]. Beyond their essential role in cohort description and subgroup assessment, clinicopathological variables should be further evaluated and expanded in independent external multimodal validation. In the internal sensitivity analysis, age, pathologic stage, tissue or organ of origin, primary diagnosis, TCGA project membership, and tissue-source-site information were examined, and combining the audited clinical variables with image-derived embeddings did not provide clear incremental discrimination over the image-only model. Future multimodal studies should therefore incorporate broader and prospectively collected variables that were unavailable or incompletely represented in the present cohort, including sex/gender, pathologist-adjudicated histological subtype, specimen type, structured pathology-report information, and center-specific technical factors. The incremental value of such multimodal integration should be tested against both image-only and clinical-only baselines in independent external cohorts using prespecified analytical pipelines, with particular attention to transportability, calibration, and clinical utility rather than model complexity alone. Taken together, these directions define a staged translational pathway: first, they externally validate the locked image-based framework; second, assess clinically confirmed endpoints and domain robustness; third, connect latent representations with pathologist-recognizable morphology; and finally, evaluate a prespecified role within prospective clinical workflows. This sequence would determine whether foundation-model-derived histopathology embeddings can contribute safely, reproducibly, and efficiently to MSI pre-screening or confirmatory-test prioritization in colorectal cancer. 5. Conclusions This study demonstrates the methodological feasibility of leakage-safe, patient-level prediction of a source-defined MSIMUT category in colorectal cancer histopathology using fixed Phikon foundation-model embeddings. Deterministic pooling of patch-level embeddings, followed by a comparatively simple logistic-regression classifier, supported strong internal discrimination under random patient-level cross-validation with the primary mean-plus-max representation (ROC-AUC, 0.915), but the same representation showed more moderate discrimination under the reconstructed source holdout (ROC-AUC, 0.788; PR-AUC, 0.593), indicating that the primary random-fold estimate was optimistic relative to source-holdout performance. Leakage-safe nested Platt calibration improved probability behavior without using outer-test outcomes for calibration-method selection, and the resulting calibrated predictions supported exploratory threshold and decision-curve analyses within the internally evaluated TCGA-derived cohort. However, the additional provenance-based analyses materially qualify the interpretation of these findings. Reconstruction of the original source TRAIN/TEST partition showed that performance was attenuated under a source-structured internal holdout, with the mean-plus-max ROC-AUC decreasing to 0.788. Patch-count analyses further showed that absolute patch burden and upstream source-preprocessing history contributed to the raw max-pooled signal and to the magnitude of performance observed under random patient-level partitioning. Although image-derived representations retained moderate discrimination in source-TEST and explicit patch-count addition did not improve source-holdout performance, the results should not be interpreted as evidence of source-independent generalizability. The lower source-holdout performance was therefore considered a key limitation of the current framework and a major reason for restricting the interpretation to internal methodological feasibility. The model should therefore be viewed as an internally evaluated methodological framework for MSI-related pre-screening research rather than as a clinically validated diagnostic tool. The predicted endpoint was the source-defined MSIMUT archive label, not a uniformly clinically adjudicated MSI-H/dMMR reference standard. All performance, calibration, threshold, decision-analytic, clinicopathological, source-provenance, and patch-count sensitivity results remain internal to the TCGA-derived cohort. Independent multicenter validation using clinically adjudicated MSI-H/dMMR outcomes, heterogeneous acquisition conditions, locked preprocessing and calibration procedures, and prespecified operating thresholds is required before any clinical application, confirmatory-testing decision, or workflow integration can be considered. evidence_text:
Multimodal alignment improves generalizability of genomic biomarker prediction in computational pathology. Computational pathology models that use digitized histopathology whole-slide images have the potential to become a cost-effective and scalable alternative to molecular assays for the prediction of genomic biomarkers, a key task in precision oncology. However, as new genomic biomarkers are discovered or quantified, large, labeled datasets must be prospectively collected to train new models. To address this challenge, we developed multimodal alignment for biomarker learning and generalization (MARBLE), a multimodal contrastive pretraining strategy that integrates structured biomarker knowledge into representation learning of histopathology images. MARBLE aligns histopathology-derived representations with representations of genomic biomarkers generated by a large language model (LLM) and a protein language model (PLM). This biologically informed alignment enables data-efficient generalization to novel, out-of-distribution biomarkers. Using the MSK-IMPACT cohort of over 40,000 patients across multiple biomarker panel versions, we design experiments grounded in real-world data to demonstrate the value of our proposed approach. Introduction  Histopathology data, particularly hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained tissue samples called whole slide images (WSIs), are routinely collected as part of cancer care. These samples are increasingly being digitized, thereby enabling the development and application of foundation models,  1   ,   2   ,   3   ,   4   ,   5   which can be used to extract robust and general-purpose visual representations. Building predictive models using these representations has been successful for routine predictive tasks, such as cancer detection and subtyping  6   ,   7   and has shown great potential for expanding the utility of WSIs to novel downstream tasks. One such use case is the computational prediction of biomarker profiles directly from histopathology images as a replacement for screening for genomic biomarkers via molecular assays ( Figure 1 A). DNA sequencing is used to assess the presence of tumor-specific genomic alterations (e.g., mutations, deletions, insertions, duplications, and rearrangements), the results of which are used to inform prognosis and guide therapy selection.  8   However, as the sequencing procedures underlying these assays are expensive and challenging to scale, direct prediction from H&E images presents a cost-effective and scalable alternative. Several works have already demonstrated encouraging performance for both single biomarkers  9   ,   10   ,   11   and larger panels.  12    Figure 1   MARBLE uses pretraining with biomarker embeddings to improve predictive performance, as demonstrated on the MSK-IMPACT panel  (A) The molecular profiling and tissue collection pipeline in cancer care: a tissue specimen undergoes DNA sequencing, routine H&E staining, and digitalization.  (B) Biomarker panel size across MSK-IMPACT versions (v.3, v.5, v.6, v.7), distribution of patient-level biomarker counts, and distribution of biomarker positivity rates.  (C) Key components of the design of MARBLE. Aggregated histopathology embeddings from a frozen pathology foundation model (Path FM) are contrasted with aggregated biomarker embeddings derived from a frozen LLM (GPT-4o + Sentence-BERT [SBERT]) and/or a frozen PLM (ESM-2), enabling cross-modal alignment through contrastive pretraining.  (D) Supervised fine-tuning of the imaging encoder for multi-label biomarker classification.  (E) Pretraining and fine-tuning cohort setups with panel-specific sample counts.                       At the same time, advances in precision oncology continue to expand the catalog of actionable genomic biomarkers, both as new oncogenes are identified and new cancer-driving alterations for existing oncogenes and tumor suppressors are characterized. For example, the MSK-IMPACT panel, a test for tumor-specific genomic biomarkers, has grown by 164 genes since it was first released in 2017 ( Figure 1 B).  8   As new cancer drivers and therapeutic targets continue to emerge, predictive models face the challenge of rapidly integrating these biomarkers in a data-efficient manner while maintaining performance on existing ones. In practice, adapting these models to novel targets often requires a large amount of labeled data, which is time consuming, costly, and potentially infeasible to obtain (e.g., for rare alterations). Addressing this limitation requires approaches that can generalize while utilizing a minimal amount of labeled samples.  We hypothesize that multimodal contrastive pretraining can overcome this limitation by structuring the visual representation space around biologically meaningful relationships. To this end, we introduce “multimodal alignment for biomarker learning and generalization” (MARBLE), a pretraining strategy that incorporates knowledge about biomarkers directly into the representation learning process, enabling downstream generalization to novel biomarkers ( Figure 1 C). Our approach aligns aggregated H&E-derived embeddings, created using a pathology foundation model (Path FM), with aggregated semantic embeddings of biomarkers.  To create biomarker embeddings, we use large language models (LLMs) and protein language models (PLMs), allowing us to explore the effect of representing biomarkers as different modalities and to exploit the specific semantics learned by their respective pretraining. Recent studies demonstrate the utility of LLMs in biological domains, from enriching protein representations via textual annotations  13   to modeling perturbations through structured LLM reasoning.  14   In parallel, PLMs encode latent information about protein function from amino acid sequences and are thus capable of capturing how mutations impact function.  15   ,   16   ,   17   PLMs have been leveraged to incorporate molecular priors into vision models, such as in the VirTues framework,  18   which fuses PLM-derived protein embeddings with image patch tokens to encode channel-specific marker information and guide multimodal representation learning in spatial proteomics.  Because tumor morphology often reflects the combined influence of several genomic alterations rather than just one ( Figure 1 B), traditional supervised approaches that treat each biomarker as an independent entity fail to capture the semantic relationships between co-occurring alterations. For example, KRAS, BRAF, and NRAS mutations all activate the MAPK signaling pathway.  19   By aligning H&E-derived embeddings with LLM- and PLM-based embeddings, we leverage the structured biological knowledge of these models to capture such relationships. This biologically informed alignment enables the model to learn that morphologically similar tissue patterns may arise from functionally related combinations of biomarkers. From principle, the construction of our method enables generalization to new biomarkers by recognizing their similarity to previously observed alterations with related mechanisms.  We evaluated the MARBLE strategy through experiments grounded in real-world data. Using earlier versions of the MSK-IMPACT panel, we performed pretraining to align image embeddings separately with LLM-derived embeddings and with PLM-derived embeddings, as well as jointly with both. The image-only component of the pretrained model was then fine-tuned to predict all of the biomarkers measured in the most recent version of the panel. Our results support the claim that alignment improves predictive performance for previously unseen biomarkers in a low-data regime and enables generalization to out-of-distribution samples. Overall, we demonstrate how our pretraining approach leads to improved, data-efficient generalization of biomarker quantification.    Results   Representing biomarkers with PLMs and LLMs  Contrastive learning aims to align representations of paired samples while simultaneously penalizing the alignment of representations of unpaired samples.  20   This approach has proven highly effective in improving the performance of modern deep learning systems and has recently gained significant interest in multimodal settings such as vision-language modeling. One example is the contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP) approach,  21   which learns a unified embedding space for images and their corresponding textual descriptions. Models with multimodal contrastive pretraining are becoming prevalent in computational pathology, spanning both vision-language  22   ,   23   ,   24   and vision-molecular  4   ,   25   ,   26   ,   27   settings. To date, the use of multimodal pretraining in computational pathology has focused on learning tile aggregation models that produce a slide embedding. In these works, the motivation rests on the assumption that the additional modality provides a generalizable supervisory signal for aggregating tile representations. Here, we investigate the distinct setting where we specifically hypothesize that pretraining will aid in out-of-distribution performance. This hypothesis is motivated by successes in representation learning from proteins and text to create PLMs and LLMs, respectively.  PLMs aim to learn rich representations of protein sequences, capturing the structural and functional properties of proteins through large-scale pretraining.  28   ,   29   The recently developed ESM-2 model  30   is a particularly noteworthy PLM because of its strong downstream performance in tasks like structure prediction and function annotation. Recently, PLM representations have been combined with imaging data in the context of spatial proteomics to capture both molecular and spatial information with the aim of enabling more accurate clinical diagnostics and biological discovery.  18   Building on this idea, we propose to leverage PLM embeddings of mutated protein products of tumor-specific genomic alterations and integrate them with H&E imaging to derive richer representations that are biologically grounded and predictive of molecular alterations.  We model in-frame variants of genomic alterations including missense, nonsense, deletion, insertion, and indel mutations. Combining the canonical UniProt sequence with the specific genomic alteration provides a sequence of amino acids. These mutated sequences can be used as input to a PLM, providing us a systematic mapping from genomic alteration to embedding. Given its recent success, we select ESM-2 as the PLM.  30   This approach produces fixed-dimension embeddings  d   P   per biomarker which are gathered into a set of      P  i   ∈   R    N  P  i   ×   d  P        where      N  P  i      is the number of embeddings for patient  i . Copy-number variations have no clear altered protein product and are excluded from the PLM representation. Additionally, MSK-IMPACT does not include data about altered protein product from frameshift mutations, so these are also excluded.  LLMs are pretrained on massive text corpora via masked language modeling or next token prediction, which implicitly encodes domain-specific knowledge in their weights.  31   Recent studies have demonstrated that this embedded knowledge can be retrieved through prompting. For instance, Med-PaLM, a variant of an LLM tuned to the medical domain, achieved expert-level performance on clinical question-answering tasks using prompt-based querying alone.  32   LLMs are typically used for their ability to directly generate text. In parallel, text embedding models provide compact vector representations of a text corpus.  We propose a systematic approach to transform biomarkers to text embeddings. Each biomarker present in the panel consists of a HUGO gene symbol (e.g., EGFR), high-level mutation information (e.g., copy-number amplification), and a cancer type (e.g., bladder cancer). For each gene, we obtain a canonical protein function description from UniProtKB,  33   an expert-curated protein knowledge base. The obtained description is then used to prompt an LLM ( Figure S1  for the complete prompt) to produce a concise description of the associated mutation and its role in the provided cancer type, including any known mechanisms of action. The resulting text description is then used as input into a text embedding model, specifically Sentence-BERT (SBERT),  34   to obtain a fixed-dimension embedding  d   L   per biomarker. This process is repeated for each patient biomarker to create a set of embeddings      L  i   ∈   R    N  L  i   ×   d  L        where      N  L  i      is the number of embeddings.    Multimodal alignment for biomarker learning and generalization  Our proposed contrastive pretraining strategy MARBLE aligns two types of biomarker representations with histopathology image representations from a patient sample ( Figure 1 C). We hypothesize and show that performing this pretraining step ahead of supervised fine-tuning improves performance, particularly when the number of labeled training samples is small. To use MARBLE, the following steps are applied. A foundation model is applied to each modality to produce instance-level embeddings. For histopathology, WSIs are divided into tiles, each embedded independently using a pretrained vision foundation model ( STAR Methods , embedding generation). For biomarkers, each genomic alteration is represented either as a textual description embedded via an LLM or as an altered protein sequence embedded via a PLM, as described in the preceding section. Both the number of tiles per patient WSIs and the number of biomarkers per patient vary across samples. Therefore, an aggregation step is performed per modality ( STAR Methods , aggregation model), and the resulting representations are used for contrastive alignment ( STAR Methods , multimodal alignment objective). After pretraining, the histopathology image-only aggregator is fine-tuned to predict multi-label biomarker status ( STAR Methods , biomarker prediction) for biomarkers that were observed and unobserved during pretraining ( Figure 1 D). Because our approach can work with LLM embeddings, PLM embeddings, or both, we evaluate the respective variants, MARBLE-LLM, MARBLE-PLM, and MARBLE.    Improving generalizability with language pretraining  We design our experiments and evaluations to mirror a real-world setting. Using the MSK-IMPACT panel genomic alterations as our target predictive task, we exploit the property that several versions of the panel have been released over time, each adding new biomarkers. This allows us to test the effect of pretraining with early versions and fine-tuning with varying numbers of labeled samples from the latest panel. Our experiments use a cohort of 40,300 patients tested with one of four MSK-IMPACT panel versions, v.3, v.5, v.6, or v.7, each with an increasing number of oncogenes ( Figure 1 B;  Table S1 ). The dataset is partitioned to use patient samples assessed with early versions of the panel, specifically v.3, v.5, or v.6, during pretraining ( STAR Methods , pretraining setup). The final predictive model is fine-tuned to predict all biomarkers from the v.7 panel, which contains 37 new oncogenes, corresponding to 53 new biomarkers ( STAR Methods , fine-tuning setup). Performance is reported using balanced accuracy for in-distribution biomarkers, those seen during pretraining and supervised fine-tuning, out-of-distribution biomarkers, those unseen during pretraining, and overall. To specifically assess sample efficiency, supervised fine-tuning is performed with v.7 samples of size 100, 1,000, and 10,000 ( STAR Methods , fine-tuning setup). Results are compared to direct supervision without contrastive pretraining (no pretraining) and pretraining with only binary presence/absence encoding of biomarkers without semantic embedding information, motivated by the THREADS  4   approach (multi-hot) (see  STAR Methods , comparison approaches for additional pretraining details). We add one additional comparison which uses an LLM to perform aggregation in place of the multiple instance learning approach ( STAR Methods , comparison approaches).  Our proposed MARBLE-LLM consistently improves out-of-distribution generalization, particularly in the low-data regime ( Figure 2 ; and  S3 ). For example, at  k  = 100, our method achieves a balanced accuracy of 62.7 ± 0.8, substantially outperforming both the supervised baseline (55.7 ± 0.6) and the multi-hot pretraining approach (57.0 ± 1.1). This advantage persists across larger sample sizes, where MARBLE-LLM continues to outperform alternatives in the out-of-distribution setting. The gains of MARBLE-LLM compared to the multi-hot and summarization approaches across all evaluation settings demonstrate the benefits of using embeddings and of learning to aggregate biomarker embeddings dynamically, respectively. Strong performance on in-distribution biomarkers is also important to consider, as it demonstrates that strong out-of-distribution generalization does not come at a cost of in-distribution performance. MARBLE-LLM also almost always has the best in-distribution performance as well. The only setting where another approach has better balanced accuracy is for the supervised model when  k  = 100 and on in-distribution biomarkers (67.4 ± 0.4 versus 66.6 ± 0.3 for supervised and MARBLE-LLM, respectively). However, because of the large gains of MARBLE-LLM on out-of-distribution biomarkers, the overall balanced accuracy of MARBLE-LLM is still higher.  Figure 2   Performance comparison of multimodal pretraining across generalization setups and data regimes  Balanced accuracy (BA) of in-distribution and out-of-distribution biomarker prediction at three data regimes ( k  = 100, 1,000, 10,000).  (A) Results for pretraining scenario 1, using v.3, v.5, and v.6 panels.  (B) Results for pretraining scenario 2 using v.3 and v.5 panels.                         Language embeddings demonstrate strong generalization performance  Detailed sequence information is only available for patients measured with the v.3 and v.5 MSK-IMPACT panels ( Table S1 ). Therefore, in a second experiment, we focus on the relative value of the different biomarker representations.  Figure 2  ( Tables S2  and  S3 ) presents the results of the three pretraining settings. For all representations, MARBLE improves out-of-distribution performance compared to the supervised approach, particularly in the low data regime. We observe that MARBLE-LLM pretraining provides stronger out-of-distribution generalization than MARBLE-PLM across all data regimes. For example, in the low-data regime at  k  = 100, LLM-based embeddings achieve a balanced accuracy (BA) of 62.7 ± 0.5, compared to 61.3 ± 0.1 with PLM-based embeddings.  When combining both PLM and LLM embeddings, MARBLE achieves consistently strong performance, often matching or surpassing the best individual approach. For example, at  k  = 10,000, the combined model achieves a performance of 68.6 ± 0.2, the highest overall and comparable to MARBLE-LLM, trained with all three previous panel versions, despite less pretraining data. These findings suggest that LLM embeddings are particularly effective for enhancing generalizability, while their integration with PLM embeddings yields complementary benefits that improve performance across both in- and out-of-distribution scenarios.  Comparison across the two panels in  Figure 2  ( Table S2 ) for MARBLE-LLM allows us to consider the impact of the size of the pretraining dataset. Generally, we observe a slight boost in performance with the larger pretraining dataset when considering overall balanced accuracy; however, it is small or even zero for out-of-distribution biomarkers. For example, at  k  = 100 in the out-of-distribution setup, LLM-based pretraining achieves 62.7 ± 0.8 on the full dataset and 62.7 ± 0.5 on the restricted subset. This observation highlights the robustness of LLM-based embeddings and suggests that the advantage in low-data regime fine-tuning can be realized even with only modest amounts of pretraining data. At the same time, using the full dataset provides a slight performance boost at larger  k  (e.g., 69.3 ± 0.2 versus 68.2 ± 0.2 at  k  = 10,000), indicating that LLM-based pretraining can still benefit from a larger pretraining cohort.    Pretraining results in improvements for many biomarkers  While the aforementioned results show the value of MARBLE at the panel level, we also wanted to understand how these improvements are distributed among the different genomic biomarkers. To do so, we conducted a paired one-sided  t  test on a per-biomarker basis ( Table 1 ). For each biomarker, balanced accuracy across five independent draws of  k  is compared between the corresponding pair of models. Overall, these results suggest that MARBLE and its variants improve performance for many out-of-distribution biomarkers with a minimal number of biomarkers exhibiting a degradation of performance. For instance, at  k  = 100, 47.2% of out-of-distribution biomarkers demonstrated significantly higher balanced accuracy with MARBLE ( p  < 0.05), while only 1.9% of biomarkers showed significantly lower performance compared to the supervised baseline. The remaining out-of-distribution biomarkers exhibited no significant difference between the models. Meanwhile, the in-distribution biomarkers had a comparable number of increasing and decreasing, resulting in an average performance that is approximately equal to the supervised baseline. Across larger fine-tuning sets ( k  = 1,000 and  k  = 10,000), the proportion of biomarkers with significantly higher performance for the MARBLE and its variants decreased, reflecting smaller gains as more labeled data became available. However, even when  k  = 10,000, MARBLE resulted in a net improvement for 24% of in-distribution biomarkers and 28% of out-of-distribution biomarkers. This statistical analysis confirms that multimodal pretraining yields the largest improvements when labeled data are scarce. Comparison between MARBLE-LLM, MARBLE-PLM, and MARBLE revealed complementary benefits, with each contributing significant gains for different subsets of biomarkers ( Table 1 ). To further characterize per-biomarker performance, we visualize the change in balanced accuracy ( Figure 3 ) and its distribution as a function of baseline performance ( Figure S3 ). The former shows the clear advantage of MARBLE and its variants: there are no settings where average balanced accuracy decreases. And although we do observe some in-distribution biomarkers decrease in balanced accuracy, they are offset by an approximately equal number of increasing biomarkers yielding no major change in performance overall. This matches our expectations, as the amount of labeled data for in-distribution biomarkers is large and therefore the effect of pretraining is more minimal. Plotting the change in performance as a function of baseline accuracy ( Figure S3 ) allows us to note that most biomarkers have predictive performance better than random and that MARBLE is able to improve performance across the range of baseline values.
