From January 2021 to December 2024, we collected surgically resected primary breast cancer tissues from MBC and FBC patients treated in hospitals across China for single-cell sequencing (10x Genomics), SeekSpace spatial transcriptome sequencing, and Visium HD spatial transcriptome sequencing, totaling 28 cases. Paraffin-embedded tissue samples from 2008 to 2019 were collected for mIHC staining and Xenium In Situ analysis. 10x Chromium scRNA-seq: Tissue processing, library preparation, and sequencing Fresh surgical tissues were transported on ice in sterile dishes containing 10 ml of 1× Dulbecco’s phosphate-buffered saline (DPBS; Thermo Fisher Scientific, catalog no. 14190144) to remove residual storage solution. Tissues were minced on ice and dissociated at 37°C for ∼40 min at 50 rpm in 0.25% trypsin (Thermo Fisher Scientific, catalog no. 25200-072) and deoxyribonuclease I (10 μg/ml; Sigma-Aldrich, catalog no. 11284932001) prepared in phosphate-buffered saline with 5% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Thermo Fisher Scientific, catalog no. SV30087.02). Cell suspensions were collected every 20 min, filtered through 40-μm strainers, subjected to RBC lysis (Thermo Fisher Scientific, catalog no. 00-4333-57), and washed with 1× DPBS containing 2% FBS. Cell viability was assessed by 0.4% Trypan blue staining on a Countess II Automated Cell Counter (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Single cells were loaded onto a Chromium Controller to generate Gel Bead-in-Emulsions. Following lysis, poly(A) and RNA hybridized to barcoded gel beads. Reverse transcription appended cell barcodes and unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) to cDNA, followed by second-strand synthesis, adaptor ligation, and amplification. Libraries were prepared according to the manufacturer’s protocol (10x Genomics, CG000206 Rev. D), quality checked using a Bioanalyzer High Sensitivity DNA kit (Agilent) and Qubit High Sensitivity DNA assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 using paired-end chemistry (2 × 150). 10x Genomics Visium HD FFPE spatial transcriptomics: Library preparation and sequencing Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) samples passing RNA QC (DV200 > 30%) were sectioned at 5 μm onto Visium Gene Expression slides (10x Genomics), baked at 42°C for 3 hours, and dried overnight. Slides were deparaffinized at 60°C, immersed in xylene, rehydrated through an ethanol gradient, and H&E stained (Mayer’s hematoxylin; Dako bluing reagent; alcoholic eosin). After whole-slide imaging, probe hybridization, probe release, and library construction were performed using the Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Reagent Kit per User Guide CG000685 (Human, 6.5 mm). Libraries were sequenced in paired-end 150–base pair mode on Illumina platforms. SeekSpace single-cell spatial transcriptomics: Library preparation and sequencing Fresh-frozen tissues were cryosectioned at 10 to 20 μm on a cryostat (Leica, −20°C). Regions of interest were placed onto SeekSpace Chips without folds and briefly warmed to ensure adhesion. Single-nucleus suspensions with spatial barcodes were prepared using the SeekSpace Single Cell Spatial Transcriptome-seq Kit (K02501-08). Nuclei were counted with AO/PI on a Countstar Rigel S2. Nuclei were divided into eight polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tubes for reverse transcription (600 to 30,000 nuclei per tube) using distinct barcoded primers with 15 annealing cycles (8°C → 42°C). After washing, nuclei were pooled and mixed with ligation reagents and then loaded with barcoded hydrogel beads and partitioning oil into SeekOne DD Chip S3. Emulsion droplets were generated on the SeekOne Digital Droplet System and incubated for 60 min at 20°C followed by 10 min at 65°C to obtain barcoded cDNA and spatial barcodes. Droplets were decrosslinked, and a second reverse transcription and PCR preamplification were performed. The preamplified product was used to construct both spatial barcode and cDNA libraries with sample indexing. Libraries were purified with VAHTS DNA Clean Beads (Vazyme N411-01), QC-checked by Qubit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Q33226 ), and Bio-Fragment Analyzer (Bioptic Qsep400) and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq X Plus (PE150). 10x Genomics Xenium In Situ transcriptomics: Assay and imaging FFPE sections (5 μm) were processed following 10x Genomics User Guides CG000578 and CG000580 . Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue and Pathways Assay (PN-1000671) was performed according to CG000760 : Sections were hybridized with probe sets at 50°C for 16 to 24 hours, washed, ligated, and amplified. Cell segmentation staining used the Xenium Cell Segmentation Staining Reagents (PN-1000661). After autofluorescence quenching and 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) staining, sections were imaged and decoded on a Xenium Analyzer (PN-1000481). Postrun H&E staining followed CG000613 . Multiplex immunohistochemistry mIHC was performed on 4-μm-thick FFPE whole-tissue sections using sequential primary-antibody staining paired with the TSA 7-color kit (abs50037, Absinbio, Shanghai), followed by DAPI staining. For example, deparaffinized slides were incubated with anti-panCK antibody (ab7753, Abcam), for 30 min and then treated with anti-rabbit/mouse horseradish peroxidase–conjugated secondary antibody (abs50015-02, Absinbio, Shanghai) for 10 min. Labeling was then developed for 10 min using TSA 520 according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Slides were washed in TBST buffer and then transferred to preheated citrate solution (90°C) before being heat treated using a microwave set at 20% of maximum power for 15 min. Slides were cooled in the same solution to room temperature. Between all steps, the slides were washed with tris buffer. The same process was repeated for the following antibodies/fluorescent dyes, in order: anti-GRIA2 (ZENBIO, R22839 ; 1:100; TSA 620), anti-panCK (Abcam, ab7753; 1:200; TSA 780), anti-NEGR1 (ZENBIO, 163125; 1:100; TSA 570), anti-APOE (Proteintech, 66830-1; 1:100; TSA 480), anti-GFRA1 (Affbiotech, DF7309; 1:250; TSA 690), and anti-CD163 (Abcam, ab182422; 1:100; TSA 520). Each slide was then treated with two drops of DAPI (abs47047616, Absinbio, Shanghai), washed in distilled water, and manually coverslipped. Slides were air dried and imaged with Pannoramic MIDI II (3DHISTECH). Images were analyzed using Indica Halo software. scRNA-seq data preprocessing The raw data were analyzed using the Cell Ranger pipeline (version 7.1.0), with gene-count data generated using the default and recommended parameters. Align the FASTQ output obtained from sequencing data with the GRCh38 reference genome using the STAR ( 59 ) algorithm. We used Seurat (version 5.0.1) R package to do all subsequent analyses. To eliminate the influence of low-quality cells such as empty droplets and multiplets, cells with expressed genes <200 or >6000 were excluded. The percentage of UMIs mapped to mitochondria was set to less than 25%. We use in Seurat:: NormalizeData, Seurat:: FindVariableFeatures and Seurat:: ScaleData functions to normalize all data. Seurat:: IntegrateLayers function was used to remove technical variability (method = RPCAIntegration). The top 50 principal components (PCs) were calculated using the Seurat::RunUMAP function. A UMAP dimensional reduction was performed on the scaled matrix using the top 50 PC analysis components to obtain a two-dimensional representation. Spatial data processing For 10x Visium HD spatial transcriptomics data, nuclei were segmented on maximum projection DAPI-stained images using a fine-tuned Cellpose model. Baysor was used to predict cell boundary segmentation based on transcript identity and location, using prior Cellpose nuclear segmentation for 10x Visium HD. The prior-segmentation-confidence parameter was set to 0.95, with min-molecules-per-cell set to the median nuclear transcript count. Baysor segmentations lacking nuclei were filtered out, whereas those containing multiple nuclei were split by assigning transcripts to the nearest nuclear centroid within segmentation boundaries. Cell boundaries were visualized as polygons using the alphashape Python package. Before downstream processing, cells with nuclear transcript count n  < 8, total transcript count n  < 20, or total transcript count n  > 800 were filtered out. Cell cluster and annotation We conducted an initial clustering analysis on the integrated data using Seurat::FindNeighbors and Seurat::FindClusters (resolution of 0.8). The cell clusters obtained from the unsupervised clustering were manually annotated on the basis of well-known marker genes. These marker genes include T cells (CD3D, CD3E, and CD3G), B cells (CD19, CD79A, and CD79B), plasma cells (IGHM, CD38, and PRDM1), mast cells (MS4A2, TPSB2, and TPSAB1), myeloid cells (CD68, LYZ, CD14, FCGR3A, S100A8, and S100A9), endothelial cells (ENG, KDR, and PECAM1), fibroblasts (COL1A1, COL1A2, FN1, and DCN), and epithelial cells (EPCAM, KRT8, KRT18, KRT19, and MUC1). Visualization was performed using the Seurat::DotPlot function, and cell identities were annotated on the basis of the expression levels and proportions of marker genes within the clusters. Next, we performed a second round of clustering to further characterize the subtypes of major cell types within the tumor microenvironment. To mitigate potential data heterogeneity caused by cell types, cell numbers, or intersample variability, we first filtered out features with an expression proportion below 50 within the cell type in the second round of clustering and used the Harmony method for batch correction. In the second clustering, we used 50 PCs for dimensionality reduction and unsupervised clustering (resolution of 1). To enhance annotation accuracy, we used an automated large language model (LLM)–based consensus annotation approach. We first identified DEGs for each cluster using Seurat::FindAllMarkers with parameters: only.pos = TRUE, min.pct = 0.25, and logfc.threshold = 0.5. The DEGs were then processed through an interactive consensus annotation system that leveraged multiple AI models (Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Qwen-Max, and GPT-4o) to provide tissue-specific cell-type annotations for MBC. The system analyzed the top 15 marker genes per cluster across a maximum of five discussion rounds with a controversy threshold of 0.8 for consensus determination. Because mLLMCelltype only broadly classified macrophages as M1 and M2 subtypes, we performed additional manual annotation of macrophage subpopulations based on highly expressed genes specific to each macrophage cluster. Spatial deconvolution (RCTD) According to the scRNA-seq dataset, spacexr (version 2.2.0) was applied to infer the cell-type composition of each bin. Specifically, the default parameters were used in the creat.RCTD function, except for minimum number of cell of >1 for each cell types and minimum of UMI counts of >1 per pixel, and mode parameter was set to “doublet” in the run.RCTD function. Cell-cell communication analysis Cell-cell communication analysis was conducted with the scRNA-seq data by using the CellChat software ( 60 ) (version 2.1.2). Specifically, only receptors and ligands expressed in >1% of cells were further evaluated, while a cell-cell communication was considered nonexistent if the ligand or the receptor was unmeasurable. Using org.Hs.eg.db annotation package (version 3.17.0). GSEA: We used GseaVis::gseaNb (version 0.0.8) R package ( https://github.com/junjunlab/ ). For input, we used preranked gene lists by avg_log 2 FC calculated from Seurat::FindAllMarkers. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes ( 62 ): We used ClusterGVis::enrichCluster (version 0.1.0) R package. Using org.Hs.eg.db annotation package (version 3.17.0): The ssGSEA analysis was conducted using the R singleseqgset package (version 0.1.2.9000). We used the human hallmark gene sets from the msigdbr package ( 63 ) (version 7.5.1) as the gene sets of interest for enrichment analysis. Differences were considered statistically significant at P  < 0.05. Developmental trajectory We inferred the developmental trajectory of human tumor cells using CytoTRACE (version 0.3.3) and Monocle (version 2.12). Tumor cells from male and female scRNA-seq samples were pooled. To reduce computational burden while preserving the original cell-subtype composition, cells were stratified by the annotated cell subtype and proportionally downsampled to ∼50,000 cells. The number of cells sampled from each subtype was calculated according to its proportion in the pooled tumor cell dataset. CytoTRACE is based on the concept of transcriptional diversity (i.e., the number of genes expressed in cells decreases during differentiation). A log 2 -normalized expression matrix was used. For Monocle 2, we constructed a CellDataSet object from the cluster-annotated Seurat object using the newCellDataSet function. We derived DEGs from each cluster using the DifferentialGeneTest function and ordered cells in pseudotime using genes with q  < 1 × 10 −5 . Dimensionality reduction was performed using the DDRTree algorithm, followed by ordering cells along the trajectory. CytoTRACE2 scores were calculated from the same downsampled tumor cell object using raw counts. The CytoTRACE2-relative score was used as an inferred measure of developmental potential within the analyzed tumor cell population, with lower scores indicating lower inferred developmental potential. CytoTRACE2-relative scores were then projected onto the Monocle trajectory. CNV inference To identify malignant and nonmalignant cells, we used two complementary methods to confidently distinguish between malignant and nonmalignant cells in each sample. To more accurately validate the identified cancer cells, we also assessed CNV levels using the R package inferCNV, with immune cells (T cells, B cells, macrophages, and mast cells) and stromal cells (fibroblasts and endothelial cells) as control groups and epithelial cells as the test group. To quantify transcriptome-inferred CNV burden, we calculated an inferCNV score for each malignant cell from the inferCNV output matrix. The score was defined as the squared sum of inferCNV values across chromosomal segments. For each sample and malignant cell group, the median inferCNV score was calculated and used for sample-level comparison. P values were calculated using two-sided t tests. TCGA data and survival analysis We used the R package easyTCGA ( 64 ) (version 0.0.4.200.0) to download the TCGA pan-cancer gene expression matrix and sample clinical information. Kaplan-Meier survival curves were plotted using ggsurvplot (version 0.4.9) function in the R package Survminer (version 0.4.9). Functional module scoring Feature scoring in scRNA-seq, SeekSpace spatial transcriptomics, and Visium HD spatial transcriptomics was calculated using the AddModuleScore function in Seurat, with the following gene sets: neurotrophic meta module (GRIA2, NEGR1, GFRA1,ROBO1,ROBO2, SHANK2, and CHGB), angiogenesis gene set (msigdb, TUMOR_ANGIOGENESIS), fatty acid gene set (msigdb, FATTY_ACID_METABOLISM), and glutamate signal gene set (msigdb, GLUTAMATE_RECEPTOR_ACTIVITY). Regulon network The regulon network was explored using the R package SCENIC (version 1.1.3), which analyzed the coexpression of transcriptional factors and their putative target genes. We built and scored gene regulatory network using the default parameters. Raw count matrix was used to build coexpression network using the runCorrelation, and runGENIE3 functions and active gene networks were identified by AUCell. Regulon activity for each cell was calculated as the average normalized expression of putative target genes. To identify differentially active transcription factors between MSTCs and other cell types, we extracted regulonAUC data from SCENIC results and calculated mean activity scores for each group. Statistical comparison was performed to identify transcription factors with significantly higher activity in MSTCs using fold change and difference thresholds (fold_change > 75th percentile, difference > 75th percentile, and mean activity > 0.005). The CSI was calculated to assess transcriptional regulatory relationships using a custom R function. CSI measures the specificity of connections between regulons based on correlation matrices, where CSI values range from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating more specific connections. We applied a CSI threshold of 0.5 and performed hierarchical clustering using Ward.D2 method to identify regulatory modules. The resulting CSI matrix and module assignments were visualized using ComplexHeatmap with custom color schemes and annotations. NMF analysis To investigate expression programs underlying tumor heterogeneity in malignant cells, we performed NMF analysis using the cNMF Python package. Patients with at least 150 malignant tumor cells were selected for analysis. For each tumor, UMI matrices were converted to counts per million by normalizing each gene by the total UMI count per cell, followed by log 2 transformation. Data were then mean centered by subtracting the average expression of each gene across all cells. We filtered genes expressed in at least 2% of cells, set all negative values to zero, and performed NMF analysis with factor numbers ( K ) ranging from 5 to 12, using 1000 iterations and a threshold of 0.4. Expression programs were initially defined as the top 150 genes per K (ranked by NMF scores). Factors appearing in fewer than 75 cells were excluded. Robust NMF programs were hierarchically clustered based on Jaccard similarity using Euclidean (1 − Jaccard similarity) distance as the distance metric. MPs were defined on the basis of representative genes and their enriched biological functions. Spatial distance analysis for neurotrophic signal distribution To quantify the spatial relationship between cells and neurotrophic signal centers, we developed a distance-based analysis approach. First, pathway scores for neurotrophic, angiogenesis, glycolysis, and fatty acid metabolism were calculated, and outliers were capped at the 95th percentile to reduce the influence of extreme values. Spatial coordinates from the tissue sections were extracted and normalized to a range of 0 to 1 using min-max normalization to standardize measurements across different tissue dimensions. Cell spatial distribution was analyzed using K -means clustering to identify density centers representing regions of high cell concentration. The optimal number of clusters was determined using the elbow method, evaluating within-cluster sum of squares for k values ranging from 1 to 10. Based on this analysis, k  = 3 was selected as the optimal cluster number. K -means clustering was performed with 25 random initializations to ensure robust cluster identification. For each cell i , the minimum Euclidean distance to the K centers d i was computed and normalized as d i ′ = d i − d min d max − d min , d i ′ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] Cells were sorted by d i ′ and binned in groups of 100 cells; within each bin, medians of d i ′ and pathway scores were computed. Pearson correlations quantified associations between spatial proximity and pathway activity. Pearson correlation coefficients were computed to assess the relationship between spatial proximity to cancer cell centers and various pathway activities, including neurotrophic, angiogenesis, glycolysis, and fatty acid metabolism scores. Spatial proximity and gene expression gradient analysis To investigate the spatial relationship between different cell types and MSTCs, we calculated the distance from each cell to its nearest reference cells. For each non-MSTC, we computed the median distance to the top- k nearest MSTCs ( k  = 3) using Euclidean distance in the spatial coordinate system. The analysis was performed using custom Python functions that used scipy.spatial.distance.cdist for efficient distance matrix calculation. We performed gene expression gradient analysis to identify genes that showed correlation with spatial distance to MSTCs. Using a modified scVelo heatmap approach, we calculated Pearson correlation coefficients between each gene’s expression and the distance to MSTCs across all immune or stromal cells. Genes were filtered to include only those expressed in more than 5% of cells. The heatmap visualization used convolution smoothing with user-defined bins ( n _bins = 10) to reveal expression trends along the spatial gradient. Statistics Two-sided tests were used. Nonparametric comparisons used Wilcoxon rank sum unless stated. Correlations used Pearson unless normality failed, in which case Spearman was reported. Multiple testing was adjusted by Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate. Exact tests, n , and effect sizes appear in the figure legends or the supplementary tables. KLRB1 (CD161) as a context-dependent prognostic marker in breast cancer: An exploratory analysis of CD4+ memory T cell infiltration: a retrospective multi-cohort study. The prognostic value of KLRB1 (CD161) in breast cancer is debated, and whether CD4+ memory T cell abundance modulates it is unclear. In this retrospective multi-cohort study we integrated The Cancer Genome Atlas Breast Invasive Carcinoma (n = 1088) and Molecular Taxonomy of Breast Cancer International Consortium (METABRIC) (n = 1980) with investigator-generated single-cell RNA-sequencing from 3 patients, public single-cell RNA-sequencing validation (GSE176078), Xenium spatial transcriptomics (19 samples) and multiplex immunofluorescence of a paired primary tumor and metastatic lymph node. Cox regression tested whether xCell-estimated CD4+ memory T cell abundance modifies the KLRB1-overall survival association. Higher KLRB1 expression was associated with favorable overall survival (TCGA hazard ratio [HR] = 0.93, P = .001; METABRIC HR = 0.82, P < .001). The CD4+ memory T cell interaction was significant under median dichotomization (TCGA P = .043; METABRIC P = .014) and after adjustment for age and tumor stage in both cohorts (TCGA P = .033; METABRIC P = .026; pooled HR 1.20, P = .0025); full adjustment for grade and subtype preserved significance in METABRIC (P = .012) but not in TCGA (P = .205). Across 3 single-cell cases KLRB1 was enriched in CD4+ memory T cells; functional profiling identified a cytotoxicity-effector T/NK signature, and TIGIT+ KLRB1+ cells showed no clear evidence of a classical exhaustion transcriptional signature. In Xenium, KLRB1+ cells proximal to CD4+ memory T cells co-upregulated TIGIT (pooled OR = 2.98) and PRF1 (OR = 1.99); multiplex immunofluorescence showed no spatial mutual exclusion. CD4+ memory T cell abundance is a hypothesis-generating candidate context modifier of KLRB1-mediated prognosis. This finding requires external validation in a subtype-stratified cohort, and the present data do not support clinical use. 1. Introduction  Breast cancer is the most common malignancy among women worldwide, with approximately 2.3 million new cases and 670,000 deaths reported in 2022. [ 1 ]  Despite advances in multimodal therapy, a substantial proportion of patients develop recurrence and distant metastasis. The integration of immunotherapy, primarily PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors combined with chemotherapy, has improved outcomes for triple-negative breast cancer, but objective response rates remain limited to 20% to 30% and durable benefit is restricted to a subset of patients. [ 2 , 3 ]  This therapeutic gap underscores the urgent need for biomarkers that capture the functional state of the tumor immune microenvironment and enable more precise patient stratification.  Within the tumor immune microenvironment, natural killer (NK) cells and T lymphocytes constitute the principal effector populations mediating antitumor immunity. [ 4 ]  Among  CD4 + subsets, memory T cells confer durable immunosurveillance, and their intratumoral abundance has been associated with favorable prognosis across multiple cancer types. [ 5 , 6 ]  The balance between effector and exhausted T cell states, governed by transcriptional programs and differentiation trajectories, [ 7 , 8 ]  is increasingly recognized as a critical determinant of clinical outcome. Regulatory T cells (Tregs), characterized by  FOXP3  expression, accumulate within tumors and suppress effector cell functions through secretion of IL-10 and TGF-β, consumption of IL-2, and direct contact-mediated inhibition via immune checkpoint receptors including  CTLA-4 ,  LAG-3 , and  TIGIT . [ 9 ]    KLRB1  encodes cluster of differentiation 161 (encoded by  KLRB1 ) ( CD161 ), a type II transmembrane C-type lectin-like receptor belonging to the NK cell receptor complex on chromosome 12p13. [ 10 , 11 ] 
 CD161  is expressed on the majority of human NK cells, NKT cells, and subsets of  CD4 + and  CD8+  T cells, including tissue-resident memory populations. [ 12 ]  Upon engagement with its ligand  CLEC2D (LLT1 ),  CD161  can deliver both co-stimulatory and co-inhibitory signals depending on cellular context. The functional complexity of this receptor-ligand axis is reflected in contradictory prognostic associations reported across cancer types. Mathewson et al. [ 13 ]  identified  CD161  to  CLEC2D  as an inhibitory checkpoint in glioma, where  KLRB1  knockout in T cells enhanced antitumor immunity in vivo. In hepatocellular carcinoma, single-cell analysis revealed that  CD161 -high  CD8+  T cells exhibited an innate-like, low-cytotoxicity phenotype associated with early relapse, [ 14 ]  illustrating the context-dependent nature of the  KLRB1 / CD161  signal. Pan-cancer analyses have confirmed that  KLRB1  expression correlates with both favorable and unfavorable prognosis depending on tumor type. [ 15 ]   In breast cancer specifically, multiple studies have reported reduced  KLRB1  expression in tumor versus normal tissue, with low expression independently predicting poor survival and altered immune infiltration patterns. [ 16 – 18 ]  Machine-learning-based immune-related gene models have further established  KLRB1  as a prognostic and immune infiltration biomarker in breast cancer. [ 17 , 18 ]  However, whether the prognostic impact of  KLRB1  in breast cancer is modified by the composition of the surrounding immune microenvironment, particularly the abundance of  CD4 + memory T cells, has not been systematically investigated.  The recent development of spatial omics technologies has opened new avenues for interrogating immune cell organization within intact tissue architecture. Xenium in situ sequencing enables subcellular-resolution detection of hundreds of targeted genes. [ 19 ]  Multiplex immunofluorescence (mIHC) provides complementary protein level spatial information, enabling quantitative analysis of cell-to-cell distances, cellular neighborhoods, and their associations with clinical variables. [ 20 , 21 ]  Single-cell profiling of breast cancer has revealed tissue-resident memory subsets associated with improved prognosis [ 22 ]  and immune ecosystems that predict treatment response, [ 23 – 25 ]  while systematic evaluation of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes supports their prognostic value across breast cancer subtypes. [ 26 – 28 ]   In the present study, we integrated large-scale transcriptomic cohorts (The Cancer Genome Atlas Breast Invasive Carcinoma [TCGA-BRCA] and Molecular Taxonomy of Breast Cancer International Consortium [METABRIC]) with investigator-generated single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) data (three investigator-generated cases: Cases A, B, and C; human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 ( HER2 )-enriched and Luminal B-like subtypes), publicly available scRNA validation, Xenium spatial transcriptomics (19 samples), and mIHC analysis of paired primary and metastatic breast cancer samples to address 3 interconnected questions: whether  CD4 + memory T cell abundance modifies the prognostic value of  KLRB1  in breast cancer; the spatial and single-cell functional states of  KLRB1+  cells; and how  KLRB1 -related immune cell organization differs between primary tumors and metastatic lymph nodes. This is a retrospective, observational, multi-cohort study.    2. Materials and methods   2.1. Study design  The study comprised 5 interconnected analytical layers. First, we performed survival analyses in the TCGA-BRCA and METABRIC cohorts to test whether  CD4 + memory T cell abundance modifies the association between  KLRB1  expression and overall survival (OS). Second, we analyzed investigator-generated scRNA-seq data from 3 breast cancer patients (Cases A, B, and C; clinicopathologic details in Methods 2.4). Third, we validated the single-cell findings in a publicly available scRNA dataset ( GSE176078 ). Fourth, we performed a cross-sample meta-analysis of 19 breast cancer samples profiled by Xenium spatial transcriptomics ( GSE311609 ). Fifth, we performed mIHC on a paired primary tumor and metastatic lymph node from 1 breast cancer patient to characterize the spatial organization of  KLRB1+ ,  FOXP3 +,  GZMB +, and CD107A + cells.    2.2. TCGA-BRCA cohort  TCGA-BRCA transcriptomic data (TPM-normalized RNA-seq) and corresponding clinical annotations were downloaded from the NCI Genomic Data Commons (GDC) Data Portal ( https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov ). Gene identifiers were converted from Entrez ID to gene symbol using clusterProfiler::bitr. Immune cell abundance was estimated using the xCell algorithm [ 29 ]  with the rnaseq = TRUE parameter, generating enrichment scores for 64 immune and stromal cell types plus 3 composite scores (ImmuneScore, StromaScore and MicroenvironmentScore), i.e. 67 features in total. OS was derived from the GDC clinical record: patients recorded as deceased were assigned an event with time equal to demographic.days_to_death; all other patients were assigned a censored observation with time equal to the longest available follow-up among all recorded diagnosis records (diagnoses.N.days_to_last_follow_up). Times were converted from days to months (÷30.4375). The analysis set was defined identically for every survival analysis reported in this manuscript (Table  1  and  Supplementary Table S1 , Supplemental Digital Content 1) as: primary tumor samples with RNA-seq expression data, successful xCell deconvolution, derivable complete OS, and non-missing  KLRB1  expression and  CD4 + memory T cell score. The resulting participant flow was: 1097 expression samples, 1096 with successful xCell deconvolution, 1096 with derivable complete OS, 1089 primary tumor samples (7 metastatic samples excluded), yielding a final analysis set of 1088 patients (544  CD4 + memory T cell low, 544 high; 150 deaths). The nomogram complete-covariate subset comprised 1073 patients (150 deaths). The same definition applied to METABRIC yielded 1980 patients (990 low, 990 high; 1143 deaths). The interaction  P  value was obtained from the  KLRB1  × group term of a Cox model. The age-adjusted value adds age at diagnosis as a covariate; the age- and stage-adjusted value additionally includes tumor stage; the fully adjusted METABRIC value further includes histological grade and molecular subtype. After adjustment for tumor stage the interaction was statistically significant in both cohorts (TCGA  P  = .033; METABRIC  P  = .026; fixed-effects meta-analysis HR 1.202, 95% CI 1.067–1.355,  P  = .0025,  I  2  = 0%).       2.3. METABRIC confirmatory cohort  METABRIC microarray expression data and clinical annotations were obtained from cBioPortal ( https://www.cbioportal.org ). Duplicate genes were resolved by retaining the probe with the highest median expression. After filtering for complete survival data, 1980 patients were included. Immune cell abundance was estimated using xCell with the rnaseq = FALSE parameter appropriate for microarray data. Because xCell applied to microarray data may underestimate low-abundance cell types, the METABRIC interaction analyses should be regarded as a confirmation of the TCGA discovery rather than as a fully independent validation.    2.4. Investigator-generated scRNA-seq (three validation cases: cases A, B, and C)  scRNA-seq was performed on tumor samples from 3 breast cancer patients (Cases A, B, and C), with matched peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) samples additionally profiled for Cases A and C. All 3 cases were profiled using the DNBelab C4 platform (MGI/BGI). Clinicopathologically, Case C had an invasive carcinoma of no special type (NST), histologic grade III, with a maximum tumor diameter of approximately 3.0 cm; no definite lymphovascular invasion or perineural invasion was identified. The nipple, skin, base, and surgical margins were free of carcinoma; the right axillary lymph nodes (0/18) showed no metastasis; the interpectoral region showed fibrofatty tissue without tumor involvement. immunohistochemistry (IHC) revealed estrogen receptor (ER) (moderate-strong positive, 80%), progesterone receptor (PR) (strong positive, 90%), AR (moderate-strong positive, 80%),  HER2  (1+, negative), CK14 (negative), P63 (negative),  TRPS1  (positive), P120 (membranous), E-cadherin (membranous), EGFR (negative), P53 (negative, nonsense-mutant pattern), Ki-67 (40%), S-100 (nerve-negative), TOPO-IIα (positive), CKpan (positive), and CD31 (delineating vasculature), consistent with an ER+/PR+,  HER2 -negative, Luminal B-like molecular subtype. Case A had an invasive ductal carcinoma of NST, histologic grade III, tumor size 5.8 × 3.2 × 2.2 cm, with perineural invasion and lymphovascular tumor thrombi; the carcinoma involved the nipple dermis; the right axillary lymph nodes were 6/21 positive for metastasis, and 2 satellite tumor nodules (0.5–0.7 cm) were present. IHC: ER negative, PR negative, AR 2+ (~90%),  HER2  3+, P120 membranous+, E-cadherin+, CK14 negative, P63 negative,  TRPS1 +, EGFR 1+, S–100 nerve+, P53+ (missense-mutant pattern), Ki-67 ~40%;  HER2 -enriched subtype. Case B had an invasive ductal carcinoma of NST, histologic grade II to III; axillary lymph nodes 0/18 and apical lymph nodes 0/2 were negative for metastasis. IHC: ER negative, PR negative, AR 2+ (~80%),  HER2  2 + (FISH-amplified), E-cadherin 2+, P120 membranous+, EGFR 1+, SOX-10 negative, CK14 negative, P53 2+, Ki-67 ~40%;  HER2 -enriched subtype (FISH-confirmed  HER2  amplification). From Case C, 3 libraries were generated. The total cell count of each library was verified from the primary sequencing data: a  CD4 5-unsorted tumor library (14,221 cells), a  CD4 5-sorted ( CD4 5+-enriched) tumor-infiltrating library from the primary tumor (referred to as the “tumor  CD4 5” library; 11,019 cells) and a matched PBMC library (referred to as the “PBMC” library; 5311 cells), enabling joint analysis of tumor-resident and circulating immune populations. The lymphoid-compartment analyses reported below aggregate the  CD4 5-sorted tumor and PBMC libraries. After quality control and removal of low-quality cells, the  CD4 5-sorted tumor and PBMC libraries comprised 16,330 cells, of which 4567 lymphoid cells (3822 T cells and 745 NK cells) were retained for the lymphoid-compartment analyses. Cell-type annotation was performed using canonical lineage markers: CD3E/CD3D for T cells; CD8A/CD8B for  CD8+  T cells;  CD4  for  CD4 + T cells;  FOXP3 /IL2RA/CTLA4 for Tregs; interleukin 7 receptor (IL7R) for memory T cells; NKG7/GNLY/KLRF1 for NK cells.  CD4 + memory T cells were defined as T cells that were  CD4 -positive, negative for CD8A/CD8B, negative for the Treg markers  FOXP3 /IL2RA/CTLA4, and positive for IL7R; this definition was applied identically to all 3 cases.  KLRB1 + cells were defined as cells with detectable  KLRB1  expression (counts > 0). Within  KLRB1 + lymphoid cells,  TIGIT -positive and  TIGIT -negative subsets were defined for stratified analysis. Per-gene odds ratios (ORs) for  KLRB1 + versus  KLRB1 − cells and for  TIGIT + versus  TIGIT − subsets were computed using Fisher exact test; depth-adjusted (sequencing depth) ORs were estimated using a logistic regression model adjusting for log10(total unique molecular identifier [UMIs]) per cell, identical to the main analyses described above. For Cases A and B, the same library preparation and quality control pipelines were applied. Data from the 3 cases were analyzed separately (per-case differential expression and OR estimation) and then summarized for cross-case concordance; no pooled integration of raw counts across cases was performed. Paired  CD4 5-sorted and  CD4 5-unsorted tumor libraries were generated for each of the 3 cases; matched PBMC libraries were additionally generated for Cases A and C, whereas Case B had no matched PBMC library. Across the 3 cases this yielded 8 libraries in total (three  CD4 5-sorted, 3  CD4 5-unsorted, and 2 PBMC libraries). For Cases A and B the paired tumor libraries were analyzed together, as the primary analysis focused on intratumoral T cell states.    2.5. Public scRNA validation ( GSE176078 )  The publicly available breast cancer scRNA-seq dataset  GSE176078  (10x Genomics) was used as an independent validation cohort. [ 30 ] 
 KLRB1 + cell definition and functional gene analysis followed the same principles as for the investigator-generated data; cell-type annotation was taken from the annotation supplied with  GSE176078 .    2.6. Xenium spatial transcriptomics  Nineteen breast cancer samples profiled by Xenium In Situ gene expression (10x Genomics) were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (accession  GSE311609 ). [ 19 , 31 , 32 ]  For each sample, gene expression counts and spatial coordinates were read using scanpy.  KLRB1 + cells were defined as cells with detectable  KLRB1  expression.  CD4 + memory T cells were defined as cells simultaneously positive for  CD4 , CD3E, and IL7R. Because some effector memory T cells may express low levels of IL7R, this definition may preferentially capture central memory  CD4  + T cells. A  KLRB1  + cell that is itself a  CD4  + memory T cell has a distance of zero to the nearest  CD4  + memory T cell and would therefore be classified as proximal irrespective of its spatial context; in the primary analysis the distance from each  KLRB1  + cell to the nearest  CD4  + memory T cell was therefore computed with the cell itself excluded, using the second-nearest  CD4  + memory T cell for cells that were themselves  CD4  + memory T cells. The complete 19-sample analysis performed with the cell included is reported as a sensitivity analysis.  KLRB1  + cells within 30 µm were classified as proximal; those beyond 50 µm were classified as distal. After random downsampling of the distal group to at most the proximal cell count (all distal cells are used when they are fewer than the proximal cells), positivity rates of  TIGIT , PRF1, FCGR3A, LAG3, and HAVCR2 were compared between proximal and distal  KLRB1  + cells using Fisher exact test. Cross-sample meta-analysis was performed using a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model on log(OR) effect sizes, pooled across samples in which the gene was detectable; the pooled effect sizes reported in the text are back-transformed to ORs for interpretability.    2.7. mIHC and spatial analysis  Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue blocks of a primary breast tumor and its paired metastatic axillary lymph node were obtained from 1 female patient who underwent surgical resection at the Affiliated Taizhou People’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University. Four-marker Opal multiplex fluorescence IHC was performed using the following primary antibodies: anti- KLRB1  (clone HP-3G10, 1:200), anti- FOXP3  (clone 236A/E7, 1:100), anti- GZMB  (clone GB11, 1:500), and anti-CD107A (clone H4A3, 1:200). DAPI was used for nuclear counterstaining. Whole-slide scanning was performed on a Vectra Polaris automated quantitative pathology imaging system at 20 × magnification. Cell detection and classification were performed in QuPath, and the centroid coordinates of each classified cell were exported. For each pairwise combination, the observed statistic was the mean nearest-neighbor Euclidean distance from each source cell to the nearest target cell. Two null models that preserve the marginal distribution of the target cells were used, each with 1000 permutations: (i) complete spatial randomness (CSR), in which the target cells were placed uniformly at random within the convex hull of all detected cells; and (ii) a toroidal-shift, in which the target point pattern was translated by a random vector with wrap-around, thereby preserving the internal clustering of the target cells while breaking any source–target association. A two-sided permutation  P  value was computed as twice the smaller tail proportion. The effect size was defined as the ratio of the observed mean distance to the mean of the null distribution, where 1.0 denotes no spatial association, values > 1 mutual exclusion, and values < 1 co-localization.    2.8. Statistical analysis  All statistical analyses were performed in R version 4.5.3 and Python (scanpy 1.12.4). Continuous variables are presented as median with range or mean with standard deviation. Cox proportional hazards regression results are reported as hazard ratios [HRs] with 95% confidence interval (CIs). To further control for potential confounding, we fitted Cox models with progressive adjustment for clinical covariates (age at diagnosis, tumor stage [early vs late], histological grade [grade 1–2 vs grade 3] and molecular subtype [Prediction Analysis of Microarray 50/Claudin-low]) where available in each cohort; cases with missing covariate values were excluded from the corresponding adjusted model. Fixed-effects meta-analysis of the age- and stage-adjusted interaction across the 2 cohorts was performed on the log HR scale. This study is reported in accordance with the STROBE statement for observational studies. Unit of inference for single-cell analyses: all single-cell comparisons were performed between cells within an individual case; cells from different patients were never pooled into a single test. Results are therefore reported as per-case (i.e. patient-level) estimates, and the evidence for generalisability is the directional concordance of these estimates across the 3 cases. Depth-adjusted ORs were estimated using logistic regression with log10 UMI per cell as a covariate. Between-study heterogeneity in meta-analysis was quantified using the I 2  statistic. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) was applied to control for multiple hypothesis testing where applicable. All hypothesis tests were two-sided. Statistical significance was defined as  P  < .05.    2.9. Data availability TCGA-BRCA and METABRIC data are publicly available from the NCI GDC and cBioPortal, respectively. Xenium data are publicly available from Gene Expression Omnibus under accession number  GSE311609 . The investigator-generated scRNA-seq datasets (Cases A, B and C;  CD4 5-sorted and  CD4 5-unsorted tumor libraries, and matched PBMC libraries where applicable) are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. All custom scripts used for the data analyses reported in the manuscript are provided as Supplementary Code S1–S4; the numerical supplementary tables are provided as  Supplementary Tables S1–S6 , Supplemental Digital Content 1 (each table in its own Word file, with its table title) and, in machine-readable form, as Supplementary Data (one Excel workbook). Purely figure-production and manuscript-assembly utilities are not included.

evidence_text:
Mapping mesenchymal diversity in the human small intestine and organoids. The organization of diverse mesenchymal populations during human small intestinal development is critical for tissue architecture and function yet remains poorly defined. Here, to construct a comprehensive, tissue-scale map of the developing human small intestine at single cell resolution, we leveraged single-cell RNA-sequencing data to build a Xenium spatial transcriptomics gene panel covering the cell diversity of the human small intestine. We defined five subpopulations occupying discrete anatomical locations within the lamina propria and submucosa-the subepithelial cells, lamina propria fibroblasts, submucosal fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells and CXCL13<sup>+</sup> fibroblasts. Our data establish molecular markers to distinguish these populations in both sequencing and imaging data. We leverage this high-resolution atlas to interrogate cell-cell signalling, benchmark pluripotent stem cell-derived human intestinal organoids and to demonstrate how this resource can incorporate relative spatial organization into tissue analysis, with broad implications for modelling development, regeneration and disease. Main  The precise organization of the small intestine, from the crypt–villus axis enabling nutrient absorption to the muscle layers coordinating with the enteric nervous system (ENS) for peristalsis, is essential for function. Cellular heterogeneity in both the adult and developing human intestine has been explored extensively using single-cell approaches to study development, homeostasis and disease  1 – 15  . While tissue-scale features such as villus morphogenesis and cellular composition are well established for intestinal epithelium, musculature and ENS  1 , 6 , 7 , 9 , 14 , 16 – 26  , the mesoderm-derived fibroblast populations (also referred to as mesenchyme and/or stroma) remain poorly defined.  In mice, recent work has redefined historical terms such as ‘fibroblast’, ‘myofibroblast’ and ‘intestinal subepithelial myofibroblast’ based on molecular identity, function or localization  27 – 40  . Subepithelial ‘telocytes’ or ‘subepithelial myofibroblasts’ are characterized by high  Pdgfra  and  Foxl1  expression, alongside two  Pdgfra -low populations:  Cd81  + / Grem1  +  ‘trophocytes’ and  Cd34  + / Pdpn  +  ‘ Pdgfra -low stroma’  27 , 41 – 43  . Distinct regional mesenchymal populations have also been shown to line the developing mouse foregut and pattern the gastrointestinal endoderm  44  , indicating functional roles tied to early spatial localization. Critically, much of this work was conducted in mice and our understanding of fibroblast populations in human development and human organoid development lags considerably  45  . A comprehensive atlas defining the identities and positions of fibroblast subtypes relative to all other cell types has not been established in humans  27  .  Here, we systematically define the molecular and spatiotemporal heterogeneity of the developing human intestine, with an emphasis on the poorly defined fibroblast populations. We integrated publicly available single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets spanning 5–21 weeks post-conception  1 , 5 , 46 , 47   to identify highly enriched marker genes, which informed the design of a 10X Xenium probe set  48 – 52   incorporating established intestinal markers and genes from key signalling and structural pathways. We interrogated a total of seven different developing human intestines spanning 7–22 weeks post-conception and across the length of the intestinal tract (duodenum, jejunum, ileum and colon). In addition, we examine full-thickness adult duodenum, and two different transplanted induced pluripotent stem cell-derived human intestinal organoid models (tHIOs)  53 – 56  .  Xenium imaging produced a cellular-resolution atlas capturing all major cell classes—epithelium, fibroblasts, smooth muscle, endothelium, ENS and immune cells—and their spatial organization. Our data identified smooth muscle cells (SMCs) plus four broad subpopulations occupying discrete anatomical locations: subepithelial cells (SECs)  1 , 7  , lamina propria fibroblasts (LPFs)  45  , submucosal fibroblasts (SMFs)  45   and  CXCL13  +  fibroblasts  7  . Applying this atlas to tHIOs derived using two distinct methods, we found subtle differences between methods, suggesting that both cellular heterogeneity and spatial organization are important measures of tHIO fidelity when compared to the in vivo human intestine  1 , 5 , 46 – 56  .  Together, this work provides a spatially resolved, tissue-scale blueprint of the developing human small intestine, establishing molecular signatures to identify and track fibroblast populations across development. By benchmarking tHIOs against this atlas, we show that both cell-type composition and precise cellular topography are critical metrics for evaluating in vitro tissues. We anticipate that these findings will advance organoid design, disease modelling and therapeutic screening. More broadly, this resource transforms our transcriptomic understanding of the gut into a three-dimensional coordinate framework applicable across developmental biology, tissue engineering and gastroenterology with high precision.    Results   Spatial transcriptomics identifies major cell classes in the developing human intestine  Using our previously published scRNA-seq data  1   (Fig.  1a,b  and Supplementary Tables  1  and  2 ), established marker genes and genes of interest, we designed a custom 292-gene Xenium panel to identify cell types and states in the developing human small intestine  1 , 3 , 7 , 28 , 29   (Fig.  1c,d  and Supplementary Table  3 ;  Methods ).    Fig. 1   Comparison of major cell type class composition between scRNA-seq and Xenium datasets describing the human fetal small intestine.   a – d , UMAP projections summarizing the major cell classes observed in human fetal small intestine as determined by scRNA-seq  1   ( a ) and Xenium spatial transcriptomics ( c ). Stacked bar graphs describing the cell population composition of the human fetal small intestine at various timepoints through development (47–142 DPC) for either the scRNA-seq dataset ( b ) or Xenium dataset ( d ). Sample labels below the graphs in  b  and  d  are coloured to indicate the developmental stage (DPC) each sample falls within. The number of cells included in each sample is indicated below the sample age.  e – g , The 105 DPC human fetal duodenum as a representative Xenium image set example: the DAPI image of the complete Xenium 105 DPC sample ( e ). Scale bar, 1,000 µm. The white box outlines the region depicted in  f  of a digital cell mask depicting the distribution of the major cell classes ( f ) annotated in  c . Scale bar, 500 µm. The white box indicates the region depicted in  g  of examples of cell subtype distribution within each major cell class identified using the Xenium panel visualized with each colour representing distinct subtypes ( g ) (from left to right): epithelium, fibroblast, SMC related, ENS, endothelium and immune subtypes. Scale bar, 100 µm. We analysed  n (scRNA-seq) = 9 biological samples,  n (Xenium) = 7 biological samples across developmental time (Supplementary Table  1 ). Cell populations are colour matched in  f  and  g ; epithelium (gold), fibroblasts (navy), muscularis mucosa (light green), other SMCs (dark green), ENS (yellow), endothelium (cyan) and immune (pink). DAPI staining of cell nuclei is depicted in grey.   Source data                    Major cell classes were identified using well-established markers:  CDH1  (epithelium),  VIM  (mesenchyme),  PECAM1  (endothelium),  PTPRC /CD45 (immune) and  TUBB3  (ENS) (Supplementary Table  4 ). Subclass markers were also included, with a focus on the fibroblast populations identified in the scRNA-seq data  1  . Xenium spatial transcriptomics was performed on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) archival tissue sections spanning 54–142 days post-conception (DPC) across all intestinal regions  16   (Fig.  1e , duodenum, jejunum, ileum, colon, and Extended Data Fig.  1a ), broadly matching the scRNA-seq stages (Supplementary Table  1 ). In total, seven biological specimens were analysed. The analysis focused on the small intestine (475,698 cells; Fig.  1d ;  Methods ); distal ileum (when included in the sample imaging) and colon were excluded due to substantial transcriptomic differences compared to the small intestine  40  .    Extended Data Fig. 1   Xenium spatial transcriptomics workflow.   a ) Workflow overview for Xenium gene expression assay. Representative Xenium images of the duodenum showing  b ) H&E,  c ) segmentation staining (PN-1000661),  d ) nuclear and cellular segmentation determined digitally using Xenium Explorer v2.0.0+ and the segmentation kit showed in  c , and  e ) example Xenium cell clustering with assigned K equal to UMAP identified and confirmed populations. Scale bars for images in  column 1 ) 50 µm and  columns 2-3)  100 µm. Colored bars indicate the developmental age group of each sample (DPC). We analyzed n(fetal) = 4 and n(tHIO) = 2 using the segmentation kit. We analyzed n(fetal) = 3 and n(adult) = 1 without the segmentation kit. Workflow in  a  created in BioRender; Spencer, J.  https://biorender.com/rkmlxdr  (2026).                   Samples were processed in two batches. The second batch included the Xenium In Situ Multimodal Cell Segmentation kit ( n  = 4; Extended Data Fig.  1b–e ), which was not available for our first batch ( n  = 3; 57, 80 and 142 DPC). This kit combined probes and antibodies targeting cell borders and interiors to improve digital cell body segmentation (Extended Data Fig.  1c ). Xenium Ranger and Xenium Explorer (10X Genomics, v2.0.0 and later) were used for segmentation and visualization (Extended Data Fig.  1d,e ). Batch 1 samples were segmented using Xenium Explorer’s internal algorithm. Resulting segmentation maps, combined with ( X ,  Y ) probe coordinates, were used for clustering and graph-based analysis (Extended Data Fig.  1e ). No notable differences in cell-type distribution or identity were observed between segmentation methods (Fig.  1d ).    Xenium captures the diversity of cell types identified in scRNA-seq data  Following cell segmentation, transcript data for small intestinal regions (duodenum, jejunum and ileum) were extracted and imported into Seurat  57 , 58   (Fig.  1c,d ). Using a pipeline analogous to our scRNA-seq pipeline ( Methods ), we generated uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) embeddings, assigned cluster identities and quantified cell-type proportion within each sample (Fig.  1c–g ). Differences in relative proportions between Xenium and scRNA-seq data were most likely technical artefacts: scRNA-seq used whole-thickness tissue dissociation, which can skew cell proportions  59 – 63  , whereas Xenium captured a fixed 5-µm cross-section preserving near-native proportions within the image plane, but are dependent upon the plane of tissue observed.  Interestingly, scRNA-seq showed slightly higher variation in the SMC and immune populations across developmental time (Fig.  1b , dark green and pink) compared to Xenium, where these populations remained consistent (Fig.  1d ). The enrichment of immune cells in scRNA-seq probably reflects their preferential recovery during single-cell dissociation. The largest proportional difference between methods was in the epithelium, which was nearly doubled in Xenium versus scRNA-seq (scRNA-seq, 11.4–18.1%; Xenium, 30.3–36.5%) (Fig.  1b,d , gold). Fibroblasts compromised approximately half of the cells in both datasets (scRNA-seq, 47.2–52.4%; Xenium, 37.9–49.3%; Fig.  1b,d , navy). Notably, both platforms identified the muscularis mucosa between 80 and 105 DPC (Fig.  1b,d , light green), consistent with prior studies demonstrating muscularis mucosa differentiation beneath the crypt domain during this developmental window  16 , 18 , 64  . Overall, spatial data enabled visualization of tissue architecture and composition that was obscured in dissociated scRNA-seq datasets.    Identification of diverse fibroblast populations within the developing intestine  Starting with human scRNA-seq data (Fig.  2a  and Supplementary Table  1 ) we extracted fibroblast populations  4 , 6 , 7 , 32 – 35   (Supplementary Table  4 ) and computationally removed four populations: (1) SMCs of the muscularis mucosa and muscularis externa, (2) vascular SMCs/pericytes, (3) actively cycling cells and (4) interstitial cells of Cajal (ICCs) (Supplementary Table  5 ). Removal of these populations, whose highly distinct transcriptomes obscured variation among non-proliferative fibroblasts, allowed the more nuanced fibroblast transcriptomes to be resolved.    Fig. 2   Identification of diverse fibroblast populations within the developing intestine using scRNA-seq and Xenium.   a , b , UMAP projections summarizing the extracted fibroblast populations observed in human fetal small intestine as determined by scRNA-seq ( a ) and Xenium spatial transcriptomics ( b ), pseudo-coloured by developmental stage.  c , d , scRNA-seq ( c ) and Xenium ( d ) UMAPs pseudo-coloured by cell type.  e , f , Dot plots displaying the markers used to annotate individual fibroblast populations for the scRNA-seq ( e ) and Xenium data ( f ).  g , h , Stacked bar graphs summarizing the fibroblast cell population composition of the human fetal small intestine at various timepoints through development (47–142 DPC) for either the scRNA-seq ( g ) or Xenium ( h ) dataset. Sample labels below the graphs in  g  and  h  are coloured to indicate the developmental stage (DPC) each sample falls within. The number of fibroblast cells included in each sample is indicated below the sample age, Xenium data was subset to reduce computational burden while maintaining relative sample contribution and cell number reflects the subset data. Cell populations are colour matched in  c – h : SECs (yellow), early LPFs (mint green), co-expressing LPFs (teal), late LPFs (cyan), SMFs (pink), and  CXCL13  +  fibroblasts (red). We analysed  n (scRNA-seq) = 9 biological samples,  n (Xenium) = 7 biological samples (Supplementary Table  1 ).   Source data                    After batch correction, scRNA-seq fibroblasts clustered broadly by developmental stage (Fig.  2a ), with each stage showing three major subpopulations: SECs, LPFs and SMFs. A fourth population,  CXCL13  +  fibroblasts, was observed in the most developmentally advanced samples (122–132 DPC) (Fig.  2c ), comprising only 5.5% of cells in the scRNA-seq data. Although Xenium fibroblasts did not segregate by age (Fig.  2b ), probably reflecting the smaller gene probe set, all four subpopulations (SEC, LPF, SMF and  CXCL13  + ) were identified (Fig.  2d ). Highly expressed marker genes for each subpopulation were defined in both datasets (Fig.  2e,f  and Supplementary Table  5 ).    Localization of SECs, LPFs, SMFs and  CXCL13  +  cells within the intestine   Localization of the SEC ( F3  + ) population  SECs in the developing human intestine have been previously described, marked by high  PDGFRA  and  F3  expression  1 , 5 , 7  . These cells reside immediately adjacent to the epithelium along the crypt–villus axis  9 , 11 , 12 , 15 , 17 , 19 , 21 , 22 , 38  . In the scRNA-seq data, SEC subpopulation proportions shifted as development progressed (Fig.  2g ), whereas Xenium proportions remained consistent across time (Fig.  2h ), suggesting that dissociation altered SEC subtype proportions during scRNA-seq preparation. Discussion  Recent single-cell approaches have shed light on rare and previously understudied intestinal populations, revealing that fibroblasts, which are historically viewed as a structurally supportive, homogeneous population, constitute a heterogeneous compartment with distinct functions  8 , 27 – 29 , 34 , 35 , 38 , 43 , 45 , 84 – 88  . While studies in the human intestine have revealed important fibroblast heterogeneity and localization  1 – 3 , 5 , 7  , the full complement of fibroblast subtypes and their spatial complexity had not been mapped in the developing or adult small intestine.  Prior spatial transcriptomic efforts characterizing cellular types and domains in the human intestine focused on the developing colon and terminal ileum using Visium technology (10X Genomics)  7  , which provides micro-domain resolution (6–10 cells per barcode) with greater sequencing depth but without single-cell resolution. The current study used an imaging-based approach achieving single-cell resolution, with the trade-off of a more limited probe panel. These approaches are complementary, and the present study extends the cellular landscape to the developing human small intestine and organoids, contributing insight into fibroblast patterning during intestinal development.  We resolved four transcriptionally and spatially discrete fibroblast lineages: SECs, LPFs, SMFs and rare  CXCL13  +  fibroblasts. Each population possessed stereotypical spatial localization from as early as 54 DPC (Fig.  8 ). While prior single-cell studies, including our own, have hinted at fibroblast heterogeneity and positional information  1 – 3 , 5 , 7 , 45  , sufficient resolution to map stereotyped tissue architecture was lacking. Here we demonstrate that (1) SECs form a continuous  PDGFRA  high / F3  high  sheath beneath the crypt–villus epithelium from as early as 7 weeks post-conception; (2) LPFs ( FABP5  +  and/or  ADAMDEC1  + ) expand within the villus core and crypt shelf during villus elongation; (3) SMFs ( SHISA3  + ) progressively consolidate between the emerging muscularis mucosa and muscularis externa; and (4)  CXCL13  +  fibroblasts arise late, clustering at the villus–crypt junction with sparse mid-villus distribution at an anatomical locus associated with lymphoid tissue formation.
