Together, these findings reconcile prior single-cell studies from different groups and establish molecular signatures with defined geographic positions across tissue compartments of the developing and adult human small intestine.  Faithfully recapitulating human tissue heterogeneity and architecture has remained a key limitation of organoid technology. Using the Xenium spatial atlas as a benchmark, we found that tHIOs generated under EGF and EREG differentiation paradigms reproduce almost the full complement of human fibroblast subtypes—SECs, LPFs and SMFs—with correctly ordered spatial topology. Subtle but informative divergences were evident: EGF-derived tHIOs retained epithelial  F3  expression and an immature  FABP5  +  /ADAMDEC1  −  LPF profile, while EREG-derived tHIOs were more mature in both respects. Neither model generated  CXCL13  +  fibroblasts, probably reflecting relative immaturity and/or absence of immune cells.  These findings highlight several important conclusions. First, cell-type abundance alone is insufficient as a fidelity metric; fibroblast positioning and stage-specific gene expression profiles must also be considered. Second, the presence of mature muscle layers (muscularis externa and muscularis mucosa) does not indicate global cellular maturation since individual cell types within tHIOs appear to mature at different rates rather than on a uniform developmental timeline ex vivo. Third, developmental maturity and incomplete patterning remain key bottlenecks to be addressed through modulation of growth factor gradients, extracellular matrix composition or co-culture with immune cells  82  . The atlas thus serves both as a quantitative quality control benchmark and as an instructive template for next-generation tissue-engineered intestine.  A limitation of this study is the shallow transcriptomic depth of the 292-gene Xenium panel, which inevitably biases clustering toward preselected markers, limits discovery of rare or novel states and reduces temporal resolution due to limited inclusion of time-dependent genes. However, the high cellular resolution of the spatial data enabled CytoSPACE  66   imputation of scRNA-seq data onto the Xenium atlas, effectively mapping full transcriptomic depth onto the spatial framework and enhancing downstream analysis such as CellChat  67 , 68   signalling inference. This approach also provides a framework for integrating high-quality data from other datasets into the atlas to drive future discovery of biological mechanisms such as niche-specific transcriptional programmes, previously unrecognized ligand–receptor interactions and testable hypotheses regarding spatially restricted mechanisms of tissue remodelling.  By integrating single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, we have refined the organization of intestinal cell types underpinning human small intestinal development and provided a quantitative scaffold for organoid engineering and disease modelling. Beyond cataloguing cell types, this work illustrates a generalizable strategy for incorporating transcriptional atlases into spatially resolved blueprints of organogenesis. As spatial multiomics technologies mature, such blueprints will be indispensable for deciphering cell–cell communication, identifying critical cell types and locations in congenital and inflammatory disorders, and engineering transplantable tissues that faithfully recapitulate human biology.    Methods   Human tissue acquisition and IRB  Normal, de-identified human fetal intestinal tissue was obtained from the University of Washington Laboratory of Developmental Biology and was conducted with approval from the University of Michigan Institutional Review Board (IRB; HUM00093465). Normal, de-identified human adult duodenum tissue specimens from research-consented deceased organ donors was obtained from the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), as FFPE blocks. Tissue from UCSF was obtained through Donor Network West in collaboration with the UCSF Viable Tissue Acquisition Lab (VITAL) Core as described previously  83  .    Statistics and reproducibility  No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size but our sample sizes are similar to those reported in previous publications  1  , no data were excluded from the analyses and the experiments were not randomized, samples were instead allocated as available. Data collection and analysis were not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments. Data distribution was assumed to be normal, but this was not formally tested. No technical replicates were performed for sequencing and Xenium imaging experiments and samples were distributed along the developmental timeline and not intended as biological replicates and are independent,  n  = 1.    Markers  The supervised lists of potential marker genes (Supplementary Table  3  and  4 ) were generated from the initial sequencing data (Figs.  1a  and  2a ) and mapped to at least one other publicly available human fetal intestine dataset  2 , 3  , then validated via FISH and Xenium imaging.    Primary tissue collection, fixation and paraffin processing  Human intestine tissue samples were collected as ~0.5-cm fragments and fixed for 24 h at room temperature in 10% neutral buffered formalin (NBF), and washed with UltraPure Distilled Water (Invitrogen, 10977-015) for three changes for a total of 2 h. Tissue was dehydrated by an alcohol series diluted in UltraPure Distilled Water (Invitrogen, 10977-015). Tissue was incubated for 60 min for each of the following solution: 25% methanol, 50% methanol, 75% methanol and 100% methanol. Tissue was stored long term in 100% methanol at 4 °C. Before paraffin embedding, tissue was equilibrated in 100% ethanol for an hour, and then 70% ethanol. Tissue was processed into paraffin blocks in an automated tissue processor (Leica, ASP300) with 1-h changes overnight.    scRNA-seq data analysis  The repositories of the raw scRNA-seq data of developing human fetal small intestine, duodenum, jejunum and ileum can be found in Supplementary Tables  1  and  2 . Data matrices for further analysis were generated using the Cell Ranger pipeline under standard parameters by the University of Michigan Advanced Genomics Sequencing Core.   Single-cell library preparation and transcriptome alignment  1    The scRNA-seq sample library was prepared as previously described, with the 10X Chromium Controller using the v2 chemistry. Sequencing was performed on an Illumina HiSeq 4000 with targeted depth of 100,000 reads per cell. Default alignment parameters were used to align reads to the pre-prepared hg19 human reference genome provided by the 10X Cell Ranger pipeline. Initial cell demultiplexing and gene quantification were also performed with the default 10X Cell Ranger pipeline.    Preprocessing and quality control filtering (full data)  Filtered gene expression matrices were imported into Seurat Version 4.1.0 in RStudio v1.4 running on R 4.1.2 for further analysis. Quality control was conducted after merging 16 single Seurat objects. Cells were excluded if they contained less than 500 or greater than 8,000 features, more than 10% mitochondria RNA and the RNA reads were less than 500 or greater than 60,000 to avoid the impact of outliers. The merged dataset was then normalized with a scale factor of 10,000 using the NormalizeData function. Highly variable features were identified using the FindVariableFeatures function. A fast version of the mutual nearest neighbours (MNN) was calculated to correct for batch effects using RunFastMNN. UMAP  90   was then constructed by the RunUMAP function with mnn reduction created by RunFastMNN with the first 30 dimensions. Nearest neighbours were found by the FindNeighbors function using MNN reduction. Cell clusters were identified by the original Louvain algorithm embedded in FindClusters with a resolution of 0.3.    Cell type annotation (full data)  The major classes of cell types in the human intestine (epithelium, fibroblast, immune, endothelium, ENS and SMC) were manually annotated using major cell population markers listed in Supplementary Table  3 . A cluster of contaminating red blood cells was identified and removed based on differential gene expression analysis. Cell counts of each major cell type across time were calculated by categorizing sample by age within developmental stage (47−75 DPC, 80 DPC, 101 DPC and 110−135 DPC).    Cell type annotation (fibroblast subset)  The fibroblast subset of the scRNA-seq dataset that was analysed for cell subtypes was defined after several rounds of quality control using Seurat v5.2.1 in RStudio 2024.12.1. with R (v4.4.1). First, the previously defined fibroblast population (Fig.  1a  and Supplementary Table  3 ) was extracted and the RNA assay was normalized using the SCTransform function with the percentage of mitochondrial reads regressing out in a second non-regularized linear, followed by the standard processing pipeline including principal component analysis, UMAP calculation, nearest neighbour discovery and cluster determination.  Then, according to the expression of gene markers listed in Supplementary Table  4  and differential gene expression analysis identified by the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, we filtered out clusters that interfered with discovery of fibroblast cell types. Specifically, we removed the active cycling cells ( MKi67, TOP2A  and  PCNA ) the SMCs ( ACTA2  and  TAGLN) , pericytes ( RGS5 ,  KCNJ8 ,  KCNL8 ,  ABCC9 ,  BGN  and  CCDC3 ) and ICCs ( KIT  and  ANO1 ). We removed these populations for two reasons. First, the clusters were notably different from the remaining cells when viewed on a three-dimensional diffusion map, they caused all other clusters to clump together. Second, these populations (other than the cycling cells) are differentiated, non-fibroblast cell types by the transcriptomic definitions we established for this study. It took several rounds of quality control to entirely remove each population, and for each round of our cell identification and quality control, we followed a similar pipeline and inspected gene expression using dot plots and feature plots. Cell counts (Fig.  2g ) of each subcell type were calculated by categorizing samples by developmental stage (47−75 DPC, 80 DPC, 101 DPC and 110−135 DPC).     Xenium slide preparation and workflow  Xenium is a spatial transcriptomics method that permits imaging of hundreds to thousands of genes on a single FFPE sample at subcellular resolution (Extended Data Fig.  1a ). A custom fetal human small intestine Xenium probe panel was designed (Supplementary Table  3 ) based on conventional markers from the adult human, conventional markers from the mouse and previously acquired or published sequencing data in the fetal human small intestine  1 , 3 , 4 , 33 , 34  .  As previously described  52  , archival tissue and tHIO FFPE samples were prepared by trimming excess paraffin from the paraffin blocks, which were then submerged in an ice bath for at least 30 min before sectioning. To prepare for section collection, the slide warmer was preheated 42 °C and used to pre-warm positive-charged microscope slides topped with molecular biology grade water (Corning, 46-000-CM). The blocks were then sectioned at a thickness of 5 μm and serial sections were collected on the prepared slides. After allowing sections to flatten out, the water was removed and sections were examined under the 4× and 10× objectives of a biological microscope to identify the optimal regions of the samples.  Using a single-edge razor blade, the corresponding area of the paraffin block was lightly scored to obtain tissue sections small enough to fit into the 10.45 mm by 22.45 mm sample placement area of the Xenium slide. Xenium slides were removed from −20 °C storage and allowed to come to room temperature 30 min before undergoing the same preparation as the microscope slides. Once the selected sections were placed on the Xenium slide, they were examined again to ensure that the fiducial frame was not obscured by any paraffin or tissue. Following water removal, sections were allowed to dry on the slide warmer for 3 h before slides were moved to a microscope slide jar for transportation to the University of Michigan Advanced Genomics Core for processing and image acquisition using the Xenium Analyzer (10X Genomics, PN-1000481).  Owing to the application of emerging technologies, the two different batches were processed for segmentation differently. In addition to the human fetal small intestine probe set, a segmentation kit (PN-1000661) was included to define cell boundaries of the second batch of samples, which resulted in more accurate cell segmentation and as a result more accurate clustering both by the Xenium Explorer program and externally.  Cell IDs and transcript counts for the small intestinal samples were exported from Xenium Explorer (v2.0.0 and later) and analysed using the pipeline described below.  Images and digital cell masks were generated and exported using Xenium Explorer. Xenium image brightness (+100%) and contrast (+20%) were enhanced equally across all exported Xenium images in Adobe Photoshop CC 2024 before figure assembly in Adobe Illustrator CC 2024.    Xenium data analysis pipeline   Extraction of Xenium data for analysis  Xenium spatial transcriptomic data were exported from Xenium Explorer version (v2.0.0 and later). The cell IDs of the fetal small intestine (duodenum–jejunum–ileum) only were included by using the XE region of interest (ROI) selection tool to define the small intestinal segments and export only cells from those regions. The colon and (for 122–142 DPC samples) distal ileum were imaged but not analysed in this study. The entirety of each tHIO sample, consisting of multiple lumen-containing organoid units were exported and analysed as single samples per condition. The whole-thickness human adult duodenum sample was exported in its entirety and analysed.    Quality control of tHIOs by identifying and removing mouse cells  Before further analysis of the tHIOs could occur, the residual mouse cells were identified and removed from further analysis based on the variety of expressed genes and total probe counts per cell (Extended Data Fig.  6 ). After validation of the removal of mouse cells and debris, the same pipeline was applied as for the human tissue samples.    Xenium cell type annotation (full data)  All Xenium data was loaded into R v4.4.1 using a standard Seurat 5.2.1 pipeline. After loading individual sample data in, cells with 0 counts were filtered out and excluded from further analysis. Each individual sample was normalized using the SCTransform function, which created a new assay with normalized transcriptomic expression values. Then principal component analysis was performed on the top 30 principal components and was applied to UMAP construction. Nearest neighbours were found with the FindNeighbors function and cells were clustered by the original Louvain algorithm at a 0.3-resolution using function FindClusters. Individual samples were carefully examined using dot plots and feature plots. The top 50 gene markers were generated by a Wilcoxon rank-sum test for each cluster for cell type annotation. The seven individual Xenium-sourced objects were then merged and cells were reclustered following the same pipeline.  When generating UMAP visualizations, cells from the later two stages (105 DPC and combined 122, 136 and 142 DPC) were randomly downsampled to 20,000 to reduce the computational burden (Fig.  1c ). Meanwhile, the whole dataset was analysed and quantified to generate cell count data in each cell type across different ages for comparison. Major populations including epithelium, fibroblast, endothelium, ENS, SMCs and immune cells were defined using the gene list in Supplementary Table  3 .  Cell IDs annotated using Seurat were imported back into Xenium Explorer and used to visualize the location of intestinal cell populations (105 DPC; Fig.  1f ). Each major cell class (epithelium, fibroblasts, SMCs, ENS, endothelium and immune) was then individually labelled to visualize subpopulations (Fig.  1g ). To carry out the labelling shown in Fig.  1g , each population highlighted was computationally extracted, subclustered and each cluster was annotated in Seurat, after which cell IDs were re-imported into Xenium Explorer for visualization.    Xenium fibroblast extraction  Different from extracting fibroblast population from a merged count matrices as we did for the single-cell sequencing data, we individually defined the fibroblast population for each sample after rigorous screening, before removing the proliferative cells, ICCs, SMCs and pericytes from the fibroblast data based on marker gene expression (Supplementary Table  4 ). Then the individual fibroblast objects were merged, clustered, annotated and quantified. Similar to the major cell type population Xenium data, the full fibroblast object was downsampled to reduce computational burden for visualization of the UMAP and to prevent visual bias due to overpopulating the object with the samples of developmental stages 122–142 DPC.  Stacked bar graphs depicting cell count distributions for major cell populations or fibroblast subtypes were generated in either Microsoft Excel (Figs.  1 ,  2 ,  5  and  6 ) or GraphPad Prism (Fig.  7 ). The annotated datasets were then re-loaded back into Xenium Explorer for visualization of the tissue architecture.     Additional analysis methods   Slingshot pseudo-time analysis of LPFs  For both the scRNA-seq and Xenium datasets, cells from all ages were integrated and LPF cells were subset into three ordered states (early LPF, LPF and late LPF). After standard preprocessing and UMAP embedding in Seurat, objects were converted to SingleCellExperiment format for trajectory analysis. Slingshot was applied using LPF annotations as cluster labels and the UMAP coordinates as the reduced dimensional space. Slingshot infers lineage structure by constructing a minimum spanning tree across clusters and fitting smooth principal curves to estimate developmental trajectories. Pseudo-time values were extracted and added back to the Seurat metadata for visualization on the UMAP. The same procedure was performed independently for both the sequencing and Xenium datasets to enable consistent pseudo-time inference across modalities.    Cell-level mapping between scRNA-seq and Xenium spatial transcriptomics using CytoSPACE  To enable cell-resolved integration between scRNA-seq data and Xenium spatial transcriptomics data, we employed CytoSPACE  66   to perform probabilistic cell-level assignment of sequencing-derived transcriptomic profiles onto spatially resolved Xenium cells.  In brief, the scRNA-seq dataset was used as a high-dimensional transcriptomic reference, while the Xenium dataset provided spatially localized cells with limited gene depth. Before mapping, both datasets were preprocessed independently using Seurat v5  91   and labelled manually. For the scRNA-seq data, standard normalization, variable gene selection and dimensionality reduction were performed. For the Xenium data, spatial cells were retained after quality control filtering and normalized based on detected transcripts.  CytoSPACE was then run using the scRNA-seq expression matrix as the reference and the Xenium expression matrix as the target. CytoSPACE computes an optimal transport-based assignment that matches each Xenium cell to the most transcriptionally similar scRNA-seq cell while respecting global cell-type composition constraints. This procedure generates a mapping table linking Xenium cell IDs (SpotID) to original scRNA-seq cell IDs (OriginalCID).    Imputation of full-transcriptome profiles into Xenium cells  Using the CytoSPACE mapping results, we transferred the full transcriptome information from scRNA-seq cells to their matched Xenium counterparts. Specifically, a named mapping vector was constructed from the CytoSPACE output     mapping.vec  =  setNames  (  OriginalCID  ,  SpotID  )  .     This mapping was aligned to the Xenium cell order. For Xenium cells with valid assignments, the raw gene expression counts from the corresponding scRNA-seq cells were extracted and re-indexed to match the Xenium cell barcodes, thereby generating an imputed gene expression matrix at single-cell spatial resolution.  This procedure resulted in a spatially resolved, full-transcriptome expression matrix, where each Xenium cell now carries both its spatial coordinates and the imputed high-dimensional gene expression profile derived from scRNA-seq.    Spatially informed cell–cell communication analysis using CellChat v2  The imputed Xenium expression matrix was then used for downstream spatial cell–cell communication analysis using CellChat  67 , 68  . As each Xenium cell retained its original spatial coordinates, we were able to perform CellChat analysis in a spatially aware context. Ligand–receptor interaction inference was conducted using the imputed expression values while incorporating spatial proximity constraints between cells.  This approach enabled us to quantify cell–cell communication networks that reflect both transcriptional states (derived from scRNA-seq) and true spatial organization (captured by Xenium), thereby overcoming the gene panel limitation of Xenium while preserving spatial fidelity.  Before running CellChat, we validated the CytoSPACE output specifically for cell duplications as the program uses a 10-cell minimum to ‘call’ a pathway as present. We found that a vast majority of cells were only duplicated a handful of times; 85.1% of cells were duplicated zero to three times and 99.4% were duplicated nine or fewer times. Only 0.61% of cells were duplicated more than ten times and those were entirely due to populations with a substantial difference in the number of cells present in the scRNA-seq dataset versus Xenium dataset.  After confirming that there would be minimal analytical artefacts due to cell duplications, we ran CellChatv2 on the CytoSPACE results of the 122/127/132 DPC sequencing data mapped onto the 142 DPC small intestine cell map.    Centroid distance calculations  For all human tissues and the two tHIO samples, the centroid for each cell was extracted from the Xenium metadata using R. Nearest neighbour queries were performed in the two-dimensional spatial coordinate space using the RANN implementation of the ANN library. For each cell centroid, we computed the Euclidean distance to the closest centroid among cells of each annotated cell type. The annotations used were the same 20 cell types used for CytoSPACE imputation; greater detail than the general class annotation, but less detail than used for full subtype annotation because some cell types varied greatly depending on developmental stage.  Minimum distance measurements (micrometre) were plotted as box plots indicating Q1, median, Q3 and mean for the minimum distance between indicated cell types within each sample. Select cell types for source and target cell were highlighted. In addition, hierarchical clustering (pheatmap) was performed, comparing the average minimum distance between each of the selected source cell types and target cell types.     Multiplex FISH and immunofluorescence  A list of probes, antibodies, fluorophores and concentrations can be found in Supplementary Table  2 . Archival tissues were selected from biologically distinct samples of similar age to at least one Xenium sample per developmental stage defined by the mesenchymal sequencing data. Paraffin blocks were sectioned to generate 5-µm-thick sections within the week before performing in situ hybridization. All materials, including the microtome and blade, were sprayed with RNase Away solution before use. Slides were baked for 1 h in a 60 °C dry oven before deparaffinization and rehydration.  Tissue slides were deparaffinized in Histo-Clear II (National Diagnostics, HS-202) twice for 5 min each, followed by rehydration in two washes of fresh 100% ethanol. The FISH protocol was then performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions (ACD; RNAscope multiplex fluorescent manual protocol, 323100-USM) with a 10-min hydrogen peroxide step, a 15-min antigen retrieval step and a 30-min protease plus treatment.  Immediately following the HRP blocking for the last channel of the FISH, slides were rinsed twice with PBS to remove excess detergent and then washed three times for 5 min in PBS, then transferred to blocking solution (5% BSA in PBS) for 1 h at room temperature in a dark, humid chamber. Slides were then incubated with primary antibody (rabbit anti-TAGLN/SM22, ab14106 (1:500) or rabbit anti-αSMA, ab5694 (1:500)) suspended in blocking solution overnight at 4 °C in a dark, humid chamber. The following day, excess primary antibody was rinsed off twice with PBS before undergoing a series of five PBS washes of 10 min each. Secondary antibody and nuclear dyes (donkey anti-rabbit 488 (1:500)), NucSpot 750/780 (1×) and DAPI (1:1,000) were added to blocking solution and slides were incubated in a dark humid chamber at room temperature for 1 h. Excess secondary antibody was rinsed off twice with PBS before going through another series of three PBS washes of 5 min each. Slides were mounted in FluorSave Mounting media (Millipore, 345789-20 ML) and allowed to dry in the dark before being sealed. Once the seal was fully dried, slides were stored in the dark at 4 °C and imaged within a week.  All imaging was done using a Nikon AXR confocal after slides were brought to room temperature. Acquisition and the alignment of multitrack FISH images was performed using DAPI and NucSpot 750/780 (Biotium, 41038) in NIS Elements v5.24.01. A minimum of three ROIs per sample region were imaged. Images were acquired using a 20× air objective with 3.00× digital zoom as multipoint, multichannel  z  stacks using resonant scanning at 2,048 × 2,048, with fluorescence averaged over four images and enhanced with Nikon Elements denoise.ai to further reduce background.  The  z -stack series were then compiled into maximum intensity projections using FIJI  92  . For publication, a representative image from each sample was selected and the brightness was further enhanced in FIJI. Imaging parameters were kept consistent for all images within the same experiment and any post-imaging manipulations were performed equally on all images from a single experiment. Final figures were assembled using Adobe Illustrator CC 2024.    tHIOs for Xenium imaging  56     Stem cell maintenance and differentiation  As previously published, stem cell lines were maintained in an undifferentiated state via media condition and regular splitting until differentiation. Stem cells underwent directed differentiation into definitive endoderm over a 3-day treatment. After three days, endoderm monolayers were differentiated into an intestinal identity. On days 4–6 of hindgut differentiation, spheroids budded from the monolayer and were collected. These spheroids were embedded in Matrigel as previously described  93  .  Organoid basal growth media was supplemented with EGF (100 ng ml −1  R&D Systems, 236-EG-01M) or EREG (10 ng ml −1  R&D Systems, 1195-EP-025/CF) with Noggin-Fc (100 ng ml −1 , purified from conditioned media) and R-Spondin1 (5% conditioned medium) for the first 3 days of culture to pattern a proximal small intestine. On the third day after embedding, media were changed to basal growth media supplemented with EGF or EREG only (no additional Noggin or R-Spondin1) and remained in this media for the duration of the experiments with media changes every 5 days. Organoids were not passaged to avoid disrupting the development and spatial organization of the key cell types seen in EREG-grown HIOs. HIOs were cultured in vitro for at least 28 days then collected for transplantation.    Mouse kidney capsule transplantation  The University of Michigan Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees approved all animal research. All mice were monitored by the investigators and veterinary staff from the University of Michigan Unit for Laboratory Animal Medicine and housed in a specific pathogen-free vivarium under a 12 h light/12 h dark cycle. Room temperature was maintained within approximately 20–26 °C, and relative humidity within approximately 30–70%, in accordance with institutional animal care standards. Food and water was available ad libitum.  HIOs were cultured in vitro at least 28 days and then implanted under the kidney capsules of adult immunocompromised NOD-scid IL2Rg-null (NSG) mice  53 – 56   (Jackson Laboratory strain no. 0005557). In brief, mice were anesthetized using 2% isoflurane and a left-flank incision was used to expose the kidney after shaving and sterilization of the area of incision with three alternating washes of hibiclens surgical soap and sterile water to prep the area after shaving. Between one and three HIOs were then surgically implanted beneath mouse kidney capsules using forceps. Before closure, an intraperitoneal flush of Zosyn (100 mg kg −1 ; Pfizer) was administered. Mice were administered a dose of analgesic carprofen during the surgery and an additional dose after 24 h. All mice were monitored daily for 10 days and then weekly until they were euthanized for retrieval of transplanted HIOs after 10 weeks.    tHIO processing for staining and histology  The tHIOs were placed in 10% NBF for 24 h at room temperature on a rocker for fixation. Fixed specimens were then washed 3× in ultrapure DNase/RNase-free distilled water (Thermo Fisher, 10977015) for 30–60 min per wash depending on its size. Next, tissue was dehydrated through a methanol series diluted in ultrapure DNase/RNase-free distilled water for 30–60 min per solution of 25% MeOH, 50% MeOH, 75% MeOH and 100% MeOH. Tissue was either immediately processed for paraffin embedding or stored in 100% MeOH at 4 °C for future paraffin processing or whole-mount staining. For paraffin processing, dehydrated tissue was placed in 100% EtOH, followed by 70% EtOH and perfused with paraffin using an automated tissue processor (Leica, ASP300) with 1 h solution changes overnight. Tissue was then placed into tissue cassettes and base moulds for sectioning. Before sectioning, the microtome and slides were sprayed with RNase Away (Thermo Fisher, 700511).  Five-µm-thick sections were cut from paraffin blocks onto Xenium slides under RNAse-free conditions (10X Genomics, PN-1000460) and submitted to the University of Michigan Advanced Genomics Core for processing and image acquisition using the Xenium Analyzer (10X Genomics, PN-1000481). In addition to the human fetal small intestine probe set, a segmentation kit (PN-1000661) was included to define cell boundaries of the second batch of samples, which resulted in more accurate cell segmentation and, as a result, more accurate clustering both by the Xenium Explorer program and externally. evidence_text:
GxP-Ready Single-Cell RNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics End-to-End Pipeline for Clinical Research. Single-cell/nucleus RNA-sequencing and Spatial Transcriptomics are powerful tools for investigating cellular heterogeneity and tissue architecture that have deepened our disease understanding. Their broader adoption in clinical and regulated settings, however, is hindered by regulatory requirements related to data integrity, regulatory compliance, reproducibility, and scalability. To address this gap, we developed NNclinSSOAP (Novo Nordisk Clinical Single-cell Spatial Omics Analytical Pipeline)-a modular, GxP-ready end-to-end computational pipeline that combines established single-cell workflows with a new Nextflow pipeline for Spatial Transcriptomics. NNclinSSOAP transforms RNA sequencing and Xenium spatial data into integrated, annotated single-cell objects and spatially resolved tissue maps. Designed to support mechanistic studies and clinical endpoint generation, it enables traceable and reproducible processing of large-scale datasets, scalable for use in HPC environments. Here, we provide a step-by-step demo case for using NNclinSSOAP that can be executed within 1.5 h on a standard laptop. All code and data are available open-source. Introduction  Single-cell/single-nucleus RNA sequencing (sc/snRNA-seq) has revolutionized biological research by enabling the study of gene expression at the resolution of individual cells and nuclei. The technology allows for the identification of cell types, the characterization of cellular heterogeneity within tissues, underlying cell–cell communication, and the understanding of complex biological processes at an unprecedented level of detail [ 1 ]. This granularity can uncover rare cell populations, specific gene expression profiles, and dynamic changes over time [ 2 ]. However, it inherently lacks spatial [ 3 ] information, which is critical for understanding the tissue architecture and the local microenvironment in which the cells reside [ 4 ]. Conversely, Spatial Transcriptomics retains high-resolution spatial information but often lacks the single-cell resolution necessary to discern the complexity of cellular interactions and the interplay of different cell types within tissues [ 5 ].  The multimodal omics approach of combining scRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics addresses their respective limitations and provides a more comprehensive overview of cellular mechanisms in tissue contexts. This enables cellular identity and spatial organization to be established concurrently, which can aid in revealing the mechanisms of action of drugs and understanding disease pathology [ 6 – 8 ].  The use of these technologies and the large data handling requirements that come with them pose challenges for use in clinical settings. Ideally, such data need to be stored and handled in a Good Experimental Practice (GxP)-compliant way and compute resources need to be large enough to handle the data volumes.  This paper addresses these critical challenges, describing the implementation and usage instructions for NNclinSSOAP (Novo Nordisk Clinical Single-cell Spatial Omics Analytical Pipeline)—a GxP-ready pipeline for running sc/snRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics together. Our approach ensures data integrity and facilitates the translation of findings into robust and reliable conclusions for downstream applications, contributing to the standardization and quality control necessary for wider application of sc/snRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics in regulated environments and clinical trial settings. Unlike applications aimed primarily at interactive exploration, NNclinSSOAP is designed as an open-source, configurable pipeline that users can adapt to their own study designs, analysis needs, and compute environments.    Pipeline Overview  The development of this paper was motivated by the need for a combined sc/snRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics workflow in a clinical research and trial endpoint analysis context. While single-cell and Spatial Transcriptomics technologies have become widely used for tissue and disease understanding for hypothesis generation, their application in regulated environments such as clinical trials presents specific challenges related to GxP requirements. Existing workflows, although effective in research settings, often do not address these requirements in a systematic way.  To meet these needs, we designed an end-to-end pipeline that integrates established methods and best practices from the broader community, with adaptations that ensure GxP-readiness and scalability. It was developed to ingest, process, and analyze sc/snRNA-seq and spatial data to generate clinical endpoints and run predefined analysis as per trial analysis plans, while providing a transparent and auditable framework suitable for clinical studies. Because of the number of samples set to be collected from multiple omics modalities, it was clear that the workflow would need to handle large data volumes and support execution in a high-performance computing (HPC) environment. To address these points, we adopted a modular, containerized architecture, enabling compliant storage and processing environments to be connected to the NNclinSSOAP pipeline.  The development process was iterative and collaborative, involving and building on cross-departmental expertise in computational biology, cloud engineering, statistics, and regulatory science. To address diverse data types and evolving analytical requirements, NNclinSSOAP was designed in a modular fashion that allows for straightforward adaptation to new datasets, data modalities, and requirements, providing flexibility and scalability for future research requirements and analyses. It is composed of 3 main components, connected as illustrated in Fig.  1  and described below:    1.  sc/snRNA-seq workflow: Handles the preprocessing, alignment, and quantification of single-nucleus RNA-seq data, leveraging nf-core/scrnaseq [ 9 ] for standardized and scalable data processing.    2.  R library/scripts: Enables advanced postprocessing, quality control, annotation, and statistical analyses of the output from the sc/snRNA-seq pipelines, ensuring robust downstream interpretation.    3.  SpatialXenium: A new Nextflow pipeline developed by us, designed to analyze multimodal data from the Spatial Transcriptomics platform Xenium [ 10 ], and optimized to run on HPCs ensuring efficient handling of large datasets. It ingests spatially resolved gene expression data and performs quality control, normalization, clustering, and spatial niche construction. The pipeline outputs processed Seurat objects (RDS), cluster/niche compositions, top marker genes, and visualizations (Principal Component Analysis [PCA], Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection [UMAP], and spatial plots). Optionally, it performs label transfer, adding cell-type annotation to the visualizations. The submodules that make up SpatialXenium are described in further detail in Box  1 .      Fig. 1. GxP-readiness  In this manuscript, GxP-readiness refers to the ability of a computational workflow to be deployed within a regulated clinical-research environment in a way that supports data integrity, traceability, reproducibility, auditability, and controlled change management. The term does not imply that the pipeline alone makes an analysis fully GxP compliant. Rather, NNclinSSOAP provides pipeline-level controls that can be combined with an institution’s validated infrastructure, standard operating procedures, access controls, and documentation practices. Relevant expectations for clinical computerized systems and analysis planning include principles described in ICH E6(R3) [ 11 ], ICH E9 [ 12 ], and FDA 21 CFR Part 11 [ 13 ].  NNclinSSOAP implements these pipeline-level controls through a modular architecture, containerized execution environments, and automatic provenance capture. The whirl package provides the functionality of executing scripts in batch and simultaneously getting a log from the individual execution [ 14 ]. Nextflow, an open-source workflow management system [ 15 ], allows each workflow step to be run as a specified module with captured parameters and process metadata, while containers help control software versions and dependencies. The entire workflow is documented automatically in BioCompute Objects (BCOs). They document the intended purpose, inputs, software and version identity, parameter settings, execution details, provenance, and output locations of an analysis, providing a standardized record that can be reviewed, repeated, and archived [ 16 , 17 ]. BioCompute is an FDA-supported standard for regulatory submissions, and can be used during regulated activities and communication with the agency [ 18 ].  In clinical use, the GxP-ready pipeline is intended to be executed after the analysis has been specified in the clinical study analysis plan. Input data, configuration files, and output objects are treated as controlled analysis artifacts. Sample metadata and QC thresholds are defined before execution where possible, the run is executed in a validated or otherwise qualified compute environment, and generated reports, logs, BCOs, and Seurat objects are retained as evidence of what was run.  In our implementation, clinical data storage and access are handled by a compliant Amazon Web Services (AWS) storage service with separate input and output locations and role-based access. For data processing, analyses were performed within a dedicated, GxP-validated compute environment developed in-house as part of the Novo Nordisk secure analytics platform. This environment operates within a cloud-based infrastructure to provide both scalability and regulatory compliance throughout the data life cycle. The flow of inputs and outputs and the environments used is shown in Fig.  1 . Other institutions can reuse the open-source code, containers, and provenance mechanisms that NNclinSSOAP provides, connecting the workflow to their own validated compute, storage, access-control, retention, audit-trail, and electronic-signature processes.  The scope of readiness is therefore layered. Elements that transfer directly with the pipeline include modular workflow definitions, container manifests, configurable analysis parameters, BCO generation, execution logs, and standard outputs for review. Elements that remain institution-specific include formal software validation or verification, training, role-based review and approval of BCOs, controlled versioning and change management of the validated pipeline, secure data retention, audit trails, and any electronic-signature practices. This distinction is important because BioCompute primarily defines what is documented. It does not replace local validation, governance, or standard operating procedures required for full GxP compliance.  Within the pipeline, GxP-readiness is also reflected in how analysis decisions are exposed rather than hidden. QC filters and label-transfer probability thresholds are explicit user-configurable parameters. Cells failing QC are excluded from downstream analysis according to documented thresholds, and low-probability labels are not silently converted into confident cell types. Instead, they are flagged as “Ambiguous” in the labeled Seurat metadata and visualizations and are accompanied by prediction files. This allows downstream users and reviewers to distinguish confident annotations from those requiring caution or manual review.    Applications  NNclinSSOAP was specifically developed for clinical trials incorporating transcriptomics as study endpoints, including sc/snRNA-seq and Spatial Xenium. As a pioneering framework in the pharmaceutical industry, particularly for cardiometabolic diseases, NNclinSSOAP has already been used in 2 mechanism-of-action trials. The first trial, focused on Alzheimer’s disease, incorporated scRNA-seq data as a primary endpoint [ 19 ], and therefore utilized only Procedure 1, which is tailored for single-cell transcriptomics. In contrast, the second trial, a clinical study in kidney disease [ 20 , 21 ], employed both Procedures 1 and 2 as it included both snRNA-seq and Xenium Spatial Transcriptomics data.  By enabling rapid and GxP-aligned data processing, this workflow sets a new standard for transcriptomic analysis in clinical trials. Looking ahead, it is broadly applicable to trials in other therapeutic areas, provided that compatible input data are available. Thanks to Nextflow’s modular architecture, the workflow can be easily adapted to accommodate additional analytical modules in the future.  Notably, the SpatialXenium Nextflow pipeline described in this paper is publicly available as part of the repository and can be integrated into new or existing Nextflow workflows, independently of the broader workflow described in the paper.    Comparison to other methods  There are numerous tools and packages available to facilitate sc/snRNA Transcriptomics data preprocessing [ 22 ]. For sc/snRNA-seq, we used the established nf-core pipeline scrnaseq as part of Procedure 1. Beyond the initial preprocessing steps, downstream processing and analysis of sc/snRNA-seq data commonly leverage widely used packages such as Seurat [ 23 ] that we use as part of our R library. Our SpatialXenium pipeline is wrapped around the Seurat suite relevant for Spatial Transcriptomics data QC, preprocessing, and analytics.  Integrated platforms for combining single-cell and Spatial Transcriptomics exist [ 24 ], but not as workflows aligned with GxP requirements. The purpose of this section is to contextualize NNclinSSOAP rather than to provide a formal benchmarking study. NNclinSSOAP builds on established community methods and combines them into a documented, containerized, and provenance-aware workflow for regulated clinical research settings. The points below therefore focus on workflow structure, traceability, reproducibility, and deployment considerations. Six main features make NNclinSSOAP different to other methods:    1.  Modularity. NNclinSSOAP not only makes it possible to run the underlying sc/snRNA-seq and SpatialXenium workflows separately, but the workflows themselves build on Nextflow modules. This simplifies both using the workflows and adapting them to future needs as well as making them scalable, a key factor in data heavy settings.    2.  GxP-readiness. Using Nextflow for building our workflows enables NNclinSSOAP to be both scalable and reproducible. Combined with BCO-based provenance capture, this supports selected GxP-relevant expectations, particularly traceability, reproducibility, and reviewability. It allows users to connect to a compute environment of choice, without compromising reproducibility, enabling analysis of data volumes at a much greater scale than in the demo case described in this paper. Full GxP compliance ultimately depends on deployment within an appropriate governed environment.    3.  The SpatialXenium pipeline. There is a publicly available pipeline, nf-core/spatialxe, currently under development. It is a flexible image- and coordinate-based reanalysis framework, focused on controlling and improving Xenium data quality through multiple segmentation and spatial-data methods. SpatialXenium differs from this, instead focusing on postprocessing and analysis of Xenium data. It provides users a fully specified, protocol-locked, and easily reproducible end-to-end pipeline, implementing Spatial Transcriptomics analysis from Seurat for Xenium data.    4.  We provide an R library capable of processing outputs generated by nf-core/scrnaseq, supporting standard Seurat workflows and downstream annotation. These scripts offer flexibility, incorporating tools such as Harmony [ 25 ] and RPCA [ 26 ] for multisample integration. For cell-type annotation, automated approaches like Azimuth [ 27 ] or SingleR [ 28 ] are supported, and user-defined reference datasets can be added. For differential treatment effect analysis, we use a pseudobulk [ 29 ] approach by aggregating counts per sample and cell type, followed by statistical assessment using edgeR [ 30 ], which enables robust testing of group-level differences while accounting for biological variability. Alternatively, other statistical methods can be integrated as needed. An overview of this workflow is illustrated in Fig.  1 .    5.  By leveraging the whirl package [ 14 ] to execute the R library, the pipeline produces a BCO along with multiple log files—one corresponding to each R script. The package offers the flexibility to modify certain domains within the BCO and to select specific scripts to run as needed.    6.  The R environment required for running these procedures is provided as a Docker container, ensuring that all necessary packages and dependencies are included and eliminating compatibility issues for the user. This approach allows the entire environment to be reliably loaded and the workflow to be executed as intended. However, one limitation is that package versions within the container may become outdated as new releases are made. Users also have the flexibility to set up and use their own custom environments if preferred.       Experimental Design   Expertise needed for implementation and interpretation  NNclinSSOAP was developed to be used by computational biologists, producing results (e.g., tables and figures) that can be interpreted and understood by medical or biological experts without a data science background. For users following the procedures step-by-step, no expertise is needed and none of the topics below need to be considered. However, some familiarity with single-cell transcriptomics and relevant training in statistical analysis of high-dimensional omics data and running analytics scripts is advisable for a smooth experience and ability to understand the outputs scientifically.  If the workflow outlined in this paper is adapted to another dataset different from the demo, carefully consider the points below. It is also recommended to read the extensive information and instructions provided in the code repository  README.md  and .md files in  /docs . For this, a broad understanding of R, Nextflow, cloud computing, containerization, and single-cell transcriptomics is needed.    Sampling strategy-dependent analysis  The datasets used in Procedure 2 contain a single sample each, one with healthy kidney tissue and the other with cancerous kidney tissue. This case facilitates analysis from the perspective of seeing differences in cell types and gene expression. Depending on a dataset’s sampling strategy, experimental design, and analysis plans, as often preregistered in a clinical trial setting, other relevant analyses and visualizations are possible, e.g., mitochondrial genes, cell cycle genes, biological sex-related genes, batch effect contribution from metadata, etc. For samples taken from the same subject at multiple time points (longitudinal data), it is possible to analyze changes over time. For samples taken at a single time point for multiple subjects (cross-sectional data), it is possible to analyze the homo-/heterogeneity within a population. Combining these 2 strategies creates a clinical trial scenario where NNclinSSOAP can be used to analyze subjects’ tissue characteristics over time as a response to treatment, comparing to a placebo group or among groups at a single time point for disease understanding. Quality control  QC thresholds should be reviewed in the context of each dataset and, where applicable, defined before downstream biological or clinical interpretation. For Xenium data, the relationship between read counts, gene detection, and QV score provides a practical check of assay quality (see Fig.  4 ). A high-quality dataset is expected to retain most informative cells and genes after filtering, with low-quality or control-probe-rich observations limited to a minority of the data. In contrast, a problematic dataset may show a large fraction of observations with low read counts, low QV scores, unusually high read-count outliers, or high control-probe proportions. The selected thresholds are captured in configuration files and execution outputs (see Fig.  2 ), supporting reproducibility and review of the filtering decisions.    Fig. 4. Expected Results  The result of following both procedures is a transformation of raw sc/snRNA-seq data into an integrated and annotated Seurat object, and raw Xenium data into a spatially resolved cell object and map. This can aid in answering clinical questions, giving the user a deeper understanding of the analyzed tissues both at a cellular expression and a structural level, as is the case in the demo case data in this paper, highlighting differences between healthy and cancer kidney tissue.  When the procedures are executed with the supplied demo data using the specified software versions, parameters and settings, deterministic tables and files are expected to be reproducible. Stochastic visualization steps such as UMAP may show minor layout differences while preserving the same biological topology and interpretation. If the paper is followed using a personal dataset, the same types of outputs are expected, but results will differ according to the input data.   Sc/snRNA-seq (procedure 1)  Executing the sc/snRNA-seq workflow (Procedure 1, step 2) generates an nf-core results folder. The demo case dataset has been run with the cellranger aligner [ 31 ], so the results are the standard cellranger outputs. The special addition is the BCO object that has been generated since the plugin is included when running the nextflow pipeline.  In the second part of the workflow (Procedure 1, steps 4 and 5), each script produces a variety of plots and output files, which are organized into dedicated folders—see Box  2  for a summary of the results file structure.    •  Quality Control (QC): QC plots document the standard Seurat workflow, starting from reading the counts matrix and progressing through to the creation of the final Seurat object (see Fig.  3 A to D). A separate folder is generated for each sample’s QC outputs, while the integrated Seurat object is stored in the parent directory.    •  Cell Annotation: This step generates visualizations such as UMAPs displaying annotated clusters and violin plot displaying the annotation scores, along with an updated Seurat object that contains cell type assignments (see Fig.  3 E and F).    •  Differential Expression analysis: For each cell type, the pipeline outputs a normalized counts CSV file, a CSV file with differential expression results, and a volcano and line plot summarizing key findings (see Fig.  3 G and H).      SpatialXenium (procedure 2)  Executing the SpatialXenium workflow (Procedure 2, step 4) produces several key outputs that can be used for clinical interpretation of the tissues analyzed, shown in Fig.  4 . By using Nextflow, reports covering errors, timing and resource usage have automatically been created. An example results file structure is shown in Box  3 . To aid with technical and clinical interpretation, key outputs from Quality Control (QC), gene expression and cell type analysis are described in further detail below:    •  Quality Control: The QC plots (see Fig.  4 A and B) summarize how many genes and reads are captured per cell and how these values are distributed across the dataset. This allows users to identify low-quality cells, technical outliers, or regions with suboptimal capture efficiency before drawing any biological or clinical conclusion, ensuring that downstream patterns (e.g. “immune poor” areas) are not artifacts of poor data quality.    •  Gene Expression: The gene expression visualizations (see Fig.  4 C and D) show how the selected markers from  assets/genes.txt  are distributed both in UMAP space and across the tissue. Clinically, these plots help confirm that canonical markers (for example, tumor, immune, or stromal genes) are expressed in the expected tissue compartments and spatial niches, supporting interpretations such as tumor–stroma interactions, immune infiltration patterns, or localization of specific disease-relevant pathways.    •  Cell Type: The cell-type plots (see Fig.  4 E and F) resulting from the label transfer display the predicted cell types in UMAP space projected back onto the tissue, with cells below the chosen probability threshold set to “Ambiguous”. This makes it clear which assignments are robust enough to support biological or clinical interpretation, which should be treated with caution. In a clinical context, these maps can be used to explore how specific cell types (e.g., cytotoxic T cells, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells) are spatially organized within lesions, margins, or normal tissue, and how this architecture might relate to disease severity or therapeutic response.       Conclusion  NNclinSSOAP offers a GxP-ready framework for scalable processing and analysis of single-cell and Spatial Transcriptomics data for clinical research and trials. Its modular design and automated provenance capture ensure transparent, reproducible, auditable, and fully traceable analyses suitable for regulated environments, e.g., clinical trials. Together, these features provide a practical, unique, and extensible foundation for deploying multimodal transcriptomics across mechanistic studies and clinical trials. Human adult and pediatric multimodal transcriptomic atlas of progression from pressure-loaded to failing right ventricle. Right ventricular failure (RVF) independently predicts mortality in heart failure, yet its pathophysiology is poorly understood. Here we present a multi-modal atlas of human right ventricular pressure loading and failure, including bulk (n = 142), single-nucleus (n = 11) and Xenium spatial (n = 9) transcriptomics in adults, plus pediatric (n = 14) and mouse pulmonary artery banding cohorts. Subclustering resolved 34 cell subtypes across 12 lineages along a two-phase trajectory. Phase 1 (non-failing to pressure-loaded) accounts for most of the transcriptional change detectable by bulk and single-nucleus RNA sequencing and is marked by loss of resident macrophage identity, fibroblast activation, endothelial expansion and erosion of tissue-protective programs. Phase 2 (pressure-loaded to RVF) produces little change in bulk RNA sequencing but is resolved by spatial transcriptomics, engaging multi-lineage fibrotic, endothelial-activation and cardiomyocyte-reactivation programs, with a gain of extracellular matrix (collagen, laminin, thrombospondin) signaling over a stable cell contact adhesion baseline. Mitochondrial respirometry revealed respiratory dysfunction in adult and mouse RVF but not pediatric RVF. Multi-lineage remodeling of the cardiac microenvironment emerges as the central molecular program of RVF, meriting further study as possible disease-modifying targets. Main  The normal right ventricle (RV) is morphologically and embryologically unique from the left ventricle (LV), precluding the categorical extrapolation of our understanding of left-side pathophysiology to the right heart  1  . Historically, cardiac research has focused on left ventricular failure (LVF), delivering multiple approved therapies, with less attention to RVF  2  . Although the most common cause of RVF is pressure overload secondary to LVF, RVF can also arise from diverse other causes  3 – 5  . Independent of etiology, RV dysfunction portends a poor prognosis: patients with LVF and concomitant RV dysfunction have approximately a two-fold increased mortality risk  6 – 8  .  Advances in LVF therapy have been driven by targeting critical pathways such as the renin−angiotensin−aldosterone system (RAAS)  9  . Attempts to generalize these therapies to the RV have been clinically unsuccessful. Neurohormonal blockade, a cornerstone of LVF therapy, has little efficacy in RVF  9  . There is, therefore, a need for exploratory research to identify RVF-specific therapeutic targets.  We conducted a multi-platform transcriptomic study of failing and non-failing human RVs, integrating bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) (142 individuals), single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) (11 individuals) and Xenium spatial transcriptomics (nine sections), with mitochondrial respirometry, flow cytometry and histological validation. We placed these findings in broader context by comparing to a mouse pulmonary artery banding (PAB) model, pediatric single-ventricle RVs, LVF and a published pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) RV transcriptomic dataset. Recent human cardiac snRNA-seq atlases remain LV centric  10 – 14   or include limited RV in genetically defined cohorts  15  . Although some include non-failing (NF) RV tissue  11 , 14 , 16  , none has stratified pressure-overload RVF progression or integrated bulk, single-nucleus and spatial modalities on matched patient tissue. Here we present, to our knowledge, the first such integrated atlas and propose a two-phase model in which multi-lineage erosion of protective programs occurs in various cell types during the transition from NF to preserved RV in the context of LVF (NF → pRV) and is followed by a pRV → RVF transition that is comparatively muted in bulk RNA expression changes but engages a broader multi-lineage signal elicited in Xenium spatial pseudobulk analyses.    Results   Cohort and multi-platform approach  From the Penn Human Heart Tissue Bank, we collected transmural RV samples from adult NF organ donors and LVF transplant recipients, the latter substratified  17 , 18   into pressure-loaded but preserved systolic function (pRV) and failing (RVF) groups (Fig.  1a  and Supplementary Tables  1 – 3 ). We applied bulk RNA-seq ( n  = 142), snRNA-seq ( n  = 11; 61,398 nuclei) and Xenium spatial transcriptomics ( n  = 9 sections; 625,305 cells; 477-gene panel); a mouse PAB model at 2-week and 2-month timepoints; a pediatric snRNA-seq cohort ( n  = 14; 10 hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS)-palliated RVs stratified by normal function or RVF and four controls); and a cross-etiology comparison with a published PAH RVF bulk dataset  19  . Source data                      Bulk RNA-seq reveals the transcriptomic landscape of RV failure progression  Principal component analysis (PCA) of bulk RNA-seq separated NF from pRV/RVF but poorly separated pRV from RVF (Fig.  1b ). Differential expression (DE) yielded many NF versus pRV/RVF differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with strong NF → pRV and NF → RVF fold change (FC) correlation (Extended Data Fig.  1a,b  and Supplementary Data  1 ). Prominent DEGs common to pRV and RVF included cardiac stress ( NPPA ,  NPPB ), chemokines ( CXCL8 – 11 ) and extracellular matrix (ECM)/angiogenic genes. Pathway enrichment highlighted immune, complement and inflammatory terms (Supplementary Data  2 ), suggesting that immune populations dominate the bulk signal. Many DEGs exhibited stepwise changes from NF → pRV → RVF, with 115 stepwise-increasing genes enriched for T cell chemotaxis, and 161 stepwise-decreasing genes enriched for mitochondrial ribosomal components (Extended Data Fig.  1c–f  and Supplementary Data  3 ). Fewer significant DEGs were identified from pRV → RVF analysis, indicating that most transcriptional remodeling precedes functional decompensation. pRV-upregulated genes enriched for oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS); RVF-upregulated genes were immune dominated (Extended Data Fig.  1g,h  and Supplementary Data  2 ).                    We also evaluated DE by weighted gene correlation network analysis (WGCNA)  20   to capture broader co-expression signals, resolving 29 gene modules, almost all of which were differentially expressed across states (Fig.  1c–e  and Supplementary Data  4 ). Two OXPHOS modules (M25 and M26) declined monotonically across NF → pRV → RVF at the module eigengene level, whereas the large resident macrophage module M1 ( CD163 ,  MRC1 ,  VSIG4 ) was highest in NF and fell sharply from NF to pRV before plateauing. In the opposing direction, an adaptive immune module (M8; T/B cell and major histocompatibility complex class II (MHC-II) genes) rose significantly from NF to pRV (Fig.  1d,e  and Supplementary Data  4 ).  To test cross-etiology generalizability, we compared our bulk data to a published PAH-associated RVF transcriptome  19  . RVF versus NF yielded 235 concordantly downregulated genes (respiratory electron transport (ETC), complex I biogenesis) and 214 concordantly upregulated genes (interferon (IFN) α/β, antiviral signaling), establishing mitochondrial decline and IFN activation as etiology shared (Fig.  1f ). By contrast, the complement cascade was divergent between cohorts, downregulated in our RVF but upregulated in PAH RVF, identifying complement activation as an etiology-specific response (Extended Data Fig.  1i  and Supplementary Data  5 ).    Single-nucleus transcriptomics resolves 34 cell subtypes across 12 lineages  Single-nucleus RNA-seq of 11 RV samples (Supplementary Tables  4  and  5 ) yielded 61,398 nuclei (2,912 genes per nucleus) and 12 major clusters (Fig.  2a,b  and Supplementary Data  6 ). Composition shifted progressively with disease: loss of cardiomyocyte nuclei and expansion of endothelial cell (EC) nuclei from NF → pRV → RVF (Fig.  2c ). This compositional shift parallels reports from LVF snRNA-seq atlases, although, notably, the non-myocyte expansion here is endothelial predominant without the fibroblast expansion typical of LVF  12  . Bulk WGCNA modules were assigned to dominant lineages (Fig.  2d ). Single-nucleus RNA-seq subclustering resolved 34 subtypes across 12 lineages: 10 cardiomyocyte, seven fibroblast, five EC, six myeloid and six lineages retained at lineage level (pericyte, smooth muscle, adipocyte, epicardial, neuronal/glial and natural killer/T) due to low counts (markers in Figs.  6b  and  7b , Extended Data Figs.  2b  and  3b  and Supplementary Data  7 ). Pseudobulk DESeq2 within each subtype across three pairwise comparisons (Supplementary Data  8  and  9 ) identified fibroblasts as most transcriptionally responsive (1,083 DEGs pRV versus NF; 806 DEGs RVF versus NF), followed by cardiomyocytes (248; 464). This difference partially reflects lower inter-patient dispersion among fibroblasts. Spatially constrained cell−cell communication reveals stage-specific signaling  Cell−cell communication inference (CellChat  29  , applied to per-patient snRNA-imputed Xenium expression under Xenium-derived spatial constraints; Supplementary Data  14 ) revealed a progressive reorganization of myocardial signaling across the NF → pRV → RVF axis (Fig.  4e,f ). Subclustering snRNA-seq resolved seven literature-grounded subtypes (Extended Data Fig.  3a,b ): Fb Resident, Adventitial, Elastogenic, Interstitial, Stressed, Pro-fibrotic and Anti-fibrotic, with fibroblast subtype proportions generally stable across disease states (Extended Data Fig.  3c ). Simultaneously, the canonical myofibroblast/matricellular markers  THBS4  (ref.   34  ) and  ACTA2  (ref.   35  ) and the activated fibroblast marker  SFRP4  were induced.  None of the snRNA-seq, bulk or panel-filtered Xenium data yielded significant fibrogenic DEGs in RVF versus pRV at the lineage level. Xenium fibroblast subtype resolution exposed a focal phase 2 program restricted to activated/matricellular subsets involving  THBS4 ,  TNC  and  PRG4  (snRNA-seq directions concordant, not significant) (Extended Data Fig.  3e ). Two literature-defined module scores anchored the two-phase split: the Koenig et al.  10   donor fibroblast identity signature collapsed sharply at NF → pRV with no further drop at decompensation (Extended Data Fig.  3f ), whereas the Fu et al.  34   matrifibrocyte commitment signature was flat at NF → pRV and trended upward only at pRV → RVF (Extended Data Fig.  3g ). This suggests that fibroblast identity erosion is phase 1 specific, whereas fibrogenic commitment is phase 2 specific. Cross-platform similarity (Extended Data Fig.  3h,i ) was strongest for Stressed and Interstitial subtypes. Spatial neighborhood analysis (Extended Data Fig.  3j–l ) placed FB Stressed, Matrix, Intermediate and CILP in myeloid-enriched niches (Xen FB Matrix–myeloid Pearsonʼs  r  = 0.93). Massonʼs trichrome/Sirius Red histology confirmed progressive fibrosis (+5.9% area per stage; Extended Data Fig.  3m ). In RVF, the fibrotic myocardium niche occupies a smaller fraction of section area (Fig.  3g ). This does not necessarily represent less fibrosis, as niche proportions are compositional. They describe how section area is partitioned between neighborhoods, not how much matrix each neighborhood contains. The rising histologic collagen burden (Extended Data Fig.  3m ), the pRV → RVF gain of ECM signaling (Fig.  4e ) and the matrifibrocyte commitment trend (Extended Data Fig.  3g ) all measure matrix content or fibroblast state and are compatible with fibrotic remodeling intensifying within existing neighborhoods while the stressed myocardium and vascular niches expand their share of the section.                    In summary, comparing pediatric to adult RVF, we found that:    Gene expression modules are largely concordant between adult and pediatric RVs.    Overall, there is substantial, but not perfect, concordance in the transcriptional changes during RVF.    Endothelial expansion is seen in both cases of RVF, although it appears driven by venous ECs in pediatric hearts versus capillary ECs in adult hearts. RVF and LVF share core transcriptional programs  Cell-type-resolved LV concordances have already emerged from the fibroblast (Extended Data Fig.  4a–c ) and myeloid (Extended Data Fig.  4d–i ) analyses above. To consolidate that picture and extend it to the bulk module and transcriptome scale, we leveraged the same Koenig et al.  10   human LV snRNA-seq dataset across the full RV WGCNA module set, which showed that RV modules were broadly conserved in LV with concordant NF-versus-DCM trends (Fig.  8g ). Findings that were common to RVF and LVF included induction of the contractile/cytoskeletal/focal adhesion module M2 (Fig.  8h ); repression of the nuclear-encoded ETC mitochondrial modules M10, M25, M26 and M28 (Fig.  8i ); and NF-versus-failing pseudobulk cardiomyocyte FCs (Fig.  8j ). One chamber-specific divergence emerged from the myeloid comparison: the RV iMac population uniquely retained TLF residency markers that were not reported in the Koenig et al. LV inflammatory macrophages. This is consistent with, although it does not prove, an RV iMac hybrid resident-like state.  Thus, the core heart failure programs (mitochondrial suppression, inflammatory activation and myofibroblast activation) are shared between RVF and LVF.     Discussion  We integrated bulk, single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomics with orthogonal mitochondrial respirometry, flow cytometry and histology to construct a multi-lineage atlas of human RVF, from which a two-phase model emerges. Phase 1 (NF → pRV) carries the dominant transcriptional burden in bulk and snRNA-seq pseudobulk and features tissue-wide erosion of protective programs, resident macrophage identity loss, fibroblast activation, endothelial expansion and anti-oxidant suppression and pan-tissue  FKBP5  loss. The compensated-to-decompensated (pRV → RVF) transition is best framed as a transcriptional set-point shift in phase 1 (approximately 95% of platform-resolved DEGs) followed by qualitatively distinct, lineage-specific phase 2 programs that include cardiomyocyte oxidative stress, EC  ANGPT2 / ADAMTS1  induction consistent with vascular remodeling and fibroblast matricellular activation.  A central and unanticipated finding is that the pediatric single-ventricle RV resists the mitochondrial failure that characterizes adult and mouse pressure overload. In adult RVF, a coordinated decline in nuclear-encoded mitochondrial transcripts, accompanied by suppression of the ERRα/PGC-1α biogenesis program, parallel impaired complex I + II respiratory function. The mouse PAB RV showed the same concordant decline: cardiomyocyte mitochondrial transcripts were coordinately downregulated (gene set enrichment, consistent with the decreased ETC gene expression reported by Hwang et al.  53  ) alongside reduced respiratory capacity, although the per-animal transcriptional effect was modest relative to the functional deficit. By contrast, pediatric HLHS-palliated failing RVs were metabolically spared. Mitochondrial transcripts were neither induced nor significantly suppressed, and respiratory capacity was preserved (Fig.  5h ). The cross-cohort respiratory pattern (Fig.  5j ), with deficits in adult and mouse but not pediatric single-ventricle RVF, together with the transcriptional data, suggests that the adult and mouse pressure-overloaded RVs undergo coupled mitochondrial transcriptional and functional decline. Conversely, the developing single-ventricle heart sustains respiratory function.  A notable feature of the RV myeloid compartment was a macrophage population marked by an immediate-early gene program, including  NR4A1 ,  NR4A3 ,  DUSP2 ,  FOS  and  JUN , which we designate as iMac. Because induction of these transcription factors is a recognized consequence of enzymatic tissue dissociation in single-cell RNA-seq, such signatures are often dismissed as technical artifact  54  . Several lines of evidence argue against that interpretation here. The program was defined in snRNA-seq, which omits the warm enzymatic dissociation step responsible for the artifact, and was independently recovered by in situ spatial transcriptomics (Xenium), in which transcripts are detected on fixed tissue without any dissociation. Furthermore, the signature was confined to a single macrophage subset and showed reproducible spatial organization, co-localizing with monocytes within discrete tissue foci—a distribution incompatible with a uniform, handling-induced stress response, which would be expected across all cell types irrespective of identity. The iMacs additionally retained resident macrophage markers that were not observed in the inflammatory macrophages of the Koenig et al.  10   left ventricular atlas, suggesting that the RV harbors an activated, resident-like macrophage state localized to sites of monocyte accrual. Whether this state reflects local activation of resident macrophages or in situ adaptation of recruited cells cannot be resolved from cross-sectional human data and will require lineage-resolved models. Regardless of origin, its presence points to a chamber-specific organization of the myeloid response in right ventricular failure.  We found evidence for disruption in GR signaling, with tissue-wide loss of the GR co-chaperone  FKBP5  and a coordinated, pan-myeloid suppression of  NR3C1  transactivation targets, although this evidence is limited to transcriptional state. Because the GR can bind both positive and negative glucocorticoid response elements (GREs) and drive either induction or repression accordingly, downregulation of GRE-associated transcripts does not by itself imply reduced GR activity. Therefore, the direction of GR signaling cannot be inferred from target gene expression alone, and functional validation of altered glucocorticoid signaling will require dedicated studies. However, the PAB model only partially reproduces this human signature ( NR3C1  targets unchanged), limiting its utility for studying RV glucocorticoid biology. Because  FKBP5  loss is observed across both tissue-resident and circulating-origin lineages, the underlying signal could reflect either local microenvironmental modulation of glucocorticoid responsiveness or systemic axis perturbation. Distinguishing these possibilities will require dedicated experimental designs.  The endothelial expansion seen in pRV/RVF across adult human, pediatric human and mice is somewhat unusual among heart failure transcriptomic studies but has been reported in the context of ischemic left ventricular cardiomyopathy  11  . We hypothesize that this reflects coronary microvascular adaptation to RV-specific hemodynamics (a thin-walled chamber perfused throughout systole as well as diastole), driving compensatory capillary/arterial expansion to maintain oxygen delivery in the setting of pressure loading, with adult  MECOM  +  arterial induction and pediatric venous-dominated expansion reflecting different developmental contexts. Phase 2 angiopoietin axis destabilization ( ANGPT2 ,  MYC ,  ADAMTS1 ) suggests that this initially compensatory vascular response transitions toward destabilization at decompensation. Functional validation will require perfusion imaging, vascular casting or interventional EC studies.  More broadly, mouse PAB reproduces the hemodynamic burden of human RVF and converges with human RVF in terms of metabolic and structural programs: suppression of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes, reduced respiratory capacity, cardiomyocyte fetal gene reactivation, endothelial expansion and progressive fibrosis. However, it diverges in immune and hormonal programs, most notably myeloid antigen presentation (MHC-II/ CIITA ) and glucocorticoid signaling and in finer features such as the arterial-biased endothelial expansion seen in mice. The model is, therefore, well suited to studying RV metabolic and fibrotic remodeling but should be applied cautiously to immune or glucocorticoid pathways.  Our atlas can be placed directly against previous cross-chamber and cross-etiology studies. In the NF human heart, the right and left ventricles are nearly transcriptionally identical. The four-chamber atlas of Tucker et al.  16   reported only approximately 24 genes differentially expressed between the ventricles, versus more than 1,000 for each atrial−ventricular contrast, implying that the RV-specific programs we resolve in failure are disease emergent rather than reflections of baseline chamber identity. Against the matched failing-LV/DCM atlas of Koenig et al.  10  , the failing RV and LV share a substantial core transcriptional program (mitochondrial suppression, cytoskeletal remodeling and immune activation)  10 , 12 , 15   with RV-specific divergence in focal programs such as glucocorticoid axis loss and reduced inflammasome induction. A rat pulmonary-artery-banding (RV) versus aortic-banding (LV) model likewise shows broadly overlapping ventricular transcriptomes at baseline (approximately 91% shared) but a distinct, stronger RV disease response, together with a conserved secreted/matrix right-heart-failure signature of approximately 50 genes spanning rat PAB and human chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH)  55  . Notably, isolated afterload modeling argues that RVF and LVF are largely distinct: only 2.2% of human LVF genes overlap the rat PAB regulated set  55  . Our predominantly LVF secondary cohort is the informative exception: its RVF shares the broad cardiomyopathic core of the failing LV, which we attribute to the common myocardial and systemic substrate of LVF-associated RVF rather than to the isolated afterload that drives the RV-versus-LV divergence seen in the banding model.  These comparisons carry translational implications. The shared core molecular pathology between LVF-associated RVF and LVF suggests that the clinical failure of LV-directed guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) in isolated RVF  9   reflects engagement of non-cardiac targets, biomechanical context, chamber geometry or upstream hemodynamic triggers rather than fundamentally divergent molecular pathways. Combined with a parallel plasma LTBP-2 biomarker study  56  , the fibrosis-related RV transcripts identified here may eventually serve as biomarkers of RV remodeling. Overall, the multi-lineage microenvironmental remodeling that we identify nominates anti-fibrotic strategies (notably, TGFBR3), immunomodulatory approaches and direct mitochondrial functional support as plausible RV-specific therapeutic avenues.  Our study has limitations. The snRNA-seq cohort ( n  = 11), although among the largest for human RV, remains modest. We address this through the larger bulk cohort ( n  = 142) and cross-platform concordance for key claims. Xenium was available for  n  = 3 per group, limiting CellChat inference, and is restricted to the 477-gene panel, so off-panel claims (notably,  POSTN ,  FKBP5 ,  TGFBR3  and  MLIP ) rest on bulk and snRNA-seq alone. Also, the phase 2 signal is quantitatively limited across platforms. Endothelial EndoMT and cardiomyocyte reactivation programs will require targeted functional validation.    Methods   Ethical compliance  This study complies with all relevant ethical regulations.
