CosMx Sample Preparation and Data Generation CosMx SMI profiling was carried out on breast and prostate tumor FFPE blocks, ID HT704B1-S1H3Fp1 and HT891Z1-S2H3Fp1, using CosMx 1K and 6K Discovery Panel respectively. FFPE blocks were sectioned at 5 µm thickness and placed on VWR Superfrost Plus Micro slides. Slides were deparaffinized via a couple of xylene and ethanol washes prior to heat-induced target retrieval at 100°C for 15 minutes using 1× Target Retrieval Solution. The tissue sections were digested using 5 µg/mL Proteinase K incubated at  40°C for 30 minutes in a hybridization chamber. Slides were washed twice with 1× PBS and incubated in 0.0004% fiducials diluted in 2× SSCT for 5 minutes at room temperature in the dark. Excess fiducials were rinsed from the slides with 1× PBS and tissue sections were fixed with 10% neutral buffered formalin (NBF) for 1  minute at room temperature. Fixed samples were rinsed twice with Stop Buffer, composed of 0.1  mol/L glycine and 0.1  mol/L Tris-base in DEPC H 2 O, and once with 1× PBS for 5 minutes each before blocking with 100 mmol/L NHS acetate in CosMX NHS acetate buffer (Bruker Spatial Biology) for 15 minutes at room temperature. The sections were then rinsed with 2× SSC for 5 minutes and incubated with hybridization solution (Denatured CosMx RNA Probe mixes) on the hybridization chamber at 37°C for 18 hours. After 18 hours, washes with stringent solution (50% formamide in 2× SSC) and 2× SSC buffer were performed to rinse of excess probes. Nuclear staining was carried out for 15 minutes in the dark in the hybridization chamber, and slides were washed with 1× PBS to remove excess stain. Cell segmentation was carried using cell segmentation mix (CD292/B2M), marker mix (PanCK/CD45), and a la carte mix (CD68) for 1 hour at room temperature in the hybridization chamber and the samples were rinsed thrice with 1× PBS and twice with 2× SSC. The Flow cells with unique barcodes were assembled on the slides, which were then loaded on CosMx SMI, running on software v1.3.1, following instructions provided in CosMx SMI Instrument User Manual (Man-10161-02-1). The Raw data and flatfiles generated were downloaded from the AtoMx platform for subsequent analysis following the manufacturer’s guidelines. https://github.com/Nanostring-Biostats/CosMxDACustomModules . Tissue Clearing, Staining, and Imaging for 3D Lightsheet Tissue was obtained through the WU Solid Tumor Tissue Bank from surgical patients after written informed consent with the aid of an attending pathologist. Briefly, each tissue block is documented by photographing, weighing, and recording a description of anatomical landmarks and is further subdivided up into 4 to 6 smaller tissue blocks. Each of the smaller blocks is then subdivided into three pieces approximately 6 mm × 6 mm × 2 mm each and processed as follows: 1) 10% NBF for histologic characterization, e.g. H&E and CODEX; 2) snap-freezing in liquid nitrogen or embedding in OCT for genomic analysis; and 3) fixation in 4% paraformaldehyde for lightsheet. The piece that is designated for lightsheet is washed in PBS after 24 hours and is then ready for tissue clearing. For tissue clearing, samples were firstly infiltrated with SHIELD polyepoxy ( 93 ) for 6 days with constant agitation at 4 C, subsequently polymerized at 37°C for 24 hours, and then delipidated using a SmartBatch+ ETC active tissue clearing platform (LifeCanvas Technologies). Samples were washed in 1× PBS for 24 hours at room temperature before proceeding to antibody staining and were permeabilized with 1× PBS containing 0.2% Triton X-100 twice for one hour each at room temperature before blocking. Samples were blocked with 6% donkey serum at 37°C with PBS containing 0.2% Triton X-100 and 10% DMSO. After blocking, samples were washed with PBS containing 0.2% Tween-20 plus 10 µg/mL heparin twice at 37°C and then incubated with fluorescently conjugated antibodies for 4 days at 37°C. Antibodies included AF488-conjugated anti-CK5 (AB_2893023) and AF594-conjugated anti-PanCK (AB_3741555). All antibodies were diluted at 1:200 in PBS containing 0.2% Tween-20, 5% DMSO, 3% donkey serum, and 10 µg/mL heparin. On day 3, Hoechst was added to the solution at 1:10,000. After staining, samples were washed at least 5 times in PBS/0.2% Tween-20/10 µg/mL heparin, exchanging the solution every 1 hour. After staining, samples were refractive index–matched to 1.52 using EasyIndex RI matching media (LifeCanvas Technologies). Whole-sample images were acquired on a Miltenyi Ultra Microscope Blaze Gaussian lightsheet platform using a 4×/0.35 MI PLAN objective. Datasets were stitched together using Stitchy (Translucence Biosystems) and visualized using Bitplane Imaris 10.1.1 (Oxford Instruments). The lateral resolution of lightsheet microscopy can be estimated as the emission wavelength divided by two times the numerical aperture, yielding 0.741 μm for the CK5 channel and 0.881 μm for the PanCK channel. Because the structures of interest do not require sampling at the theoretical resolution limit, we used a lateral sampling interval of 1.62 μm. The axial resolution of our FLSM setup is determined by the thickness of the light sheet (7 μm) and was sampled at the Nyquist frequency. CODEX Preparation and Imaging Carrier-free monoclonal or polyclonal anti-human antibodies were purchased (Supplementary Table S4) and verified using IF staining in multiple channels. After the screening, antibodies were conjugated using the Akoya Antibody Conjugation Kit (Akoya Biosciences, SKU 7000009) with a specific barcode (Akoya Biosciences) assigned according to the IF staining results. Several common markers were directly purchased through Akoya Biosciences. Keyence protocol: CODEX staining and imaging were performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions (CODEX User Manual - Rev C). Briefly, 5 μm FFPE sections were placed on APTES (Sigma, #440140) coated coverslips and baked at 60°C overnight before deparaffinization. The next day, tissues were incubated in xylene, rehydrated in ethanol, and washed in ddH2O before antigen retrieval with TE buffer, pH 9 (Genemed, #10-0046), in boiling water for 10 minutes in a rice cooker. The tissues were then blocked using the blocking buffer (CODEX staining kit SKU 7000008) and stained with the marker antibody panel to a volume of 200 µL for 3 hours at room temperature in a humidified chamber. Imaging of the CODEX multicycle experiment was performed using a Keyence fluorescence microscope (model BZ-X810) equipped with a Nikon CFI Plan Apo λ 20x/0.75 objective, the CODEX instrument (Akoya Biosciences), and CODEX Instrument Manager (CIM; Akoya Biosciences). The raw images were then stitched and processed using the CODEX processor (Akoya Biosciences). After multiplex imaging was completed, H&E staining was performed on the same tissue. Panels for each codex section are listed in Supplementary Table S4. Phenocycler protocol: The immunostaining procedure was conducted using the PhenoCycler-Fusion sample kit (Akoya, cat. #7000017) following Akoya’s user guide. Selected FFPE samples were sectioned at 5 μm thickness, placed on charged slides (Fisherbrand, cat. #1255015), and dried at 42°C on a heat block. Prior to deparaffinization, the slides were baked at 65°C overnight. Deparaffinization was done using two times Xylene followed by rehydration in a graded series of ethanol (two times 100%, 90%, 70%, 50%, and 30%) and two times Milli-Q water (ddH2O). Antigen retrieval was performed for prostate cancer in 1× Tris-EDTA (pH 9) using a rice cooker for 18 minutes, and for breast cancer tissue for 20 minutes. After equilibrating to room temperature, sample slides were washed twice in the hydration buffer and then equilibrated in the staining buffer for 30 minutes. Subsequently, slides were incubated with all antibodies diluted in 200 µL staining buffer containing N Blocker, G Blocker, J Blocker, and S Blocker for 3 hours at room temperature in a humidified chamber. After staining, slides were washed twice in the staining buffer and fixed with 1.6% paraformaldehyde in the storage buffer for 10 minutes. Samples slides are then washed three times in PBS and incubated in ice-cold methanol for 5 minutes, followed by three times washes in PBS and incubation in the final fixative solution for 20 minutes. After three additional PBS washes, slides were stored in a storage buffer for a maximum of 3 days before imaging. The reporters were prepared following Akoya’s PhenoCycler-Fusion user guide and dispensed into a 96-well black plate. The experimental template for the PhenoCycler-Fusion Run was designed using Akoya’s PhenoCycler Experiment Designer software. Details about antibodies used for each codex run are available in Supplementary Table S4. The experimental run was executed using Akoya’s Fusion 1.0.8, and final images were generated on the PhenoImager Fusion microscope using default settings. 3D Serial Sectioning Procedure FFPE blocks were chilled on ice for at least 20 minutes before sectioning. Tissue was cut at a thickness of 5 μm to capture the full surface of the sample, continuing until the regions of interest were fully included. Once the optimal surface exposure and section quality were achieved, tissue ribbons were cut continuously until the tissue was exhausted or the required number of sections was obtained. The sections were labeled sequentially (U1, U2, U3, etc.) during the sectioning process. Upon completing the sectioning, the ribbons were gently placed on a clean surface and divided into smaller ribbons, each consisting of 8 to 10 sections. These smaller ribbons were slowly transferred to a water bath, ensuring they floated in a line without folds or breaks. Any section that folded or broke prior to slide mounting was discarded, whereas its section number was retained. The sections were carefully loaded one by one onto regular glass slides, Visium slides, or Xenium slides in the planned sequence. Subsequently, the slides were processed according to spatial platform–specific protocols. Section retention for each sample can be viewed in Supplementary Table S7. 3D Serial Section Registration Prior to registration, imaging data underwent the following transformations. Multiplex, Xenium, and CosMx images were converted to grayscale images of the nuclear intensity channel. The images were then downscaled by a factor of 5 before key point selection. For Visium and Visium HD, H&E images (also downsampled by a factor of 5) were used for keypoint selection. For registration, we used the BigWarp tool (arXiv:1511.01154), which was packaged in the Fiji/ImageJ software application. To register each collection of serial images, we use the first serial section as the fixed image and the second image as the moving image. After the second image is warped to the first image, the second image is used as the fixed image for the transformation of the third image. Key point registration proceeds in this fashion for all images in the serial section experiment. A total of 4 to 10 key points were selected per image transformation. Once key points were selected, a moving field was exported from BigWarp for each image transformation (thin plate spline). This dense displacement field (DDF) was then upscaled by a factor of 5 so it could be used to warp the full-resolution image data. The DDF was then also used to register corresponding point-based data (transcript locations for CosMx and Xenium, spot locations for Visium, and grid locations for Visium HD). The code used for registration is available at https://github.com/ding-lab/mushroom/blob/main/README.md#manuscript-materials . Breast 3D Connectivity Analysis We constructed 3D region volumes to analyze connectivity of serial section breast cancer cases (HT704B1, HT206B1, and HT397B1) using Xenium, CODEX, and H&E sections in a three-part process: (i) protein abundance prediction from H&E slides, (ii) automated epithelial region annotation, and (iii) interconnected region reconstruction. Due to gaps between Xenium and CODEX sections, we decided to fill in these gaps using H&E sections. Because H&E has no inherent marker for epithelial cells, we trained a deep learning model to predict marker abundance using H&E as input. To enable volumetric reconstruction of epithelial connectivity across serial sections, we used a deep learning model to approximate epithelial marker abundance in intervening H&E sections. This model was used exclusively for epithelial region segmentation to support 3D connectivity analysis. For training, we used an adjacent CODEX and H&E section to train a separate model for each of the three serial section cases. At inference time, the input to the model was an H&E section, and the output was protein abundance for certain CODEX markers (Supplementary Table S8). Model architecture, training methodology, and inference time mechanics are described below. Architecture and training parameters can be found in Supplementary Table S8. We use a U-net (arXiv:1505.04597) with a ResNet-18 backbone (arXiv:1512.03385, arXiv:2110.00476) followed by a prediction head composed of 2D convolutions for protein abundance prediction. We train a separate model for each case. For training, we select adjacent CODEX and H&E sections. The images are preprocessed in the following manner. First, each channel of the H&E and CODEX image is normalized by mean and standard deviation. Natively, these images are too large to pass through the model, so they must be tiled for training and inference. As such, we shred each image into 256 × 256 pixel tiles. However, when using tiles we remove the morphologic context of the area outside the tile that may be useful for protein abundance prediction. Appending additional regional context to a tile is one way to remedy this issue ( 94 ). To give each tile context of morphology outside its immediate surroundings, we also train additional Unets in parallel with their input being zoomed-out, low resolution (2×, 4×, 8×, and 16×) views centered on the given tile. After the forward pass through each Unet, the resulting activations are then concatenated prior to input into the prediction head. With this procedure, we are able to give each high-resolution tile regional morphologic context helpful to protein prediction. The model was implemented using the Pytorch Python library (arXiv:1912.01703). During training, we randomly select image tiles from a uniform distribution across the 2D section. Each tile is then horizontally or vertically flipped with 50% probability. Most serial H&E sections were imaged in the same batch to minimize batch effects across slides. As such, we did not perform other color-based image augmentations to the input image tiles. Following the forward pass through the Unet and prediction head, we are left with a C × W × H tensor in which height and width are the same shape as the input image tile and c is the number of CODEX proteins being predicted. For model loss, we use mean squared error (MSE) between the predicted values and the ground truth protein abundance, in which the ground truth values are the protein abundance in the CODEX section adjacent to the H&E section. Each model was trained for 640,000 steps with a batch size of 64. Following training, we performed model inference over all H&E serials sections, which generated protein abundance values for every H&E section. We then used expression of epithelial marker genes to identify epithelial regions (encompassing normal, DCIS, and IDC morphology) in an automated fashion. First, we selected epithelial marker genes for each sample based on what genes and proteins were available in a given Xenium or CODEX panel. First, we tiled all inputs to a resolution of 15 μm per pixel. To tile Xenium data, the area covered by the Xenium section was split into 15-µm grid squares. We then summed the aggregate expression counts of all cells within each grid square. For CODEX and H&E, we rescaled the images to a resolution of 15 μm per pixel. We selected a 15-µm tiling resolution because the primary objective was region-level epithelial segmentation. Given minor registration uncertainty and occasional missing serial sections, volumetric continuity is fundamentally constrained by z-axis sampling density rather than in-plane resolution. The 15-µm resolution provided an appropriate balance between epithelial segmentation accuracy and consistency with intersection spacing. A cutoff value was then defined via manual inspection for each of these markers in a case-independent fashion. The cutoff value was then applied in the following way to segment epithelial regions. First, all pixels with a value greater than the cutoff value were considered epithelial pixels. Then a binary hole filling algorithm was applied to fill holes in regions, for this we use the scipy.ndimage.binary_fill_holes function from the scipy Python package (arXiv:1907.10121). Interconnected areas of epithelial pixels were then identified by constructing a N × H × W array in which N is the total number of Xenium, CODEX, and H&E sections for a case. Each voxel was either positive (epithelial) or negative (nonepithelial). Adjacent epithelial voxels were considered connected. We used the skimage.morphology.label function from the scikit-image Python package ( 95 ) to then identify connected 3D regions. Manual Annotation of Interconnected Epithelial Regions We use manual region annotation to label interconnected epithelial regions for connectivity analysis and 3D ROI path construction. First, we generate an OME-TIFF for each region of interest. The OME-TIFF stores a stack of pseudo-color images representing each serial section. The OME-TIFF was then viewed with the QuPath ( 96 ) image viewing platform. Manual epithelial region annotation was then performed in QuPath. Annotated region coordinates were then exported in GeoJSON format ( https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7946 ) for downstream visualization and analysis. Selection and Annotation of 3D Serial Section ROIs ROIs were selected based on areas of region morphology. Searching for interconnected morphology was conducted with the Imaris 3D image viewing platform. We generated pseudo-color images for each serial section as described in the manual annotation section above, with these images then being converted to an .ims file using Imaris, following which we were able to view each pseudo-color image to identify interconnected epithelial regions undergoing noninvasive to invasive transition (normal, HGPIN, and GP3 in prostate; DCIS, MI, and IDC in breast). Cross sections of these transitioning regions were then annotated using the approach described in “Manual Annotation of Interconnected Epithelial Regions” (Supplementary Tables S9 and S10). Gene Discovery Overview We selected ROIs that had interconnected noninvasive to invasive morphology. Each 2D cross section of the interconnected structure was segmented to enable tracing of the continuity and transitions between progression states, enabling a more detailed understanding of the spatial and molecular dynamics of the progression within a singular structure. This analysis would not be possible with traditional, nonserial 2D image sections. To identify genes differentially expressed in IDC compared with DCIS, we leveraged both 2D and 3D ST datasets (Xenium, CosMx, Visium, and Visium HD). For 2D cohort-level gene discovery, we used both automated and manual annotation methods on ST sections. Automated differential gene expression discovery was performed in Xenium, CosMx, and Visium HD sections. This involved identifying epithelial regions and assessing myoepithelial intensity using basal layer markers, which were then correlated to gene expression (see “2D automated gene discovery”), allowing the identification of genes associated with myoepithelial integrity (Supplementary Table S11). To supplement the automated approach, we also implemented a manual workflow in which areas of DCIS ( n = 5+) and IDC ( n = 5+) morphology were randomly manually selected in Visium sections (Supplementary Table S12; see “2D manual gene discovery”). DEG identification was subsequently performed based on these manual annotations. For 3D ROI-level gene discovery, we identified DEGs specific to 3D ROIs to characterize gene expression changes across progression states within a single interconnected epithelial structure (Supplementary Tables S13 and S14). For 3D gene discovery, we use two approaches: morphology-based and path-based (see “3D gene discovery”). Briefly, for morphology-based, regions were annotated (DCIS, MI, or IDC in breast; normal, HGPIN, or GP3 in prostate) and expression differences between groups were quantified with the Student t test and fold change. In path-based discovery, regression was run on expression values for each region along the path of the transitioning epithelial structure. Together, this dual-layered approach provided a comprehensive view of the gene expression landscape, revealing key molecular pathways and biological processes involved in invasive transition. Manual curation and visual inspection further refined the identification of genes specific to luminal epithelial cells and linked to breast cancer progression. 2D Automated Gene Discovery We used both manual and automated methods for 2D DEG discovery. For automated discovery, we first annotated epithelial regions across Xenium, CosMx, and Visium HD sections with invasive and noninvasive morphology in the dataset. For Xenium and CosMx, the process consisted of first tiling all inputs to the same resolution: 10 µm per pixel. We then identified epithelial regions in an automated fashion. First, all tiled sections were normalized by standard deviation at the gene level. An epithelial mask was then constructed by thresholding each grid for EPCAM >1.0. This mask was then run through a hole-filling algorithm to fill in gaps present due to transcript sparsity and necrosis. All positive grids (i.e., pixels) were considered epithelial pixels. We then used the skimage.morphology.label function from the scikit-image Python package ( 95 ) to identify areas of connected pixels. Interconnected pixels with a tiled area of less than 10 were filtered out. These remaining areas of pixels were considered epithelial regions. For Visium HD, we had two annotation methods based on the data available. For sections that were included in the 3D stacked serial section dataset, we used outputs from the U-net model from “Breast 3D Connectivity Analysis” as epithelial “expression”. We then generated epithelial masks in an identical manner to the previous paragraph. For Visium HD sections that were not part of the stacked 3D dataset, we underwent the same procedure as Xenium and CosMx with the following changes: the normalized expression image was Gaussian-blurred (alpha = 5), and EPCAM was thresholded at 0.1. The expression image was Gaussian-blurred to account for the additional sparsity introduced by tiling with 2-µm Visium HD squares. Following identification of regions, we quantified feature expression for three areas of the region: the region itself (i.e., luminal cells), the region boundary (i.e., basal layer), and the area surrounding the region (i.e., TME). Masks were generated to identify pixels belonging to each of these areas and were defined in the following ways. The “region” mask is the same as the epithelial mask previously described but shrank by 10 μm. The “boundary” mask was defined by the area between the epithelial mask and the epithelial mask expanded by 20 μm. The “TME” mask was defined by expanding the epithelial region 40 μm and subtracting the “boundary” and “region” masks. Region area masks were not allowed to expand into another region’s area. The skimage.segmentation.expand_labels function from the scikit-image ( 95 ) Python package was used to expand epithelial regions. Expression was then quantified for each region, boundary, and TME mask. With expression values in hand, we were able to correlate feature expression within regions (“region” mask) to boundary (“boundary” mask) expression of basal layer markers. A positive correlation value for a feature in a section indicates that for regions within that section, intra-region expression of that gene is associated with higher expression of basal layer markers in the region boundary (i.e., the genes expression is associated with regions having a more intact basal cell layer). Negative correlations indicate the opposite association. The same metric was also obtained for the area outside regions (“TME” mask) in order to identify TME genes associated with region basal layer expression. We defined the TME as the peritumoral region extending 100 µm from the epithelial boundary. This distance captures stromal and immune cells within biologically relevant interaction range of tumor epithelium, consistent with spatial oncology studies that define cellular neighborhoods on the scale of tens to hundreds of μm ( 97 – 99 ). A 100-µm margin balances inclusion of the immediate invasive niche while minimizing incorporation of distant stromal regions unlikely to directly influence epithelial transition. Due to marker absence in panels between and within spatial platforms, the same basal layer marker could not be used for every section. The basal layer marker for a section was determined by selecting a gene out of the following list of markers: ( KRT5 , KRT14 , KRT15 , LAMB3 , and ACTA2 ). For each sample, we iterated through the marker list, and once a basal marker gene was found to be in that sample, we used that gene as the marker gene for that sample. Additionally, for TNBC cases, in which the cell of origin tends to be basal, we used ACTA2 as the basal layer marker. Supplementary Table S11 contains correlation values for this analysis. 2D Manual Gene Discovery We also used manual annotation for Visium sections, in which resolution of expression is limited and not amenable to the techniques used in 2D automated gene discovery. For this, we implemented a manual workflow where a minimum of five areas each of normal, DCIS, and IDC in breast—or normal, HGPIN, and GP3+ in prostate—morphology were randomly manually annotated. Mean feature expression was then calculated for each area, and the Student t test was used to quantify differences between different morphologies. Annotated barcodes (Supplementary Table S12) and comparison statistics (Supplementary Table S11) can be found in the supplement. 3D Gene Discovery We further strengthened our gene discovery approach with multiplatform, 3D serial section DEG discovery. With this approach, we were able to quantify gene expression changes throughout a single region as it transitioned from noninvasive to invasive morphology. For this we use two methods, morphology group–based and path-based comparisons. For both approaches, we used regions annotated as described in “Manual Annotation of Interconnected Epithelial Regions”. Expression and correlation values can be found in supplementary Tables S13 and S14, respectively. For morphology group–based discovery, regions were annotated for morphology (DCIS, MI, or IDC in breast; normal, HGPIN, or GP3 in prostate), and mean gene expression was calculated for each region. We then, on a data type–specific basis, used the Student t test and fold change to quantify differences between morphology groups where possible. Due to variation in rate and location of region transition, the same spatial platform did not always capture each morphologic state for every interconnected region. Fold change was calculated as [( b + 1) − ( a + 1)]/( a + 1), in which a and b are arrays of expression values associated with different morphology groups. For path-based discovery, we calculated a single correlation value across multiple spatial platforms for each interconnected region. First, expression values for each data type were z-scaled within each data type. We then ran a linear regression on the scaled expression values for each Xenium, CosMx, and Visium HD cross-section in the transitioning region. Values were ordered from least invasive end of the interconnect region to the most invasive. As such, positive correlations indicate increased expression toward the invasive end of the region, whereas negative values indicate the opposite, with increased expression in less-invasive areas of the region. 3D TAM Proximity Analysis For the six Xenium sections from sample HT704B1, we performed a 3D proximity analysis to evaluate the spatial relationship between macrophages and epithelial regions. First, TAMs were subtyped into two populations: SPP1 + TAMs and MS4A6A + TAMs. Cell annotation was based on transcript detection using the following criteria. A cell was classified as an SPP1 + TAM if it contained at least one transcript of any macrophage marker ( CD68 , CD163 , CSF1R , or CD14 ), at least one transcript of SPP1 , and zero EPCAM transcripts. Similarly, a cell was classified as an MS4A6A + TAM if it contained at least one transcript of any macrophage marker ( CD68 , CD163 , CSF1R , or CD14 ), at least one transcript of MS4A6A , and zero EPCAM transcripts. Next, we computed the shortest 3D distance from each TAM to the nearest epithelial region using spatial coordinates across all sections. For each epithelial region, we calculated a basal-layer intensity score, defined as the z-scored transcript counts of basal-layer boundary markers described in the “2D Automated Gene Discovery” “Methods” section. Higher basal-layer intensity scores correspond to regions with stronger basal integrity, consistent with less invasive DCIS morphology, whereas lower scores indicate reduced basal integrity characteristic of more invasive IDC regions. This approach assigns each TAM the basal-layer intensity score of its nearest epithelial region, providing a quantitative measure of the invasiveness of the epithelial environment in which each TAM resides. IF Validation Immunostaining was performed as described ( 100 ). FFPE blocks were sectioned at 5 µm thickness and placed on Superfrost Plus slides and baked at 60°C overnight before deparaffinization. The next day, tissues were deparaffinized in xylene, rehydrated in ethanol, and washed in ddH2O before heat-induced antigen retrieval with 0.1 mmol/L Tris-EDTA buffer pH9 (#NB900-62085, Novus) for 10 minutes using a steamer. These slides were incubated with 100 mmol/L glycine for 2 × 10 minutes and a blocking solution (5% inactivated normal donkey serum and 10 mg/mL BSA) for 1 hour at room temperature. Subsequently slides were incubated with primary antibodies in a humidified chamber overnight at 4°C. After washing with PBST 3 × 5 minutes, samples were incubated with secondary antibodies for 1 hour at room temperature and washed with PBST 4 × 5 minutes. After incubation with Hoechst for 5 minutes, the slides were washed again in PBST for 5 minutes and mounted with VectaMount AQ Aqueous Mounting Medium (#H-5501-60; Southern Biotech). Primary antibodies used were from Abcam: rabbit monoclonal anti-ANPEP (AB_10866195;1:100), rabbit polyclonal anti-ALDH1A3 (AB_2937054;1:100), rabbit polyclonal anti-FASN (AB_732316,1:100), and rabbit monoclonal anti-GDF15 (AB_3099455, 1:100); LSBio: rabbit polyclonal anti-EPHA6 (AB_3741541; 1:100); Life Technologies: mouse monoclonal anti-PanCK (AB_10942225;1:200) and anti-CK5 (AB_2538529, 1:200) antibodies and Alexa Fluor 488-, 594-, and 647-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:1,000); and R&D Biosytems: goat polyclonal anti–E-cadherin (AB_355568;1:100). The fluorescence images were obtained using Keyence Fluorescence Microscope (BZ-X810; Keyence). Normal, precancer, and cancer regions were annotated using Napari, and average intensities were calculated within each region. Breast and Prostate Cancer Proliferation and Migration Assays Human breast and prostate cancer cell lines ETCC-006 ( CVCL_6G19 ), ETCC-010 ( CVCL_6G22 ), and PC3 ( CVCL_E2RM ) were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) in (March, 2022). Cell line profiling was not performed by the authors following receipt from the ATCC. Cells were used for experiments within 10 passages after thawing and were not maintained in culture for longer than 2 months. Cells were routinely tested for Mycoplasma contamination using the MycoAlert Mycoplasma Detection Kit (Lonza, #LT07-318), and the most recent test was performed in (August, 2025), with negative results. Cells were cultured in RPMI-1640 medium (Gibco, #11875093) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Gibco, #16140071) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco, #15140122) and maintained at 37°C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO 2 . For prostate cancer experiments, we initially screened four commonly used prostate cancer cell lines for expression of the candidate genes ( GDF15 , FASN , ALDH1A3 , and ANPEP ). Among these, only PC3 cells expressed all four genes and were therefore selected for subsequent functional assays (Supplementary Fig. S11). To knock down the expression of the target gene ( MGP and PLAT in breast cancer cells and GDF15 , ANPEP , ALDH1A3 , and FASN in prostate cancer cell), lentiviral particles encoding specific shRNA as well as control shRNA were purchased from Sigma using the pLKO.1 vector. Cells were seeded in six-well plates and transduced with lentivirus in the presence of 10 μg/mL polybrene (Sigma-Aldrich, #TR-1003-G). After 48 hours, cells were selected using 10 μg/mL puromycin (Sigma-Aldrich, #P8833) for 7 days to establish stable knockdown cell lines. Cells surviving puromycin selection were expanded and used for downstream experiments within five passages. Knockdown efficiency was confirmed by RT-qPCR. The shRNA sequence for MGP and PLAT was GCGGTAGTAACTTTGTGTTAT and CAAGGTTTACACAGCACAGAA, respectively. GDF15, FASN, ALDH1A3, and ANPEP shRNA target sequence was CCGGATACTCACGCCAGAAGT, CATGGAGCGTATCTGTGAGAA, GCTGTATTAGAACCCTCAGAT, and ACCAGTACAGCGAGGTTAATG, respectively. Total RNA from cell lines was extracted using RNA extraction Kit (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. RNA concentration and purity were determined using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer. One microgram of total RNA was reverse transcribed using a cDNA synthesis kit (Themo Fisher Scientific, High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit with RNase Inhibitor, #4374966). qPCR was performed using SYBR Green Master Mix (BIO-RAD, iTaq Universal SYBR Green Supermix, #1725121) on a QuantStudio or ABI 7500 system. Relative gene expression was calculated using the 2 −ΔΔCt method, with ACTB and GAPDH as the internal control. The primer sequence for MGP was TCCGAGAACGCTCTAAGCCT; GCAAAGTCTGTAGTCATCACAGG. The primer sequence for PLAT was AGCGAGCCAAGGTGTTTCAA; CTTCCCAGCAAATCCTTCGGG. The primer sequence for ACTB was CATGTACGTTGCTATCCAGGC; CTCCTTAATGTCACGCACGAT. The primer for GAPDH was purchased from Integrated DNA Technologies (Ref #580480971; 580480972). The primer sequence for FASN was TTCTACGGCTCCACGCTCTTCC; GAAGAGTCTTCGTCAGCCAGGA, and that for GDF15 was GTTAGCCAAAGACTGCCACTG; CCTTGAGCCCATTCCACA. The primer sequence for ALDH1A3 was TGGATCAACTGCTACAACGC; CACTTCTGTGTATTCGGCCA. The primer sequence for ANPEP was GACCAAAGTAAAGCGTGGAATCG; TCTCAGCGTCACCCGGTAG. Cell proliferation was assessed using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8; Dojindo). Cells (2,000–4,000 per well) were seeded in 96-well plates in triplicate. At indicated time points (e.g., 0, 24, 48, 72, 96 and 120 hours), 10 μL of CCK-8 solution was added to each well and incubated for 2 hours at 37°C. Absorbance at 450 nm was measured using a microplate reader (BioTek or Thermo). Normal control, MGP -KD (knockdown), PLAT -KD, GDF15 -KD, FASN -KD, ALDH1A3 -KD, and ANPEP -KD cells were seeded in six-well plates and grown to about 100% confluence. A straight scratch was made using a sterile 200-μL pipette tip across the cell monolayer. Detached cells were removed by washing with PBS, and fresh serum-free medium was supplemented. Images were captured at 0 hours and after 24 hours using a light microscope (×5 magnification). The wound area was measured using ImageJ software, and migration was quantified as the percentage of wound closure. evidence_text:
Weighted sliced inverse regression for scalable supervised dimensionality reduction of spatial transcriptomics data. With the rise of spatially resolved transcriptomics biotechnologies, performing spatially-aware analysis of the resulting data is crucial to maximise advances in biological understanding. Dimensionality reduction is a first step in most analyses of spatial transcriptomics data, and common approaches that preserve total variation of gene expression features do not usually preserve biologically meaningful spatial variation. To this end, we develop weighted sliced inverse regression (wSIR), a sufficient dimension reduction technique that aims to retain the predictive power of the spatial coordinates. wSIR is applicable to multiple distinct spatial transcriptomic datasets and is highly scalable, with over 100, 000 cells processed in under two minutes on a standard laptop. The feature loadings are interpretable, and new non-spatial data can be projected into wSIR's low-dimensional space for downstream analyses. We examine wSIR's performance and demonstrate its biological relevance through two case studies in human breast cancer and mouse early embryonic development. Introduction  Spatial transcriptomics is becoming a widespread method for profiling hundreds to thousands of genes at single-cell resolution in their spatial context for a variety of tissues  1  . There is great potential to uncover the complexity of tissue organisation and discover new biological aspects in normal processes and the emergence of disease. Current analysis of spatial transcriptomics data has emerged primarily as an extension of the last 5–8 years of single-cell transcriptomics research ( https://www.scrna-tools.org/ ), with several key analytical steps often borrowed from single-cell analysis, including normalisation, filtering and dimensionality reduction techniques. Dimensionality reduction, in particular, is a crucial step in analysing complex high-dimensional data, including single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, as several other downstream analysis steps rely on this  2 – 4  . For example, clustering of cells is typically performed using graph-based approaches on low-dimensional embeddings rather than the original gene expression matrix to avoid the curse of dimensionality. As such, effective and appropriate dimensionality reduction of spatial transcriptomics data is an important challenge in the analysis of these data.  Despite the rapidly accelerating generation of spatial transcriptomics data, it is not straightforward how to incorporate spatial coordinates and gene expression measurements to form a low-dimensional representation of the data. Popular dimensionality reduction approaches such as principal component analysis (PCA) do not utilise spatial coordinates; it focuses on finding orthogonal linear combinations of the gene expression data to preserve the largest amounts of their total variation. Other classical statistical approaches can be adapted to perform a ‘spatially-aware’ dimensionality reduction, such as partial least squares (PLS) and linear discriminant analysis (LDA). PLS treats spatial coordinates in each dimension as separate responses and may not be well suited to account for the complex spatial associations between the spatial coordinates and the gene expressions. LDA is sensitive to the arbitrary choice of allocation of the spatial coordinates into distinct classes. Given these challenges, new approaches have emerged that aim to integrate gene expression and spatial coordinates to arrive at meaningful dimensionality reduction. Some innovative approaches, such as GraphPCA  5   and SpatialPCA  6  , improve PCA by incorporating an additional step, such as augmenting the PCA objective function with a spatial penalty term, including a cell-cell kernel function, utilising experimental trajectory information, or incorporating PCA into a hierarchical model, respectively. Dimension-Reduction Spatial-Clustering (DR-SC)  7   and PRECAST  8   assume factor-analysis models with low-dimensional embeddings are spatially clustered based on a smooth hidden Markov model. Other approaches have adapted different modelling strategies, such as nonnegative matrix factorisation, to utilise spatial information  9 – 11  . In another line of research, several methods have utilised a dimensionality reduction step to cluster cells or spots in a ‘spatially-aware’ manner, including STAMP  12  , stLearn  13   and FAST  14  . Other approaches used bespoke techniques utilising deep learning to learn from spatial gene expression and images jointly  15  , or exploited higher order interactions to identify clusters of interest  16  . Additionally, some methods are developed to utilise the spatial transcriptomic data as a reference to predict the latent spatial coordinates of scRNA-seq-derived data, such as CellContrast  17   and Tangram  18  .  In statistics research, advances in sufficient dimension reduction (SDR) have emerged in the last few decades. SDR is a technique that enables dimensionality reduction of features so that the ability to predict the response variables is best preserved. Among SDR methods, sliced inverse regression (SIR), which was originally proposed in the seminal paper of ref.   19   is still the most popular due to its simplicity, flexibility and computational efficiency  20  . Despite many developments of SIR to handle complex settings, to the best of our knowledge, SIR has not been adapted to be suitable for single-cell or spatial transcriptomics data. While several approaches have been developed for spatial dimensionality reduction, many are prohibitive in terms of computational scalability and runtime, and are limited in their ability to project new gene expression data into a low-dimensional space.  Given these challenges, we have developed  w eighted  S liced  I nverse  R egression (wSIR), an innovative statistical approach that performs SDR to preserve the association between the gene expressions and the spatial information. wSIR takes into account the slice-slice correlation induced from spatial transcriptomics data, and enables the projection of non-spatial gene expression data into the low-dimensional spaces. Due to its linearity, wSIR is highly scalable and can be applied to massive single-cell spatial transcriptomics datasets across multiple distinct samples. In this paper, we describe the wSIR approach, explore its properties and demonstrate its superior performance compared to other statistical methods. Furthermore, we will also employ wSIR to uncover additional insights from spatial transcriptomics data in two real biological contexts in human breast cancer and mouse development.    Results   Scalable spatially-aware dimensionality reduction with weighted sliced inverse regression (wSIR)  Given the challenges in effectively describing spatial transcriptomics data, we developed a linear sufficient dimension reduction approach named weighted sliced inverse regression (wSIR). Assuming a  n  ×  p  gene expression matrix  X  with  n  samples and  p  features, and a corresponding  n  ×  q  responses  Y , sufficient dimension reduction is a class of statistical techniques that aims to estimate a  d  ≪  p  vector-valued function of the data  f ( X ) so that  Y ⊥ X ∣ f ( X ), that is, that  Y  and  X  are conditionally independent given the reduced data  f ( X ). Sliced inverse regression (SIR), which was invented in ref.   19   is an example of linear sufficient dimension reduction, where  f ( X ) is assumed to be a linear combination of the  X , i.e.  f ( X ) =  X  B  with  B  a  p  ×  d  matrix. Under mild technical conditions, SIR has been shown to be a powerful technique in the area of linear SDR due to its ability to preserve complex and nonlinear patterns within the data [refs.   20 – 22  , among many others]. One important challenge in implementing such an approach to spatial transcriptomics, however, is that SIR does not account for possible spatial relationships among the slices, prompting our development of a novel weight component to SIR to create wSIR (‘Methods’).  Briefly, wSIR takes in spatial transcriptomics data with appropriately normalised, centred and scaled gene expression values, alongside spatial coordinates that can belong to one or more distinct tissues or samples (Fig.  1 a). The observations within each sample are then grouped according to their proximity in physical space into distinct ‘slices’, alongside the corresponding gene expression data (Fig.  1 b). Then, a slice-slice correlation matrix is estimated by taking into account the physical proximity of the centroids of each slice per sample (Fig.  1 c, ‘Methods’), where the closer the two slices are, the higher the corresponding value in the correlation matrix. On each slice, gene expression values are averaged over each gene. Following this step, the slice-mean gene expression and slice-slice correlation matrix are subjected to an eigendecomposition to obtain the eigenvectors, which are finally multiplied by the inverse of the sample covariance matrix of the gene expression to the wSIR direction (loadings). A sample-level scores (embeddings) matrix is then formed by multiplying the original data by the loadings matrix, representing the low-dimensional embedding of the data (Fig.  1 d). This procedure enables the projection of new, unseen, potentially non-spatial data to the same low-dimensional embedding via matrix multiplication. Overall, wSIR enables interpretation of important genes via examination of the loadings matrix, as well as further downstream analysis (such as clustering) on the spatial transcriptomic data, alongside mapping of non-spatial (e.g. scRNA-seq resolved) transcriptomic data to a spatially-informed low-dimensional space. As a linear dimension reduction method, wSIR’s computational cost is comparable to PCA and more scalable than other existing spatially-aware dimension reduction methods (Supplementary Fig.  1 ) that either use a cell–cell adjacency matrix and/or require fitting sophisticated statistical or deep learning models. We generated an input data matrix  X  containing  p  = 20 features and  n  = 500 samples, alongside  q  = 2-dimensional spatial coordinates in Cartesian space corresponding to a rough doughnut shape (Fig.  2 a, left column, Methods). We split features so that some features were (1) uncorrelated with spatial coordinates, (2) some features were correlated with the radial position of the sample and (3) some features were correlated with the angular position of the sample, all with varying degrees of total noise. We then performed other common approaches for supervised or unsupervised dimensionality reduction, including GraphPCA  5  , PLS and PCA. We found that in this simulation, the corresponding scores generated by the first and second wSIR’s directions were highly correlated with the angle and radius, respectively, where, in contrast, GraphPCA and PLS were only able to partially recover the spatial pattern. As expected, PCA did not capture the spatial pattern and rather captured the non-spatial variables that were simulated to have the highest amount of variation (Fig.  2 a). Since the spatial patterns correspond to angle and radius, we conclude that wSIR is capable of prioritising the underlying linear signals in the gene expression data, which encode the non-linear relationship with the spatial positions of each cell. The main tuning parameters of interest are (1) the number of tiles to partition the spatial coordinates, and (2) Alpha ( α ), representing the scaling factor applied to the slice-slice correlation matrix (‘Methods’). We note that for certain selections of these tuning parameters, the wSIR approach becomes equivalent to SIR ( α  = 0) and PCA (i.e. when the number of slices approaches the total number of observations in the dataset). For this exploration, we used two case study datasets from single-cell resolved transcriptomic technologies in mouse development and human breast cancer stemming from seqFISH and 10x Genomics’ Xenium platform, respectively  23 , 24   (‘Methods’). For each combination of these tuning parameters, the quality of the low-dimensional embedding was measured by the bias-corrected distance correlation (BCDC, Methods) between it and the true spatial coordinates. The resulting heatmaps for each dataset (Fig.  2 b, c) show that, overall, wSIR obtains a higher BCDC than SIR, and that a high value of BCDC is maintained for parameter choices deviating from the ‘optimal’ choices. This indicates that the performance of wSIR is relatively robust to the choice of parameters, and that a selection of a sub-optimal combination of parameters is likely to still yield useful results.  We also conducted a sensitivity analysis of wSIR to the slicing mechanisms. By default, slicing is implemented based on a rectangular grid of the spatial coordinates. We implemented two different transformations of this grid, one by rotating it to a certain degree, and the other by shifting it to the right and upward by an amount proportional to the height and width of the smallest rectangle in the original grid. Supplementary Fig.  2  demonstrates that the BCDC between wSIR loadings (with  α  = 4 and  k  = 8) and the true spatial coordinates are robust to both these transformations. Comparisons were based on in-sample performance metrics, as cross-validation was not feasible in this setting: our objective was to project  non-spatial  gene expression data into a spatially informed low-dimensional embedding, with spatial coordinates of the query cells used only for post-hoc accuracy assessment. Existing spatially aware methods do not support such out-of-sample projection and therefore cannot be evaluated on a held-out test set. We found that wSIR consistently resulted in the highest BCDC values when performed on each embryo of the mouse development data and on each sample of the Xenium breast cancer dataset, indicating its ability to preserve spatially relevant patterns from gene expression data (Fig.  2 d, e). When we examined an additional metric of neighbourhood preservation (‘Methods’), by taking the Jaccard index of local neighbourhoods of cells according to physical space and the low-dimensional embeddings, we found that, overall, wSIR was best able to faithfully recapitulate the local neighbourhoods of cells, especially as the sizes of neighbourhoods increased as a percentage of the test sets (Fig.  2 f, g).  We next compared wSIR with popular non-spatial dimensionality reduction methods, including PCA, GraphPCA, LDA, PLS and SIR (i.e. wSIR with  α  = 0). We conducted cross-validation studies to perform the comparison, as all these methods are capable of producing low-dimensional embeddings of gene expressions on a test set without using the spatial coordinates there. For the mouse development dataset, we performed cross-validation by selecting two of the three biological samples as reference and query, and repeating for each of the six combinations (Supplementary Fig.  4 ). For the human breast cancer data, we repeatedly randomly selected subsets of the cells to treat as reference and took the remainder of the cells as query. Following this, we found that wSIR consistently resulted in higher BCDC and higher Jaccard values (Supplementary Fig.  4 ).  Finally, we also examined the performance of wSIR when performed in multiple samples. For the mouse development dataset, we found wSIR has a higher BCDC and higher Jaccard values on a test embryo when trained in two other embryos altogether than when trained in only one embryo (Supplementary Fig.  5 ). Following the wSIR analysis of all the cells belonging to the mouse development dataset, we focused on the cells belonging to the ‘Endothelium’ cell type, as we noticed these cells were especially diverse according to the wSIR low-dimensional embedding (Fig.  3 e), with some cells appearing closer to ‘Cardiomyocytes’ and ‘Allantois’ in the UMAP representation. We subset the Endothelium cells and performed wSIR followed by graph-based clustering (Fig.  3 f), resulting in four identified clusters. Visualising the original locations of these cells indicates that the clusters correspond to distinct anatomical regions, such as the posterior region, which includes the allantois (cluster 1) and the endocardium (cluster 4) (Fig.  3 g). This enables researchers to: (1) identify gene sets with important spatial roles, such as those involved in axial patterning during mouse development, and (2) uncover spatially localised cellular subtypes, such as vascular endothelial subsets arising in distinct anatomical regions. These findings underscore the potential of wSIR as a powerful tool for integrating spatial context into high-dimensional analyses, offering new insights into the spatial organisation of cellular and molecular processes.    Spatial prediction, pseudospace and domain detection approaches are improved by using wSIR  Since we have shown wSIR’s ability to generate low-dimensional embeddings that are useful in uncovering spatial biology, we wondered if wSIR, as a linear dimensionality reduction approach, would be useful as an input into more complex modelling approaches. To examine this, we turned to a popular method, named Tangram  18  , that uses deep learning to map single-cell gene expression data to spatial transcriptomics references. Tangram typically takes in a filtered gene expression matrix as input and returns a prediction of the physical locations of single cells, given a spatial omics reference dataset. Using the mouse development data, we performed Tangram with three input types: (1) gene expression counts, (2) PCA scores and (3) wSIR scores. We used five different metrics to evaluate the performance of the predicted coordinates (‘Methods’). Overall, we found that using wSIR as the input to Tangram resulted in the best performance evidenced by the highest BCDC, Jensen–Shannon divergence, Spearman correlation, the smallest MSE and the shortest run time (Fig.  3 i). Visually, we noticed that predicted coordinates using wSIR aligned well with previously known organisation of cell types in the developing embryo (Fig.  3 j). Overall, this investigation indicates that wSIR is a useful initial analytical step prior to applying other bespoke analyses, and is versatile in the range of downstream applications that can be employed.  We next wondered if wSIR may be useful in uncovering axes of biologically relevant variation in space. To this end, we used a recently published human thymus spatial omics dataset  29   where a continuous cortico-medullary axis (CMA) was defined. The CMA represents a continuous, rather than discrete, shift from tissue areas most associated with the cortex and medulla of the thymus. We used the nine spatial omics-resolved samples to perform wSIR dimension reduction alongside PCA, followed by trajectory ‘pseudospace’ inference using Slingshot  30   (‘Methods’). We observed that both approaches were able to recapitulate the CMA well, with Spearman correlations of 0.39 and 0.22 for wSIR and PCA, respectively (Supplementary Fig.  6 a, b), and fairly close concordance between wSIR and PCA overall (Spearman correlation 0.57). Overall, this analysis demonstrates wSIR’s ability to prioritise spatially relevant and continuous gene expression variation.  Since tissue domain detection is a key analysis task in exploring spatial omics data, we examined wSIR’s ability to produce meaningful and stable spatial domains compared to other state-of-the-art methods. While wSIR is fundamentally an approach to embed observations into a reduced dimension space, it can be coupled with unsupervised learning to generate spatially-informed clusters or domains. To facilitate this comparison, we used one real dataset (DLPFC, ‘Methods’) and one synthetic simulation dataset (as per  8  , ‘Methods’) that contained what can be considered ‘ground truth’ domain labels. When we compared wSIR’s derived domains against those of other methods, including DR.SC, PRECAST, SpatialPCA and STAMP for the real DLPFC dataset, we observed comparable performance in terms of pseudo- R  2  and ARI (Supplementary Fig.  7 a–d). Similarly, for the synthetic data, we observed both comparable performance in terms of BCDC, neighbourhood similarity and pseudo- R  2  (Supplementary Fig.  8 a–c), as well as observing a consistent visual recapitulation of the striped spatial patterns in this dataset (Supplementary Fig.  8 d, e). Overall, these analyses demonstrate wSIR’s ability to facilitate downstream detection of discrete spatially relevant domains. The human breast cancer dataset stems from an experimental study where slices from the same tissue block were also subjected to spot-level spatial transcriptomics via the 10x Visium platform  24  . Discussion  In this paper, we have introduced wSIR, an approach to perform spatially-aware dimensionality reduction of single-cell and spot-level spatial transcriptomics data. wSIR can handle multiple distinct biological samples, and enables mapping of non-spatial gene expression data to a low-dimensional embedding that is informed by spatial coordinates. We have implemented wSIR as an R package, with scalability due to efficient Rcpp implementation. We have shown relatively superior performance of wSIR compared to other dimensionality reduction approaches, and demonstrated wSIR’s applicability in two real-world biological contexts.  A current limitation of wSIR is that an initial step of feature selection is needed for very large datasets, e.g. whole transcriptome data. While there are works in statistics research on implementing sparsity to SIR via the Lasso  21  , future work would focus on incorporating such regularisation approaches to the wSIR context in terms of both the slicing mechanisms for spatial transcriptomics data, and taking the slice-slice correlations into account. Adding further complexity to the modelling step could be met with a decrease in computational scalability, so future work would focus on ensuring that any algorithmic advance is not met with a large drop in computational efficiency.  We have shown that wSIR is quite robust to changes in the slicing mechanism, such as location shifts, but we have not fully examined the impact of other types of slicing mechanisms that, for example, take into account the density of cells in a tissue. Given this, there is a future opportunity to investigate whether an ‘adaptive’ slicing mechanism may be beneficial in balancing between large enough sample sizes for analytical stability and small enough sample sizes to retain subtle spatial patterns.  A key advantage of wSIR is its ability to take into account multiple samples to generate a single low-dimensional loading and embedding. We currently do so by assuming that the slice-slice correlation of slices belonging to separate samples is zero. With the increase in throughput of spatial transcriptomics studies and the inevitable rise in variety and complexity of the studies  31  , it is important to consider different levels of replication. For example, datasets can contain distinct spatial samples that are 2D slices from the same 3D tissue block across multiple individuals, and care will need to be taken to build an appropriate slice-slice correlation matrix in these situations. Currently, wSIR would be limited in assuming that such 2D slices from the same 3D block are not spatially correlated at all, potentially reducing the ability of wSIR to leverage this information. There are algorithms that computationally ‘register’ 2D samples into a 3D structure, but there is a potential circularity issue in using gene expression data to register spatial coordinates, then using spatial coordinates to reduce the dimensionality of gene expression data. Future work could consider tackling these tasks jointly, potentially leading to more accurate results.  We envisage wSIR being used in a variety of contexts, especially as spatial transcriptomics data becomes more widespread. Effectively using spatial information is a challenge in contemporary spatial transcriptomics analyses, and simply using tools designed for scRNA-seq can hinder the ability to draw insight in terms of spatial biology. We believe that wSIR is helpful in uncovering spatially relevant variation, but may be limited in identifying non-spatial but still biologically relevant variation. As such, wSIR should be considered as one of many tools that analysts can use for understanding their complex and high-dimensional spatial omics data. Overall, we see the potential of wSIR to ensure that spatially relevant variation is not lost, and to enable a more comprehensive understanding of spatial biology in several contexts.  While wSIR is computationally efficient because it is a linear dimension reduction method, it may not be the case that linear combinations of gene expression are able to predict the spatial outcomes. To that end, future research could adapt the idea of wSIR to non-linear sufficient dimension reduction methods, such that those recently developed by ref.   32  . From a theoretical standpoint, properties of wSIR, such as consistency and optimality, similar to those developed by refs.   33 , 34  ,  35  , can also be investigated.    Methods   A brief review of sliced inverse regression  Dimension reduction (DR) refers to statistical methods aiming to reduce the dimension, typically the number of columns, of a dataset to address the curse of dimensionality and remove noise from the data. Let  X  be an  n  ×  p  matrix of gene expression features, where  n  is the number of observations (cells), and  p  is the number of genes, where  p  is typically large. Dimension reduction methods aim to find a low–dimensional score  n  ×  d  matrix  V , with  d  ≪  p , where different methods differ in what information of  X  (e.g. total variances, graph structures) need to be retained as much as possible in  V .  In our spatial transcriptomic context, in addition to  X , we have an  n  ×  q  matrix of response  Y  containing spatial coordinates of cells with  q  = 2 or  q  = 3. Therefore, we aim to find such a matrix  V  so that  V  preserves the ability of  X  to predict  Y   20  , i.e.  Y ⊥ X ∣ V , with ⊥ denoting statistical independence and ∣ denoting conditioning. This is precisely the aim of ‘sufficient dimension reduction’, which is an active research area that gains increasing popularity among practitioners. Among sufficient dimension reduction methods, SIR is the most widely used due to its generality, simplicity, and computational efficiency. Since its first introduction, SIR has been adapted into many complex settings, including missing data  36 , 37   and high-dimensional features with  n  ≪  p   17 , 21  . Nevertheless, most recent works on SIR assume a univariate response, i.e.  q  = 1. While a few works have extended SIR to the multivariate response settings  38 , 39  , our paper is the first to propose SIR for responses with spatial coordinates. Without the loss of generality, we assume each column of the feature matrix  X  is centred.  As a linear sufficient dimension reduction method, SIR assumes  V  =  X  B , where  B  is a  p  ×  d  loading matrix  B  such that  Y ⊥ X ∣ V . This conditional independence relationship is invariant for any rotation of  V  by an orthonormal  d  ×  d  matrix  C , i.e.  Y ⊥ X ∣ V  is equivalent to  Y ⊥ X ∣( V  C ), so the loading matrix  B  is only identifiable up to rotation. Compared to non-linear sufficient dimension reduction methods, linear dimension reduction methods are more interpretable and scalable, and they enable a straightforward projection of a new dataset into the lower-dimensional space.  The basic algorithm for SIR is as follows. Let  z   h   be a  p  × 1 column vector consisting of the average of all the standardised covariates within the  h th slice for  h  = 1,…,  H . In the second step, let    M  =    n    −  1      ∑    h  =  1    H      n    h      z    h      z    h    ⊤      be a sample covariance matrix of these sliced means, where  n   h   is the number of observations within the  h th slice. There are two main challenges of adapting the above basic SIR algorithm to our settings with spatial coordinate responses. First, it is not clear how to form slices. Second, each slice in our setting corresponds to one spatial location, so these slices are spatially correlated with each other. Nevertheless, in the basic SIR algorithm, this spatial information is ignored after the slices are formed. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a general weight matrix into the computation of the sample covariance matrix of the sliced mean, where the off-diagonal elements are explicitly used to account for the correlation among the slices. In general, the number of cells/spots within each slice should be large enough to benefit from the SIR mechanism, noting that in the extreme case, if each cell/spot is within its own slice, then the approach is akin to PCA. While there are practical discussions around slicing in the SIR literature  22   and general heuristics can be followed (e.g. at least 25 cells), the number of slices is treated as a tuning parameter and a selection is made according to the largest cross-validated BCDC.     wSIR: Spatial weighting matrix to handle correlations among the slices  In the second step of the basic SIR algorithm, we can write the matrix  M  in the form    1   M  =    Z    H    ⊤    D    Z    H    ,   D  =    diag     (     p    1    ,  …  ,    p    H     )   ,     where  Z   H   is the  H  ×  p  matrix whose  h th row is the vector of average of the standardised covariates and  p   h   =  n   h  / n  for  h  = 1,…,  H , and  H  is the number of tiles. Selecting tuning parameters for wSIR  For these other parameters in the wSIR algorithm, including the number of tiles  H  and the coefficient  α  in the computation of the weight matrix, we use a 10-fold cross-validation. Specifically, we split our data into a training set ( X  train ,  Y  train ) and a validation set ( X  val ,  Y  val ). This distance correlation metric is widely used in the statistics literature to measure the dependence between two datasets, encompassing both linear and non-linear relationships among them  41 – 43  . We outlined the computation of this metric below.    Applying wSIR to multiple samples  When we use multiple samples in the training set for a dimension reduction procedure, we must account for possible differences between both the gene expression data and the spatial coordinate systems (e.g. coordinate (0, 0) in one sample may not correspond to coordinate (0, 0) in another sample). These concerns can both be addressed by the weight matrix. In the weight matrix, a value of 0 corresponds to no spatial correlation between the tiles. For a pair of tiles from different samples, we set the corresponding entry in the weight matrix to 0.  The weight matrix has a dimension      ∑    s  ∈  S    ∣  S  ∣      H    s    ×    ∑    s  ∈  S    ∣  S  ∣      H    s     , where  S  is the set of all samples,  s  is one of the samples, and  H   s   is the number of tiles in sample  s . For any entry  w   i  j   of the weight matrix  W , it will take the value 0 if tiles  i  and  j  come from different samples. If they are from the same sample, its value will be calculated in the usual way as if there was only one sample in the wSIR computation. As a result, we are not assuming any spatial correlation between tiles from different samples.  Because of the structure of the weight matrix  W , when wSIR is applied to multiple samples, there are few constraints on the samples included. Performing wSIR together would only add value if there is some spatially-relevant information that is common to all samples, so having a shared tissue origin is required. The procedure also requires that the gene sets in all the samples are the same. Further, because wSIR does not include any batch correction stage, it is assumed that the input to wSIR will have already undergone batch correction. Note that we also do not need shared or aligned coordinate systems between the samples, because wSIR will automatically set the element in the weight matrix corresponding to two tiles from different samples to zero.    Ranking variables by importance in wSIR  Following the fitting of wSIR, we examine the estimated loadings matrix      B   ^     to obtain a ranking of the variables that are most relevant in the dimensionality reduction. Recall that the matrix  B  is only identifiable up to an orthogonal rotation, but the ranking of variables within each column of  B  is generally not invariant to such a rotation. Hence, we remove the effect of rotations by computing the corresponding  p  ×  p  projection matrix    P   (   B   )   =  B     (     B    ⊤    B   )     −  1      B    ⊤     . Then, a measure of importance for the  j th gene expression feature is the corresponding diagonal element of    P   (     B   ^    )    , i.e.      a    j    =     [   P   (     B   ^    )    ]     j  j      for  j  = 1,…,  p . The values of  a   j   range from 0 to 1, with      ∑    j  =  1    p      a    j    =  d   ; a higher value of  a   j   indicates the  j th feature is more important. Intuitively, a high value of  a   j   indicates a relatively large loading of the  j th gene expression feature in  at least  one of the  d  dimensions; a low value of  a   j   indicates the corresponding gene expression has a small loading in  all  dimensions. This measure of variable importance is commonly used in sufficient dimension reduction, see for example refs.   44   and   45  .  We then rank the variables in descending order according to these scores. The user may select a set number of top-ranked variables as relevant, e.g. the top 50 genes. We note that this approach to ranking variables is also applied to the loadings estimated using PCA.    Projecting non-spatial data using wSIR  Since a fitted wSIR model only involves the feature-level information of spatial omics data, non-spatial data can be projected into the spatially-aware low-dimensional space as estimated from spatial data. This is done by employing the same projection      V    val    =    X    val      B   ^     for centred and scaled non-spatial gene expression data.     Comparison with existing methods  We compare wSIR with PCA, LDA, PLS, GraphPCA (GPCA), DR-SC, PRECAST, SpatialPCA and STAMP. PCA forms the low-dimensional scores  Z  that preserve as much as total variability in  X ; as a common practice, we kept the number of PCs to be 50 for all downstream analyses  46  . For LDA, we create a categorical response variable with  H  categories, each corresponding to one slice. LDA finds  H  − 1 linear combinations of  X  that separate these categories. PLS finds the components that maximise the sample covariance between  X  and the spatial coordinates  Y ; we selected the number of low-dimensional components by cross-validation as implemented in the plsr function of the pls R package  47  . GPCA is a regularised version of PCA; it aims to construct low-dimensional scores  Z  of  X  that minimise the reconstruction error while preserving the graph structures among the cells. GPCA requires an  n  ×  n  cell-cell adjacency matrix, which is obtained from computing  k -nearest neighbour graph on the spatial coordinates  Y . As implemented in the GraphPCA Python package, the default choice is  k  = 5 for the ST platform, and the regularisation parameter for the graph constraint is fixed at 0.5. SpatialPCA is a spatially-aware dimension reduction approach that augments the PCA objective function with a regularisation term to preserve the neighbouring structure of the original data in the low-dimensional embeddings. DR-SC performs dimension reduction assuming low-dimensional embeddings follow a finite Gaussian mixture model, where the probability that two observations belong to the same cluster depends on their spatial coordinates; PRECAST extends DR-SC to multiple samples and accounts for possible batch effects and misalignment among these samples. Finally, STAMP is a Bayesian topic model, which uses a graph convolutional network with inputs being gene expression and an adjacency matrix built from the spatial coordinates, to perform dimension reduction and infer the contribution of each gene to each topic. Genotype-driven tumor ecosystems drive immune evasion and immunotherapy resistance in melanoma.

Background

Genetic and transcriptional alterations in cancer cells shape their interactions with immune and stromal compartments, thereby influencing tumor progression, immune evasion, and response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Yet, how these interactions are spatially organized within melanoma and how they relate to clinical outcome remains incompletely understood.

Methods

We used spatial multi-omic profiling on melanoma tissues from patients, compared those with loss-of-function mutations in the Neurofibromin 1 (NF1) tumor suppressor gene to those with intact NF1, and integrated these results with functional studies and subsequent gene expression changes observed in patient-derived melanoma models and an immunotherapy-resistant syngeneic mouse model.

Results

Spatial multi-omic analysis of melanoma tissues from patients identified 12 meta-niches composed of distinct cell populations with unique molecular features. Although all tumors contained these meta-niches, those enriched in immunosuppressive cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and macrophages were significantly more common in tumors with NF1 loss. Conversely, niches enriched in cytotoxic CD8+ T cells were significantly reduced. In both human and mouse melanoma, NF1 loss was associated with impaired antigen-presentation programs and reduced CD8+ T cell infiltration. Mechanistically, EGFR signaling emerged as a prominent feature of NF1-deficient melanoma ecosystems and correlated with reduced expression of antigen-presentation genes and T cell exclusion. EGFR inhibition restored the expression of antigen-presentation programs and enhanced antitumor immune responses in a syngeneic Nf1 knockdown model resistant to ICIs.

Conclusions

These findings define spatially organized, functionally distinct meta-niches enriched in NF1-mutant melanoma that may contribute to their aggressive disease features and poor ICI response. Our study links an understudied melanoma driver to specific immune-evasion mechanisms and identifies EGFR inhibition as a candidate strategy to improve outcomes in patients with NF1-mutant melanoma resistant to immunotherapy.
