DeSpaST: deconvoluting spatial transcriptomics signals to cell-level resolution using histology images. Advances in spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies enable spatially resolved gene expression profiling, yet most platforms remain limited to spot-level resolution, where each measurement aggregates signals from multiple cells and obscures cell-specific programs and microenvironmental interactions. Existing computational approaches either provide limited sub-spot refinement or rely on matched single-cell RNA sequencing references that are costly and difficult to obtain. Here, we present DeSpaST (Deconvoluting Spatial Transcriptomics Signals to Cell-Level Resolution Using Histology Images), a dynamic edge-conditioned graph convolutional network that deconvolves spot-level ST data into cell-level gene expression profiles using only paired histology images. DeSpaST extracts nucleus-level morphological features, constructs directed cellular interaction graphs, and integrates spatial and transcriptional information through message passing. Validated across four cancer datasets with orthogonal Xenium, immunofluorescence, ablation, and interslice evaluations, DeSpaST enhances spatial resolution, facilitates downstream cellular-level analyses, and provides deeper insights into tissue biology. Background  Spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies have made significant progress in transitioning transcriptomic research from the cell level to a 2D spatial cell system. This transition is crucial for investigating cell–cell communication, tissue heterogeneity, and the tumor microenvironment, offering new insights into intricate biological processes. In contrast to single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), which requires tissue dissociation, ST technologies profile gene expression and preserve the spatial composition of cells within the native tissue environment [ 1 ]. ST technologies (e.g. 10× Genomics Visium [ 2 ], Nanostring GeoMx DSP [ 3 ], HDST [ 4 ], and Slide-seq [ 5 ]) utilize unique spatial barcodes to label the spatial locations and capture the gene expression at thousands of barcoded spatial locations (referred to as spots) within one experiment [ 6 ]. While these methods achieve high detection efficiency, their spatial resolution is inherently limited. The barcoded spot area (Spot diameter: 10× Genomics Visium: 55 μm, Nanostring GeoMx DSP: 10 μm [ 7 ], and Slide-seq: 10 μm [ 8 ]) encompasses a diverse population of cells, ranging from a few cells up to 200 cells [ 9 ]. To accurately distinguish the mixed-cell populations and uncover biological inferences from the ST data, it is essential to develop computational models that can enhance the resolution of ST data.  Several computational methods have been developed to improve the spatial resolution of ST data. Bayesian-based methods such as BayesSpace [ 10 ] refine gene expression to sub-spot resolution, only yielding modest improvement. Deep-learning-based approaches such as SPOTlight [ 11 ], Tangram [ 12 ], cell2location [ 13 ], and CARD [ 14 ] integrate ST data with scRNA-seq data, mapping related gene expression cells to ST coordinates or reconstructing the ST landscape from various cell combinations. However, the reliance on scRNA-seq data significantly raises the experimental costs and introduces constraints, including limited cell types and potential biases in spatial reconstruction accuracy.  Instead of relying on the scRNA-seq data, integrating histology images with ST data presents a more feasible and promising way to enhance ST resolution. Most ST platforms, such as Visium and HDST, typically provide corresponding histology images, like hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining images, which offer high-resolution morphological and spatial information for individual cells across the tissue sections. Deep-learning-based methods such as TESLA [ 15 ], XFuse [ 16 ], and iStar [ 17 ] have been developed to integrate the histology image with ST data to enhance ST resolution. However, these methods primarily enhance resolution at the pixel level but fall short of achieving cell-level gene expression resolution. Furthermore, these methods focus on extracting pixel level histological features [e.g. pixel intensities in red, green, blue (RGB) channels], neglecting true cell features and cell–cell interactions, which compromises model accuracy. A specialized model that directly incorporates actual cell-level features is necessary to improve the biological application of ST data.  Many fundamental biological questions—including the delineation of cell-type boundaries, characterization of the tumor microenvironment, and inference of cell–cell communication—inherently require cell-level resolution. However, true single-cell spatial assays such as Xenium or MERFISH remain expensive, limited in gene panel size, and not universally available, making spot-level ST the dominant modality in practice. Moreover, matched scRNA-seq data from the same tissue, which several existing deconvolution methods depend on, is not always obtainable and may introduce additional biases when tissue dissociation alters cell-type composition. A computational approach that can reliably infer cell-level expression directly from spot-level ST data and routine histology images therefore addresses a practical and widely encountered gap in the field.  In this work, we developed an innovative model called DeSpaST (Deconvoluting Spatial Transcriptomics Signals to Cell-Level Resolution Using Histology Images), which incorporates the cell level features from histology image with ST data using dynamic edge–conditioned graph convolution neural network ( Fig. 1 , and  Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Starting with a histology image, we perform cell segmentation and explicitly extract cell morphological and spatial interaction features, followed by constructing the cellular graphic interaction structures of the tissue. We then build a graph deconvolution model that combines ST data with these morphological features and interaction structures to deconvolute spot-level gene expression into cell-level gene expression profiles. In contrast to the previous methods that primarily rely on pixel-level information and use convolutional neural network (CNN)-like structures to encode the features, which often failing to capture cell–cell interaction information. DeSpaST leverages the graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to fully capture the cellular interaction topologies by constructing cellular interaction graphic structures. Unlike conventional CNNs, GCNs operate on non-Euclidean data structures, enabling comprehensive modeling of diverse cellular interaction topologies. DeSpaST offers several practical advantages. First, it does not require scRNA-seq references, reducing experimental cost and avoiding dependence on matched dissociated-cell datasets. Second, it leverages morphology and local tissue architecture to improve spatial localization and denoising within spots, which is particularly valuable in heterogeneous tumors where boundaries and niches vary over short distances. Third, DeSpaST’s inferred cell-level expression supports downstream analyses that are difficult at spot resolution, such as cell-type mapping at cellular granularity, spatial domain characterization, and trajectory inference. In our experiments, these advantages manifest as improved agreement with orthogonal measurements (e.g. Xenium), clearer spatial patterns, and improved recovery of spatial domains, with robustness supported by ablations demonstrating that performance depends on both transcriptional input and morphology rather than visual cues alone. Together, these considerations motivate DeSpaST as a practical and interpretable approach for cell-level resolution inference from spot-based ST, while clarifying the conditions under which it is most reliable.    Result   Overview of the DeSpaST model  DeSpaST requires only two inputs: a histology image and ST data ( Fig. 1a ). Histology images offer the individual cell spatial organization and morphology characterization, while the ST data provide gene expression at the spot level. To explicitly extract the cell spatial and organization characterizations from the histology image, we first employed the HD-staining deep-learning algorithm [ 18 ,  19 ] to segment and classify the cell nucleus from the tissue image. Alternatively, other methods for cell or nuclei segmentation could also be applied at this step. We then extracted the morphology features for each cell to construct the cellular graphic structures (see  Fig. 1a  and  Method  section for details). DeSpaST builds the graphic convolution networks by performing the four following steps: (i) extract image patches based on the spot coordinates in the ST data; (ii) construct a directed cellular graphic structure for each patch using nearest neighbors based on the Euclidean distance from a cell to its neighbors; and (iii) derive features from the directed cellular graphic structures to incorporate the spatial and morphology information of the cells into the graph convolutional network. Each node in the graph represents a cell. Node features include cell size, shape, and other morphological features. Edges denote spatial and morphological relationships between cells. Edge features include cell spatial proximity, cell connectivity angle, and interaction edge categorization ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ) [ 4 ]. The model is then constructed using two convolutional layers and one fully connected layer ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). All cell nodes are updated through a message passing from all neighboring nodes in each convolutional layer, which incorporates both morphological and cell–cell spatial interaction features of neighboring cells. In this study, we demonstrate DeSpaST’s ability in accurately capturing cell-level gene expression to overcoming spatial resolution limitations in ST data, using breast, lung, and ovarian cancer datasets as examples. DeSpaST offers a new convenient tool for advancing biomedical research, with broad applicability to diverse spatial transcriptomics datasets.    DeSpaST effectively enhances gene expression resolution  To assess the efficacy of DeSpaST, we applied the model to a well-studied breast cancer 10× Visium dataset [ 20 ]. We then conducted a comparative analysis of DeSpaST’s performance against the TESLA model [ 15 ], which is a machine-learning framework designed to enhance gene expression to pixel-level resolution [ 15 ]. DeSpaST demonstrated notable advancements in elucidating gene expression patterns. To illustrate, we present two marker genes,  MS4A1  and  ERBB2 , as representative examples ( Fig. 1b ). The  MS4A1  gene encodes the surface molecule CD20, which serves as a widely recognized marker indicative of B-cell lineage [ 21 ].  ERBB2  encodes the human epidermal growth factor receptor-2 (HER2) protein [ 22 ], which is used as a tumor marker in breast cancer diagnosis [ 23 ,  24 ]. For each gene, the cell-level gene expression profile from DeSpaST, spot-level gene expression pattern from Visium ST data, and the pixel-level gene expression patterns from TESLA ( Fig. 1b ), iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3a  and  b ) were plotted separately. Compared to Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse, DeSpaST showed the gene expression profiles with highest clarity and precision for both genes, successfully enhancing the gene expression resolution. Notably, the gene expression patterns from DeSpaST correlated well with the pathologist-annotated regions. DeSpaST high  ERBB2  gene expression cells closely matched the pathologist-annotated tumor regions. Also, the DeSpaST high  MS4A1  expressed cells were well aligned with the annotated immune cell regions. In contrast, Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse did not achieve the same level of visual clarity as DeSpaST in these regions. The  MS4A1  gene expression profile is particularly noteworthy because it is nearly imperceptible in the Visium ST data and in the reconstructions produced by TESLA ( Fig. 1b , right), iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3b ), whereas DeSpaST accurately discerns the  MS4A1  gene expression pattern and immune cell regions.  Remarkably, DeSpaST’s cell-level gene expression predictions demonstrate its capability and reliability in distinguishing between different cell layers. In three specific areas ( Fig. 1c  and  d , and  Supplementary Fig. S4 ), pathologists meticulously annotated the invasive carcinoma and immune cell regions to delineate their boundaries in the H&E images. The gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST effectively differentiated between these immune cell and tumor cell regions. DeSpaST accurately captured the elevated expression of ERBB2 in tumor regions and the elevated expression of MS4A1 in immune cell regions. The distinct gene expression patterns of MS4A1 and ERBB2 predicted by DeSpaST ( Fig. 1c  and  d  ,  and  Supplementary Fig. S4b ) precisely delineated the tumor and immune boundaries. In contrast, Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse could not accurately delineate these cell layers and boundaries ( Supplementary Fig. S3a  and  b ); instead, they only provided ambiguous patterns, which indicates a lack of precision in defining the regions. Moreover, as shown in  Supplementary Fig. S4c , DeSpaST demonstrated exceptional potential in precise cell type annotation. Beyond the highly expressed ERBB2 tumor region, DeSpaST identified an additional layer outside the tumor region with abundant MS4A1 expression, which had not been previously annotated. Upon closer examination of the H&E image by the pathologist, the layer was found to be a lightly stained layer, containing fibrous connective tissues interspersed with inflammatory cells, crucial for restricting tumor expansion. This finding of interspersed immune cells is consistent with the MS4A1 gene expression pattern predicted by DeSpaST.    DeSpaST accurately predicts cellular-level gene expression  The above comparison between pathology annotation and DeSpaST highlights the resolution enhancement power of DeSpaST. To further evaluate the model’s performance, we conducted a direct and comprehensive comparison of cellular-level expression for individual genes. In addition to the Visium spot-level gene expression measurement, Janesick  et al . [ 25 ] also measured the cellular-level gene expression of hundreds of genes through the Xenium experiment. We applied DeSpaST to this breast cancer Visium dataset from Janesick  et al . [ 25 ], segmented and classified the cell nucleus from the H&E image ( Supplementary Fig. S5 ), and deconvolving spot-level ST signals into cell-level gene expression profiles. Despite the inherent limitations of adjacent-section comparisons (e.g. local distortion, cell displacement, and microenvironmental differences), DeSpaST showed strong concordance with Xenium in spatial distribution patterns. For example, for the breast cancer marker gene  CCND1  [ 26 ,  27 ] ( Fig. 2a ) and T-cell marker gene  CD69  [ 28 ,  29 ] ( Fig. 2b ), DeSpaST accurately predicted the gene expression patterns, in agreement with the observed patterns in the Xenium. Both Visium and TESLA failed to resolve these patterns adequately, especially in the complex tissue regions. Consider the top of the tissue section ( Fig. 2c  and  Supplementary Fig. S6a ) where intricate tumor and immune cell domains are present. Only DeSpaST successfully captured gene expression within intricate microenvironments ( Fig. 2d  and  e ), accurately reflecting the patterns observed in the Xenium experiment. Conversely, TESLA and Visium failed to capture these spatial variations in gene expression, resulting in unclear expression patterns. In the case of the  CD69  gene ( Fig. 2b ), the Visium ST data are noisy and lack a clear expression pattern. Although TESLA reduces some noise, it fails to capture the inherent gene expression patterns accurately. In contrast, DeSpaST effectively eliminates noise and accurately discerns the true gene expression pattern.    Figure 2   Evaluation of DeSpaST in cell-level gene expression prediction. With the gene pattern identified by DeSpaST, our next step involves a quantitative assessment of the performance enhancement achieved by the DeSpaST model. To facilitate this assessment, spot-level gene expression was reconstructed by taking the average expression of cells inside each spot. For quantitative comparison across methods, we reconstructed spot-level expression by averaging the predicted cellular expressions within each Visium spot and then computed gene-wise Pearson correlations against Xenium for DeSpaST, raw Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3 ). DeSpaST exhibits a stronger correlation to Xenium ( r  = 0.754 for  CCND1  gene and  r  = 0.665 for  CD69  gene) than both Visium ( r  = 0.477 for  CCND1  gene, and  r  = 0.239 for  CD69  gene) and TESLA ( r  = 0.720 for  CCND1  gene, and  r  = 0.424 for  CD69  gene) ( Fig. 2f  and  Supplementary Fig. S3c ). Similar enhancements in clarity and noise reduction in gene expression patterns were observed in other genes as well, such as the  ERBB2  and  MS4A1  genes ( Supplementary Fig. S7 ). DeSpaST demonstrated strong consistency with Xenium experiments for both of these genes, achieving a correlation of  r  = 0.850 for the  ERBB2  gene and  r  = 0.610 for the  MS4A1  gene ( Supplementary Fig. S7c  and  d ). In addition to the above genes, to assess transcriptome-wide generalizability, we computed spot-level Pearson correlations for all examined Xenium genes and summarize the overall trend using correlation density plots ( Fig. 2g ;  Supplementary Fig. S3c ): DeSpaST achieves higher overall agreement with Xenium (median  r  = 0.518) than Visium (median  r  = 0.198) and TESLA (median  r  = 0.479), and the top 20% highest-density region summary consistently favors DeSpaST, indicating systematic improvement beyond a small set of marker genes.  To address the concern that histology-guided models might rely on visual cues and to validate key graph-construction hyperparameters, we performed a comprehensive set of ablation and sensitivity analyses ( Supplementary Fig. S8 ). First, randomizing the input transcriptional counts (“Random count”) caused a substantial collapse in performance—gene-wise correlation with Xenium dropped (CD69:  r  = 0.188; CCND1:  r  = 0.379), the overall summary decreased (top 20% high-density mean correlation: 0.174), and downstream spatial domain agreement deteriorated (NMI: 0.033; ARI: 0.0196)—demonstrating that accurate transcriptional signals are essential and that morphology alone cannot recover meaningful spatial expression. Second, randomizing morphology features (“Random image info”) also reduced performance relative to the full model (e.g. CD69:  r  = 0.423 versus 0.665; top 20% high-density mean: 0.202 versus 0.582; NMI: 0.169 versus 0.194; ARI: 0.0910 versus 0.1167), indicating that morphology provides complementary information but is not solely responsible for DeSpaST’s gains. Finally, we evaluated the robustness of the k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) cell-graph parameter by varying        on the breast dataset: extreme values were suboptimal (e.g. top-20%-density mean correlation = 0.161 at        and 0.220 at       ), while intermediate values (      –12) consistently achieved higher performance (0.58–0.64) and stable domain-detection agreement, supporting our choice of        as a balance between locality and connectivity ( Supplementary Fig. S8 ). Together, these analyses show that DeSpaST integrates both transcriptional and morphological information and that its performance is stable across a biologically reasonable range of neighborhood sizes.  To further test whether the deconvoluted outputs preserve biologically meaningful spatial structure beyond individual marker genes, we evaluated each method using a downstream spatial domain detection task on the breast cancer 10× Visium dataset [ 20 ]. As shown in ( Supplementary Fig. S9 ), we used the manually annotated domains as ground-truth labels. For each tool, we took the predicted cell-by-gene expression matrix together with per-cell spatial coordinates as input, constructed (i) an expression kNN graph in PCA space and (ii) a spatial kNN graph in 2D coordinate space, fused them into a hybrid connectivity matrix, and inferred domains using Leiden community detection (parameters reported in Supplementary Information). We then quantified concordance with manual annotations using NMI and ARI ( Supplementary Fig. S9b ; higher is better). DeSpaST achieved the best agreement with manual labels (NMI = 0.194; ARI = 0.117), outperforming iStar (NMI = 0.182; ARI = 0.056), XFuse (NMI = 0.033; ARI = 0.011), and TESLA (NMI = 0.143; ARI = 0.031), indicating that DeSpaST’s deconvolution better preserves domain-level organization for downstream spatial analyses.  Supplementary Fig. S9c  further visualizes the inferred domains from each method, where DeSpaST produces domain boundaries that are qualitatively more consistent with the expert annotations.  The remarkable cell-level resolution achieved by DeSpaST creates new possibilities for examining cell–cell communications within a spatial context. For instance, within the cellular milieu surrounding the breast ducts ( Supplementary Fig. S10 ), we detected elevated expressions of breast cancer marker genes  CCND1  and  ERBB2  ( Supplementary Fig. S10a  and  c ). In contrast, immune cell marker genes  CD69  and  MS4A1  ( Supplementary Fig. S10b  and  d ) exhibited high expression in the outside layer adjacent to the tumor cells. The gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST align with the Xenium gene panel, while TESLA failed to predict them accurately. DeSpaST’s findings suggest possible interactions between immune and tumor cells, highlighting its potential for further studies on the tissue microenvironment and cell–cell communication.    DeSpaST accurately captures the cell-level protein expression  As products of gene expression, protein expressions are generally correlated with differentially expressed mRNAs [ 30 ,  31 ]. Next, we evaluate whether the gene expression patterns obtained by DeSpaST could reflect protein expressions at the cell level [ 25 ]. We plotted and compared the  MS4A1  and  ERBB2  gene expression patterns with the corresponding HER2 and CD20 protein immunofluorescence (IF) signals ( Fig. 3a  and  b ). Interestingly, the gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST closely align with protein expression profiles, while Visium and TESLA are not able to capture them. We calculated the correlations between predicted  MS4A1  gene expression and Xenium IF CD20 protein signals. DeSpaST exhibits superior performance compared to TESLA and Visium with higher correlation ( r  = 0.622 for DeSpaST versus  r  = 0.420 for Visium and  r  = 0.401 for TESLA;  Fig. 3c ). DeSpaST also demonstrated a notably higher correlation of ERBB2 gene expression with HER2 protein expression ( r  = 0.839) when compared to Visium ( r  = 0.821) and TESLA ( r  = 0.660), as illustrated in  Fig. 3d . Although Visium and TESLA also showed good correlations with the HER2 IF signals, DeSpaST significantly outperformed them in predicting fine-grained details gene expression patterns ( Supplementary Fig. S11 ). Notably, only DeSpaST accurately captured the comprehensive pattern of ERBB2 gene expression, depicting the tumor’s shape around the breast duct in alignment with IF protein signals. In contrast, Visium and TESLA predicted a vague outline of ERBB2 expression, lacking finer details and failing to depict a clear pattern. Application of DeSpaST for cell type identification  Given the highly precise cell-level gene expression predicted by DeSpaST, we employed DeSpaST for downstream analysis. This involved leveraging the predicted cell-level gene expression to delineate the spatial distribution of various cell types. Unlike ST data, where one spot may contain multiple cells, DeSpaST’s cellular-level resolution offers a superior depiction of cell-type distribution. Utilizing DeSpaST’s gene expression predictions as input, we applied the cell-type identification algorithm ScType [ 32 ] to assign the cell type to each single cell. The resulting cell-type profiles were mapped back onto the spatial location and detected locations for tumor cells, lymphocytes, fibroblasts, and macrophages ( Supplementary Fig. S12a ). To validate the cell-type distribution by DeSpaST, we implemented the ScType algorithm with the Xenium data and plotted the cell-type distribution in  Supplementary Fig. S12b . The spatial distributions of annotated cell types from DeSpaST closely resemble the cell types obtained from Xenium, which further substantiate the accuracy of DeSpaST. To reveal the tumor’s immunological response, we specifically focus on tumor cells and immune cells ( Fig. 4a  and  b ). Both DeSpaST ( Fig. 4a ) and Xenium panel ( Fig. 4b ) delineated similar tumor and immune cell regions. Heterogeneous areas are found at the upper and middle portion of the tissue where tumor and immune cells closely interact, which indicates the recognition and attack of activated immune cells that impede tumor spread. Discussion  In this paper, we presented DeSpaST, which is a graphic deconvolution model that integrates the cell morphology features from histology images with spatial transcriptomic data to predict the cellular resolution gene expression for cells across the tissue section. Unlike other methods that only enhance the ST resolution, DeSpaST stands out as the first model to directly infer cell-level gene expression from histology images and ST data. DeSpaST is innovative and beneficial in that it takes advantage of the histology images and explicitly models the spatial organization of cells. By constructing the cellular graphic structure, cell morphology and interaction information from histology images were successfully input to the GCN model as nodes and edges, respectively. GCN, with its capability to handle complex non-Euclidean structures, enables deconvolution at cell-level resolution by well aligning with the diverse and intricate cellular interaction topologies. We demonstrated the high accuracy, resolution, robustness, and efficacy of DeSpaST in this paper. This model can be easily applied to diverse types of tissues and ST data.  The cellular-level gene expression inferred from DeSpaST offers powerful support to many biomedical applications. In this study, we applied DeSpaST’s output to the spatial cell type annotation and inferred the pseudotime trajectories of tumor development. DeSpaST offers the cellular resolution for cell type identification compared to traditional spot-level cell type identification. DeSpaST clearly illustrates the cell types for individual cells, enabling the revelation of cell–cell interaction in the tumor microenvironment and providing valuable insights into tumor immunology studies. Pseudotime analysis further uncovers the pseudo-temporal trajectories of tumor progression, revealing distinct clusters of early- and late-stage cancer cells. The high precision of DeSpaST establishes a reliable foundation for subsequent spatial transcriptomics analyses, such as deriving differentially expressed genes and exploring cell–cell communication inference.  A key limitation of our evaluation is that the Xenium measurements used for validation are obtained from an adjacent FFPE section, rather than the exact same section profiled by Visium. Although adjacent-section validation is often necessary in practice because assays are destructive or mutually exclusive, it is inherently imperfect: consecutive sections can exhibit local tissue distortion during sectioning and mounting, cell displacement, partial-volume differences, and subtle microenvironmental heterogeneity (e.g. immune infiltration near boundaries). These factors can weaken strict quantitative comparability even when broad spatial trends remain visually similar. Therefore, the agreement we observe between DeSpaST predictions and Xenium should be interpreted primarily as qualitative and semi-quantitative evidence that DeSpaST recovers coherent spatial gene-expression patterns and microenvironmental structure, rather than as an absolute quantitative ground truth at single-cell resolution. To mitigate this limitation, we emphasize evaluations that do not require one-to-one cell correspondence across sections—such as region-level pattern concordance, marker-consistent localization, and spot-level correlations computed after aggregating predicted cells within each Visium spot—and we further assess whether predicted cell-level signals support consistent tissue organization using downstream spatial domain analyses.  Beyond the cross-section validation constraints discussed above, several additional limitations should be noted. First, DeSpaST’s accuracy depends on the upstream nucleus segmentation step; segmentation errors such as missed nuclei, over-segmentation, or misclassification propagate to the graph construction and deconvolution. Second, genes with very low or near-zero expression in the Visium data are inherently difficult to deconvolve, as there is minimal transcriptional signal to distribute among cells. Third, standardized simulation frameworks that jointly model realistic histology with spatially structured single-cell expression are not yet available, and matched single-cell spatial datasets with paired Visium and H&E inputs remain scarce, precluding direct ground-truth validation at single-cell resolution. Despite these limitations, DeSpaST demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple complementary evaluation criteria and tissue types.  In addition to uncovering cellular gene expression in ST data, DeSpaST holds the potential for deconvoluting cellular protein expression in spatial proteomics. Recently, numerous spatial proteomic methods have been developed to enable the direct detection of protein molecules with spatial variability. However, the resolution remains limited, typically operating at spot sizes around 20–100 μm [ 42–45 ]. The application of DeSpaST to improve the resolution of spatial proteomics encourages further exploration of spatially cellular protein expression.  DeSpaST is designed for broad applicability, leveraging histology images and ST data as input to uncover cellular-level expression. Its capabilities can be further extended by incorporating additional data sources. For example, if single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data are available from the same tissue or a similar sample, DeSpaST can integrate it as a cell type constraint, potentially improving the deconvolution accuracy. This is particularly valuable when dealing with very weak sequencing signals in ST data, as scRNA-seq offers higher sequencing depth. An additional enhancement for DeSpaST could involve its extension to 3D spatial transcriptomes. Recently, spatially resolved transcriptomic atlases in high-dimensional data have emerged to revolutionize the understanding of cell interaction and gene regulation within the organ. Organ-level 3D spatial transcriptomics [ 46–48 ] or proteomics [ 49 ] were reconstructed from serial 2D tissue sections. DeSpaST, with a potential 3D GCN version, could leverage these data’s complexity to learn 3D spatial cell features and deconvolute gene expression. This is particularly relevant as current 3D spatial transcriptomes often miss data between sections. DeSpaST can potentially address this gap and provide a more complete picture of the 3D spatial transcriptomic landscape.    Method   Datasets   Human breast cancer datasets 1  Two human breast cancer datasets were employed for constructing and validating the DeSpaST model. The first human breast cancer dataset consists of Visium ST data for DCIS and Invasive Carcinoma FFPE human breast cancer tissue. This dataset contains 2518 spots, with 5244 median genes per spot and a sequencing depth of 32 524 reads per spot.    Human breast cancer datasets 2  The second human breast cancer dataset is associated with a recently released Xenium  in situ  platform [ 25 ]. This research conducted a comprehensive analysis with three complementary technologies (Chromium, Visium, Xenium) on a single breast-cancer FFPE tissue. The Visium output ST data were used to deconvolute the cell-level gene expression using DeSpaST, which contains 4992 spots, with 5712 median genes per spot and 40 003 mean reads per spot. The Xenium panels were used as a reference standard to evaluate DeSpaST’s cell-level resolution prediction. Additionally, IF staining was performed after Xenium to assess the expression profiles of HER2 and CD20 proteins. The results from both the Xenium panel and the subsequent IF staining were then used to verify the effectiveness of DeSpaST.    Human ovarian cancer dataset  The human ovarian cancer dataset is obtained from 10× Genomics and contains 4674 spots, with 8792 median genes per spot.    Human lung cancer dataset  The human lung cancer dataset is obtained from 10× Genomics and contains 6195 spots, with 10 087 median genes per spot.     Spatial transcriptomics data preprocessing and image feature extraction  Spatial transcriptomics data were first preprocessed prior to analysis. Gene expression values in the spot barcode profile matrix were normalized to counts per million (CPM). To mitigate the impact of outliers, the normalized CPM values were scaled to the 95th percentile.  The cell morphology features were extracted from H&E images using HD-Staining (Histology-based Digital Staining of Pathology Images) [ 18 ], which is an automatic deep-learning model that simultaneously segments and classifies cell nuclei, as well as provides morphology information about each identified cell nucleus. The extracted morphological features encompassed the centroid position, cell area, convex area, eccentricity, extent, filled area, major axis length, minor axis length, orientation, perimeter, solidity, and probability. In addition, we further enriched DeSpaST by incorporating 1024-dimensional intermediate box features and 256-dimensional mask features derived from the HD-Staining model. These cell morphological features were incorporated into the construction of DeSpaST.    Cellular graphic structure construction  We initially divided whole-slide H&E images into 250 × 250-pixel patches centered on the Visium spots. In total, we generated 2518 patches for the 10× Visium human breast cancer dataset, 4992 patches for the Janesick  et al . [ 25 ] human breast cancer dataset, 4674 patches for the human ovarian cancer dataset, and 6195 patches for the human lung cancer dataset. For each patch, we first obtain each cell location by performing cell segmentation, then construct a directed graph structure by connecting the cells based on their spatial proximity. This graph structure was designed to incorporate at least eight nearest neighbors. Pairwise Euclidean distances between cell coordinates were computed to identify the nearest neighbors. For those patches with very low cell density (<8 cells), DeSpaST dynamically resized the patch to include at least eight neighboring cells. These directed graph structures captured the spatial relationship and connectivity among cells in the tissue.  Each graph structure consisted of two main components: nodes and edges. Nodes represent morphological features extracted through HD-Staining for individual cells. These node features have undergone global scaling as part of the preprocessing. Edges store information on edge categorization and edge spatial representation ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). Edge categorization is determined based on the types of cells connected by each edge, which provides insight into the type of interactions between the connected cells. Here, we included a total of 49 combinations of edge categorizations across seven cell types ( Supplementary Fig. S2a ). Edge spatial representation refers to the spatial aspects of cell interactions, including the Cell Connectivity Angle and Spatial Proximity. Cell Connectivity Angle indicates the connectivity between neighboring cells and the directionality of these connections. Spatial Proximity reflects the physical distance between cells. Both nodes and edges collectively constitute the cellular graphic structure, which synergistically contributes to the definition of complex cellular relationships. Image registration and result comparison   Immunofluorescence image and Xenium panel registration to hematoxylin and eosin images  In order to register the IF image and Xenium panel to the Visium corresponding H&E images and facilitate the comparison to the protein/RNA expression experiment, we employed skimage.transform package for image transformation. DeSpaST model validation  We validate DeSpaST through the assessment of RNA expression and protein expression by utilizing data from the Xenium panel and IF images, respectively. Using the spatial information from Visium spot locations, we reconstructed the spot-level expression for DeSpaST, TESLA, Xenium panel, and IF protein expression. The accuracies of Visium ST data, TESLA, and the DeSpaST model were evaluated using the Pearson correlation coefficient with the Xenium panel and IF image.     Cell type analysis  To assign cell types to each predicted single cell, we adopted a fully automated cell-type identification algorithm, ScType [ 32 ], which utilizes the Xenium-tested marker gene as the selected cell markers. The cellular level gene expression predicted by DeSpaST was used as input. The Seurat package was used to normalize the data with the default LogNormalize method. We then use the Seurat FindNeighbors function with parameter dims = 1:50 and FindClusters function with resolution = 0.9, which results in 23 clusters. ScType was also applied with Xenium Breast Cancer Cell Marker panel. Each cluster was assigned to the cell type with the highest score, and clusters assigned the same cell type were merged into larger clusters.    Pseudotime analysis  The gene expression of tumor cells predicted by DeSpaST was extracted for pseudotime analysis. We first reduced the gene expression dimension using principal component analysis (PCA). Then, cell clustering was performed using the Leiden algorithm, which is a fast approach to ensure that all cells are well connected for downstream optimal trajectory inference [ 55 ]. Partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) [ 56 ] is used to construct a topological graph based on the cell partitions. The cluster with high expression of  ALDH1A 3 [ 33 ,  34 ], a gene marker of cancer stem cells, was selected as the trajectory root node. The Diffusion Pseudotime (DPT) method [ 57 ] was then applied to estimate pseudotime values, which represented the tumor cell dynamics. All analyses were performed using the SCANPY [ 58 ] Python packages.    Spatial domain detection  To assess whether each deconvolution method preserves biologically meaningful spatial structure at the domain level, we performed downstream spatial domain detection using the predicted cell-by-gene expression matrix together with per-cell spatial coordinates as inputs. For each method, we first constructed two neighborhood graphs: (i) an expression kNN graph in a low-dimensional transcriptomic space, obtained by PCA on the predicted expression matrix and kNN graph construction using Scanpy, yielding an expression connectivity matrix       ; and (ii) a spatial kNN graph in the 2D coordinate space using Euclidean neighbors, yielding a symmetric binary adjacency matrix       . We then fused these graphs into a hybrid connectivity matrix via a linear combination,        where       balances spatial proximity and transcriptional similarity. Finally, we applied Leiden community detection on       to infer spatial domains for each tissue section, using identical processing across methods; all parameters are reported in the Supplementary Information. Domain assignments were benchmarked against manual domain annotations (when available) using Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) and the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI).    Key Points    DeSpaST introduces a dynamic edge-conditioned graph convolutional network for deconvolving spot-level ST data into true cell-level-resolution gene profiles.    DeSpaST integrates spatial and morphological features from histology images to model cell–cell organization and improve accuracy.    Extensively benchmarked across multiple cancer datasets, outperforming existing methods in resolution and precision.    DeSpaST enables diverse applications, including cell-type annotation, tumor trajectory analysis, and cell–cell communication discovery, demonstrating its potential to provide new insights in various biological contexts. title: STWave: Fine-Scale Spatial Structure Discovery in Microscopic-Resolution Spatial Transcriptomics via Patchwise Wavelet Graphs.
xenium_reason: Text indicates reuse of public Xenium data
evidence_text:
STWave: Fine-Scale Spatial Structure Discovery in Microscopic-Resolution Spatial Transcriptomics via Patchwise Wavelet Graphs. The advent of microscopic-resolution spatial transcriptomics ( μST ) enables the mapping of tissue complexity at subcellular resolution. However, the massive increase in data volume introduces a critical "memory wall," significantly limiting the applicability of existing computational methods on deployable hardware platforms. In addition, traditional single-scale modeling approaches often struggle to disentangle weak biological signals from technical noise. To overcome these challenges, STWave is proposed as a scalable framework for spatial domain identification. Specifically, STWave first enables efficient computation during both training and inference by leveraging a decoupled patch-based learning strategy, thereby mitigating hardware limitations without sacrificing global contextual information. Furthermore, STWave adopts a discrete wavelet transform to encode gene expression features across multiple scales, effectively capturing both global trends and fine-grained details. Extensive experimental results show that STWave attains state-of-the-art clustering performance while maintaining exceptional computational efficiency, enabling scalable analysis of ultra-large spatial transcriptomics datasets under constrained computational resources. Across platforms including Visium HD, Xenium, and CosMx, the proposed STWave accurately resolves complex tissue structures, enabling the identification of distinct immune niches within the tumor microenvironment and revealing fine-grained developmental substructures. These results support STWave as a robust and efficient tool for large-scale μST  analysis. Introduction  Spatial biology is rapidly entering the era of microscopic‐resolution spatial transcriptomics (    μ  ST    )[ 1 ], which enables whole‐transcriptome mapping at subcellular resolution with unprecedented spatial precision below     1   μ  m    [ 2 ]. Next‐generation ST platforms, including Visium HD [ 3 ], Xenium [ 4 ], GeoMx [ 5 ], and Stereo‐seq [ 6 ], have surpassed physical resolution limits through advanced molecular barcoding and imaging‐based capture strategies. For consistency, we use the term “spot” to denote the smallest addressable spatial sampling unit across all platforms. However, the gain in spatial precision incurs a substantial increase in sampling density [ 7 ]. To interrogate an equivalent tissue area, the required number of spatial spots increases exponentially. As a result, the massive scale and pronounced sparsity of     μ  ST     data have created substantial computational challenges, widening the gap between biological resolution and current analytical feasibility [ 8 ].  Under this computational constraint, existing analysis pipelines encounter a practical “memory wall.” Most graph‐based clustering approaches, including Louvain [ 9 ] and stLearn [ 10 ], encode spatial context using simplified adjacency structures, which hinders both the scalability and reconstruction of fine‐scale cellular neighborhood organization. Similarly, probabilistic modeling approaches, including BayesSpace [ 11 ], BASS [ 12 ], and SpatialPCA [ 13 ], incur prohibitively high computational and memory costs as the number of spatial spots increases, hindering their application to large‐scale, whole‐tissue analyses. In parallel, state‐of‐the‐art deep learning–based methods, such as STAGATE [ 14 ], GraphST [ 15 ], conST [ 16 ], and SEDR [ 17 ], generally require the entire tissue‐level graph to be loaded into memory during training and inference. As ST datasets scale to millions of spots, existing approaches encounter severe scalability constraints. Even methods that introduce partitioned or mini‐batch training frequently require full‐graph loading during inference, failing to alleviate the underlying scalability bottleneck. However, the challenge of effective analysis extends beyond computational cost. A more fundamental limitation lies in adequately modeling complex biological heterogeneity across multiple scales [ 18 ]. Most existing methods preferentially model single‐scale variation, focusing on dominant high‐variance spatial patterns that reflect global tissue organization [ 19 ]. Consequently, fine‐grained tissue substructures and subtle molecular transition regions are often obscured by the high noise level inherent to     μ  ST     data [ 7 ]. The computational limitations of existing methods necessitate the development of a scalable framework capable of handling million‐spot datasets while modeling biological variation across multiple scales and remaining computationally efficient.  To address these challenges, we design a scalable framework for ultra‐large     μ  ST     data, which is referred to as STWave. By adopting a decoupled patch‐based learning strategy, STWave efficiently processes datasets containing hundreds of thousands of spots on standard, biologist‐accessible hardware. Unlike existing approaches, STWave adopts patch‐based computation during both training and inference, thereby avoiding full‐slice graph loading and maintaining low peak GPU memory usage as tissue size increases. In addition, the framework incorporates a discrete wavelet transform to address the intrinsic sparsity of ST data and perform multi‐resolution analysis. Specifically, it decomposes gene‐expression signals into approximation coefficients, which encode global expression structural patterns, and detail coefficients, which preserve localized high‐frequency signals. These multi‐scale features are integrated using a graph attention network, enabling the amplification of weak signals and attenuation of noise without constructing a massive global graph.  We evaluated STWave through comprehensive benchmarking across multiple platforms and conditions. In ultra‐large‐scale simulation studies, STWave exhibited excellent scalability, processing 6 40 000 spots in less than 20 min with a GPU memory footprint of 2.47 GB, while achieving leading clustering performance. In the 10x Visium DLPFC benchmark, STWave outperformed 17 competing methods, achieving an improvement of about 20% in clustering performance. In addition, STWave resolved fine‐grained biological structures on subcellular‐resolution platforms, including the identification of specific immune niches, such as     S  P  P   1  +      macrophages in Visium HD colorectal cancer samples, and the delineation of the     F  o  x  g  1    ‐driven dorsal forebrain in Stereo‐seq mouse embryos. Furthermore, on Xenium and CosMx datasets, STWave improved molecular sensitivity and specificity while substantially reducing computational cost compared with recent partition‐based methods. Collectively, these results indicate that STWave provides a robust, accurate, and computationally efficient solution for analyzing large‐scale datasets characteristic of the     μ  ST     era.    2  Results   2.1  Overview of STWave  STWave is a scalable deep learning framework that integrates wavelet representations to delineate spatial domains in     μ  ST     data. STWave takes gene expression and spatial coordinates as input and partitions tissue sections into localized patches. Within each patch, spatial graphs are constructed and wavelet transforms are applied to extract multi‐scale features. The model is trained with a reconstruction loss (defined in Equation ( 14 )) and subsequently performs batched inference over the full tissue to generate low‐dimensional embeddings that preserve both spatial context and gene expression. This patch‐based design enables scalable analysis by avoiding full‐slice loading. The overall workflow of STWave is illustrated in  Figure   1 .   FIGURE 1   Schematic overview of the STWave framework. (a) STWave pipeline. The framework partitions a microscopic‐resolution ST slice into patches based on spatial coordinates and constructs local graphs. It shuffles these patches for iterative training and then performs patch‐based sampling inference to reconstruct the global result. (b) Data preprocessing. STWave decomposes gene expression signals into approximation coefficients (CA) and detail coefficients (CDs) using a 1D discrete wavelet transform. Simultaneously, it constructs spatial networks and pruned networks based on spatial locations and pre‐clustering results. (c) STWave model architecture. The unsupervised neural network utilizes Graph Attention Network (GAT) layers and linear layers for feature extraction. An attention fusion layer integrates the reconstructed features, while a dual‐term loss function jointly optimizes the model by minimizing reconstruction errors in both the wavelet and gene‐expression domains. (d) Downstream analysis tasks. The learned representations empower various applications, including substructure detection, fine‐scale spatial clustering, amplification of gene expression signals, and visualization via UMAP with PAGA trajectory inference.                      To achieve scalability, we first partition each tissue slice into an     m  ×  m     grid according to spatial coordinates, enabling patch‐wise training that effectively bounds peak memory usage. Within each patch, we construct a spatial neighborhood graph to model local connectivity and a pruned graph that removes noisy edges based on preliminary clustering assignments. In parallel, to capture biological heterogeneity across multiple spatial resolutions, we apply a one‐dimensional (1D) discrete wavelet transform as a multi‐scale encoding step. This operation decomposes the sparse expression profile of each spot into approximation coefficients that encode coarse tissue‐level patterns and detail coefficients that preserve fine‐grained, localized variations. These coefficients, combined with the graph structures, enable the model to learn robust representations. Finally, the network is optimized using a dual‐domain loss strategy: one component reconstructs the wavelet coefficients to preserve signal structure, while the other reconstructs the raw gene expression matrix to ensure biological fidelity.  In addition, STWave improves downstream task performance. With dual‐domain reconstruction, the model suppresses technical noise while amplifying weak yet biologically informative molecular signals. Here, signal amplification refers to an increase in the relative visibility of spatially coherent marker signals in the reconstructed expression map, rather than an absolute increase in raw transcript counts. Mechanistically, the wavelet‐domain reconstruction preserves multi‐scale signal structure, the expression‐domain reconstruction maintains gene‐level fidelity, and graph‐based aggregation reinforces signals that are spatially consistent across neighboring spots while reducing isolated technical noise. This results in refined gene expression profiles that preserve intricate biological patterns. Consequently, the learned embeddings support high‐precision spatial clustering, enabling the detection of fine‐grained tissue substructures and distinct boundaries. These spatially aware representations provide a foundation for downstream analyses, enabling visualization using methods such as UMAP and reliable trajectory inference with PAGA. Overall, STWave integrates patch‐based computation with multi‐scale modeling to efficiently analyze ultra‐large spatial datasets, eliminating the need for complex or specialized hardware configurations.    2.2  STWave Outperforms Seven Algorithms in Simulation  To evaluate the performance of STWave on ultra‐large ST data, we generated simulated datasets [ 20 ] based on the Human Lung Cell Atlas and benchmarked STWave against seven baselines: STAGATE, conST, GraphST, SEDR, SpaceFlow [ 21 ], PAST [ 22 ], and SpaSEG [ 23 ]. We conducted a two‐part evaluation. To assess computational efficiency, we recorded CPU memory usage, GPU memory usage, and wall‐clock time. To evaluate clustering performance, we measured the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) [ 24 ], Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) [ 25 ], and Homogeneity Score (HS) [ 26 ]. All experiments were performed on the same hardware to ensure fair comparison, using an H20 GPU with     96     GB of memory and a CPU with     256     GB of memory.  We evaluated scalability under constrained computational resources to determine whether STWave can analyze ultra‐large ST data when other methods fail. Across all simulated datasets, STWave achieved the highest clustering fidelity, as indicated by the mean ARI (    0.625  ±  0.076    ) and NMI (    0.701  ±  0.061    ), while maintaining low GPU memory consumption ( Figure   2a,d  and Figure  S1 ). Notably, STWave analyzed the     640000    ‐spot dataset within     20     min, using     2.47     GB of GPU memory and     30.34     GB of CPU memory. In contrast, although SpaSEG achieved the shortest runtime under the same setting, it required higher GPU (    19.67     GB) and CPU (    75.76     GB) memory and yielded lower ARI, NMI, and HS (Figure  2b,d , Figures  S1  and  S2  and Tables  S2–S4 ). Across all scales, STWave maintained low and stable GPU memory usage, a critical advantage for analyzing ultra‐large datasets. By comparison, conST, GraphST, and SEDR failed when the number of spots exceeded     80000    . Other methods performed adequately on smaller datasets but deteriorated beyond     240   000     spots. For instance, PAST achieved an ARI of     0.209     at     640   000     spots (Figure  2d  and Figure  S2 ). Collectively, these results demonstrate that STWave delivers accurate clustering with modest computational and memory requirements, enabling the analysis of ultra‐large ST datasets where competing methods either fail or demand substantial resources.   FIGURE 2   STWave shows robust performance on simulated datasets.  (a)  GPU usage of deep learning methods at different data sizes.  (b)  Runtime of different methods at different data sizes.  (c)  The top left panel shows an annotated spatial pattern in a setting with     480  ,  000     spots. Spatial clustering results are shown for STWave (top right), PAST (bottom left), and SpaSEG (bottom right). Results for all methods are provided in the supplementary file.  (d)  ARI performance of each method at different data sizes.  (e)  The left panel shows an annotated spatial pattern in the     3   20   000    ‐spot setting. The boxed region indicates the selected area. The right panels show STWave clustering within the selected region at     1   60   000    ,     2   40   000    , and     4   80   000     spots, arranged from top to bottom.                      We next compared clustering visualizations to assess robustness across scales. STWave maintained stable performance and produced well‐defined spatial domains. At     480   000     spots, SpaceFlow and SpaSEG achieved ARI values of     0.350     and     0.312    , respectively, with noticeably over‐smoothed spatial domains. In contrast, STWave recovered finer structural details and achieved an ARI of     0.670    , approximately     100  %     higher than SpaSEG (Tables  S5  and  S6 ). To examine scalability in a controlled setting, we used the     320  ,  000    ‐spot dataset as a reference and generated datasets with     160000    ,     240000    , and     480000     spots to mimic different resolutions. As dataset size increased, STWave progressively recovered finer spatial patterns (Figure  2c,e  and Figures  S3–S8 ). We further identified a practical operating point: when each patch contained approximately     10  ,  000     spots, STWave achieved a favorable balance among GPU memory usage, CPU memory usage, runtime, and clustering accuracy (Table  S7 ). Together, these results demonstrate that STWave is robust to scale and maintains consistent performance on ultra‐large ST datasets.    2.3  STWave Deciphers the Tumor Microenvironment in Colorectal Cancer  As one of the most prevalent cancers, colorectal cancer poses a significant global health challenge [ 27 ,  28 ]. Recent evidence increasingly highlights the pivotal role of immune cells in modulating the trajectory of the disease [ 29 ]. Tumor‐associated macrophages are a prominent and highly active component of the tumor microenvironment, where they play a critical role in tumor initiation and the progression of colorectal cancer [ 30 ]. ST captures gene expression in its native tissue context, enabling a more comprehensive characterization of the tumor microenvironment [ 31 ]. In this study, we analyzed a Visium HD colorectal cancer dataset from 10x Genomics aggregated at an     8   μ  m  ×  8   μ  m     spatial resolution. The dataset comprised     545913     spatial spots and     18  ,  085     genes [ 32 ]. To evaluate spatial domain identification, we benchmarked STWave against STAGATE as a representative spatial method and principal component analysis (PCA) as a standard non‐spatial baseline.  Across spatial resolutions, STWave reconstructed tissue architecture with high fidelity and robustness, preserving the morphology and continuity of colonic glands while accurately resolving cord‐like and tubular glandular structures. In contrast, STAGATE and PCA produced fragmented and noisy partitions, exhibiting oversegmentation and undersegmentation within the same regions ( Figure   3a,c ). The improvements achieved by STWave were systematic and included sharper boundaries, sustained connectivity of fine glandular units, and reduced cross‐region leakage. Additionally, STWave revealed biologically informative cell populations that were not detected by competing approaches. Notably, STWave identified a distinct cluster of     S  P  P   1  +      macrophages encircling a calcified region (Figure  3b ), consistent with prior observations [ 20 ]. The calcified regions in the H&E panels and the corresponding STWave‐identified spatial domains are delineated by blue outlines in Figure  3b , providing direct localization of the calcified foci and their surrounding macrophage‐enriched structures. The same regions were further compared with the matched PCA and STAGATE results in Figure  S25 , where the calcification‐associated domains were clearly preserved by STWave but were fragmented or spatially mismatched in the baseline results.     S  P  P   1  +      macrophages are associated with immune regulation and patient prognosis [ 33 ,  34 ,  35 ]. These cells assemble into spatially organized clusters, chains, or gland‐like rings surrounding tumor cells, patterns that are difficult to capture without robust spatial representations. Their absence in the results produced by STAGATE and PCA highlights STWave's superior ability to preserve low‐abundance yet biologically meaningful spatial signals.   FIGURE 3   STWave enables the identification of fine structures in a human colorectal cancer dataset.  (a)  Spatial clustering visualizations of STWave (left), STAGATE (middle), and PCA (right).  (b)  H&E‐stained images of five selected regions and their corresponding STWave spatial clustering results, taken from region b boxed by a black dashed line in Figure  3a . Blue outlines in the upper H&E panels mark calcified regions, and blue outlines in the corresponding lower STWave clustering panels mark the spatial domains identified by STWave around these regions.  (c)  H&E‐stained images (top left) of region c boxed by a black solid line in Figure  3a , with the corresponding clustering result of STWave (top right), STAGATE (bottom left), and PCA (bottom right).  (d)  Dot plot (left) of genes with high expression in domain     11     identified by STWave, as shown for region d boxed with a black solid line in Figure  3a , showing spatial mean expression (top right) and pathway enrichment (bottom right) computed with the Python package gseapy.  (e)  Spatial expression plot of     C  X  C  L  8    . The blue box indicates the region of interest defined by the overlap between the     C  X  C  L  8    ‐high region and the corresponding STWave‐identified spatial domain.  (f)  Separate spatial clustering result of STWave, consistent with Figure  3e . The box marks the same overlap region of interest.  (g)  Separate spatial clustering result of STAGATE, consistent with Figure  3e . The box marks the same region for comparison.                      Moreover, STWave uncovered tumor subregions with distinct transcriptional programs and well‐defined spatial organization (Figure  3d ). Highly expressed genes were organized into coherent spatial modules, and enrichment analyses indicated significant upregulation of immune‐associated pathways. These patterns are consistent with an enhanced anti‐tumor immune response driven by active immune cell infiltration within the tumor microenvironment [ 36 ]. In addition, STWave identified a spatially localized subregion with elevated     C  X  C  L  8     expression (Figure  3e,f ), indicative of a pro‐tumor inflammatory niche. The boxes in Figure  3e–g  indicate the region of interest defined by the overlap between the     C  X  C  L  8    ‐high region and the corresponding STWave‐identified spatial domain. As ST technologies advance toward subcellular resolution, the exponential increase in spot numbers poses a substantial memory barrier for existing analytical tools. Our framework addresses this challenge by introducing a unified pipeline tailored for ultra‐large ST datasets. It enables routine analysis of hundreds of thousands of spots on standard computing platforms without compromising biological resolution. By formulating spatial domain identification as a joint problem of computational efficiency and signal enhancement, STWave offers a robust solution for decoding tissue heterogeneity at microscopic scales.  The effectiveness of STWave arises from two core mechanisms that jointly balance scalability and accuracy. First, the partition‐and‐sample strategy addresses the memory bottleneck by enabling patch‐based computation during both training and inference. Second, the integration of a discrete wavelet transform mitigates extreme sparsity and noise characteristic of subcellular‐resolution data. Specifically, approximation coefficients capture global tissue patterns, whereas detail coefficients preserve sharp spatial boundaries. The dual‐domain reconstruction loss further encourages the model to learn representations that are consistent across the wavelet and gene‐expression domains, effectively suppressing technical noise while retaining weak but biologically meaningful signals.  Extensive validation across diverse ST platforms underscores STWave's ability to uncover biologically meaningful patterns that are overlooked by existing approaches. Beyond improvements in standard quantitative metrics, STWave consistently resolved subtle yet clinically relevant structures. For example, in colorectal cancer, it delineated the spatial niche of     S  P  P   1  +      tumor‐associated macrophages and pro‐tumor inflammatory regions enriched for     C  X  C  L  8    . In mouse embryonic development, STWave uniquely identified a dorsal forebrain subregion defined by     F  o  x  g  1    , in close agreement with established histological knowledge. Moreover, STWave outperformed 17 baselines on the Visium DLPFC benchmark, demonstrating superior resolution of fine‐grained cortical layers. These results indicate that the combination of multi‐scale modeling and efficient partitioning enables robust generalization across diverse biological contexts and ST technologies.  Despite these advantages, several limitations suggest directions for future improvement. Fixed‐size patching may disrupt continuous spatial structures at boundaries, which could be alleviated by adaptive or overlapping strategies. To quantify this effect, boundary and interior regions were compared on the Xenium human breast cancer dataset under different boundary ranges. The boundary‐region ARI and NMI remained comparable to the corresponding interior‐region values, suggesting that the patch‐based strategy did not introduce substantial performance degradation at patch boundaries in this dataset (Table  S14 ). In addition, representing gene expression as a 1D sequence does not fully capture gene‐gene regulatory relationships; graph‐based embeddings or order‐invariant transforms may provide more expressive alternatives. Finally, extending STWave from two‐dimensional (2D) sections to three‐dimensional (3D) reconstruction or multi‐modal integration would further enhance its applicability.    4  Experimental Section   4.1  Data Description  We evaluated STWave on a collection of ST datasets spanning multiple technologies and spatial resolutions. The study encompasses five platforms: 10x Genomics Visium HD, 10x Genomics Xenium, NanoString CosMx SMI, BGI Stereo‐seq, and 10x Genomics Visium. Among these, Visium HD achieves near‐cellular resolution with     2  ×  2   μ  m     features across a     6.5   mm  ×  6.5   mm     tissue area, with measurements that can be aggregated into coarser spatial spots ranging from     8     to     16   μ  m    . Xenium is an imaging‐based in situ platform that provides single‐cell to subcellular resolution using ready‐to‐use panels of 5000 genes, with options for small add‐ons or fully custom designs. NanoString CosMx SMI similarly achieves single‐cell to subcellular resolution and supports RNA panels targeting about 6000 genes in both FFPE and fresh‐frozen tissues. Stereo‐seq employs DNA nanoball–patterned arrays on flexible chip formats, enabling spatial binning from subcellular to multicellular scales. In contrast, the Visium platform profiles transcriptomes using 55     μ  m     circular spots across a     6.5   mm  ×  6.5   mm     capture area, providing multicellular resolution with one to ten cells per spot. Collectively, these platforms span spatial resolutions from multicellular to subcellular scales, motivating the development of methods that preserve fine‐grained biological detail while maintaining computational efficiency.  To evaluate the accuracy of spatial domain identification, we benchmarked STWave on a human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) dataset comprising 12 tissue slices from three donors, with each capture area containing about 4000 spots and 33 538 genes. To assess performance at single‐cell and subcellular resolutions, we analyzed a diverse array of high‐resolution ST datasets: a Visium HD human colorectal cancer slice (P2) containing 5 45 913 spots and 18 085 genes; two Xenium datasets, including a human breast cancer dataset featuring 1 67 780 spots across 313 genes and a human kidney cancer dataset containing 56 510 spots across 377 genes; and a CosMx SMI lung cancer dataset consisting of 87 589 spots and 960 genes. The longitudinal Stereo‐seq mouse embryo series (stages E13.5–E16.5) was further utilized, with the E16.5 sample totaling 1 55 741 spots and 28 579 genes. To test high‐resolution scalability under resource‐constrained environments, we generated a series of simulated datasets from the Human Lung Cell Atlas, spanning     5  ×   10  3      to     6.4  ×   10  5      spots. This comprehensive collection covers a continuous spectrum from small‐scale to ultra‐large‐scale data. Collectively, these benchmarks evaluate whether STWave preserves spatial fidelity and maintains manageable resource consumption as data volume increases, while highlighting where baseline methods succumb to oversmoothing of fine structures, boundary fragmentation, or computational failure.    4.2  Data Preprocessing  Gene expression data were processed using Scanpy. For datasets containing at least 3000 genes, highly variable genes were identified from the raw counts using the Seurat v3 method, and the top 3000 highly variable genes were retained. The resulting expression matrix was then normalized on a per‐spot basis and log‐transformed. For datasets with fewer than 3000 genes, all genes were retained before normalization and log transformation, as in the Xenium human breast cancer and CosMx SMI human lung cancer datasets.    4.3  Spatial Neighbor Graph Construction  We construct a spatial graph based on the Euclidean distances between spot coordinates. Spatial relationships are encoded as an undirected    k   ‐nearest‐neighbor graph, denoted      G  spatial   =   (   V  spatial   ,   E  spatial   )     , where     V  spatial     denotes the set of spots and     E  spatial     denotes the set of undirected edges connecting neighboring spots. The adjacency matrix is denoted      A  spatial   ∈    {  0  ,  1  }    n  ×  n      , where    n    is the number of spots. For vertices    i    and    j   , we set      a  spatial   i  j    =  1     if    j    belongs to the set of    k    nearest neighbors of    i   , and      a  spatial   i  j    =  0     otherwise. Each spot is connected to its    k    nearest neighbors, and the resulting graph is treated as undirected. In our experiments, we set     k  =  8     for simulated data, Visium HD, Xenium, and Stereo‐seq datasets, and     k  =  6     for standard 10x Visium datasets.  Based on the constructed spatial graph, STWave prunes edges that are unlikely to convey meaningful local information. We first embed the gene expression matrix using PCA and obtain an initial partition of spots via the Louvain algorithm. Edge pruning is then performed in two stages. In the first stage, edges connecting spots assigned to different clusters are removed to prevent premature information propagation across heterogeneous regions. In the second stage, spurious long‐range connections are eliminated using distance‐based outlier detection with an Isolation Forest [ 46 ]. Specifically, edges with unusually large Euclidean lengths (e.g., exceeding the global mean plus one standard deviation) are flagged and removed. The resulting pruned graph is denoted      G  pruned   =   (   V  pruned   ,   E  pruned   )     .    4.4  Wavelet Representation of Gene Expression  ST data are high‐dimensional and sparse, characterized by pronounced zero inflation, technical noise, multi‐scale texture, and fragile tissue boundaries.
