       h  i  3      =   σ  1      1  Q    ∑   q  =  1   Q     ∑   j  ∈   S  i     a  t   t   i  j   q     W  3  q     h  j  2    ,       
 
 
 (10) 
       h  i  4      =   W  4     [    h  i   3  _  spatial    ∥   h  i   3  _  pruned     ]   ,       
 where     W  3     and     W  4     are trainable parameters.     H  3     and     H  4     are the corresponding layer outputs. The final reconstruction is      C  ^   =   H  4   ∈   R   n  ×   d  wc       . This design couples attention‐driven neighborhood aggregation with linear projection to achieve graph‐informed reconstruction.    4.7  Inverse Wavelet Transform  To more accurately recover spot‐level gene expression patterns, we apply the inverse discrete wavelet transform (IDWT) to both the reconstructed coefficient matrix     C  ^     and masked coefficient matrix     C  mask    . Specifically, we reverse the concatenation defined in Equations ( 3 ) and ( 4 ) to recover scale‐specific wavelet components. For each spot    i    (    i  =  1  ,  …  ,  n    ), a split operator maps the reconstructed coefficient vector      c  ^   i     to the set     (   a  J   ,   d  J   ,  …  ,   d  1   )    , where    J    denotes the number of wavelet decomposition levels.  We then perform the IDWT to recover the signal. The single‐level reconstruction is
 
 (11) 
        a   J  −  1     [  r  ]       =   ∑   k  =  0    N  −  1     h  ∼    [   r  −  2  k   ]     a  J    [  k  ]    +    ∑   k  =  0    N  −  1     g  ∼    [   r  −  2  k   ]     d  J    [  k  ]   ,       
 where     a  J     and     d  J     denote the approximation and detail coefficients at decomposition level    J   , respectively;     h  ∼     and     g  ∼     are the reconstruction low‐pass and high‐pass filters;    N    is the signal length at the current level; and    r    indexes the reconstructed samples. Iteratively applying Equation ( 11 ) from level    J    down to level     1     yields the reconstructed gene expression vector       x  ^   i   ∈   R  m      for spot    i   .  Stacking the reconstructed vectors      x  ^   i     across all spots yields the reconstructed expression matrix       X  ^   wc   ∈   R   n  ×  m      . Applying the same inverse discrete wavelet transform to the masked coefficient matrix     C  mask     produces      X  ^   mask    , which preserves low‐frequency approximation components while suppressing high‐frequency noise. Together, the pair     (    X  ^   wc   ,    X  ^   mask   )     provides complementary reconstructions that support robust downstream analysis.    4.8  Attention Fusion Mechanism  We integrate      X  ^   wc     and      X  ^   mask     using an attention‐based fusion module. The reconstruction      X  ^   wc     retains high‐frequency details but exhibits attenuated low‐frequency structure, while      X  ^   mask     preserves global low‐frequency trends while discarding fine‐scale variations. To balance these complementary properties, we employ spot‐level or gene‐level attention to adaptively weight the two reconstructions, yielding a more accurate and biologically faithful expression profile. Formally,
 
 (12) 
       γ  m      =    exp     a  m  ⊤    [     X  ^   wc   ∥    X  ^   mask    ]       ∑   j  =  1   2   exp     a  j  ⊤    [     X  ^   wc   ∥    X  ^   mask    ]      ,   m  ∈   {  1  ,  2  }   ,       
 
 
 (13) 
       X  ^      =   γ  1   ⊙    X  ^   wc    +    γ  2   ⊙    X  ^   mask   ,       
 where     γ  m     denotes the learned attention coefficient, and the vectors     a  m     are trainable parameters, while    ⊙    represents element‐wise multiplication. This fusion mechanism enables complementary integration of low‐frequency structural information and high‐frequency detailed signals.    4.9  Loss Function  The objective function of STWave is formulated as a dual‐term loss that jointly optimizes reconstruction fidelity in both the wavelet and gene‐expression domains. The first term measures the reconstruction error of wavelet coefficients, preserving essential multiscale structural features, while the second term enforces accurate recovery of gene expression in the original space. The overall loss    L    is defined as
 
 (14) 
    min  L  =  α   1  n    ∑   i  =  1   n    ∥    C  i   −    C  ^   i    ∥  +    1  n    ∑   i  =  1   n    ∥   X  i   −    X  ^   i   ∥   ,    
 where     C  i     and      C  ^   i     denote the original and reconstructed wavelet representations for spot    i   , respectively;     X  i     and      X  ^   i     are the corresponding original and reconstructed gene expression vectors;    n    is the total number of spots; and    α    is a tunable hyperparameter controlling the contribution of the wavelet‐domain reconstruction term.    4.10  Training and Inference  After partitioning the original tissue slice into spatial patches, we randomize the patch order and train the model iteratively on each patch. As described above, the spot‐level expression vector is treated as a 1D discrete signal and transformed via a 1D discrete wavelet transform to obtain multiscale coefficients. These coefficients are processed by the autoencoder to generate reconstructed wavelet representations. The inverse discrete wavelet transform is then applied to map the reconstructed coefficients back to gene expression space, yielding a patch‐level reconstructed profile. In parallel, detail coefficients are masked and passed through the same inverse transform to produce a complementary reconstruction emphasizing low‐frequency structure. An attention‐based fusion module adaptively integrates the two reconstructions. Model training is guided by the loss function in Equation ( 14 ) and proceeds for a predefined number of epochs.  After training, inference is performed at the patch level to minimize GPU and CPU memory usage. Using the stored spot index sets, patch‐wise predictions are mapped back to their original spatial coordinates on the full tissue slice. This design substantially reduces computational overhead while preserving reconstruction fidelity (Figure  2a  and Figure  S1 ). The reconstructed expression profiles, together with the learned graph‐informed embeddings, are subsequently used for downstream tasks such as clustering, visualization, and spatial analysis.    4.11  Spatial Clustering  Following the above procedure, each spot is represented by a graph‐informed embedding and a reconstructed gene expression profile. We use the learned embeddings for spatial domain identification with standard clustering algorithms, including Mclust [ 48 ], Louvain [ 9 ], and Leiden [ 41 ]. For tissue slices with manual annotations, we apply Mclust and set the number of clusters to match the annotated domains. When annotations are unavailable or when latent spatial structure is to be discovered, we employ Louvain or Leiden clustering with an appropriately selected resolution. To ensure fair evaluation on annotated benchmarks, we follow the recommended settings for each method and tune the resolution parameters such that the inferred number of domains equals the annotation count, enabling balanced comparisons across methods.    4.12  Parameter Sensitivity Analysis  To evaluate the impact of the dual‐domain reconstruction loss weight    α    (defined in Equation ( 14 )) on model performance, we conducted a sensitivity analysis on the     12     human DLPFC slices. We varied the hyperparameter    α    from     5     to     30     in increments of     5     to assess its impact on clustering performance. As summarized in Tables  S10  and  S11 , STWave exhibits a clear performance trend, achieving optimal results at     α  =  20    . At this setting, the model attains the highest clustering accuracy, with a mean ARI of     0.642     and a mean NMI of     0.654    .  Further analysis of mean and variance across different    α    underscores the robustness of STWave. Although performance peaks at     α  =  20    , clustering accuracy remains stable throughout the evaluated range, indicating limited sensitivity to moderate hyperparameter variations. Notably, at     α  =  20    , the standard deviation of NMI is minimized (    0.045    ), while the standard deviation of ARI remains low (    0.089    ). This consistently low variance across 12 tissue slices suggests that a fixed setting of     α  =  20     generalizes well across samples without requiring slice‐specific tuning. To further assess whether this setting transfers beyond DLPFC, the same sensitivity analysis was performed on the Xenium human breast cancer dataset and the mouse embryo dataset using three independent random seeds. On the Xenium dataset,     α  =  20     achieved the highest ARI (    0.441  ±  0.026    ) and a comparable NMI (    0.549  ±  0.001    ) across the tested range. On the mouse embryo dataset,     α  =  20     achieved the highest ARI (    0.415  ±  0.018    ) and NMI (    0.612  ±  0.001    ) (Tables  S12  and  S13 ). These results demonstrate that STWave exhibits a stable optimization landscape and strong generalization performance.     Conflicts of Interest  The authors declare no conflicts of interest. title: Cell-resolved spatial mapping of antibody-drug conjugate targets in breast cancer.

evidence_text:
Cell-resolved spatial mapping of antibody-drug conjugate targets in breast cancer.

Background

Antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) activity and target-dependent on-target/off-tumor toxicity depends in part on which cells express the target antigen, a feature that bulk assays cannot resolve.

Methods

We analyzed a publicly available whole-transcriptome CosMx breast tumor dataset including 154,816 cells and 18,934 genes. Eleven clinically relevant ADC targets were profiled across seven annotated lineages. Findings were contextualized using TCGA-BRCA bulk transcriptomes (1,097 tumors and 114 normal tissues) and assessed in two public Xenium breast cancer specimens.

Results

HER2 (ERBB2), TROP2 (TACSTD2), HER3 (ERBB3), NECTIN4 and MUC1 were enriched in tumor epithelium. B7-H3 (CD276) was highest in endothelial and myoepithelial cells, with similar mean expression in stromal and tumor cells. PSMA (FOLH1) was enriched in endothelium. TCGA-BRCA tumor-normal differences did not identify these cellular sources. No overall-survival association remained after multiple-testing correction or covariate adjustment. HER2 and TROP2 tumor enrichment recurred in both Xenium specimens, whereas EGFR was not tumor restricted.

Conclusions

Cell-resolved spatial profiling separated ADC targets enriched in tumor epithelium from those expressed in vascular and stromal compartments. B7-H3 and PSMA localization was consistent with prior immunohistochemical reports and is confirmatory. These RNA-level results do not establish surface-protein abundance, ADC response, or clinical toxicity. Low-abundance microenvironmental findings remain based on a single discovery specimen and require protein-level validation. Protein-level confirmation, and correlation with ADC efficacy and toxicity, are required before these maps can inform clinical decisions. Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) link a target-specific antibody to a cytotoxic payload and are now central to breast-cancer treatment [ 2 ]. Trastuzumab emtansine established the class in HER2-positive disease [ 3 ], extending median progression-free survival from 6.4 to 9.6 months and median overall survival from 25.1 to 30.9 months relative to lapatinib plus capecitabine. Trastuzumab deruxtecan and the TROP2-directed agents Sacituzumab govitecan and datopotamab deruxtecan have since broadened their use across breast cancer subtypes [ [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. In the long-term DESTINY-Breast04 analysis, investigator-assessed median progression-free survival was 8.8 versus 4.2 months (hazard ratio, 0.36), and median overall survival was 22.9 versus 16.8 months (hazard ratio, 0.69), with trastuzumab deruxtecan versus treatment of the physician's choice in HER2-low advanced breast cancer [ 4 ]. In the final ASCENT analysis, Sacituzumab govitecan improved median progression-free survival to 4.8 versus 1.7 months (hazard ratio 0.41) and median overall survival to 11.8 versus 6.9 months (hazard ratio 0.51) in metastatic triple-negative breast cancer [ 5 ]. HER3, NECTIN4 , folate receptor-α, B7-H3, MUC1 and CEACAM5 are among the additional targets in clinical development [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]; the molecular alterations of MUC1 and their therapeutic exploitation have been reviewed recently [ 11 ]. For an ADC, tissue-level abundance is not enough. The target must also be located on the relevant cells. Expression in stroma, vasculature or normal epithelium can contribute to target-dependent on-target/off-tumor toxicity, but ADC toxicity is multifactorial and also reflects payload cytotoxicity, platform-related properties, and host factors [ 12 ]. The clinical burden can nonetheless be substantial. In the updated DESTINY-Breast04 analysis, adjudicated drug-related interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis occurred in 12.1% of patients receiving trastuzumab deruxtecan, including 1.1% grade 5 events [ 4 ]. In the final ASCENT analysis, the most common grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events with Sacituzumab govitecan included neutropenia (52%) and diarrhea (12%) [ 5 ]. Conversely, target-negative tumor cells may escape direct binding, although a membrane-permeable payload can affect neighboring cells through a bystander effect [ 13 ]. Bulk assays and tissue-averaged immunohistochemistry do not resolve the cellular source of a target signal. The broader importance of tissue architecture extends beyond ADCs to other tumor-directed delivery platforms, including nanocarriers influenced by vascular permeability and retention, as well as stimuli-responsive nanoparticles under development for breast cancer [ 14 , 15 ]. Cell-resolved target assessment is already used in the chimeric antigen receptor T-cell field to anticipate on-target/off-tumor effects [ 16 ]. For ADCs, bulk surveys have catalogued target expression across tumors and normal tissues, including a 54-target pan-cancer analysis [ 17 ]. A post-mortem breast cancer series also compared metastases with matched normal organs [ 18 ]. In high-grade serous ovarian cancer, dissociated single-cell RNA sequencing identified clinical ADC targets that were most often restricted to cancer cells [ 19 ]. Spatial profiling has therefore been proposed as a means of interpreting target availability in tissue context [ 20 ]. Breast single-cell atlases have examined heterogeneity in ERBB2 and TACSTD2, but primarily within the malignant epithelial compartment [ 21 ]. Few studies have spatially identified multiple ADC targets across malignant and non-malignant compartments in breast cancer. Imaging-based transcriptomics can provide this information while preserving histological structure [ [22] , [23] , [24] , [25] ]. We therefore mapped 11 ADC targets in a publicly available whole-transcriptome breast cancer specimen, examined the recurrence of selected patterns in two public Xenium specimens, and compared the findings with TCGA-BRCA bulk transcriptomes. The study is descriptive. Its purpose is to identify which cells contribute to each target transcript and to show where tissue-level abundance may obscure that source. Materials and methods Single-cell spatial dataset We used the public CosMx Spatial Molecular Imager Human Whole Transcriptome FFPE breast dataset (Bruker Spatial Biology, "breast discovery" release, sample S0) [ 22 ]. The dataset contains one tumor specimen, which served as the discovery sample. Selected findings were examined in two additional public Xenium specimens (the cross-specimen Xenium analysis). We obtained the cell-by-gene matrix, cell metadata, and cell polygons from the public repository. The complete dataset contained approximately 645,000 cells. To make the analysis tractable using standard hardware, we drew a reproducible random subsample (seed = 1) and retained cells with at least 50 detected RNA molecules. This yielded 154,816 cells. Removing negative-control and system-control probes left 18,934 genes. Global coordinates were converted from pixels to micrometers using a scale of 0.12028 µm per pixel. We also split the retained cells into two random halves and compared cell-type mean target-expression matrices to assess sensitivity to subsampling. Clustering, annotation and differential expression Analyses were performed in R 4.5.2 with Seurat 5.5.1 [ 26 ]. Counts were log-normalized to counts per 10,000, then subjected to a natural-log transformation. We scaled the 2,000 most variable genes and used 30 principal components to construct a shared-nearest-neighbor graph. Louvain clustering was run at resolution 0.5, followed by UMAP embedding. Clusters were assigned to seven lineages using module scores for canonical markers and established breast cell-type signatures [ 27 ]. The lineages were tumor epithelial, fibroblast/stromal, myeloid, B/plasma, T, myoepithelial, and endothelial. One-versus-rest Wilcoxon rank-sum tests identified positive cell-type markers, with at least 10% detection, a minimum log2 fold-change of 0.25, and at most 500 cells per group. P values were adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg method. These cell-level tests treat cells from one specimen as independent observations. We therefore used them to describe within-sample marker specificity and placed greater weight on effect sizes than on nominal P values. ADC-target analysis We examined eleven clinically relevant ADC targets: ERBB2 (HER2), TACSTD2 (TROP2), ERBB3 (HER3), NECTIN4, FOLR1 (FRα), CEACAM5 (CEA), CD276 (B7-H3), MUC1, MET, EGFR and FOLH1 (PSMA). For each cell type, we calculated mean log-normalized expression and the number and fraction of cells with detectable expression. Per-cell expression was also mapped in tissue coordinates. Cross-platform single-target detection comparison To describe cross-platform differences in single-target detection, we compared ERBB2 and TACSTD2 between the whole-transcriptome CosMx dataset and a 313-gene Xenium breast panel [ 23 ]. For each dataset, we calculated the fraction of tumor cells with zero counts for the target gene. The assays were applied to different specimens and used different chemistries and panel sizes; this descriptive comparison was not designed to isolate a platform or panel-design effect. Receptor subtype, spillover control and spatial organization For each target, we report the number and fraction of expressing cells, along with the mean expression. This provides cellular support for findings in low-abundance microenvironments. To assess whether FOLH1 and CD276 enrichment could reflect transcript spillover across cell boundaries, we built a k-nearest-neighbor graph (k = 10) from cell centroids. We calculated the proportion of tumor-epithelial neighbors for each cell, then compared expression in the enriched lineage between cells with few (<25%) and many (>50%) tumor neighbors. The receptor phenotype was inferred from tumor-cell expression of ESR1, PGR, and ERBB2 , with GATA3 and MKI67 as context. This RNA-based classification is not equivalent to immunohistochemical receptor status. Cell-type neighborhood enrichment followed the approach implemented in Squidpy [ 28 ]. For each ordered cell-type pair, we compared the observed number of graph edges with a null distribution from 100 permutations of cell-type labels and expressed the result as a z-score. Bulk transcriptomic contextualization (TCGA-BRCA) TCGA-BRCA gene-level expression (log2(normalized count + 1)) and clinical data were obtained from the UCSC Xena TCGA hub [ 29 , 30 ]. Sample barcodes identified 1,097 primary tumors and 114 solid-tissue normals. In this dataset, NECTIN4 is recorded under its alias PVRL4 and was mapped accordingly. Tumor-versus-normal differences were tested for each target by the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment. Overall survival was derived from vital status and time to death or last follow-up. The full survival cohort contained 1,080 patients. For each target, we fitted a univariable Cox model using continuous expression and performed a median-split log-rank test. We interpreted these P values in the context of the 11 tested targets and did not search for additional endpoints and subgroups. Multivariable Cox models were fitted separately in the 808 patients with complete data for age, pathologic stage, and PAM50 intrinsic subtype. Cross-specimen validation on Xenium We analyzed two additional public Xenium breast cancer specimens: the Human Breast invasive ductal carcinoma sample and the breast cancer reference block [ 23 ]. The invasive ductal carcinoma specimen came from a different patient. Public metadata did not establish patient-level independence of the reference block. We used the vendor-supplied graph-based clusters and assigned cells to the same lineages by marker scores. Four ADC targets were represented in the Xenium panel: ERBB2, TACSTD2, MUC1, and EGFR . For each target, we compared detection fractions between tumor epithelial and non-tumor cells. Detection fraction was chosen because absolute expression is not directly comparable across platforms with different panel sizes and sequencing depths. Results A seven-lineage single-cell spatial map of the breast tumor Unsupervised clustering produced 15 clusters, which were assigned to seven cell types ( Fig. 1 ). Tumor epithelium was the largest compartment (95,803 cells; 61.9%). Fibroblast/stromal and myeloid cells each accounted for 10.3%, followed by B/plasma cells (6.9%), T cells (5.3%), myoepithelial cells (2.7%), and endothelial cells (2.6%). Quality-control distributions are shown in Supplementary Fig. S2. These populations occupied coherent tissue regions, with tumor epithelium forming contiguous fields and glandular structures ( Fig. 1 B). One-versus-rest testing identified 4,449 positive markers. The leading markers matched the assigned lineages, including PIP, SERHL2, and MLPH in the tumor epithelium; COL1A1, LUM, and POSTN in the stroma; and EGFL7, PLVAP, and FLT1 in the endothelium ( Fig. 2 ; Supplementary Table S4). The same correspondence was seen for myeloid ( APOE, LYZ, C1QC ), B/plasma ( IGKC, IGHA1, JCHAIN ), T ( GNLY, GZMA, ITGAE ) and myoepithelial cells ( ACTA2, MCAM, CSPG4 ). Fig. 1 Single-cell spatial map of the breast tumor. (A) Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) of 154,816 analyzed cells from one CosMx breast tumor specimen, colored by seven annotated cell types. (B) Spatial distribution of the same cells using tissue coordinates in micrometers. Each point represents a cell centroid. The same cell-type color key is used in both panels. Fig. 2 Cell-type marker expression in the discovery specimen. The five positive one-versus-rest markers with the largest average log2 fold change are shown for each of seven cell types. Dot color represents mean log-normalized expression across all cells in the indicated lineage, including zero-count cells. Dot size represents the fraction of cells with a nonzero gene count. The size-key values are fractions: 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75 correspond to 25%, 50% and 75%, respectively. Expression was normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and transformed using ln(1 + x). Marker-test results are provided in Supplementary Table S4. ADC targets show tumor-enriched and microenvironment-enriched patterns The eleven ADC targets followed two broad patterns ( Fig. 3 ). MUC1 (mean log-normalized expression 0.82), HER2/ ERBB2 (0.68), NECTIN4 (0.60), TROP2/ TACSTD2 (0.52) and HER3/ ERBB3 (0.39) were highest in tumor epithelium. Their mean expression in non-malignant compartments was 0.14 or lower. Spatial maps showed that HER2 and TROP2 expression were associated with the tumor-epithelial regions of the section ( Fig. 4 ). Fig. 3 ADC-target expression across cell types. Dot plot of 11 antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) targets in the CosMx discovery specimen. Dot color represents mean log-normalized expression across all cells in each lineage, including zero-count cells. Dot size represents the fraction of cells with a nonzero gene count; size-key values of 0.1-0.4 correspond to 10%-40%. Expression was normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and transformed using ln(1 + x). MUC1, HER2, NECTIN4, TROP2 and HER3 had their highest mean expression in tumor epithelium. B7-H3 was highest in endothelial and myoepithelial cells, and PSMA was highest in endothelium. Cell counts and detection fractions are provided in Supplementary Table S1. These measurements concern RNA expression. Fig. 4 Spatial expression of representative ADC targets. Per-cell expression of HER2 (ERBB2, upper left), TROP2 (TACSTD2, upper right), PSMA (FOLH1, lower left) and B7-H3 (CD276, lower right) in the CosMx discovery specimen. Each point represents a cell centroid. The four panels use the same tissue coordinates and a common expression color scale. Expression was normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and transformed using ln(1 + x). The maps show transcript localization and do not establish surface-protein abundance. Other targets were expressed preferentially outside the tumor compartment. B7-H3/ CD276 was highest in endothelial (0.35) and myoepithelial cells (0.31), followed by fibroblast/stromal and tumor cells (both 0.16). PSMA/ FOLH1 was concentrated in endothelium (0.47), whereas mean tumor-cell expression was 0.05. This distribution agrees with the reported localization of PSMA to tumor-associated neovasculature rather than breast carcinoma cells [ 31 ]. FOLR1 and CEACAM5 remained low across all cell types in this specimen (≤0.10). The microenvironmental findings were supported by the number of cells expressing (Supplementary Table S1). PSMA was detected in 20.0% of endothelial cells (817 of 4,076) and 3.2% of tumor cells. B7-H3 was detected in 16.0% of endothelial cells, 12.9% of myoepithelial cells, and 9.5% of tumor cells. Low PSMA expression in tumor cells argues against tumor-derived transcript spillover as the main explanation for endothelial enrichment. In the neighborhood analysis, endothelial cells with fewer than 25% tumor neighbors still had a mean PSMA expression of 0.39 (n = 2,282), compared with 0.05 in tumor cells. B7-H3 enrichment in stroma, endothelium and myoepithelium was also retained in cells located away from tumor epithelium (Supplementary Table S2). Single-target detection differed between platforms and specimens In the CosMx whole-transcriptome specimen, 60% of tumor cells had zero ERBB2 counts, and 68% had zero TACSTD2 counts. In the targeted 313-gene Xenium specimen, the corresponding fractions were 3.5% and 11%. Because the assays were applied to different tissue specimens and used different chemistries and panel sizes, these differences cannot be attributed solely to assay design. They nevertheless caution against interpreting a zero count as absence of target expression over spatial transcriptomic platforms. Tumor receptor phenotype and spatial organization Among tumor cells, ERBB2 was the most highly expressed receptor gene (mean 0.68; detected in 36.6% of cells). ESR1 (0.09; 5.8%) and PGR (0.04; 2.7%) were low. This RNA profile is compatible with, but not diagnostic of, a HER2-enriched or hormone-receptor-negative phenotype. The HER2 and TROP2 findings should therefore be interpreted in the context of these receptors. Neighborhood analysis showed strong self-association of the tumor epithelium (z = 507) and negative associations with all non-malignant cell types. The largest negative values were observed in myeloid cells (z = -308) and fibroblast/stromal cells (z = -294). Among non-malignant populations, fibroblasts co-localized most strongly with myeloid cells (z = 131), whereas endothelial cells co-localized most strongly with myoepithelial cells (z = 137; Supplementary Fig. S3). Subsampling had little effect. Two random halves of the retained cells produced nearly identical cell-type mean target-expression matrices (Pearson r = 0.998). HER2 and TROP2 tumor enrichment recurs in additional Xenium specimens Both Xenium specimens were public datasets distinct from the CosMx discovery sample, although only the invasive ductal carcinoma specimen was known to come from a different patient. We therefore assessed cross-specimen recurrence without treating the reference block as a separate patient-level replicate (Supplementary Fig. S4, Supplementary Table S3). Because panel content and sequencing depth differed, the comparison used detection fractions. Ranking cell types by mean expression gave the same ordering. Tumor epithelium had the highest HER2/ ERBB2 and TROP2/ TACSTD2 expression in all six specimen-by-target comparisons. In the invasive ductal carcinoma specimen, for example, TROP2 was detected in 84% of tumor cells and 26% of non-tumor cells. MUC1 showed the same pattern where it was included in the panel. EGFR differed. In both Xenium specimens, EGFR was detected as often as or more often in non-tumor cells, with the highest levels in myoepithelial cells. Bulk tumor-versus-normal expression In TCGA-BRCA (1,097 tumors and 114 normal tissues), six targets were higher in tumor tissue: CEACAM5 (log2 fold-change +4.1), MUC1 (+2.1), CD276 (+0.85), ERBB3 (+0.85), NECTIN4 (+0.75) and ERBB2 (+0.54). All adjusted P values were below 0.001 ( Fig. 5 ; Supplementary Table S5). TACSTD2 did not differ between groups (log2 fold-change -0.29; P = 0.06). Four targets were lower in tumors: FOLR1 (-3.8), EGFR (-3.5), MET (-2.4) and FOLH1 (-1.6). These bulk contrasts are influenced by tissue composition and do not identify the cell type expressing the gene. B7-H3 illustrates the distinction, as it was higher in bulk tumor tissue but arose mainly from endothelial, myoepithelial and stromal cells in the spatial data. Fig. 5 ADC-target expression in TCGA-BRCA tumors and normal tissues. Box plots show log2(normalized count + 1) expression of 11 ADC-target genes in primary tumors (n = 1,097; red) and solid-tissue normal samples (n = 114; blue). The center line is the median, boxes span the 25th-75th percentiles, and whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range. Points beyond the whiskers are outliers. The y-axis range differs between gene panels. Two-sided Wilcoxon comparisons and Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P values are reported in Supplementary Table S5. No ADC target shows a strong association with overall survival Among the 1,080 patients with survival data, no univariable association remained significant after correction for eleven targets. The lowest nominal P values in this full cohort were observed for NECTIN4 in the continuous Cox model (P = 0.040) and the median-split log-rank test (P = 0.053; Supplementary Fig. S1; Supplementary Table S6). The complete-covariate subset contained 808 patients. In this subset, CEACAM5 had a nominal univariable association (P = 0.019), which weakened after adjustment for age, pathologic stage, and PAM50 subtype (hazard ratio 1.22; P = 0.071; Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P = 0.478). No target was associated with overall survival after covariate adjustment (Supplementary Table S7). These analyses do not support a strong single-gene prognostic effect, although the unselected cohort and limited event count constrain the inference. Discussion At the RNA level, the eleven ADC targets separated into two expression patterns in the discovery specimen. HER2, TROP2, HER3, NECTIN4 and MUC1 were concentrated in tumor epithelium. Among these, MUC1 had the highest mean expression, consistent with its long-standing status as a tumor-associated antigen and with continuing efforts to exploit MUC1 alterations therapeutically [ 11 ]. B7-H3 and PSMA were more prominent in stromal or vascular compartments. Bulk and tissue-averaged assays cannot resolve this difference in cellular source. Recovery of the established PSMA neovascular pattern provides an internal check on the cell assignments. These data do not estimate the therapeutic index, which also depends on surface protein abundance, internalization, expression in vital normal tissues, and payload and linker chemistry. Localization alone does not indicate whether a compartment contains sufficient antigen to affect treatment. PSMA is a useful caution. We detected FOLH1 in 20% of endothelial cells, but quantitative immunohistochemistry found PSMA staining in only a small minority of breast-cancer neovessels [ 32 ]. Those authors questioned the viability of PSMA-directed theranostics in this disease. A cell type can therefore be the dominant source of a low-abundance transcript without presenting a clinically meaningful antigen burden. Our study locates the RNA signal but does not quantify surface protein or predict efficacy or toxicity. The bulk and spatial examinations answered different questions. TCGA-BRCA identified targets whose total expression differed between tumor and normal tissue. It could not show whether the signal came from malignant cells. B7-H3 was higher in bulk tumor tissue but mapped mainly to endothelium, myoepithelium, and stroma in the spatial specimen. This is not a contradiction. Tumor-versus-normal contrasts are influenced by tissue composition, so we do not interpret bulk upregulation as evidence of tumor-cell specificity. Prior work defines the limits of the study's novelty. Single-cell surveys have already been used to identify non-malignant expression of CAR-T targets [ 16 ]. ADC-target catalogues are available for pan-cancer and breast cancer tissues [ 17 , 18 ], and dissociated single-cell data have been used to assess ADC target restriction in ovarian cancer [ 19 ]. B7-H3 expression in tumor endothelium and fibroblasts has been reported [ 33 ], as has PSMA expression in breast cancer neovasculature [ 31 , 32 ]. Our contribution is narrower. We assign 11 ADC-target transcripts to cell types in intact breast tissue, including the myoepithelial compartment, and assess selected targets in 2 additional specimens using another platform. The recovery of the known B7-H3 and PSMA localizations supports the approach but does not constitute a new biological discovery. Tumor epithelium occupied spatially segregated regions, apart from stromal, immune, and vascular populations (Supplementary Fig. S3). Together with the neighborhood control, this pattern makes simple transcript spillover an unlikely explanation for the B7-H3 and PSMA findings. The discovery tumor had low ESR1 and PGR expression and comparatively high ERBB2 . HER2 and TROP2 localization should therefore be interpreted within the context of their respective receptors rather than generalized across all breast cancer subtypes. Cross-specimen support was strongest for HER2 and TROP2. Their enrichment in tumor epithelium recurred in both Xenium specimens and on a second imaging platform. The invasive ductal carcinoma specimen came from a different patient, but the public metadata did not establish patient-level independence for the reference block. The evidence therefore represents recurrence across three specimens and two platforms, not three independent patients. EGFR was highest in myoepithelial cells in both Xenium specimens, showing that tumor restriction cannot be assumed for every target. B7-H3 and PSMA were absent from the targeted panel, so their localization remains based on the discovery specimen. The survival analyses provide no evidence that any target is an independent prognostic marker. Nominal associations differed between the full cohort and the complete-covariate subset and did not survive correction for or adjustment for covariates. This null result should not be read as proof that the target expression has no prognostic relevance in any subgroup. The cohort was unselected, the number of events was limited, and we deliberately avoided exploratory analyses by subtype or alternative endpoints. Translating these transcript-level maps into clinical decisions will require protein-level measurement and direct correlation with ADC efficacy and toxicity. We regard this as the central next step, rather than a peripheral caveat. A practical sequence would begin with multiplexed immunofluorescence or imaging mass cytometry on matched tissue sections, using the lineage markers applied here to reproduce the cell assignments alongside antibodies directed against the ectodomains engaged by ADCs. Simultaneous RNA and protein co-detection on the same section would then allow the transcript-to-protein relationship to be assessed cell-by-cell rather than assumed. Compartment-resolved quantitative scoring, as applied to PSMA in breast-cancer neovasculature [ 32 ], could subsequently convert localization into an estimate of antigen burden within each compartment. Clinical correlation would require complementary study designs. For efficacy, pretreatment tumor blocks from patients subsequently treated with a defined ADC could be scored separately for tumor-cell and microenvironmental target protein expression and related to objective response and progression-free survival. Assessment of toxicity would require additional evidence from relevant normal tissues and organ-specific adverse events in ADC-treated cohorts, because protein expression within the tumor microenvironment alone cannot establish on-target/off-tumor toxicity. Only outcome-linked studies of this kind can determine whether compartment-specific expression patterns such as those reported here for B7-H3 and PSMA have measurable clinical consequences. The spatial framework may also be relevant beyond ADCs. Nanoparticle and other tumor-directed delivery systems are influenced by vascular permeability, stromal barriers, and the organization of the tumor microenvironment [ 14 , 15 ]. Although these mechanisms differ from antigen-dependent ADC targeting, they reinforce the broader value of resolving delivery-relevant compartments within intact tissue. Until protein-level and outcome-linked data become available, however, the present findings should be interpreted as a hypothesis-generating guide to where such validation should be directed, not as evidence of ADC efficacy or safety. Limitations The whole-transcriptome discovery analysis is based on one tumor. HER2 and TROP2 were examined in two additional public Xenium specimens, but only one was clearly documented as a different patient. B7-H3 and PSMA were not present in the targeted validation panel. Their low-abundance stromal and vascular patterns, therefore, require confirmation in larger, patient-level cohorts across breast cancer subtypes. Cell annotations were marker-based rather than reviewed against matched histopathology. Differential expression tests also treated cells from a single specimen as independent units, which can inflate statistical confidence. Effect sizes and marker identity are more informative here than nominal cell-level P values. Public metadata did not consistently provide specimen-level sex and gender information, and these variables were not analyzed. Whole-transcriptome imaging was sparse for individual genes, limiting per-cell quantification. The bulk and survival analyses were based on a single cohort, and no signal of survival remained after adjustment. Most importantly, every target measurement was messenger RNA. ADC binding depends on the availability of an accessible cell-surface protein, whose RNA abundance cannot be measured directly. We did not assess protein localization, internalization, drug response, or toxicity. The findings are therefore descriptive and hypothesis-generating. Conclusion Single-cell spatial transcriptomics separated ADC targets enriched in tumor epithelium from targets expressed in stromal and vascular cells. HER2 and TROP2 showed the most consistent tumor enrichment across the three profiled specimens, whereas EGFR did not. These RNA-level findings should inform the design of protein-level, multi-patient validation studies. They cannot substitute for direct measurement of surface antigen or ADC activity. Compartment-resolved protein confirmation, followed by correlation with ADC response and toxicity in treated cohorts, is the necessary next step before any of these observations is applied clinically. Ethics approval and informed consent This study used only publicly available, de-identified datasets and involved no direct participant contact or new data collection. Ethical approval and informed-consent procedures for the source studies were reported in the original dataset publications. No additional ethics approval or informed consent was required for this secondary analysis. The funders had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, manuscript preparation, or the decision to submit the article for publication. Declaration of competing interest The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this article. Data and code availability All analyzed datasets are publicly available. The discovery dataset was the CosMx SMI Human Whole Transcriptome FFPE breast dataset (breast discovery release, sample S0; Bruker Spatial Biology; https://nanostring.com/products/cosmx-spatial-molecular-imager/ffpe-dataset/ ). The validation datasets were the Xenium Human Breast invasive ductal carcinoma specimen (Xenium_V1_FFPE_Human_Breast_IDC_With_Addon) and the Human Breast Cancer reference block (Xenium_FFPE_Human_Breast_Cancer_Rep1) from the 10x Genomics Datasets portal ( https://www.10xgenomics.com/datasets ). TCGA-BRCA gene expression and clinical data were obtained from the UCSC Xena TCGA hub ( https://tcga.xenahubs.net ). Analysis scripts and package versions are provided in the Supplementary_Code.zip file. Supplementary Tables S1-S7 and Fig. source data are provided as machine-readable Excel workbooks.

Protocol for integrated multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling using Xenium and MACSima. Combining same-section spatial transcriptomics with high-plex protein imaging enables comprehensive characterization of the tissue microenvironment while preserving spatial information. Here, we present a protocol for multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling using Xenium transcriptomics and MACSima cyclic protein imaging. We describe steps for tissue preparation, hybridization, and RNA imaging, followed by slide recovery, antigen retrieval, and MACSima imaging cyclic staining (MICS). We provide Python scripts for data registration and integration to generate a single-cell multimodal map of the tissue microenvironment. Graphical abstract                     Highlights    •  Multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling on a single tissue section    •  Detailed Xenium and MACSima workflow protocol for single-section spatial multi-omics    •  Registration and integration of transcriptomic and proteomic data at single-cell level      Publisher’s note: Undertaking any experimental protocol requires adherence to local institutional guidelines for laboratory safety and ethics.    Combining same-section spatial transcriptomics with high-plex protein imaging enables comprehensive characterization of the tissue microenvironment while preserving spatial information. Here, we present a protocol for multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling using Xenium transcriptomics and MACSima cyclic protein imaging. We describe steps for tissue preparation, hybridization, and RNA imaging, followed by slide recovery, antigen retrieval, and MACSima imaging cyclic staining (MICS). We provide Python scripts for data registration and integration to generate a single-cell multimodal map of the tissue microenvironment.     status  released    display-pdf  yes    is-olf  no    is-manuscript  no    is-preprint  no    is-journal-matter  no    is-scanned  no    is-retracted  no       Collection date 2026 Dec 18.       Before you begin   Protocol overview  This protocol describes multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling on the same tissue section using Xenium (10x Genomics) and MACSima Imaging Cyclic Staining (MICS, Miltenyi Biotec). The workflow was established using human tonsil and tumor tissue sections; however, it can be adapted to other tissue types with appropriate optimization of RNA probe panels, antibody panels, and tissue processing conditions.    Innovation  This protocol introduces a novel workflow for multimodal spatial profiling by integrating Xenium spatial transcriptomics with highly multiplexed protein imaging using MICS on the same formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue microarray (TMA) section. Alternative multimodal workflows have demonstrated the combination of Xenium with other hyperplex protein imaging platforms, including PhenoCycler and COMET.  1   ,   2   Building upon these advances, this protocol provides the first detailed experimental and computational workflow for integrating Xenium with the current-generation MACSima platform, which supports significantly higher antibody plexity than comparable technologies. This workflow for sequential Xenium and MACSima analysis includes optimized requirements and procedures for sample processing, antigen retrieval, and iterative cyclic immunofluorescence that preserve tissue integrity and enable single-cell RNA and protein measurements on the same section. In addition to the experimental workflow, this protocol provides scripts for accurate registration of Xenium and MACSima imaging data, enabling direct correlation of transcriptomic and proteomic features within the same spatial framework. Importantly, both the laboratory workflow and computational approach can be adapted to other spatial multi-omics combinations, offering a flexible framework for integrating transcriptomic and proteomic data. Together, these advances address key technical challenges in spatial multi-omics and provide a reproducible and scalable approach for multimodal tissue analysis.    Institutional permissions  Experiments involving human-derived tissues require approval from the appropriate institutional ethics committee. Researchers must ensure that ethical approval is obtained and that informed consent is secured from all donors prior to sample collection. All specimens used in this study (see  key resources table ) were obtained with informed consent and handled in accordance with institutional regulations and approved protocols.    Tissue selection and preparation 
   1.  Obtain FFPE TMA samples with preserved morphology and RNA integrity.   
          CRITICAL:  Following proper handling, storage, preparation and sectioning of the FFPE tissues according to the demonstrated protocol  Xenium In Situ for FFPE – Tissue Preparation Handbook  (10x Genomics,  CG000578 ) is critical to ensure preservation of morphology and RNA integrity.  
   2.  Optimize sectioning conditions, such as rehydration time for the block and floating time of the sections in the water bath of the Section Transfer System (STS) before mounting on slides to prevent cutting artefacts.    3.  Assess tissue quality, morphology and RNA integrity of the blocks prior to mounting on Xenium slides by performing DAPI staining, H&E staining, and/or DV200 analysis.    4.  Place sections on Xenium slides and store them according to standard protocol (10× Genomics,  CG000578 ).   a.  If the tissue blocks are of optimal quality, section them at 4–6 μm thickness using a microtome and mount the sections on Xenium slides.    b.  Dry the slides appropriately as per standard protocol (10x Genomics,  CG000578 ).      
          Pause point:  Slides can be stored at room temperature (RT, 20°C–25°C) or at 4°C in tubes with desiccant sachets for up to 4 weeks prior to deparaffinization and Xenium workflow.  
   Xenium assay version compatibility 
    Note:   The workflow for sequential Xenium and MACSima is compatible with the v1 as well as the 5K Prime Xenium assay versions. It is also compatible with the Xenium In situ Multimodal Cell Segmentation which has now become standard in the Xenium workflows. Since the MACSima workflow uses directly conjugated antibodies, the antibodies in the Xenium multimodal cell segmentation kit do not pose a risk of cross-detection (10x Genomics,  CG000750 ).  
   Xenium probe panel design 
   5.  Select a pre-designed Xenium probe panel and/or design a custom Xenium probe panel (to be used as a standalone panel or as an add-on to the pre-designed panel) targeting genes of interest relevant to the biological question.    6.  Validate the custom probe panel performance in control samples, if available.   
    Note:   Perform add-on panel design in line with the guidelines provided in the  Technical Note: Xenium Add-on Panel Design  (10x Genomics,  CG000643 ). Transcript abundance and cell type specificity should be taken into consideration when designing a panel.

    Step-by-step method details 
    Note:   The protocol was optimized for the Xenium Prime 5K workflow with Cell Segmentation Staining, using a Prime 5K Human pan Tissue and Pathways panel (10x Genomics, PN-1000724) and a custom 100-gene add-on panel. For alternative Xenium workflow formats, workflow parameters may require adaptation. Xenium processing should always be performed according to the corresponding manufacturer-recommended protocols. In addition, performance of downstream antibody staining following Xenium processing may vary depending on the selected Xenium assay configuration.  
  Preparation of FFPE TMA sections 
          Timing: 3 days when performing steps consecutively. Approximately 1.5 days are required for sectioning optimization, slide mounting, drying, and quality assessment. Another day is required for sectioning, mounting to Xenium slides, and drying. Half a day is required for deparaffinization, rehydration, and decrosslinking of sections.   
 This step describes the preparation of FFPE TMA samples for the Xenium Prime 5K workflow, including sectioning of the FFPE blocks, tissue mounting, deparaffinization, and decrosslinking of sections. Sample preparation is performed according to the demonstrated protocol  Xenium In Situ for FFPE – Tissue Preparation Handbook  (10× Genomics,  CG000578 ).           CRITICAL:  Sectioning conditions, such as rehydration time of the FFPE TMA block in ice-cold water, should be optimized depending on tissue type, degree of dehydration, and the age of the paraffin block. Similarly, the floating time of sections in the water bath prior to mounting on Xenium slides needs to be adjusted to prevent wrinkling, folding, or tearing of the sections.     1.  Assess tissue quality and RNA integrity.    Note:   Evaluate tissue quality and RNA integrity of the FFPE TMA samples prior to placement of sections onto Xenium slides by performing DAPI staining, H&E staining, and/or DV200 analysis.     a.  Mount serial sections on SuperFrost Plus slides and deparaffinize according to the standard protocol (10x Genomics,  CG000578 ).    b.  Perform DAPI and H&E staining as outlined in the demonstrated protocol (10x Genomics,  CG000578 , Appendix).    c.  Image the slide to assess nuclear integrity, tissue morphology, sectioning artefacts, and the presence of necrotic or degraded regions.    d.  For RNA quality assessment, collect approximately four 10 μm sections (for samples ≤ 6.5 × 6.5 mm) for RNA extraction and DV200 analysis.          CRITICAL:  Samples with DV200 values below 30 % are considered suboptimal and may result in reduced median transcript counts per cell in downstream Xenium analysis.         2.  Section the FFPE TMA block and dry the sections.          CRITICAL:  During sectioning, maintain RNase-free conditions by wiping the microtome with RNase Zap ™ solution and filling the water bath of the STS with nuclease-free water.     a.  Prepare the FFPE TMA block for sectioning by rehydrating it in ice-cold Milli-Q water for a previously optimized duration (typically 10–30 min, depending on tissue type and degree of dehydration).    b.  Trim the block until the area of interest is fully exposed. For previously sectioned TMA blocks, discard the first 5–10 sections to obtain uniformly hydrated and intact tissue sections prior to collection.    c.  Section FFPE TMA block at a thickness of 5 μm using a microtome. Let the sections slide via the STS into its water bath filled with nuclease-free water and maintained at 42°C–45°C.    d.  Incubate the sections in the water bath for a previously optimized duration (typically 10 s to 3 min for most FFPE tissues) to allow the section to fully flatten and to minimize wrinkles, folds, or tearing prior to mounting.          CRITICAL:  Excessive incubation times in the water bath may lead to tissue distortion or reduced adherence during downstream processing.      e.  From the water bath, mount the sections carefully onto the Xenium slides (10× Genomics, PN-1000465), within the designated sample area.          CRITICAL:  Avoid placing the sections covering the fiducials, specifically the top and bottom fiducials.            CRITICAL:  Monitor the section adhesion on Xenium slides throughout the workflow to ensure that sections remain intact and properly attached during all processing steps.      f.  Following section placement, incubate the slides at 42°C for 3 h to promote adhesion of the sections to the Xenium slide surface.    g.  After incubation, place the slides in 50 mL Falcon tubes containing desiccant and store them overnight (16–24 h) at RT (20°C–25°C) to allow complete drying of the tissue sections.          Pause point:  Following section mounting, Xenium slides can be stored at RT (20°C–25°C) or at 4°C in the presence of desiccant sachets for up to 4 weeks prior to deparaffinization and further processing with the Xenium workflow.         3.  Perform deparaffinization, rehydration, and decrosslinking of the sections.   a.  Incubate the slides at 60°C for 2 h, followed by cooling at RT (20°C–25°C) for 7 min prior to further processing.    b.  Sequentially incubate the slides in two Coplin jars containing xylene for 10 min each.    c.  Perform two washes in 100 % ethanol for 3 min each.    d.  Perform two washes in 96 % ethanol for 3 min each.    e.  Perform one wash in 70 % ethanol for 3 min.    f.  Perform a final rinse in nuclease-free water for 20 s.    Note:   Xylene and ethanol incubation steps should be performed in a fume hood.      g.  Assemble the slides into Xenium cassettes.    h.  Perform decrosslinking using the  Xenium Prime Sample Preparation Reagents  (10x Genomics, PN-1000720) (included in the  Xenium Prime Sample Preparation with Cell Segmentation with Slides  kit, 10x Genomics, PN-1000742).    i.  Immediately proceed with the Xenium in situ gene expression workflow.         Probe hybridization for Xenium Prime  in situ  gene expression 
          Timing: 2–3 days; with the Xenium  in situ  multimodal cell segmentation staining, the workflow spans 3 days: day 1 includes priming and probe hybridization. Day 2 comprises post-hybridization washes, ligation, amplification, and cell segmentation staining. Day 3 includes post-staining washes, autofluorescence quenching, and nuclear staining. Without cell segmentation staining, the workflow spans 2 days: day 1 includes priming and probe hybridization. Day 2 comprises post-hybridization washes, ligation, amplification, autofluorescence quenching, and nuclear staining.   
 This section describes the preparation of deparaffinized and decrosslinked FFPE TMA sections for the Xenium workflow, enabling subsequent imaging and analysis using the Xenium Analyzer. The entire workflow is performed according to the  Xenium Prime In Situ Gene Expression with optional Cell Segmentation  user guide (10x Genomics,  CG000760 ) using the  Xenium Prime Sample Preparation with Cell Segmentation with Slides  reagents (10× Genomics, PN-1000742).    4.  Perform priming and probe hybridization.   a.  Hybridize priming oligos to decrosslinked RNA.    b.  Perform RNase treatment and a polishing reaction to release the RNA strand from the hybridized oligos, thereby enabling subsequent hybridization of Xenium probes to the target RNA (10× Genomics,  CG000760 ).    c.  Perform hybridization overnight (16–24 h) at 50°C in a thermocycler (Bio-Rad, C1000) using the Xenium Prime 5K probes ( Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue and Pathways Assay  kit, 10× Genomics, PN-1000671) together with an optional custom human add-on panel comprising up to 100 additional genes.       5.  Perform post-hybridization washes, ligation, and amplification.   a.  Perform post-hybridization washes to remove unbound probes, followed by ligation of hybridized probes, and enzymatic rolling circle amplification to generate amplified signal products for downstream imaging.       6.  Perform optional multimodal cell segmentation staining.   a.  To facilitate morphology-based cell segmentation, perform overnight (16–24 h) staining using the Xenium cell segmentation staining reagents, which label nuclei, cell boundaries, and intracellular RNA-rich regions according to the manufacturer’s instructions (10× Genomics,  CG000760 ).       7.  Perform autofluorescence quenching and nuclear staining.   a.  After amplification (and optional cell segmentation staining), perform autofluorescence quenching, brief drying at 37°C for 5 min and subsequent nuclear staining according to the manufacturer’s instructions.    b.  Upon completion of the workflow, store the slides in 0.05 % PBST until imaging and analysis using the Xenium Analyzer.                Pause point:  After completion of the Xenium sample preparation workflow and prior to loading onto the Xenium Analyzer, slides can be stored in 0.05 % PBST at 4°C in the dark for up to 1 week using a new Xenium cassette lid.      Note:   During the drying step following autofluorescence quenching, inspect the slides to ensure that the Xenium slide fiducials, particularly the top and bottom fiducials, remain free of tissue coverage. If fiducials are obstructed, carefully remove the tissue from these regions at the end of sample preparation, as covered fiducials may interfere with subsequent imaging and alignment on the Xenium Analyzer.      Note:   At the end of sample preparation, clean the underside of the Xenium slides using 70 % ethanol and lint-free wipes to remove residues and prevent fibers or debris from interfering with subsequent imaging.     Xenium  in situ  gene expression imaging 
          Timing: 2.5–5 days; half a day is needed for hands-on preparation, including buffer preparation and setup of the Xenium Analyzer. An additional 2–5 days are required for instrument run time, depending on the Xenium assay version (e.g., Xenium v.1, Xenium Prime 5K), whether cell segmentation staining is performed, and the size and number of ROIs.   
 This section describes the setup and operation of the Xenium Analyzer for imaging and preliminary analysis of FFPE TMA sections prepared using the Xenium workflow.           CRITICAL:  In cases where a custom panel (add-on or standalone) is used, obtain the corresponding JSON file for the panel and upload it to the Xenium Analyzer prior to initiating the run.            CRITICAL:  Slides processed using different Xenium workflows cannot be run simultaneously in the same instrument run. However, slides processed with different probe panels within the same workflow can be run together during a single instrument run.      Note:   For the Xenium Prime workflow, ensure that the Xenium Analyzer software version is XA v3.0 or higher.     8.  Prepare buffers and set up the Xenium Analyzer.   a.  Prepare all required buffers and decoding reagents and set up the Xenium Analyzer for processing of slides generated using the Xenium workflow according to the  Xenium Analyzer User Guide  (10× Genomics,  CG000584 ). Use the  Xenium Prime 5K Decoding Reagents  (10× Genomics, PN-1000740),  Xenium Decoding Consumables v2  (10× Genomics, PN-1000726), and  Xenium Reagent Bottles  (10× Genomics, PN-1000730).          Note:   Transfer the  Xenium Prime Decoding Reagent Module B  (sealed in the mylar bag) from −20°C to 4°C at least one day before the run and allow it to thaw at 4°C for 16–72 h.      Note:   Prepare the Xenium Probe Removal buffer in a fume hood due to the hazardous nature of DMSO.     9.  Define ROIs.   a.  Following the overview scan, define one or more ROIs consisting of fields of view (FOVs) that encompass the tissue of interest while excluding blank areas, and initiate the run.          Note:   Up to eight ROIs can be defined per slide.      Note:   For TMAs, define a single ROI encompassing all FOVs containing TMA cores and excluding blank FOVs.     10.  Clean the instrument and store slides.   a.  After completion of the run, clean the instrument according to the standard protocol (10× Genomics,  CG000584 ).    b.  Replace the buffer on the slides with 1 mL 0.05 % PBST and store the slides at 4°C until further processing.       11.  Store and prepare post-Xenium slides for transport.   a.  Fill two 50 mL Falcon tubes with 0.05 % PBST up to the brim.    b.  Remove the Xenium slides from the Xenium cassettes and place each of them in a 50 mL Falcon tube filled with 0.05 % PBST. Ensure that the slides are completely submerged.    c.  Seal the lid of the Falcon tube with parafilm.    d.  Transport them at 4°C on cool packs.          Note:   For long term storage, transfer the slides into a 50 mL Falcon tube and replace the 0.05 % PBST weekly to prevent contamination or sample drying.      Note:   Alternatively, slides may be stored or transported in 50 mL Falcon tubes containing MACSima Running Buffer. In this case, exchange the buffer every four weeks.            Pause point:  Slides can be stored in MACSima Running Buffer at 4°C. In our experience, slides stored for up to nine months still yielded MACSima data meeting established QC criteria; longer storage periods have not been systematically evaluated.      Note:   Slides can be stored long term at this stage while awaiting Xenium analysis results and potential adjustment or optimization of the downstream antibody panel.     Post-Xenium sample preparation for MACSima imaging cyclic staining 
          Timing: 4–5 h; quencher removal requires approximately 30 min. Preparation of the TEC buffer and antigen retrieval require approximately 2–3 h, while DAPI pre-staining and removal of dust particles prior to imaging require an additional 30 min.   
 This step describes the preparation of FFPE TMA sections for MICS after the Xenium run and includes quencher removal, antigen retrieval, DAPI pre-staining, and dust particle removal. Following Xenium imaging, perform quencher removal as recommended in  Xenium In Situ Gene Expression – Post-Xenium Analyzer H&E Staining  (10x Genomics,  CG000613 ) to reduce residual Xenium-associated background signals and improve compatibility with downstream cyclic immunofluorescence imaging using MACSima.    12.  Remove the quencher (see  problem 1  in  troubleshooting ).   a.  In a fume hood, prepare quencher removal solution by weighing 17.4 mg sodium hydrosulfite and transfer it to a conical tube containing 10 mL Milli-Q water.    b.  Cap the tube tightly and vortex for 10 s until the reagent is fully dissolved.    c.  Keep the solution at RT (20°C–25°C) until use.          CRITICAL:  Prepare quencher removal solution immediately before each use to ensure optimal performance, as its effectiveness decreases after 10 min.      Note:   Because sodium hydrosulfite is hazardous, prepare the solution in a fume hood.      Note:   Vortexing may be performed outside the fume hood if the tube is tightly capped.      Note:   Do not use alternative chemicals for quencher removal.      d.  Add 10 mL quencher removal solution into the slide mailer.    e.  Prepare three slide mailers with 10 mL Milli-Q water each.    f.  Gently immerse Xenium slide into the slide mailer with quencher removal solution and incubate for 10 min at RT (20°C–25°C).    g.  Immerse slide in each Milli-Q water containing slide mailer for 1 min, then move to the next one.    h.  Transfer the Xenium slide into a 50 mL Falcon tube filled with MACSima Running buffer until further use.    Note:   Alternatively, transfer Xenium slide into a MACSwell One Small imaging frame ( Figure 1 A, right) and add 1.5 mL quencher removal solution. After 10 min incubation at RT (20°C–25°C), wash slide with 1.5 mL Milli-Q water three times, waiting for 1 min each time.      Note:   Residual purple staining after Xenium processing indicates the presence of autofluorescence quencher and should disappear following successful quencher removal ( Figure 1 B).         13. Expected outcomes  Successful implementation of this protocol results in the generation of a multimodal spatial dataset containing both transcriptomic and proteomic information from the same FFPE TMA section. The wet-lab workflow provides practical guidance for the critical experimental steps required for successful Xenium and MICS procedures, including tissue preparation, Xenium processing, post-Xenium slide recovery, antigen retrieval, antibody staining, and multiplexed imaging. Important considerations and troubleshooting insights are provided throughout to help users optimize tissue integrity, RNA and protein signal quality, and overall assay performance. Following Xenium spatial transcriptomics and subsequent MICS, users obtain high-resolution spatial maps of RNA transcripts and protein markers while preserving tissue morphology and spatial context. The experimental workflow enables detection of thousands of RNA targets using the Xenium platform together with highly multiplexed protein profiling using MICS. The workflow is expected to enable comprehensive multimodal characterization of individual cells by combining Xenium transcriptomic information with highly multiplexed and customizable protein profiling. The increased antibody plexity and flexibility of MACSima compared with the protein-detection capabilities of Xenium and other hyperplex protein imaging platforms, such as PhenoCycler and COMET, enable broader phenotypic and functional characterization, particularly in complex immune and tumor microenvironments. Following image registration and protein channel intensity quantification, transcriptomic and proteomic measurements are linked at single-cell resolution, generating a combined RNA-protein expression matrix for each cell together with its spatial coordinates within the tissue. The resulting dataset can be used to identify and characterize cellular phenotypes, investigate cell states, study cell-cell interactions, and explore tissue organization by integrating complementary transcriptomic and proteomic information. In addition, the image registration and data integration framework provided in this protocol can be adapted to combine Xenium data with other multiplex imaging modalities.  Users should expect preservation of tissue integrity throughout the workflow, successful recovery of Xenium-processed slides for downstream protein imaging, and generation of registered multimodal datasets suitable for downstream spatial and single-cell analyses. Depending on tissue quality, RNA integrity, antibody performance, and imaging conditions, signal intensity and the number of detected transcripts or proteins may vary between samples.  After step 35 (SpatialData assembly), the output Zarr store contains aligned images from both modalities, transformed cell and nucleus segmentation polygons ( Figure 7 D), the gene expression count matrix with cell-type annotations, and spatially filtered transcript coordinates. The data can be visualized interactively with napari using the napari-spatialdata plugin, where all layers overlay correctly in a shared coordinate space.  After step 36 (protein quantification,  Figure 6 D), each cell in registration.aligned_data[”rna_protein_table”].X contains numeric columns for each MACSima antibody. A cross-modal concordance between RNA-based cell-type annotations and protein measurements can serve as an additional quality metric for the overall registration and quantification workflow. This concordance could be visually explored by plotting heatmaps showing the expression of corresponding RNA and protein markers for each of the identified cells using standard tools such as scanpy.  7   The correlation coefficients between transcript counts and mean protein expression per cell for pairs of corresponding markers can also be used for a quantitative evaluation of the concordance between RNA and protein measurements.  2    After step 37 (registration quality assessment), the color overlay should show white overlap at nuclear positions, with minimal red-only or green-only fringes ( Figure 7 C).    Quantification and statistical analysis  The per-cell protein quantification (step 36,  Figure 6 D) yields absolute fluorescence intensity values (mean of aligned pixel values within each cell mask). These values are instrument- and acquisition-specific and should be used for within-experiment comparisons. Cross-experiment normalization (e.g., percentile normalization or z-score per channel) may be necessary when integrating multiple MACSima runs. It is important to note that errors in per-cell protein quantification could substantially affect downstream analysis. Per-cell protein quantification depends on accurate image registration and cell segmentation, as fluorescence intensity is calculated from the pixels within each cell mask. The sensitivity to segmentation errors may vary according to subcellular localization: nuclear markers are generally less affected by small changes in cell boundaries, whereas membrane-associated markers may be more sensitive to segmentation inaccuracies, particularly at cell-cell interfaces. Cytoplasmic markers typically show intermediate sensitivity. Applications requiring improved or alternative segmentation, advanced segmentation approaches can be evaluated and compared with the default segmentation approach to assess their suitability for the respective tissue and marker composition. Therefore, segmentation quality and image alignment should be carefully assessed before interpreting per-cell fluorescence intensities.  The combined RNA and protein measurements are stored in a single AnnData table within the SpatialData Zarr store. Downstream analyses, including joint RNA and protein cell-type classification, ligand-receptor interaction inference, and spatial neighborhood analysis, can be performed using standard tools (e.g., scanpy,  7   squidpy,  28   LIANA  29  ) applied to the exported AnnData table.    Limitations  Antibody performance may vary between tissue types. For example, we observed tissue-dependent variation in staining performance in the data generated in the scope of this workflow. Therefore, as described in  before you begin  (step 7) and in  problem 2  in  troubleshooting , antibody performance should be validated in the tissue type of interest e.g., by performing a mock Xenium-MACSima.  The SIFT-based registration relies on sufficient structural similarity between the Xenium DAPI morphology focus image and the MACSima DAPI staining. If tissue morphology is substantially altered between the two acquisitions (e.g., due to tissue loss, folding, or deformation during antigen retrieval), registration may fail or produce locally poor alignment. In such cases, non-rigid (deformable) registration methods may be required but are not implemented in this workflow (see  problem 6  in  troubleshooting ).  The per-cell protein quantification uses the Xenium cell segmentation labels projected onto the MACSima images. Any residual registration error directly propagates into protein allocation. Cells at the boundary of registration artifacts or at the tissue edge may receive inaccurate protein measurements.  The current computational workflow performs image registration of MACSima images to the Xenium coordinate system. As with any image transformation and resampling procedure, image registration involves interpolation of pixel values. Therefore, minor changes in pixel intensities may occur in the registered images. In our experience, these effects were not observed to materially impact the intended downstream analyses, including RNA-protein based cell annotation and spatial characterization of tissue microenvironments.  The scripts process each TMA core independently. Cross-core normalization of protein signal intensities is not performed automatically and must be applied by the user if comparing protein levels across cores or slides, due to the technical variation within staining intensities. There are several normalization methods (e.g., Y score, ComBat, MxNorm or mean division) that can fail to consider skewed patterns that arise from this type of data. Thus, we recommend using a more reliable non-parametric normalization methods that can be employed in both pixel and feature level, such as UniForm.  30      Troubleshooting   Problem 1: Insufficient quencher removal after Xenium-processing (related to step 12 in the protocol)  Occasionally, incomplete removal of the Xenium autofluorescence quencher using quencher removal solution (10 mM sodium hydrosulfite) may be observed, indicated by persistent lilac discoloration of the tissue section ( Figure 1 ). Start the run and define ROIs as mentioned in step 9.    -  After the mock Xenium run is complete, replace the buffer on the slides with 0.05 % PBST and store at 4°C until quencher removal and subsequent MICS imaging (step 12 onwards).       ○  Alternatively, a mock Xenium run can also be performed in an off-the-Xenium-Analyzer setting. In this case, mount the serial section onto a SuperFrost Plus slide. The sample preparation workflow from deparaffinization to nuclei staining is exactly as mentioned above. Following sample preparation, incubate slides in Probe Removal Buffer (30 min at RT, 20°C–25°C) followed by Wash Buffer (30 min at RT, 20°C–25°C), at least 4 cycles each, to mimic buffer exposure during the Xenium Analyzer processing. Buffers are prepared as per the  Xenium Analyzer User Guide  (10x Genomics,  CG000584 ).       •  An antibody should be considered compatible when it fulfills the following criteria (see  Figure 3 ):   ○  Specific staining pattern: Signal is restricted to the expected cell population and subcellular localization.    ○  High signal-to-background ratio: Positive cells are clearly distinguishable from surrounding tissue with minimal nonspecific background.    ○  Reproducible performance: Comparable staining is observed across technical replicates or appropriate control tissues.    ○  Preserved staining after Xenium processing: The staining pattern is consistent with the expected biology, previous MACSima or immunohistochemistry validation, and comparable to reference databases.       •  The resulting images ( Figure 3 ) allow users to identify antibodies that fulfilled ( Figures 3 C, 3D, 3E, 3G, and 3H) or failed ( Figures 3 B and 3F) these criteria.   
   Problem 3: Autofocus failure with large ROIs during MICS (related to step 22 in the protocol)  Selecting tissue sections that cover the entire Xenium imageable area as a single, large ROI during ROI definition on the MACSima instrument occasionally resulted in autofocus instability during imaging. Such issues manifested as blurry FOVs or blurry images in the output folders ( Figure 5 ). In our experience, ROIs larger than approximately 100 FOVs were more prone to the aforementioned focusing issues.    Potential solution 
   •  Divide large imaging areas into smaller ROIs to improve autofocus performance and overall image quality.    •  Select the image contrast-based focusing approach instead of constant height-based focusing for your MICS experiment.    •  Cover the MACSwell frame with adhesive, pierceable aluminum foil to prevent evaporation and drying of the sample during extended imaging cycles, as insufficient liquid coverage may lead to autofocus and imaging issues.    •  If the tissue to be imaged is larger than the above-mentioned limitation, consider splitting it into several (non-overlapping) ROIs.    •  For TMAs, every core should be imaged as a separate ROI.    •  We suggest using the slides from a mock Xenium run to test suitable ROI sizes and decide on the best autofocusing method.   
   Problem 4: SIFT registration fails or produces identity affine matrix  A failed or bad quality registration could be due to the identification of too few matching keypoints between the Xenium and MACSima DAPI images.    Potential solution  Verify that the correct DAPI file is used (cycle-0 stained DAPI with “_S_” flag, not the baseline “_B_“ image). Try reducing scale_factor from 3 to 2 for higher-resolution feature detection. If images have very low contrast, adjust the CLAHE parameters in preprocess_reg().  21   Confirm that the Xenium morphology focus images contain the expected core region by visually inspecting the cropped image.    Problem 5: Xenium positions do not match MACSima ROI position  If some Xenium positions do not match the MACSima ROI positions, these cores were probably not captured during MACSima scanning (e.g., edge cores or tissue damage).    Potential solution  Do not include these positions in the roi_map_file CSV file, so that they are skipped in the full-slide processing script (“match_rois_cores_fullslide.py”).    Problem 6: Variable registration offset across the tissue  The presence of a misalignment between the Xenium DAPI image and the registered MACSima image that is not constant in magnitude and direction across the image shows that a global affine transformation is insufficient to register the images correctly. A visual inspection of the overlaid Xenium and registered MACSima DAPI image allows for the easy identification of this issue by showing a non-uniform alignment quality across the image. This heterogeneous misalignment is more common for larger ROIs and typically arises from tissue deformation or folding between acquisitions, lens distortion in either imaging system, different tissue mounting geometry, or non-linear shrinkage or expansion of the section.    Potential solution  A non-rigid (deformable) transformation is required.     Note:   Non-rigid (deformable) transformation is not addressed in this protocol, as only a single transformation type was tested. This represents a current limitation; users are advised to adapt the methodology as needed for their specific application. Recommended alternatives are RAMI2D  31   or ST-align.  32       Additional computational problems and diagnostic tips  Other possible computational problems could lead to TMA cores being skipped or output folders not being written due to lack of disk-space ( Table 4 ). For troubleshooting the user can refer to the error message to identify the cause of the problem and correct their workflow or report it as an issue on the GitHub repository associated with this protocol ( https://github.com/scOpenLab/MACSimaXenium ).
