X-SPEAR: An Extensible Framework for Spatial Panel Evaluation and Refinement Introduction  Targeted in situ transcriptomics platforms such as 10x Genomics Xenium measure hundreds to thousands of genes at subcellular resolution in intact tissue, so that cell types, subtypes and states can be identified in their spatial context ( Janesick et al., 2023 ). They require the user to choose the gene panel before the experiment. The panel is usually chosen from an annotated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) or single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) reference, and the choice determines which cell identities the experiment can resolve. A probe that hybridises to unintended transcripts can also produce misleading spatial signal, so the designed probes need checking.  Several computational methods select markers or probe sets for this purpose: differential-expression rankings such as the Wilcoxon rank-sum test ( Wilcoxon, 1945 ); specificity scores such as COSine similarity-based marker Gene identification (COSG) ( Dai et al., 2022 ); minimal marker combinations such as Necessary and Sufficient Forest (NS-Forest) ( Aevermann et al., 2021 ); and probe-set optimisation such as Spapros ( Kuemmerle et al., 2024 ). Two problems remain. First, single-gene markers are often insufficient for rare populations, closely related subtypes and transient states, and methods that find gene combinations usually reduce each cell type to one combination, which fails if any of its genes is poorly detected. Second, a gene’s detection in a targeted spatial assay differs from its detection in the single-cell reference. Across the ovarian cancer panel studied here, the median gene is detected in Xenium in only about half as many cells as in the matched reference, and the loss varies strongly from gene to gene. A marker that looks excellent in the reference may be nearly invisible in situ. The methods we compare choose genes from the reference as measured and do not model this loss.  Here we present eXtensible Spatial Panel Evaluation And Refinement (X-SPEAR), a framework with two modules. The first is Decision-rule Aggregation for Rare-cell Typing (DART), which learns short Boolean gene rules and selects several gene-disjoint rules for each cell type. Before learning, DART thins the reference to each gene’s measured single-cell-to-Xenium detection rate, so that rules relying on poorly detected genes score poorly and are not chosen. The detection rates come from a  Xenium prior : a previous experiment in which a single-cell reference and a Xenium run were both measured, usually on a different tissue, because a designer never has Xenium data from the target sample before ordering its panel. The second module checks the probes of any panel, whichever method chose it, for predicted off-target transcripts that are expressed in other cell types. The current version targets cell-type marker selection for Xenium. The “X” denotes extensibility, toward other targeted platforms and other selection objectives.  We first ask which Xenium priors help DART, using every combination of prior and target among five paired single-cell and Xenium datasets. We then benchmark DART against the Wilcoxon test, COSG, NS-Forest and Spapros on three targets (ovarian cancer, mouse brain and cervical cancer), with a deployment rule throughout: nothing measured on the target’s Xenium informs the panel, and its labels are used only for scoring. With a Xenium prior from a different tissue, DART outperformed all four methods at matched panel size on every target. Its rules agree with the downstream classifier and name interpretable marker programs. On 45 mouse retinal ganglion cell (RGC) subtypes, held out within a single-cell atlas, DART matched the best methods and led COSG and NS-Forest at every subtype abundance.    2  Results   2.1  X-SPEAR designs a detection-aware panel and checks its probes  X-SPEAR takes an annotated single-cell reference of the tissue to be profiled, together with a Xenium prior, and returns a Xenium gene panel with evidence for classification performance and probe-level off-target risk ( Fig. 1 ). It is a Python package that can be used as a library, from the command line or as a pipeline of twelve stages (below). Panel design with DART proceeds in three steps ( Fig. 2 ).  The first step is detection-aware thinning. For each gene, a keep probability      p   keep       is the ratio of its detection rate (the fraction of cells with a nonzero count) in the Xenium prior’s Xenium run to its detection rate in that experiment’s single-cell reference ( Methods ). Each nonzero count of the single-cell reference is kept with probability      p   keep       and zeroed otherwise, so that the thinned reference reproduces each gene’s expected in situ detection. The prior’s cells need no labels, and the target’s Xenium is never used.  The second step is rule learning. Three learners propose candidate Boolean rules for each cell type: thresholded conjunctions such as     G  e  n  e  A  >   t  1   ∧  G  e  n  e  B  ≤   t  2     , which require one gene to be high and another to be low. The Asymmetric Tree Panel Finder (ATPF), developed here, grows decision trees whose splits isolate one target cell type rather than separating all classes. R ule F it  ( Friedman and Popescu, 2008 ), a rule-ensemble method, is applied to random-forest and gradient-boosted ensembles; it extracts rules from the trees and keeps those with nonzero      L  1     -penalised coefficients.  The third step is orthogonal selection. Candidates are ranked by      F  1      minus a penalty per additional gene, and up to     K     rules are kept per cell type, sharing at most      O   max       genes. The default is gene-disjoint rules        O   max    =  0      . The panel is the union of the selected rules’ genes.  The off-target module reads the probe report that the Xenium Panel Designer returns for a submitted panel, which lists each probe’s predicted off-target genes. For each marker it draws a dotplot of the marker beside its off-target genes across the reference’s cell types. A probe whose off-target genes are expressed in cell types that the marker does not mark would add false signal there and should be replaced; the dotplot shows which probes these are. Because the check needs only the probe report and the reference, it applies to a panel from any selection method ( Section 2.12 ).  X-SPEAR’s pipeline runs these steps as twelve numbered stages, each configured by its own file and each optional ( Fig. 3 ). Stages 00–04 load and prepare the single-cell reference: ingest, quality control, a cap on the cells per cell type, normalisation and, if wanted, an embedding. Stage 06 thins a copy of the reference to the Xenium prior’s detection rates, and stage 07 selects the panel, with DART (as four substages: rule learning, rule scoring, ranking and orthogonal selection) or with one of the other selectors compared here. Stage 10 exports the panel together with the reference bundle that the Xenium Panel Designer takes, and stage 11 checks the probe report it returns. Where a labelled Xenium run of the target exists, stages 05, 08 and 09 load it, label its cells with a classifier trained on the reference and score the labels, as the evaluations in this study do. Every selector writes the same panel file, which is all the later stages read, so the classification, export and off-target stages serve a panel from any method. The interfaces and each stage are described in the  Methods  ( Section 4.1 ).    2.2  Datasets  We used five paired datasets, each with a single-cell reference and a Xenium run, and one single-cell atlas ( Table 1 ). Three pairs serve as  targets , which need cell-type labels on the Xenium cells to score a panel: ovarian cancer, cervical cancer and mouse brain. All five pairs serve as Xenium priors. Ovarian and cervical cancer are the reference cases: formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue profiled with the 10x Genomics Chromium Flex assay (Flex) and Xenium Prime 5K on the same tissue block, with 10x’s cell-type annotation of the Xenium cells. Mouse brain adds a fresh-frozen (FF) target of another species. The mouse retina pair supplies a same-species prior for mouse brain; it has no cell-type labels, so it cannot be a target. The breast cancer pair is used only as a prior: its Flex reference and its Xenium run come from different tumours, so it is not suitable as a target. The mouse RGC atlas, with 45 annotated subtypes, has no Xenium counterpart with subtype labels, so it is used for a held-out single-cell benchmark of fine subtypes.  Several other datasets were considered and set aside. A skin melanoma pair was removed because its single-cell reference turned out to be from mouse lemur while its Xenium run was human, so its detection rates measured a species mismatch. A dermatomyositis skin pair had a nearly flat detection profile from a shallow reference and was not validated. A second ovarian cancer Xenium dataset was measured with an earlier 5K panel version lacking about 30% of the genes, and in situ whole-transcriptome Atera data show no detection loss to correct, so neither tests detection-aware design. A human spleen pair was set aside because the source of its Xenium run could not be documented.    2.3  Detection loss is large, gene-specific and reproducible across experiments  A Xenium prior is only useful if a gene’s detection loss measured in one experiment predicts its loss in another. On the ovarian cancer Xenium, the median gene is detected in 52% as many cells as in the matched single-cell reference (4,259 genes detected in at least 0.1% of reference cells), and the loss varies widely between genes ( Fig. 4a ). The loss is reproducible. Per-gene      p   keep       in ovarian and cervical cancer, two different tissues profiled on the same Xenium panel, correlate at Spearman     ρ  =  0.88     over 3,056 shared genes. That is more strongly than the genes’ single-cell detection breadth correlates between the two tissues (    ρ  =  0.62    ), so      p   keep       captures a property of the gene and its probes rather than shared biology ( Fig. 4b ).    2.4  Designing a panel without the target’s Xenium  Every panel in this study is designed and evaluated in the same way ( Fig. 5 ). Three datasets are involved. The  single-cell reference  is annotated single-cell data of the target tissue; the panel is chosen from its genes. The  Xenium prior  supplies per-gene detection rates from a previous experiment that measured both a single-cell reference and a Xenium run; only its detection rates are used. The  target Xenium  is the Xenium run of the target tissue. Its Xenium cells were split into two spatial halves by a checkerboard, and only the held-out half was scored. Nothing from the target Xenium informs the panel. To score a panel, a classifier is trained on the single-cell reference restricted to the panel’s genes, it predicts the cell type of every held-out target Xenium cell, and the predictions are compared with the target’s labels by macro      F  1     , the unweighted mean of the per-cell-type      F  1      scores.    2.5  A Xenium prior helps when it matches the target’s chemistry and species  We first asked which Xenium priors help DART. For each target we designed DART panels with every available prior, and with none, and compared them at the target’s default panel size ( Fig. 6 ;  Methods ). The target’s own Xenium is shown as an upper bound that no designer has before ordering.  The prior that helped most, other than the target’s own, always matched the target’s chemistry and species. For the two human FFPE tumours it was the other tumour, profiled with the same Flex reference and Xenium chemistry: cervical cancer raised ovarian cancer from 0.470 macro-     F  1      without a prior to 0.563, against 0.600 with the target’s own Xenium, and ovarian cancer raised cervical cancer from 0.517 to 0.612 (own 0.666). The breast pair, of the same chemistry but with its reference and Xenium run from different tumours, helped less (0.520 and 0.538). For the fresh-frozen mouse brain, the fresh-frozen mouse retina prior helped (0.643 to 0.673; own 0.700), whereas every human FFPE prior lowered accuracy, by 0.05 to 0.13. Conversely, the two fresh-frozen mouse priors helped ovarian cancer little (+0.011 and +0.025) and lowered cervical cancer (−0.016 and −0.033). A prior from the other species reaches only the genes whose human and mouse symbols agree, about half of the target’s genes ( Methods ). The best results therefore need a prior of the same chemistry and species as the planned experiment, which can come from a different tissue.    2.6  Benchmark against existing marker-selection methods  We then compared DART with four existing methods: the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, COSG, NS-Forest and Spapros. Each target used a Xenium prior from a different tissue, chosen by how closely its samples match the target’s and not by any score on the target: for ovarian and cervical cancer, each other (FFPE tissue with a Flex reference and Xenium Prime 5K on the same block), and for mouse brain, the mouse retina pair, the only other mouse pair, which like the target is fresh-frozen tissue with a single-nucleus reference and the mouse 5K panel ( Fig. 7 ). The other methods select genes from the single-cell reference as measured, as they are normally used. Because panel size drives accuracy, DART was run with     K  =  1–10     rules per cell type and the Wilcoxon test and COSG with 1–12 genes per cell type, and methods were compared at matched realised panel size by interpolating along each accuracy curve. NS-Forest’s panel barely changes with its budget (21–24 genes on ovarian cancer and one identical panel on each of the other targets), and Spapros was run at its default size, so neither gives an accuracy curve and DART was compared with them at their own panel sizes.    2.7  DART outperforms existing marker-selection methods  At matched panel size, DART outperformed the Wilcoxon test, COSG, NS-Forest and Spapros on every target ( Fig. 8 ;  Table 2 ). These rules name recognisable marker programs ( Table 3 ). For the interferon-high inflammatory tumour cells of the ovarian cancer reference, DART’s four gene-disjoint rules use  MX1  (in a conjunction that also requires  ESR1  high and  NAMPT  and  CD200  low),  IFIT1 ,  IFIT3  and  DDX58 , all interferon-stimulated genes. A ranked gene list carries no threshold and does not say which genes act together.  Panels are deployed with a classifier that never sees the rules, yet the classifier’s coefficients recover them ( Table 4 ). A “    g  e  n  e  >  t    ” condition in a cell type’s rule carries a positive coefficient for that type in 98–100% of cases on the three Xenium targets and in 96.5% across the 45 RGC subtypes. The rules are therefore an accurate, human-readable account of why the classifier calls a cell type.    2.11  Fine retinal ganglion cell subtypes  The Xenium targets have 6–14 broad cell types, which a single marker usually separates; on them most DART rules use one gene. RGCs, the projection neurons of the retina, comprise more than 40 transcriptionally related subtypes ( Tran et al., 2019 ;  Sanes and Masland, 2015 ), many without a unique marker. No Xenium dataset has RGC subtype labels, so we evaluated the 45 subtypes of a published atlas by five-fold out-of-fold prediction within the single-cell data ( Methods ): each panel is designed on four folds and scored on the held-out fold. Here 75% of DART’s rules are multi-gene conjunctions, with a mean of 2.4 genes per rule (    K  =  4     panels of the five folds), against 7–15% on the three Xenium targets.  DART, the Wilcoxon test and Spapros reached the same accuracy at matched size, about 0.955 to 0.96 macro-     F  1      from 150 genes upward ( Fig. 11a ): DART scored 0.959 with 184 genes and 0.960 with 223, the Wilcoxon test 0.957 with 191 and 0.958 with 224, and Spapros 0.956 with 175. It makes three contributions:
    Detection-aware design from a Xenium prior.  The gap between a gene’s detection in a single-cell reference and in Xenium is large, gene-specific and reproducible across tissues. Thinning the reference to a previous experiment’s detection rates anticipates that gap before ordering. The prior should match the planned experiment’s chemistry and species, and it can come from another tissue; a mismatched prior can lower accuracy.     DART.  With a Xenium prior from a different tissue, DART outperforms the Wilcoxon test, COSG, NS-Forest and Spapros at matched panel size on every target we tested, and reaches the Wilcoxon test’s best accuracy with 42–69% fewer genes. Its rules name interpretable marker programs and agree with the classifier that uses the panel. On fine RGC subtypes it matches the best methods, leads COSG and NS-Forest at every subtype abundance, and no single probe is load-bearing.     A method-independent off-target check.  Dotplots of each marker beside its predicted off-target genes show which probes would add signal in the wrong cell types, for a panel chosen by any method.     Two limitations matter most. First, the benefit depends on a suitable Xenium prior: for the best results, the prior should come from the same assay chemistry and the same species as the target. Second, the evaluation labels of the Xenium targets derive from reference-based annotation: 10x’s for ovarian and cervical cancer and our own label transfer for mouse brain. The comparisons are therefore within the reference’s annotation scheme, although an independent annotation of the ovarian section agreed with the evaluation labels on 82.8% of cells at the level of five lineages ( Supplementary S3 ).  The thinning, selection and off-target modules are separable. Other targeted platforms can be supported once a detection profile and a probe-design output exist for them, and the same architecture can host objectives beyond cell-type identification, such as panels that preserve differential expression across conditions or spatial niches.    4  Methods   4.1.  The X-SPEAR software   Interfaces.  X-SPEAR is a Python package (Code availability statement) with three interfaces. As a library,  design_panel  takes an annotated single-cell reference, a dataset configuration and, optionally, a Xenium prior, and returns the panel’s genes, the selected rules (each with its cell type, thresholds, precision and recall) and the full pool of candidate rules.  Panel.reselect  selects again from that pool at another     K     or      O   max       without relearning; this study used it for the RGC panels with     K  =  1–3    .  classify  labels a target’s cells with a panel, and  metrics.evaluate  scores the labels. A dataset configuration, one JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) file, names the reference’s cell-type column, the cell types to leave out, and the renames and exclusions that map the target’s labels onto the reference’s. On the command line,  xspear design, xspear classify  and  xspear evaluate  wrap these calls.  xspear prior  lists and exports the Xenium priors shipped with the package,  xspear profile  depth-normalises priors and  xspear kcurve  plots accuracy against     K     ( Supplementary S6 ).  xspear init  writes annotated configuration files for the pipeline, and  xspear run  runs it, in full or for chosen stages.    Pipeline. The stages of the pipeline ( Fig. 3 ) pass files to each other. Every selector writes the panel’s gene list, which is all that stages 08–11 read, and DART also writes its rules. Each stage records its outcome, with the package version and commit, in a run manifest, and a stage does not start if an earlier one failed. Stage 00 loads counts (an AnnData h5ad file or a Matrix Market (MTX) matrix) and can attach Ensembl gene identifiers from a gene transfer format (GTF) file or mygene.info (needed for the export bundle), merge per-cell metadata and assign a group label such as the sample of origin. Stage 01 computes quality metrics and keeps cells with 500–8,000 detected genes and genes detected in at least three cells; it can also filter on mitochondrial fraction and call doublets with Scrublet ( Wolock et al., 2019 ). Stage 02 caps the cells per cell type (3,000, seeded). Stage 03 normalises counts per 10,000, or per median library size, applies     log  (  1  +  x  )     and can flag highly variable genes. Stage 04, off by default, computes principal components, a neighbour graph, a uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) ( McInnes et al., 2018 ) and Harmony integration ( Korsunsky et al., 2019 ). Stage 05 loads the target Xenium and its labels, which are used only for scoring. Stage 06 resolves a Xenium prior and thins a copy of the reference to it ( Supplementary S6 ); every data-driven selector of stage 07 uses the thinned copy, and the classifier of stage 08 uses the original. Stage 07 runs DART as four substages, 07a rule learning, 07b rule scoring, 07c ranking and 07d orthogonal selection ( Sections 4.3  and  4.4 ; defaults     K  =  4    ,      O   max    =  0     and 1,000 estimators per ensemble, as in this study). It can instead run the Wilcoxon test, COSG or NS-Forest (10 genes per cell type by default), read a curated marker list, run Spapros or its reference probe sets (principal components, differential expression, highly variable genes and random genes), or adopt an existing panel. Stage 10 writes the panel and, for the Xenium Panel Designer, a reference bundle of counts, gene and cell tables and cell types. Stage 11, off by default, is the off-target check ( Section 4.9 ). This study ran stage 00 to load the references of the three Xenium targets and called the functions behind stages 06, 07 and 11 from its analysis scripts; the capping, splitting and scoring described below are in the paper repository. Cells can also be labelled by voting with DART’s rules instead of a classifier ( Supplementary S5 ). NS-Forest and Spapros give no curve, so DART’s curve was interpolated at their panel sizes; NS-Forest’s margin is the mean over its three budgets.    Seed variability.  The reference thinning and every learner were repeated at four seeds (1, 2, 3 and 42; the benchmark uses 42), and each seed’s DART curve (    K  =  1–6     and     8    ) was compared with the other methods’ panels exactly as in the benchmark. Across seeds, the standard deviation of DART’s margin over a method was 0.005–0.017 macro-     F  1      (0.006–0.008 over the Wilcoxon test), and that of DART’s macro-     F  1      at a single     K     was up to 0.024. A DART panel’s genes partly change between seeds (mean pairwise Jaccard index 0.62–0.74 at     K  =  4    ).    Compute.  Compute was measured on this study’s own runs, one job per target and method on the same cluster. For DART, the Wilcoxon test, COSG and NS-Forest, the job loaded the benchmark’s design slice and timed the method’s selection call exactly as the benchmark makes it (DART with the target’s Xenium prior,     K  =  4    ,      O   max    =  0     and 1,000 estimators; DART and NS-Forest with eight worker processes), recording the wall time of the call, the CPU time of the process and its workers, and the peak memory of the largest process. For Spapros, the scheduler summary of its job gave the same quantities, which also cover loading and preparing the data.     4.8  Single-cell out-of-fold evaluation on RGC subtypes  The RGC atlas (34,029 cells, 45 subtypes) was restricted to the 4,911 genes of the mouse Xenium 5K panel and split into five folds, stratified by subtype (scikit-learn  StratifiedKFold , shuffled, seed 42). For each fold, every method selected its panel from the other four folds only, so the held-out cells never influenced their own panel. Each panel was scored as on Xenium (Benchmark protocol), with the four training folds as the training cells and the held-out fold as the test cells. The predictions of the five folds were pooled, and macro-     F  1      and per-subtype      F  1      were computed over all 34,029 cells. title: SpaCut: Transcript-Aware Morphology Fusion for Robust Cell Segmentation in Subcellular Spatial Transcriptomics.

evidence_text:
SpaCut: Transcript-Aware Morphology Fusion for Robust Cell Segmentation in Subcellular Spatial Transcriptomics. Subcellular Spatial Transcriptomics (SST) offers unprecedented opportunities to decipher tissue architecture at subcellular resolution. Consequently, accurate cell segmentation is a fundamental prerequisite for analyzing SST data, as precise transcript assignment is essential for downstream single-cell interpretation. Existing methods often overlook the spatial organization of transcripts, rely on simplified geometric priors, or struggle to coordinate transcript-derived features with morphology-derived spatial guidance. This limitation restricts their adaptability to irregular cell shapes, often leading to transcript misassignment. To address this, we propose SpaCut, a unified deep learning framework designed to effectively integrate transcriptomic feature learning with dynamic morphological guidance. SpaCut comprises a Gene-Wise Attention (GWA) module and a Nuclei-Guided Attentive Fusion (NGAF) module. GWA encodes the high-dimensional transcript map and aggregates features across multiple depths. NGAF uses the encoded transcript features to modulate distance-based nuclear softmasks and refine nucleus-anchored cell boundaries through progressive training. Extensive evaluations across seven datasets from diverse platforms (including Xenium, CosMx, MERSCOPE, and Stereo-seq) demonstrate that SpaCut significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both segmentation accuracy and consistency with single-cell reference data. The source code is available at https://github.com/wenwenmin/SpaCut. Introduction  Elucidating how cells organize into tissues and interact within their environment is fundamental to biomedical research [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ]. Subcellular Spatial Transcriptomics (SST) technologies enable the measurement of gene expression within intact tissues at subcellular resolution [ 4 ,  5 ]. However, deriving biological insights from these data requires accurately attributing transcripts to individual cells through the segmentation of the spatial domain. The precision of this segmentation directly impacts downstream analyzes, such as cell type annotation and cell–cell communication [ 6 ,  7 ,  8 ]. Specifically, segmentation errors introduce bias: over‐segmentation incorporates extracellular noise or signals from neighboring cells, distorting spatial gene expression patterns; conversely, under‐segmentation results in the loss of valid transcripts, leading to incomplete gene expression profiles. Therefore, accurate cell segmentation is essential for the effective analysis of SST data [ 9 ,  10 ].  Currently, SST technologies vary significantly in key parameters such as resolution and gene profiling capacity [ 11 ]. Imaging‐based platforms, such as Vizgen's MERSCOPE [ 12 ] and 10    ×     Genomics' Xenium [ 13 ], offer high resolution (     ∼  100   nm     ) and capture efficiency for targeted gene panels. Notably, NanoString's CosMx [ 14 ] expands this capability, detecting thousands of genes while maintaining subcellular precision. Meanwhile, sequencing‐based platforms like Stereo‐seq [ 15 ] stand out by offering whole transcriptome analysis, capturing over 10000 genes with a resolution of 0.5      μ  m     . This distinction leads to different data characteristics: imaging methods generally prioritize high capture efficiency for specific gene sets, whereas sequencing methods deliver comprehensive genome‐wide profiles [ 16 ,  17 ]. Consequently, developing a unified cell segmentation method that adapts to these diverse data characteristics and resolutions remains a significant challenge.  Existing cell‐segmentation methods for SST can be broadly grouped into three categories: image‐based, transcript‐based, and integrative image–transcript approaches. Image‐based approaches [ 18 ,  19 ,  20 ,  21 ,  22 ,  23 ] primarily rely on deep neural networks trained on large‐scale annotated cellular images. Leveraging architectures such as U‐Net [ 24 ] or Transformers [ 25 ], these frameworks extract visual features like staining intensity and texture, determining cell boundaries based solely on visual information. Although tools like Cellpose [ 18 ] and StarDist [ 19 ] excel at nuclear detection, they are unable to capture complex gene expression patterns outside the nuclear region. This limitation extends to commercial platforms like 10    ×     Xenium and Vizgen, which rely on similar nuclear‐based strategies. Consequently, they often face challenges such as inaccurately large cells resulting from Xenium's default dilation or transcript loss due to Vizgen's conservative segmentation.  Transcript‐based methods instead infer cellular assignments primarily from molecular distributions. Baysor [ 26 ] utilizes Markov Random Field modeling to partition molecules based on compositional consistency, allowing it to function independently of histological images. Conversely, ProSeg [ 27 ] adopts a simulation‐based Cellular Potts Model. While it uses nuclear centroids for initialization, it primarily drives boundary expansion by optimizing the probabilistic likelihood of transcript distributions. Although these methods excel in regions with poor staining, inferring boundaries solely from transcript distributions often results in imprecise segmentations that do not correspond well to imaging data.  Integrative image–transcript methods seek to overcome the complementary weaknesses of these two categories by incorporating molecular information into morphology‐guided boundary inference. JSTA [ 28 ] jointly optimizes cell segmentation and cell‐type annotation using reference expression profiles, whereas SCS [ 29 ] combines imaging and sequencing data by learning the relative position of each transcript spot to its cell center. BIDCell [ 30 ] introduces biologically informed self‐supervised losses to relate spatial gene expression to nuclear morphology and reference cell‐type information. UCS [ 31 ] adopts a two‐stage nucleus‐anchored framework that combines transcript‐derived foreground features with distance‐based nuclear softmasks. Despite these advances, encoding sparse transcript distributions and adaptively integrating them with nucleus‐derived spatial priors remain challenging.  To address these challenges, we propose SpaCut, a transcript‐aware, nucleus‐guided framework for cell segmentation (Figure  1 ). The Gene–Wise Attention (GWA) module projects raw gene channels into a learned feature space and recalibrates transcript‐derived features to suppress noise and generate a coarse cellular foreground map. The Nuclei‐Guided Attentive Fusion (NGAF) module then uses these features to modulate distance‐based nuclear softmasks and refine nucleus‐anchored boundaries according to local transcript distributions. A progressive training strategy first learns foreground localization and subsequently freezes the transcript encoder while optimizing instance‐specific boundary refinement. Benchmarking against representative methods across seven datasets spanning Xenium, CosMx, MERSCOPE, and Stereo‐seq showed that SpaCut achieved higher segmentation accuracy and greater consistency with single‐cell reference profiles.    FIGURE 1   Overview of the SpaCut architecture. (A) Spatial transcriptomics data are transformed into tensor representations, where each gene corresponds to an individual slice (gene map). The input nucleus segmentation is further used to generate training labels (     Y  1      and      Y  2     ) for Stage 1 and Stage 2, respectively. (B) Backbone network of SpaCut. (C) Two key modules of SpaCut, including the depthwise separable convolution (DSConv) module and the feature‐wise linear modulation (FiLM) module. (D) Downstream analysis enabled by SpaCut.                     2.  Results   2.1.  Overview of SpaCut  To achieve accurate cell segmentation from SST data, we propose SpaCut. Designed to leverage both high‐dimensional gene expression maps and nucleus segmentation from nuclei staining, the network first employs a Gene‐Wise Attention (GWA) Module to encode the gene expression data into refined features. This module functions as a robust encoder, capturing spatial context while adaptively re‐weighting gene importance. The encoded features are then utilized in two sequential stages. First, a classification head generates a coarse foreground localization map, distinguishing cellular areas from the background. Simultaneously, discrete nuclei segmentations are smoothed into continuous softmasks via signed distance mapping. Subsequently, the Nuclei‐Guided Attentive Fusion (NGAF) Module integrates the nucleus softmask as a spatial prior. It employs a FiLM‐inspired mechanism where gene features generate a spatial coefficient map to dynamically modulate this prior, guiding the expansion from the nucleus to the precise cellular boundaries. SpaCut adopts a progressive training strategy: it first uses the Weighted Cross‐Entropy Loss (     L  fg     ) to train the foreground localization; it then freezes the encoded features and employs the Weighted Cross‐Entropy Loss (     L  cell     ) to train the NGAF module for individual cell boundary refinement. By jointly optimizing for foreground consistency and individual cell precision, SpaCut effectively produces robust cell segmentation.    2.2.  SpaCut Enables Accurate Cell Segmentation Across Diverse Spatial Transcriptomics Platforms and Tissue Architectures  To comprehensively assess SpaCut's generalization capability, we evaluated its performance across seven datasets spanning four leading SST platforms: 10    ×     Genomics Xenium, NanoString CosMx SMI, Vizgen MERSCOPE, and BGI Stereo‐seq. These datasets cover epithelial, stromal, and neural tissues, capturing a broad range of cellular morphologies and tissue architectures. This diversity introduces substantial segmentation challenges, specifically complex cellular morphologies and varying data quality across different technologies. SpaCut effectively handles this biological and technical variability, achieving accurate and consistent cell segmentation across these highly heterogeneous platforms.  The proposed SpaCut framework demonstrates robust and accurate performance in cell segmentation across diverse SST platforms. In Xenium Human Pancreas and Mouse Colon datasets (Figure  2A,B ), where 10    ×     Genomics annotations serve as the ground truth, SpaCut produces segmentation masks that closely align with reference boundaries. Compared with UCS and Baysor(prior), it yields smoother and biologically coherent boundaries while effectively avoiding the over‐segmentation observed in UCS. Such robust performance is similarly observed in the Xenium Lung Cancer dataset (Figure  2C ), where SpaCut precisely delineates elongated fibroblast‐like cells and irregular stromal cells in the tumor microenvironment, outperforming competing methods that often distort cellular morphology. In the Stereo‐seq Mouse Brain dataset (Figure  2D ), SpaCut maintains compact and morphologically consistent segmentations under sparse transcript density and high spatial resolution—conditions where transformer‐based models such as SCS tend to produce fragmented boundaries. In the Vizgen Ovarian Cancer dataset (Figure  2E ), we leveraged Vizgen's underestimated default segmentation results as “nuclei” inputs to assess cross‐platform adaptability. By reinterpreting segmentation masks as nuclear priors, SpaCut improves transcript coverage and accurately incorporates regions of high gene expression (     P  <  0.001     ), thereby increasing the number of assigned transcripts per cell for downstream analyzes. Finally, in the CosMx Human Pancreas dataset (Figure  2F ), SpaCut achieves results highly consistent with NanoString's full‐cell reference annotations, despite relying solely on nuclear fluorescence and transcript information. Additional same‐region visual comparisons across multiple datasets and platforms are provided in Figures  S1  and  S2 . These panels show that SpaCut retains coherent local boundaries under diverse microscopy backgrounds and transcript‐density patterns. Collectively, these results highlight SpaCut's strong cross‐modality generalization and robust performance under nuclei‐only staining conditions, which is a crucial capability for most SST datasets lacking whole‐cell stains.    FIGURE 2   Generalizability of SpaCut across six datasets. (A) Xenium human pancreas dataset; (B) Xenium mouse colon dataset; (C) Xenium human lung cancer dataset; (D) Stereo‐seq mouse brain dataset; (E) Vizgen ovarian cancer dataset; and (F) CosMx human pancreas dataset. SpaCut achieves accurate cell segmentation across diverse spatial transcriptomics platforms, consistently outperforming existing methods. Notations such as “SpaCut (10    ×    )”, “SpaCut (Cellpose)”, and “SpaCut (Vizgen)” indicate that the nuclei segmentation inputs are derived from the corresponding sources.                   We further evaluated the robustness of SpaCut on the Xenium Breast Cancer dataset by randomly subsampling transcripts at varying ratios (80%, 60%, 40%, and 20%) (Figure  3A ). This approach intentionally introduces signal sparsity to assess algorithmic stability under challenging, low‐quality conditions. Using the original dataset (100% transcripts) as the ground truth, we benchmarked the performance of SpaCut against BIDCell and UCS across these subsampled levels. SpaCut maintained robust performance and remained consistent with the H&E image even at the lowest signal level (20%) (Figure  3B ). This stability is corroborated by the F1‐score analysis(Figure  3C ), demonstrating its ability to preserve segmentation accuracy under noisy conditions. In contrast, competing methods showed a marked decline as signal density decreased. BIDCell suffered a sharp drop in accuracy with increasingly fragmented boundaries, while UCS exhibited moderate sensitivity to reduced signals. These results highlight SpaCut's robustness to handle noisy and incomplete datasets, maintaining reliable cell segmentation in various spatial transcriptomics datasets.    FIGURE 3   Robustness evaluation under transcript‐level subsampling on the Xenium breast cancer dataset. (A) To simulate varying signal intensities, transcriptomic data were subsampled to 80%, 60%, 40%, and 20% for  ERBB2  visualization. (B) Segmentation results of SpaCut, BIDCell, and UCS under different subsampling ratios. (C) Quantitative F1 score comparison demonstrating that SpaCut maintains consistently high accuracy across all subsampling levels, whereas BIDCell shows a sharp performance drop and UCS exhibits moderate sensitivity to reduced signals.                   SpaCut also remained robust to transcript corruption on Xenium Human Lung Cancer, achieving the highest instance F1 and AJI among the three evaluated methods across all tested conditions. Its F1 decreased from 0.8227 on the clean input to 0.7767 after 80% transcript loss and 0.7765 after adding 80% background transcripts (Figures  S3  and  S4 ). Together with the cross‐platform benchmarks, these results support the generalizability and robustness of SpaCut across diverse SST datasets.    2.3.  SpaCut Achieves State‐of‐the‐Art Segmentation Accuracy on Xenium Datasets  To comprehensively evaluate the performance of SpaCut, we conducted rigorous benchmarking on three representative Xenium spatial transcriptomics datasets, including Human Lung Cancer, Human Pancreas (FFPE), and Mouse Colon (FF) datasets. Unlike most publicly available Xenium data, which often lack reliable ground truth annotations, the Xenium 2.0 platform provides dual‐channel fluorescence imaging that simultaneously stains both nuclei and cell boundaries. This dual labeling provides reliable ground truth for segmentation evaluation. Using this reference, we compared SpaCut with a suite of representative segmentation methods. Segmentation performance was quantified using two established metrics including the Aggregated Jaccard Index (AJI) and the F1 score at an Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold of 0.4 (See Table  1 ). Specifically, it achieved leading AJI scores of 0.7461, 0.7454, and 0.6151 on the lung, pancreas, and colon datasets, respectively, substantially outperforming all competitors and reflecting higher agreement with the reference annotations. The corresponding F1 scores—0.9381, 0.8953, and 0.8980—further confirm its advantage. As shown in Figure  4 , SpaCut consistently achieves higher F1 scores across a wide range of IoU thresholds. This stable advantage under different matching thresholds demonstrates the robustness of our model in accurately identifying cell boundaries. In contrast, image‐based approaches showed lower performance across these datasets. These methods rely primarily on nuclear morphology, whereas SpaCut additionally integrates spatial transcriptomic information to support cell‐boundary delineation. The horizontal axis denotes the IoU matching threshold, and the vertical axis shows the corresponding instance‐level F1 score. Increasing the IoU threshold imposes a stricter overlap criterion; methods that retain higher F1 scores therefore achieve more accurate cell‐instance detection and boundary delineation.                   Qualitative results further support these quantitative observations. As shown in Figure  2A–C , SpaCut generates sharp and continuous cell boundaries across various tissue types. In regions with dense cellular packing, it accurately preserves cell morphology, while existing methods often yield fragmented or blurry boundaries. This improvement stems from SpaCut's joint modeling of local morphological features and spatial transcriptomic signals, which enables precise cell segmentation even in complex and heterogeneous tissue environments.  In summary, both quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that SpaCut achieves state‐of‐the‐art segmentation performance on Xenium datasets. Its effectiveness arises from the joint modeling of morphological and transcriptomic spatial features, leading to accurate cell segmentation. This capability provides a strong foundation for reliable downstream spatial transcriptomics analyzes.    2.4.  SpaCut Achieves Multi‐Scale Morphological and Transcriptomic Consistency on Xenium Breast Cancer  To comprehensively evaluate the performance of SpaCut in cell segmentation and annotation, we conducted a multi‐scale benchmarking analysis using the Xenium Human Breast Cancer dataset (Figure  5 ). As shown in Figure  5A , SpaCut shows stronger alignment with the H&E staining compared to existing methods. Regions with clear nuclear staining are accurately segmented, while low‐contrast or background areas are correctly ignored—errors that are frequently observed in the segmentation results of 10    ×    . Baysor (prior) tends to generate overly smooth and enlarged masks that merge adjacent cells, while Baysor (no prior) often produces fragmented boundaries. Cellpose‐SAM and Cellpose3 achieve nucleus‐centered segmentation that aligns well with dark‐stained regions and effectively separates close nuclei, but they frequently undersegment cytoplasmic or lightly stained areas.    FIGURE 5   SpaCut demonstrates accurate transcriptional and morphological consistency on the Xenium breast cancer dataset. (A) Visual comparison of segmentation boundaries overlaid on H&E images. SpaCut exhibits better morphological consistency with histological structures compared to baselines. (B) Quantitative statistics comparing cell count, transcript recovery, genes/transcripts per cell, and sparsity across methods. (C) Gene‐level quality assessment. Scatter plots display the fraction of cells expressing each gene in segmented cells (    y    ‐axis) vs. nuclei (    x    ‐axis). (D) Morphological validation. Left: Correlation between cell and nucleus elongation across cell types. (E) Overall morphology correlation plotted against average transcripts per cell, demonstrating SpaCut's effective balance between transcriptional sensitivity and morphological preservation.                   To quantitatively evaluate segmentation performance, we further analyzed both cell‐level and gene‐level statistics (Figure  5B,C ). At the cell level, five representative metrics—cell count, total transcripts, genes per cell, transcripts per cell, and cell sparsity were used to examine the trade‐off between segmentation outcomes and transcripts capture. Baysor (no prior) tends to over‐segment, producing numerous small cells with sparse transcript counts, while the nuclei dilation method used in the 10    ×     official pipeline generate segment large cells that include background or neighboring signals. In contrast, SpaCut achieves a balanced segmentation profile, recovering a biologically consistent number of cells with stable per‐cell gene and transcript distributions. At the gene level, we compared the proportion of cells expressing each gene between segmented masks and nuclei‐based expression to assess cytoplasmic transcript recovery. Methods with points near the diagonal recover little beyond nuclei, whereas SpaCut shifts more genes above the diagonal, indicating improved cytoplasmic transcript recovery and transcriptome completeness. Across the three Xenium datasets, SpaCut achieved the highest correct cytoplasmic recovery among non‐reference methods (0.6964–0.7324) and the highest assignment F1 (0.7619–0.8371). Although several conservative image‐only methods captured fewer extracellular transcripts, they recovered substantially fewer correct cytoplasmic transcripts. These results support a favorable recovery–contamination balance rather than an advantage driven solely by larger masks (Table  S1  and Figure  S5 ).  Finally, we examined how well each method preserves cellular morphology by correlating nuclear elongation (x‐axis) with cell‐mask elongation (y‐axis) (Figure  5D ). Image‐based models such as Cellpose and Cellpose‐SAM show high morphology correlations but exhibit lower average transcript counts per cell, suggesting that their segmentations primarily follow nuclear boundaries and underrepresent cytoplasmic regions. In contrast, SpaCut shows strong nuclear–cell shape agreement while achieving comparable transcripts per cell than competing methods(Figure  5E ), suggesting improved transcript recovery beyond the nucleus. UCS and BIDCell also display consistent nuclear–cell coupling, whereas Baysor (no prior) exhibits weak correlation and Cell 10X achieves only moderate agreement. Before post‐processing, shuffling or removing transcripts reduced instance F1 from 0.8638 to 0.7389 and 0.7032, respectively, and the full model outperformed fixed‐dilation and analytic‐softmask controls. Ablation Studies and Computational Performance  We evaluated the contributions of NGAF and GWA through component ablations on three Xenium datasets (Table  S9 ). Within NGAF, removing spatial attention or the concatenation of the original and modulated nuclear softmasks reduced segmentation performance, indicating that both spatially selective aggregation and retention of the nuclear prior contribute to boundary refinement. Within GWA, removing the depthwise‐separable convolution and channel‐recalibration block (DSC_CA) also decreased AJI and F1. Replacing multi‐depth feature fusion with only the deepest feature map caused the largest single‐component reduction on Xenium Human Lung Cancer, lowering AJI and F1 from 0.7465 and 0.9395 to 0.6805 and 0.8871, respectively. Simultaneously removing spatial attention and DSC_CA further degraded performance, particularly on Xenium Mouse Colon. Overall, the complete model achieved the best AJI and F1 on all three datasets, supporting complementary roles for transcript‐feature encoding, multi‐depth aggregation, and nucleus‐guided fusion.  SpaCut also maintained a favorable balance between runtime and segmented‐cell count across the Xenium, Stereo‐seq, and CosMx benchmarks (Figure  S16  and Tables  S10 – S12 ).     3.  Discussion  In this study, we introduce SpaCut, a robust cell segmentation framework for subcellular spatial transcriptomics based on a deep transcript–morphology fusion approach. SpaCut integrates a Gene‐Wise Attention (GWA) Module with a Nuclei‐Guided Attentive Fusion (NGAF) module. The former encodes high‐dimensional gene expression data to capture spatial context and suppress noise, while the latter dynamically modulates nuclear priors to guide cell boundary expansion based on actual transcriptomic signals. Finally, a progressive training strategy is employed to synergize global foreground localization with precise instance‐level boundary refinement.  We evaluated the effectiveness of SpaCut on seven datasets from four representative platforms, including Xenium, CosMx, MERSCOPE, and Stereo‐seq. The experimental results show that SpaCut consistently achieves higher segmentation accuracy (F1 score) and instance‐level quality (AJI) than state‐of‐the‐art baselines across various tissues. Beyond these metrics, we validated the biological relevance of our method. Unlike image‐based approaches that rely solely on nuclei, SpaCut leverages gene expression to identify cytoplasmic regions, thereby recovering valid transcripts located outside the nuclear boundary. Furthermore, transcript subsampling experiments demonstrated the model's robustness. SpaCut maintained accurate cell structures even with only 20% of the original transcripts, confirming its ability to handle the signal sparsity and technical noise often found in spatial transcriptomics.  We conducted systematic ablation experiments to dissect the impact of both architectural components and input quality on segmentation outcomes. These studies revealed that the GWA and NGAF modules are mutually indispensable: the former is critical for decoding sparse transcriptomic signals via deep feature aggregation, while the latter is essential for transforming rigid nuclear priors into biologically accurate cell boundaries. Furthermore, we investigated the dependency on nuclear segmentation quality. Our analysis reveals that segmentation performance is significantly correlated with the accuracy of the initial nuclear anchors. While high‐quality nuclei inputs unlock the full potential of SpaCut for precise boundary refinement, suboptimal inputs lead to performance degradation. This observation underscores that reliable nuclear detection serves as a critical prerequisite for the subsequent transcript‐driven expansion. Collectively, these findings validate the efficacy of the dual‐module strategy while highlighting the importance of upstream data quality.  Future work will focus on reducing the dependence on nuclear anchors by incorporating explicit multi‐anchor merging and anchor‐free candidate recovery for tissues containing multinucleated cells or weak or missing nuclear signals. We will also explore confidence‐aware nuclear guidance and adaptive post‐processing to improve robustness when upstream nuclear masks are imperfect.  In summary, SpaCut offers an effective and unified solution for analyzing subcellular spatial transcriptomics data, outperforming state‐of‐the‐art methods in segmentation performance. By integrating transcriptomic and morphological information for robust boundary inference across heterogeneous platforms, SpaCut facilitates more accurate downstream analyzes of tissue heterogeneity and cellular interactions.    4. For NanoString CosMx datasets, the platform's inherent field‐of‐view (FOV) structure was leveraged for model training. Each FOV was processed independently, with separate models trained to accommodate inter‐regional transcriptomic diversity across different tissue areas. This FOV‐specific approach ensures optimal performance while respecting the platform's natural data organization.    4.3. To provide a comprehensive evaluation, the F1 score was computed at the instance level across various matching thresholds.  Instance‐level F1 Score: Instead of pixel‐level evaluation, we measure the detection and segmentation accuracy of individual cells. The spatial overlap between a predicted cell mask (    P    ) and a ground truth cell mask (    G    ) is quantified by the Intersection over Union (IoU):
   (17)     IoU   (  P  ,  G  )   =    |  P  ∩  G  |    |  P  ∪  G  |        Given an IoU threshold     τ    , a predicted cell is considered a True Positive (TP) if its maximum IoU with a ground truth cell satisfies      IoU  (  P  ,  G  )  ≥  τ     . Predicted cells that fail to meet this threshold are counted as False Positives (FP), and ground truth cells without a valid matching prediction are counted as False Negatives (FN). Based on these instance‐level counts, Precision, Recall, and the F1 score are calculated as:
   (18)     Precision  =    T  P    T  P  +  F  P         (19)     Recall  =    T  P    T  P  +  F  N         (20)     F1  @  τ  =  2  ·    Precision  ×  Recall    Precision  +  Recall    =    2  ·  T  P    2  ·  T  P  +  F  P  +  F  N        By varying the matching threshold     τ     (e.g., from 0.1 to 0.9), we obtain an F1‐IoU curve that reflects the model's robustness under increasingly strict segmentation criteria.  Aggregated Jaccard Index (AJI): AJI evaluates instance‐level segmentation quality by measuring overlap between predicted and ground truth cell instances:
   (21)     AJI  =     ∑   i  =  1   N    |   G  i   ∩   P   σ  (  i  )    |      ∑   i  =  1   N    |    G  i   ∪   P   σ  (  i  )     |  +    ∑   j  ∈  U     |   P  j   |         where      G  i      represents the     i    ‐th ground truth cell instance,      P  j      denotes the     j    ‐th predicted cell instance,      σ  (  i  )      is the predicted instance with maximum overlap to      G  i     ,     N     is the number of ground truth instances, and     U     is the set of unmatched predicted instances. The AJI ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating better instance‐level segmentation performance.    4.8.  Experiment Settings  Experiments were conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU with PyTorch 2.0.1 [ 41 ] and Python 3.9. The SpaCut framework employed a progressive training strategy optimized by Adam with a learning rate of      10   −  4      . Specifically, the GWA Module was trained for 10 epochs with a batch size of 128, while the NGAF module was subsequently trained for 10 epochs with a batch size of 1 and frozen encoder features. Loss weights       w  1   ,   w  2   ,   w  3   ,   w  4       were set to 1 to ensure balanced supervision. Data augmentation included random discrete rotation (0     , 90     , 180     , 270     ) and vertical flipping. All experiments were independently repeated five times with different random seeds, and the final results were reported as the mean     ±     standard deviation across runs. SpaCut uses the same post‐processing pipeline as BIDCell [ 30 ], consisting of several standard morphological operations. Standard morphological post‐processing may remove fragmented regions but can also modify correctly delineated boundary pixels. Its effect is therefore condition‐dependent, and it is treated as an optional cleanup step rather than a procedure expected to improve all quantitative metrics. For downstream single‐cell processing, spatial neighborhood analysis, and visualization, we utilized Scanpy [ 38 ] and Squidpy [ 42 ].    4.9.  Baseline Methods  To benchmark SpaCut across complementary segmentation paradigms, we selected eleven representative methods spanning integrative, transcript‐based, and image‐based approaches: BIDCell [ 30 ], Proseg [ 27 ], SCS [ 29 ], UCS [ 31 ], Baysor [ 26 ], DeepCell [ 22 ], SAM [ 21 ], Cellpose [ 18 ], Cellpose‐SAM [ 20 ], StarDist [ 19 ], and MEDIAR [ 23 ]. Their algorithmic principles and execution configurations are summarized below.  
 BIDCell  [ 30 ]: BIDCell is a self‐supervised framework for cell segmentation in subcellular spatial transcriptomics. It integrates biologically informed loss functions with single‐cell RNA‐seq references to model relationships between gene expression and cell morphology. We used the documented Xenium configuration.  
 Proseg  [ 27 ]: Proseg is a probabilistic segmentation method that adapts the Cellular Potts model within a Metropolis–Hastings sampling framework. It infers cell boundaries by optimizing the likelihood of transcript distributions and includes transcript repositioning to reduce spurious co‐expression. The default configuration was used.  
 SCS  [ 29 ]: SCS employs a transformer‐based neural network to combine gene‐expression profiles with high‐resolution imaging information. It learns the relative position of each spot to its corresponding cell center and groups spots through gradient‐flow tracking. We used the default parameters provided by the authors.  
 UCS  [ 31 ]: UCS uses a two‐stage nucleus‐anchored framework. Its first network extracts transcript‐derived foreground features, and its second network combines these features with distance‐based nuclear softmasks for per‐anchor cell prediction. The model was run using the documented implementation and dataset‐specific settings.  
 Baysor  [ 26 ]: Baysor uses a Bayesian mixture model that accounts for spatial morphology and transcriptional composition when assigning molecules to cells. Both spatial‐prior and no‐prior configurations were evaluated using the documented settings.  
 DeepCell  [ 22 ]: DeepCell is a deep‐learning framework for whole‐cell and nuclear segmentation in tissue images. It uses a ResNet50‐based backbone with a feature‐pyramid architecture trained on TissueNet. We used the official pretrained model.  
 SAM  [ 21 ]: The Segment Anything Model uses a Vision Transformer trained on the SA‐1B dataset and provides promptable zero‐shot segmentation. We used the official pretrained weights in the image‐based comparison.  
 Cellpose  [ 18 ]: Cellpose predicts spatial gradient‐flow fields and forms cellular instances by grouping pixels that converge to common sinks. We used the official pretrained weights.  
 Cellpose‐SAM  [ 20 ]: Cellpose‐SAM combines the Cellpose flow‐field formulation with a SAM‐based image encoder to improve generalization across microscopy images. We used the official pretrained model without architecture‐specific retraining.  
 StarDist  [ 19 ]: StarDist represents nuclei as star‐convex polygons and predicts radial distances to their boundaries together with object probabilities. We used the official pretrained weights.  
 MEDIAR  [ 23 ]: MEDIAR is a transformer‐based framework for cell‐instance segmentation in multimodal microscopy images. We evaluated it with the official pretrained model. title: FmH2ST: foundation model-based spatial transcriptomics generation from histological images.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: FmH2ST: foundation model-based spatial transcriptomics generation from histological images. Spatial transcriptomics (ST) reveals gene expression distributions within tissues. Yet, predicting spatial gene expression from histological images still faces the challenges of limited ST data that lack prior knowledge, and insufficient capturing of inter-slice heterogeneity and intra-slice complexity. To tackle these challenges, we introduce FmH2ST, a foundation model-based method for spatial gene expression prediction. Equipped with powerful foundation models pretrained on massive images, FmH2ST employs a dual-branch framework to integrate prior knowledge from foundation model and fine-grained details from spot images. The foundation model branch employs a multilevel feature extraction strategy to obtain enriched features with slice context for capturing inter-slice heterogeneity, and a dual-graph strategy to obtain spatial and semantic enriched features for modeling intra-slice complexity. The spot-specific learning branch leverages multiscale convolutions, Transformer, and graph neural network to extract fine-grained spot features. The outputs of two branches are adaptively fused for better prediction under a collaborative branch learning strategy. Experimental results show FmH2ST outperforms state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets. FmH2ST can denoise the raw gene expressions, reveal cancer spatial heterogeneity and gene co-expression patterns, and support the inference of gene regulatory networks. Overall, FmH2ST is effective for predicting ST, with potential applications in clinical diagnostics and personalized treatment.

evidence_text:
Automated tumor regression grade assessment and survival prediction in esophageal cancer via weakly supervised multiple instance learning.

Introduction

Esophageal cancer remains a major global health burden and is among the leading causes of cancer-related deaths. Accurate evaluation of tumor regression grade (TRG) after neoadjuvant therapy is essential for assessing treatment response and guiding postoperative management. However, conventional TRG assessment relies heavily on subjective histopathological assessments, leading to considerable inter-observer variability and limited reproducibility. We aimed to develop an objective and automated TRG assessment framework using artificial intelligence for digital pathology.

Methods

A retrospective analysis was conducted on 157 patients with esophageal cancer and 1,298 hematoxylin and eosin-stained whole-slide images. Three slide-level pathology foundation models and three multiple instance learning methods were evaluated within a patient-level multiple instance learning framework, enabling weakly supervised TRG prediction based solely on patient-level labels.

Results

The proposed framework achieved a classification accuracy of 82.7% and demonstrated strong agreement with manual pathologist grading. Notably, artificial intelligence-derived TRG score provided superior prognostic stratification compared with conventional assessments, showing significant associations with progression-free and overall survival.

Discussion

This study presents a foundation-model-driven, patient-level multiple instance learning framework for automated evaluation of TRG in esophageal cancer. This approach offers a standardized, reproducible, and clinically interpretable solution that reduces the workload of pathologists and improves prognostic precision. These findings highlight the potential of weakly supervised AI pathology in advancing personalized treatment assessment and decision-making in digital oncology.

evidence_text:
Development and Usability Assessment of a Health Education Conversational Agent for Patients With Gastric Cancer: Action Research Study.

Background

To provide patients with gastric cancer with adequate health education information for effective overall management is crucial, while traditional manners exposed certain challenges. Conversational agents have increasingly been adopted for health care use to provide innovative solutions for patient education.

Objective

This study aimed to develop a health education embodied conversational agent to focus on gastric cancer disease using an action research approach and test its accuracy, usability, and user experience among patients and other related stakeholders.

Methods

The AI-guided conversational agent was developed based on the OpenMEDLab 2.0 foundation model and the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. A 4-phase action research approach was adopted to implement this system at a gastric cancer center in China. Diagnose and plan phase used participatory observation and in-depth interviews to explore current health education models and patients' needs for health education. Act and implement phase was used to develop and deploy the conversational agent. Evaluate phase comprised 3 rounds of alpha testing to assess accuracy and RAG knowledge hit rate, and 1 round of beta testing to assess the usability and relevance. Reflect phase conducted in-depth interviews to gain insights into users' experiences. Data collection was conducted from September 2023 through April 2025. Participants include patients, clinical nurses, nursing managers, surgeons, clinical psychologists, and dietitians. Thematic analysis and multiple-group chi-square tests were performed, respectively, for qualitative and quantitative data. A 2-sided P value of <.05 was considered statistically significant.

Results

A total of 44 patients, 13 nurses, 3 nursing managers, 2 surgeons, 1 clinical psychologist, and 1 dietitian were recruited during the study procedure. Favorable outcomes in terms of accuracy and usability were achieved. The accuracy of the agent in 3 rounds was 67% (37/55), 71% (44/62), and 82% (31/38), respectively; RAG knowledge hit rates reached 86% (47/55), 98% (61/62), and 100% (38/38). Significant differences (P<.01) in RAG knowledge hit rates were observed. The mean chatbot usability questionnaire score was 91.9 (SD 3.6), while the mean content relevance score was 3.75 (SD 0.9). Three themes of user experiences were identified: perceived usefulness, ease of use, and intention to use, revealing potential in reducing staff workload and reinforcing patient education.

Conclusions

This study provided insights into how the action research approach can inform the development and usability assessment of a gastric cancer health education conversational agent, also illustrating the value of RAG technology. Additional assessments and improvements are warranted to confirm the effectiveness and safety.

title: RNABag: A Generalizable Transcriptome Foundation Model for Precision Oncology across Biopsy Modalities

evidence_text: RNABag: A Generalizable Transcriptome Foundation Model for Precision Oncology across Biopsy Modalities Transcriptomic data is highly sensitive to cancer state and progression, making transcriptome-based foundation models a great promise for diverse clinical ontological inference. However, analyses of transcriptome are conventionally hindered by technical batch effects and limited generalization across platforms. Here, we introduce RNABag, a foundation model designed to generalize well to external datasets. In particular, the model only focuses on highly variable genes to reduce noise; and extensive data augmentation was utilized to pretrain RNABag to learn robust representations, invariant to batch variations. We demonstrate that RNABag achieves superior performance in pan-cancer tissue-of-origin classification and cancer detection in internal validation sets, as well as in zero-shot generalization to external cohorts and in-house clinical samples. Furthermore, RNABag, after specialized finetuning, exhibits strong capabilities in a wide range of clinical applications. The model effectively stratifies patient survival and predicts relapse risks, highlighting key molecular pathways driving tumor progression. Crucially, we extend RNABag’s utility to liquid biopsies, achieving high diagnostic accuracy in plasma cfRNA and tumor-educated platelets (TEPs), thereby supporting its application in non-invasive cancer monitoring. Interpretability analysis revealed pivotal role of tumor immune escape in the cancer induced plasma cfRNA signals. In summary, our study indicates that cancer states and progression may be monitored in details and precision via comprehensive modeling of transcriptome across biopsy modalities.

evidence_text:
A Melanoma Brain Metastasis CTC Signature and CTC:B-cell Clusters Associate with Secondary Liver Metastasis: A Melanoma Brain-Liver Metastasis Axis.

Abstract

Melanoma brain metastasis is linked to dismal prognosis and low overall survival and is detected in up to 80% of patients at autopsy. Circulating tumor cells (CTC) are the smallest functional units of cancer and precursors of fatal metastasis. We previously used an unbiased multilevel approach to discover a unique ribosomal protein large/small subunit (RPL/RPS) CTC gene signature associated with melanoma brain metastasis. In this study, we hypothesized that CTC-driven melanoma brain metastasis secondary metastasis (“metastasis of metastasis” per clinical scenarios) has targeted organ specificity for the liver. We injected parallel cohorts of immunodeficient and newly developed humanized NBSGW (huNBSGW) mice with cells from CTC-derived melanoma brain metastasis to identify secondary metastatic patterns. We found the presence of a melanoma brain–liver metastasis axis in huNBSGW mice. Furthermore, RNA sequencing analysis of tissues showed a significant upregulation of the RPL/RPS CTC gene signature linked to metastatic spread to the liver. Additional RNA sequencing of CTCs from huNBSGW blood revealed extensive CTC clustering with human B cells in these mice. CTC:B-cell clusters were also upregulated in the blood of patients with primary melanoma and maintained either in CTC-driven melanoma brain metastasis or melanoma brain metastasis CTC–derived cells promoting liver metastasis. CTC-generated tumor tissues were interrogated at single-cell gene and protein expression levels (10x Genomics Xenium and HALO spatial biology platforms, respectively). Collectively, our findings suggest that heterotypic CTC:B-cell interactions can be critical at multiple stages of metastasis.

Significance

This study provides important insights into the relevance of prometastatic CTC:B-cell clusters in melanoma progression, extends the importance of the CTC RPL/RPS gene signature beyond primary metastasis/melanoma brain metastasis driving targeted organ specificity for liver metastasis ("metastasis of metastasis"), and identifies new targets for clinical melanoma metastasis therapies.

title: A unified framework for identification of cell-type-specific spatially variable genes in spatial transcriptomic studies.

evidence_text: A unified framework for identification of cell-type-specific spatially variable genes in spatial transcriptomic studies. Characterizing cell-type-specific spatially variable genes (SVGs) within tissue context is essential for exploring the landscape of complex biological systems in spatial transcriptomic (ST) studies. In this paper, we present a unified framework, the Mixture of Mixed Models (MMM), designed to directly model RNA count data and identify cell-type-specific SVGs while accounting for cell type composition and correcting for platform effects. Through a comprehensive simulation study and the analyses of eight publicly available ST datasets from various tissues and technologies with different resolutions, we demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of MMM in identifying cell-type-specific SVGs. Notably, our integrative analysis with genome-wide association studies reveals that the cell-type-specific SVGs identified by MMM in a mouse brain study exhibit significant heritability enrichment in brain-related phenotypes. This finding suggests that cell-type-specific SVGs play a vital role in elucidating the mechanisms underlying complex traits and diseases. When applying MMM to analyze a high-resolution Xenium human breast cancer dataset by accounting for the uncertainties in cell segmentation, we find that certain cell-type-specific SVGs may contribute to cell-cell communications, thereby regulating the tissue microenvironment. Furthermore, we show the versatility of MMM by applying it to the 3D tissue models constructed from multiple ST slices, highlighting its utility in analyzing the 3D ST data.
