Results can be plotted statically or visualized interactively through a napari-based viewer ( Sofroniew et al . 2024 ). 2.2 Data structure on sample level The sample level data structure of InSituPy ( InSituData ) is compatible with any spatially resolved omics data consisting of a count or abundance matrix, image data and optionally segmentation masks or transcript locations. Within an InSituData object, data is organized in six data categories: image data ( images ), transcript locations and identities ( transcripts ), omics data from arbitrarily shaped spatial units such as spots or tissue compartments ( units ), single-cell omics data ( cells ), histological annotations ( annotations ), and histological regions ( regions ) ( Fig. 1D ). While spatial units and cells both represent bounded areas with associated measurements, cells are treated independently as they possess unique properties including distinct nuclear and cellular boundaries. Both the cells and units attributes are further subdivided into layers, allowing integration of results from multiple cell segmentation algorithms or different types of spatial units. Each layer consists of two attributes: a table containing spatial omics data as an AnnData ( Virshup et al. 2021 ) object, paired with either a boundaries attribute storing nuclear and cellular segmentation masks (for cells ) or a shapes attribute containing polygons (for units ). Each data modality can be loaded individually using the respective loading functions ( Fig. 1C ). Image and transcript data is loaded lazily and only loading times for cellular data, annotations and regions increase with dataset size ( Fig. S2A , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). Analysis results can be saved in an InSituPy project folder. To optimize writing performance, the framework distinguishes between static data (i.e. data that remains unchanged during analysis such as raw image data and transcript locations) and variable data (i.e. data that is modified during analysis such as spatial omics data and histological data). When saving to an existing project, only variable data is written to disk, significantly reducing save times ( Fig. S2B , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). For data handling, the framework uses different state-of-the-art packages ( Table S2 , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). In case of histological data, InSituPy differentiates between regions and annotations ( Fig. 1B and D ). Annotations can be any histological annotation (e.g. “tumor”), while regions are meant to delineate the positions of TMA cores or different tissue sections within the same dataset. 2.3 Multi-sample and multi-modal data assembly InSituExperiment objects can be assembled using three strategies ( Fig. 1E ): (i) from histological regions, e.g. TMA cores; (ii) from individual InSituData objects; (iii) from a configuration file containing data directories and corresponding metadata. For transcriptomic methods such as Xenium In Situ and Visium, dedicated reading functions and alignment tools are implemented, facilitating the joint analysis of single-cell and spot-based spatial omics approaches ( Fig. S3A , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). Further, technology-agnostic import workflows are documented, enabling integration of additional platforms. For spatial proteomic technologies based on multiplex immunofluorescence (e.g. co-detection by indexing ( Schürch et al. 2020 )), a technology-agnostic workflow using QuPath ( Bankhead et al. 2017 ) and InstanSeg ( Goldsborough et al. 2024 ) has been implemented. This workflow enables import of one or more samples into InSituPy ( Fig. S3B , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). In addition, functionality to quantify immunofluorescence signal intensity per cell from aligned images has been implemented as well ( Fig. S3C , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). The quantification algorithm processes images in tiles, avoiding full image loading into memory and enabling analysis on standard hardware with limited RAM ( Fig. S3D , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). 2.4 Interoperability with SpatialData To ensure interoperability with analysis packages from the scverse ecosystem ( Virshup et al. 2023 ), InSituPy provides bidirectional conversion functions between InSituData or InSituExperiment objects and the SpatialData format ( Fig. S4 , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). While SpatialData’s flat, keyword-based structure offers flexibility, it can become unwieldy when working with complex, multi-modal datasets. InSituPy addresses this limitation through a hierarchical data structure that provides organized access to different data modalities and improves scalability for larger datasets. In addition, the conversion functions provide access to spatialdata-io readers, extending InSituPy’s compatibility to technologies beyond its native readers. Benchmarking the InSituPy Xenium reader against its spatialdata-io counterpart revealed that spatialdata-io required substantially longer reading times and higher memory consumption, making it difficult to load very large datasets on normal computers and highlighting the advantage of technology-specialized readers over more generalized ones. 2.5 Automated image registration The non-destructive nature of spatial omics methods such as Xenium or CODEX ( Black et al. 2021 ) enables the subsequent histological staining of sections. To simplify integration of pathological annotations, InSituPy provides an automated registration pipeline that aligns the nuclear image acquired during the spatial omics measurement with subsequently stained images ( Fig. 1F ). The pipeline employs Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) to identify features in both images ( Lowe 2004 ), followed by the Fast Library for Approximate Nearest Neighbors (FLANN) for feature matching ( Muja and Lowe 2009 ). The random sample consensus algorithm (RANSAC) then selects the most robust feature matches to calculate an affine or perspective transformation matrix for image registration. Registered images are saved alongside quality control metrics and integrated into the InSituData object for downstream analysis. 2.6 Data visualization and annotation using the InSituPy viewer A precise registration of the images is a prerequisite for the addition of histological annotations to the datasets and for visualizing the results of the single-cell spatial omics analyses in their histopathological context. This is particularly important for morphological quality control and for leveraging the translational potential of spatial omics analyses. Histological annotations can be either imported from external software such as QuPath ( Bankhead et al. 2017 ) or from a napari-based viewer ( Sofroniew et al. 2024 ) ( Fig. S5 , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). The viewer provides various functionalities for data examination, including visualization of spatial omics data and cellular boundaries, localization of specific cells, and adding and displaying annotations or regions ( Figs. S5 and S6 , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). Added regions or annotations can be synchronized with the source InSituData object via a dedicated button. In case of multi-sample datasets stored as InSituExperiment object, individual datasets can be visualized and annotated in parallel. 2.7 Data analysis using InSituPy Leveraging the InSituExperiment object structure, InSituPy facilitates multi-sample analysis workflows through simple and streamlined syntax. Analyses can be performed within or between samples, and depending on the biological question, can be focused on specific regions, annotations, or cell types ( Fig. 1G ). Currently available analyses include cellular composition evaluation, the measurement of cell type densities, differential gene expression analysis and pseudobulk analysis. Further, InSituPy offers interfaces to external tools such as STRING, Enrichr and g:Profiler for GO term enrichment analysis, decoupler for enrichment analysis, and squidpy for spatial analyses ( Kuleshov et al. 2016 ; Raudvere et al. 2019 ; Szklarczyk et al. 2019 ; Badia-i-Mompel et al. 2022 ; Palla et al. 2022 ). Since omics data is stored in the AnnData format, all scverse functions are expected to be compatible with InSituPy. Further, InSituPy provides plotting functionalities to visualize the results of multi-sample datasets ( Fig. S1H , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). Together, these functionalities allow a histomorphology-informed analysis of gene expression changes in multi-sample spatial omics datasets. A complete step-by-step analysis has been demonstrated using published breast cancer Xenium In Situ data ( Janesick et al. 2023 ) and revealed differentially expressed genes within one cancer cell subtype between different histological regions ( Supplementary Methods and Figs. S7 and S8 , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). In addition, we provide a tutorial on how to import previously published data of a pulmonary fibrosis TMA (Vannan et al. 2025) into an InSituExperiment object and perform preprocessing steps ( Fig. S9 , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). 3 Discussion In this work, we introduce InSituPy, a comprehensive Python-based framework, designed to simplify the handling, analysis, and visualization of multi-sample spatial omics data. While state-of-the-art Python-based analysis frameworks such as SpatialData ( Marconato et al. 2025 ) or Squidpy ( Palla et al. 2022 ) focus on a sample-level analysis, InSituPy allows handling of data at both the sample and experiment levels. With functions to read, write, query and analyze the datasets, InSituPy lays the foundation for large spatial omics projects, including multiple tissue sections or tissue microarrays from large patient cohorts. For the multi-sample analysis of such datasets, InSituPy provides functionalities to conduct analysis within and across samples using a simple syntax. On a sample level, currently published frameworks such as SpatialData structure the data based on the geometric properties of the modalities, e.g. as shapes or points. In contrast, InSituPy introduces a hierarchical data structure which groups the modalities into biologically meaningful layers, making analyses more intuitive and more accessible for non-bioinformaticians and medical experts. To allow interoperability between both frameworks, we implemented bidirectional conversion functions, giving InSituPy users access to data analysis workflows developed for SpatialData. In the future, we aim to further strengthen the support of SpatialData while also introducing advanced data formats for metadata handling such as ehrapy ( Heumos et al. 2024 ). A central step in the analysis of spatial omics data is the alignment of concurrently generated image data, which often requires laborious manual steps. Based on previously published analysis pipelines ( Wirth et al. 2023 ) and similarly to R-based tools like VoltRon ( Manukyan et al. 2023 ), InSituPy uses the computer vision toolbox OpenCV to facilitate an efficient and automated alignment of images from histological or immunofluorescent stainings. To verify results and develop hypotheses during analysis, interactive visualization of the data is crucial. Based on the napari framework ( Sofroniew et al. 2024 ), InSituPy offers visualization of image data and cellular omics data of multiple datasets as well as the handling of histological annotations or regions, facilitating the integration of pathological expert knowledge and opening new ways of generating hypotheses and driving translational research. All functionalities were demonstrated on a Xenium In Situ breast cancer dataset; however, InSituPy’s data structure is suitable for all types of imaging-based and sequencing-based spatial transcriptomics as well as spatial proteomics methodologies. Technology-agnostic data import strategies are available and explained in the documentation. Furthermore, InSituPy supports bidirectional conversion with SpatialData objects, enabling data import from various spatial omics technologies through the spatialdata-io ecosystem while maintaining InSituPy’s biology-inspired hierarchical structure for downstream analysis. Notably, benchmarking of InSituPy’s native Xenium reader against its spatialdata-io counterpart also highlights that specialized readers optimized for specific data formats can significantly improve loading performance. In conclusion, InSituPy represents the first Python-based framework for multi-sample spatial omics analysis that seamlessly integrates sample-level and experiment-level data handling. Through its biology-inspired hierarchical structure and comprehensive documentation, InSituPy establishes standardized analysis workflows that improve accessibility for non-bioinformaticians and disease experts. Malignant epithelial states drive immune dysfunction in ampulla of Vater carcinoma.

Background

Ampulla of Vater (AoV) carcinoma is a rare malignancy arising at the junction of intestinal and pancreatobiliary epithelium. Its heterogeneous clinical behavior and histological diversity have hindered therapeutic advances, and the cellular basis of this heterogeneity remains unclear. We aimed to construct a single-cell transcriptomic atlas of AoV carcinoma, with a focus on identifying epithelial subtypes and their interactions with the tumor microenvironment (TME).

Methods

We performed single-cell RNA sequencing on eight primary AoV tumors and four matched normal tissues. Comprehensive clustering and transcriptomic analyses identified cell-type composition, epithelial heterogeneity, and tumor-immune interactions. Findings were validated using deconvolution of bulk RNA-seq data from 62 AoV carcinoma patients. Results Malignant epithelial cells were categorized into four distinct subtypes: Int-Wnt, PB-KRAS, Int-Hypoxia, and Cycling stage. PB-KRAS cells exhibited stem-like transcriptional programs and high genomic instability. Deconvolution analysis of bulk RNA-seq data from the independent AoV cohort revealed that enrichment of the PB-KRAS subtype correlated with tumor recurrence and poor survival. Our immune profiling analysis discovered a significant association between PB-KRAS subtype and GZMK+ CD8+ T cells, which are in a pre-dysfunctional state, alongside SPP1+ macrophages exhibiting immunosuppressive traits. Spatial transcriptome data further supports the immunosuppressive natures of TME around PB-KRAS subtype malignant epithelial cells in AoV carcinoma.

Conclusions

Our study presents a single-cell atlas of AoV carcinoma, highlighting the molecular diversity of malignant epithelium and its association with the immune microenvironment. The PB-KRAS subtype emerges as a stem-like, immunosuppressive tumor state associated with poor prognosis, providing insights for future therapeutic targeting. Background Ampulla of Vater (AoV) carcinoma is a malignancy arising from the ampulla of Vater, the anatomical convergence of the common bile duct, pancreatic duct, and duodenum. This unique anatomical location gives rise to both histological and molecular heterogeneity, reflecting contributions from intestinal and pancreatobiliary lineages. AoV carcinoma is often categorized into intestinal and pancreatobiliary subtypes, which exhibit distinct prognostic and therapeutic characteristics [ 1 , 2 ]. However, this binary classification does not fully account for the molecular diversity and variable clinical behavior observed among patients [ 3 ]. Previous genomic studies have provided important insights into the molecular landscape of AoV carcinoma. Notably, Yachida et al. [ 4 ] identified frequent mutations in the ELF3 gene, implicating it as a potential driver of tumorigenesis. Similarly, Gingras et al. [ 5 ] reported recurrent ELF3 inactivation and widespread dysregulation of the WNT signaling pathway. While these studies advanced our understanding of AoV carcinogenesis, they were based on whole-exome sequencing and bulk transcriptome profiling, which lack the resolution to capture cell type-specific transcriptional programs and the complexity of tumor-microenvironment interactions. As a result, the biological basis of epithelial heterogeneity and the functional contributions of non-malignant cell populations remain poorly understood. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) offers a powerful approach to address these limitations by enabling high-resolution, cell-type-resolved transcriptomic profiling [ 6 ]. This technology facilitates the identification of cellular subpopulations, and intercellular communication networks that are not accessible through bulk sequencing methods. Despite its potential, scRNA-seq has not yet been applied to AoV carcinoma, leaving fundamental gaps in our understanding of its cellular and transcriptional architecture. Therefore, our study is essential to move beyond bulk-level genomic insights and establish a high-resolution, cell-type-resolved atlas of AoV carcinoma. In this study, we present the first single-cell transcriptomic analysis of AoV carcinoma. Using scRNA-seq on primary tumor specimens, we identify distinct epithelial subtypes characterized by unique oncogenic and reveal their associations with the immune landscape and clinical outcomes. This work establishes a foundational single-cell atlas of AoV carcinoma and provides new insights into its cellular diversity with potential translational implications. Methods Study patients This study included 70 patients histologically diagnosed with AoV adenocarcinoma between September 2005 and March 2023 at Samsung Medical Center (SMC), of whom eight underwent single-cell RNA sequencing and 62 underwent bulk RNA sequencing. Patient demographics and clinical characteristics, including age, gender, tumor stage according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 8th edition, tumor differentiation, adjuvant chemotherapy administration, and survival data, were retrospectively collected. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board at SMC (IRB No. SMC-2022–06-076) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. All participants provided written informed consent for the future research use of their pathology specimens. Single-cell RNA sequencing Fresh tumor and adjacent normal tissue specimens were obtained from patients with AoV carcinoma before treatment through Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) for scRNA sequencing. Acquired tissues are collected in MACS® Tissue Storage Solution (Miltenyi Biotec., Auburn, CA, USA) on ice and processed to the single cell dissociation immediately. Biopsy tissues are placed on a petri dish with a small volume of enzyme mixture solution (Tumor Dissociation Kit, Miltenyi Biotec.) and minced into small pieces under 1–2 mm with surgical blades. Minced pieces are transferred to gentleMACS TM C-tube containing enzyme mixture solution. By choosing an appropriate program of gentleMACS TM Dissociator, tissue pieces are further dissociated three times with two interval incubations for 30 minutes at 37 °C under continuous rotation using the MACSmix TM Tube Rotator. Resuspended samples are applied to a cell strainer (70 μm) and washed with 10 ml of DMEM/F12 media with 1% FBS. After a centrifugation at 400xg for 5 minutes, cells were resuspended in an appropriate volume of media and counted with trypan blue staining or acridine orange/propidium iodide staining. Optionally, erythrocytes are removed by red blood cell lysis solution for 10 min before counting. We initiated the cell preparation process by employing the LUNA-FL™ Automated Fluorescence Cell Counter (logos biosystems). Detailed guidelines for cell preparation were sourced from the 10x Genomics Single Cell Protocols Cell Preparation Guide and the Guidelines for Optimal Sample Preparation flowchart. Libraries were meticulously constructed using the Chromium controller in accordance with the 10x Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3’ v3.1 protocol (10x Genomics). In brief, cell suspensions were diluted in nuclease-free water, aiming to achieve a targeted cell count of 10,000. The diluted cell suspension was mixed with a master mix and subsequently loaded onto a Chromium Next GEM chip, along with Single Cell 3’ V3.1 gel beads and partitioning oil. Within the droplets formed in the chip, RNA transcripts from individual cells underwent unique barcoding and reverse transcription. Pooled cDNA molecules then underwent sequential processes, including end repair, addition of a single ‘A’ base, and adapter ligation. Subsequently, the resulting products were subjected to purification and enrichment through polymerase chain reaction (PCR), ultimately yielding the final cDNA library. To ensure library quality and quantify the purified libraries, we adhered to the qPCR Quantification Protocol Guide (KAPA). Furthermore, library qualification was performed using the Agilent Technologies 4200 TapeStation from Agilent Technologies. The sequenced libraries were processed using the HiSeqX platform from Illumina to obtain the requisite data for our study. Data preprocessing and quality control Raw sequencing data were processed using CellRanger (v7.0.1; 10x Genomics) [ 7 ], with alignment to the GRCh38 reference genome via STAR. CellBender (v 0.2.2) [ 8 ] was applied to each sample to eliminate background RNA contamination. Doublets were detected using Scrublet (v 0.2.3) [ 9 ], with thresholds determined according to simulation-derived scores. we excluded low-quality cells with fewer than 500 detected genes and a mitochondrial gene proportion exceeding 20%. Seurat (v4.3.0) [ 10 ] was used for downstream processing, including normalization, variable gene selection, scaling (regressing out total UMI counts, mitochondrial gene proportion, and cell cycle scores), principal component analysis, and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) projection. Clustering was performed using the FindNeighbors and FindClusters functions, with dimensionality assessed via JackStraw and ElbowPlot methods. Cell type annotation was conducted using SingleR (v2.0.0) [ 11 ] and further validated through the expression of canonical lineage markers. Major cell types were identified using EPCAM (epithelial cells), COL1A1 (fibroblasts), VWF (endothelial cells), CD3D (T cells), CD14 (myeloid cells), and CD79A (B cells). For more granular annotation of immune and stromal subsets, we utilized the following marker sets: CD4 for helper T cells, CD8 for cytotoxic T cells, FOXP3 for regulatory T cells (Tregs), and NCAM1 and NCR1 for NK cells. Myeloid sub-populations were defined by C1QC (macrophages), LYZ and S100A9 (monocytes), CD1C (dendritic cells), and CPA3 and KIT (mast cells). B cell lineages were further distinguished using CD79A and MS4A1 (B cells), CD38 and CD27 (plasma cells). Subclustering analyses were performed on major immune and stromal compartments following additional doublet removal [ 12 ]. Identification of epithelial subtypes using cNMF To identify transcriptional programs within epithelial cells, we applied consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF) (v0.2) [ 13 ] to the normalized gene expression matrix. The number of components (k) was varied from 2 to 15, and the optimal solution was selected based on silhouette scores and Frobenius reconstruction error. Copy number variation inference To infer copy number alterations at the single-cell level, CopyKAT (v1.1.0) [ 14 ] was applied with default parameters. T cells were used as a reference for normal diploid profiles. CNV scores were computed for individual epithelial cells and summarized across samples to evaluate subtype-specific genomic instability. Transcription factor regulatory network inference Regulatory network analysis was performed using the pySCENIC (v0.12.1) [ 15 ] pipeline. Regulon activity scores were computed from raw UMI matrices to identify transcription factor-target gene modules, and average activity scores were calculated per subtype for downstream comparative analyses. Modular score and stemness estimation The CytoTRACE algorithm (v0.3.3) [ 16 ] was used to infer the differentiation potential of malignant epithelial cells. CytoTRACE computes transcriptional diversity and expression correlation to derive stemness scores, ranging from 0 (fully differentiated) to 1 (highly undifferentiated). This approach enables the identification of less differentiated, stem-like cell states at single-cell resolution. To evaluate functional characteristics of epithelial subtypes, including stemness potential, we calculated gene module scores using AddModuleScore function in the Seurat package. This approach determines the average expression of a specific gene program at the single-cell level, which is then normalized by subtracting the aggregated expression of control feature sets. To ensure a robust baseline, all analyzed features are binned based on their average expression levels, and control features are randomly selected from each bin. This process effectively accounts for technical noise and the influence of overall gene expression profiles. The stemness gene set was constructed using previously reported stemness-associated markers [ 17 ]. Functional enrichment analysis Differentially expressed genes were selected based on adjusted p -values and fold changes. Functional enrichment analysis was performed using EnrichR (v3.2) [ 18 ], employing the hypergeometric test with default parameters to identify overrepresented pathways and biological processes. We employed the hypergeometric test with default parameters to identify overrepresented pathways and biological processes from the MSigDB Hallmark gene set collection. Cell-cell communication analysis Ligand-receptor interaction analysis was conducted using CellPhoneDB (v5.0.0) [ 19 ] to identify potential intercellular communication events between cell types. Significant interactions were inferred via permutation testing using default parameters. Pseudotime trajectory analysis To infer the developmental hierarchy of epithelial subtypes, we performed pseudotime trajectory analysis using the Monocle2 R package (v2.30.0) [ 20 ]. To minimize potential biological variations across patients, we utilized the integrated data generated via the FindIntegrationAnchors and IntegrateData functions from the Seurat package. For trajectory ordering, we selected the top 30 differentially expressed genes from each epithelial cluster. Dimensionality reduction was performed using the DDRTree algorithm. Bulk RNA sequencing and processing For bulk RNA sequencing, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor tissues from an independent cohort of surgically resected 62 AoV carcinoma patients were analyzed. Transcript-level quantification was achieved using RSEM (v1.3.0) [ 21 ], aligned to the GRCh38 genome with GENCODE v33 annotation. Gene-level expression matrices were derived for integrative analyses with single-cell data. Proportions of each subtype were estimated in bulk RNA-seq samples using MuSiC (v1.0.0) [ 22 ]. Xenium in situ hybridization and spatial analysis Surgically resected FFPE tissue samples from AoV tumor patients were profiled using Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue and Pathways Panel (10x Genomics). FFPE tissue sections (5 µm) were prepared on Xenium slides using Xenium Prime Sample Preparation Reagents. RNA quality was assessed by calculating the percentage of RNA fragments > 200 nucleotides (DV200) extracted from tissue sections, and H&E staining were also used to assess tissue morphology and region of interests by a specialized pathologist before performing the Xenium in situ hybridization. Slides were deparaffinized, rehydrated and decrosslinked, followed by hybridization with Xenium 5K Priming Oligos and probes targeting messenger RNA. Probes were ligated, amplified and washed, with subsequent antibody staining for cell segmentation. Autofluorescence quenching and nuclei staining were performed and slides they were stored in phosphate-buffered saline with tween-20 (PBS-T) at 4 °C. The Xenium Analyzer (version 3.1) was used for imaging, decoding, segmentation and cell assignment, following the manufacturer’s protocols. During the initial quality control and filtering step, cells with a transcript count below 100 were classified as low-quality and excluded from all downstream analyses. For cell type classification, we utilized our own scRNA-seq dataset as the reference. Cell assignment was performed using the FindTransferAnchors and TransferData functions within the Seurat package, employing default parameters. Cells with a prediction score below 0.5 were classified as unknown and excluded from further downstream analyses. Survival analysis The clinical relevance of epithelial subtypes was evaluated using survival analysis. Kaplan-Meier curves were generated using the survival and survminer R packages (v0.5.2). Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression models were implemented using the coxph function to assess associations with overall survival and disease-free survival. Statistical analysis All statistical analyses were performed in R. Pair-wise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were utilized to analyze the proportional differences between groups within each cell type/subset. Significance is displayed as *, p  < 0.05; **, p  < 0.01; and ***, p  < 0.001. For comparisons among multiple groups, the Kruskal-Wallis test was used to determine global significance, followed by Dunn’s test for pairwise post-hoc comparisons with adjustments for multiple testing. Statistical significance for multiple comparisons is presented as adjusted p -values (Padj), indicated as follows: *, Padj < 0.05;, Padj < 0.01; and ***, Padj < 0.001. Pearson correlation was employed to calculate the correlation between the proportions of each pair of cell subsets, and Spearman correlation was used for the co-ecosystem analysis. Results Patient characteristics This study included 70 patients (scRNA-seq: n  = 8 and bulk RNA-seq: n  = 62) with AoV carcinoma. Median age was 61.5 years (range, 36–83 years) and 33 were male (47.1%). Tumor stage (AJCC 8th edition) was I-III in the majority of patients (67/70, 95.7%), with only one patient classified as stage 0 and two as stage IV. During a median follow-up of 9.7 years (interquartile range, 6.4–12.7 years), 27 deaths (38.6%) occurred (Table S1 ). Single-cell transcriptomic profiling reveals diverse cellular composition in AoV carcinoma To investigate the cellular architecture of AoV carcinoma, we performed scRNA-seq on tumors ( n  = 8) and matched adjacent normal tissues ( n  = 4) (Fig. 1 a). After quality filtering, a total of 34,672 cells were analyzed and grouped into 18 clusters, which were subsequently classified into six major cell types based on cell type marker gene expression (Fig. 1 b–c). UMAP visualization revealed that while immune cells were broadly shared across patients, epithelial cell clusters displayed strong patient-specific transcriptional profiles, consistent with the absence of batch effects and reflecting inter-patient variation driven by tumor-specific copy number alterations [ 23 , 24 ] (Fig. 1 d). We further examined the distribution of cell types across individual samples, revealing substantial inter-patient heterogeneity in cellular composition (Fig. 1 e). Some tumors were highly enriched in epithelial or myeloid populations, whereas others showed greater T cell infiltration. These findings highlight the cellular complexity of AoV carcinoma and underscore the diversity of tumor-immune microenvironments across patients. This analysis revealed strong patient-specific clustering patterns (Fig. 2 a), indicating pronounced transcriptional differences between tumors. We then applied consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF) to the epithelial transcriptomes, identifying four robust molecular subtypes (NMF-1 to NMF-4) (Fig. S1 a-b). Although each subtype included epithelial cells from multiple patients, their relative proportions varied markedly across samples (Fig. 2 b). This suggests that, while certain transcriptional programs are shared among tumors, their dominance is highly patient-specific, reflecting substantial inter-patient heterogeneity. Intestinal markers ( CDX2 and KRT20 ) were strongly expressed in NMF-1 and NMF-3, whereas pancreatobiliary markers ( KRT7 and MUC1 ) were predominantly enriched in NMF-2. These findings support the biological relevance of the identified subtypes and their alignment with previously described histological features [ 2 , 25 ]. Functional enrichment analysis revealed distinct transcriptional programs characterizing each subtype (Fig. 2 d and Table S2 ): NMF-1 was enriched for Wnt/β-catenin signaling (designated Int-Wnt), NMF-2 for KRAS signaling (PB-KRAS), NMF-3 for hypoxia-related pathways (Int-Hypoxia), and NMF-4 for cell cycle-associated signatures (Cycling). We categorize these four programs as three lineage-driven, differentiated subtypes and one progenitor/functional subtype (NMF-4, Cycling). To further characterize the regulatory landscape underlying epithelial heterogeneity, we performed regulon activity analysis across epithelial cells. This analysis revealed that multiple transcription factor regulons were differentially activated in a subtype-specific manner (Fig. S1 c). MSX1 activity was predominantly elevated in the Int-Wnt subtype compared to the PB-KRAS and Cycling subtypes. HNF1B activity reached its highest levels in the PB-KRAS subtype, showing a significant increase over the Cycling subtype and a strong upward trend compared to the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtypes. SIRT6 activity was notably enriched in the Int-Hypoxia subtype, while CDX1 was most active in the Cycling subtype, significantly surpassing the levels in the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia groups (Fig. S1 d). The MSX1 is a known WNT/β-catenin responsive transcription factor implicated in promoting intestinal tumorigenesis [ 26 ]. Similarly, the enrichment of HNF1B in the PB-KRAS subtype is relevant, as its overexpression has been shown to enhance the expression of liver progenitor cell markers and stemness in liver cancer cells [ 27 ]. Finally, the activation of the SIRT6 regulon in the Int-Hypoxia subtype is consistent with its known role in enhancing the stability of HIF-1α, a process linked to epithelial-mesenchymal transition under hypoxic conditions [ 28 ]. These regulon profiles were concordant with the transcriptional programs defined by cNMF, further supporting the molecular distinction among AoV epithelial subtypes. Collectively, these results demonstrate that epithelial cells in AoV carcinoma exhibit diverse transcriptional states driven by lineage-specific and oncogenic programs, with subtype composition varying substantially between tumors. PB-KRAS subtype exhibit distinct genomic instability and stem-like properties To interrogate the degree of genomic instability underlying each epithelial subtype, we first analyzed copy number variation (CNV) profiles inferred from single-cell transcriptomes. Notably, CNV patterns were strongly patient-specific, indicating inter-patient variability in genomic alterations (Fig. 3 a). At the single-cell level, CNV scores were markedly elevated in tumor epithelial cells compared to non-epithelial controls, with the PB-KRAS subtype exhibiting the highest levels of genomic aberrations (Fig. S2 a). To validate these findings at the sample level, we averaged CNV scores across epithelial cells within each sample and compared them across subtypes. This analysis confirmed that the PB-KRAS subtype exhibits the highest CNV burden among all epithelial subtypes (Kruskal-Wallis, p  = 0.00013; Fig. 3 b). These results indicate that genomic instability is unevenly distributed among AoV epithelial subtypes and is particularly pronounced in PB-KRAS subtype. For pairwise post-hoc comparisons, Dunn’s test was used to adjust for multiple comparisons. *Padj < 0.05, ** Padj < 0.01, *** Padj < 0.001; n.s., not significant Given that high genomic instability is frequently associated with aggressive phenotypes and enhanced self-renewal capacity [ 29 ], we next investigated the functional and developmental hierarchy of these subtypes. Based on its highest CNV burden, we specifically focused on evaluating the stem-like properties of the PB-KRAS subtype. We first focused on the Cycling subtype. Given its cell cycle-associated transcriptional program and the enrichment of progenitor-associated regulons, such as CDX1 (Fig. S1 d), we hypothesized that it represents a less differentiated, progenitor-like state. To infer the developmental potential across all subtypes, we employed CytoTRACE [ 16 ], a computational tool that infers developmental potential using transcriptional entropy. As expected, the Cycling subtype exhibited high CytoTRACE scores (Fig. 3 c and Fig. S2 b), supporting its identity as a less differentiated, progenitor-like state. Surprisingly, the PB-KRAS subtype, which otherwise presents as a differentiated lineage, exhibited the highest CytoTRACE scores (Fig. 3 c and Fig. S2 b), suggesting unexpected stem-like features. This combination—a seemingly differentiated state with high developmental potential—defines a non-canonical stemness phenotype. This suggests that, unlike the canonical progenitor-like Cycling subtype, the PB-KRAS subtype represents a distinct, highly aggressive stem-like epithelial state that deviates from the typical differentiation pathway. To further examine this possibility, we calculated stemness scores based on a curated stem cell gene signature [ 17 ]. The PB-KRAS subtype exhibited elevated stemness scores that were comparable to those of Cycling cells, while remaining notably higher than the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtypes (Kruskal-Wallis, p  = 0.00043; Fig. 3 d and Fig. S2 c). To provide dynamic evidence of this developmental hierarchy, we performed pseudotime trajectory analysis using Monocle2 [ 20 ]. The resulting trajectory delineated a clear lineage progression originating from the Cycling subtype, passing through the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtype, and ultimately culminating in the PB-KRAS subtype at the terminal end (Fig. 3 e). Notably, despite its terminal position on the pseudotime axis—which typically denotes a fully differentiated state—the PB-KRAS subtype harbored exceptionally high developmental potential, consistent with its elevated CytoTRACE (Fig. 3 f) and stemness scores (Fig. 3 g). This paradoxical terminal stemness suggests that PB-KRAS cells do not merely follow a conventional differentiation path but may undergo a coordinated transcriptional reprogramming or de-differentiation process, re-acquiring progenitor-like properties at an advanced stage of lineage development. We next sought to determine the potential molecular drivers of this phenotype, focusing on KRAS , the defining feature of the PB-KRAS subtype. Expression of KRAS was significantly upregulated in PB-KRAS subtype compared to the Int-Wnt subtypes (Fig. 3 h and Fig. S2 d), whereas CNV at the KRAS locus showed no significant difference among the subtypes (Fig. 3 i). Consistent with this, correlation analysis at the sample level revealed a moderate positive correlation between CNV score and stemness score ( r  = 0.5, p  = 0.014, Fig. S2 e). Furthermore, the expression of KRAS showed a strong positive correlation with both stemness score ( r  = 0.6, p  = 0.002, Fig. S2 f) and CNV score ( r  = 0.59, p  = 0.002, Fig. S2 g). These findings collectively highlight the robust association of both genomic instability and KRAS expression with the enhanced stem-like properties of the PB-KRAS subtype. Since KRAS knockdown in pancreatic cancer cells is known to reduce stemness characteristics [ 30 ], these observations suggest that the transcriptional upregulation of KRAS , rather than genomic alterations, is the likely contributor to the stemness signature of the PB-KRAS subtype. Among these, the Int-Wnt subtype was the most abundant, followed by Int-Hypoxia and PB-KRAS, whereas the Cycling subtype was relatively rare across samples (Fig. 4 a and Table S3 ). Spatial profiling reveals an immunosuppressive microenvironment in PB-KRAS subtype regions To investigate the spatial relationships between cellular subtypes and the tumor microenvironment, we performed Xenium in situ analysis on two representative AoV carcinoma samples, categorized as intestinal type and pancreatobiliary type based on the consensus judgment of experienced pathologists examining the tumor sections (Fig. 5 f). We first used single-cell RNA sequencing to estimate the major cell types and then mapped their spatial distribution across the tissue (Fig. 5 g). To investigate subtype-specific spatial patterns, we next identified and distinguished specific regions within the tumors, focusing on the AoV-ST1 sample, which are characterized by high proportions of Int-Hypoxia, and the AoV-ST2 sample, which are characterized by high proportions of the PB-KRAS subtype (Fig. 5 h). Importantly, the classification of regions derived from scRNA-seq mapping into Int-Hypoxia high (AoV-ST1) and PB-KRAS high (AoV-ST2) categories showed strong agreement with the initial pathological classification. Visualization of the spatial maps revealed a striking co-localization between the PB-KRAS subtype and Tc-GZMK cells (indicated by triangle-shaped dots), with a denser infiltration observed in the PB-KRAS high sample (Fig. 5 h). Quantitative analysis confirmed this observation: the PB-KRAS high sample exhibited a markedly higher proportion of PB-KRAS cells (among all epithelial cells) and a corresponding elevation in the proportion of Tc- GZMK cells (among all T cells) compared to the Int-Hypoxia high sample (Fig. 5 i). To further validate the spatial association between these populations, we performed a nearest neighbor distance analysis using the Xenium spatial coordinates. Our results revealed that Tc- GZMK cells were located significantly closer to PB-KRAS cells, with a mean minimum distance of 114.3 µm, whereas the distance to Int-hypoxia cells was nearly three-fold higher at 321.4 µm (Fig. 5 j). To visually confirm the presence of the Tc- GZMK population, we performed multiplex immunofluorescence using MACSima Imaging System ( n  = 3 per each group; see supplementary methods). Although this population was relatively sparse, pancreatobiliary subtype enriched samples showed higher infiltration of Tc- GZMK cells, whereas intestinal subtype dominant tumors displayed sparse Tc- GZMK infiltration (Fig. S5 a-b). Quantification confirmed that the proportion of Tc- GZMK cells was significantly higher in Pancreatobiliary subtype compared to intestinal subtype tumors ( p  = 0.0375; Fig. S5 c). These initial findings collectively suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype is associated with a distinctive and highly infiltrated tumor microenvironment. These refined annotations enabled a more precise characterization of cell-type-specific contributions to the tumor microenvironment. SPP1 -expressing macrophages have previously been associated with immunosuppressive and pro-tumorigenic functions [ 32 , 33 ]. This analysis identified several significant signaling axes, including PTN-ALK, FGF2–FGFR1, and FGF19–FGFR1, which were specifically enriched in the interaction between the PB-KRAS subtype and SPP1 + macrophages (Fig. S6 c). Notably, FGF2 is a well-established mediator known to promote the polarization of tumor-associated macrophages toward a pro-tumorigenic, M2-like state within the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment [ 34 ]. These findings suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype may develop within, or contribute to, a uniquely immunologically conditioned microenvironment enriched in tumor-promoting macrophages and pre-dysfunctional CD8 + T cells. This immune landscape may underlie the aggressive behavior and recurrence-prone nature of this epithelial subtype. Further mechanistic studies are warranted to clarify the functional significance of these immune–epithelial interactions and evaluate their potential as therapeutic targets. Discussion This study presents the first single-cell transcriptomic analysis of AoV carcinoma, offering a high-resolution landscape of its epithelial and immune cell composition. Previous genomic investigations, primarily based on whole-exome sequencing, have significantly advanced our understanding of AoV carcinoma by identifying recurrent alterations such as ELF3 mutations and WNT pathway dysregulation [ 4 , 5 ]. However, these bulk approaches lack the granularity required to resolve cell type-specific programs and microenvironmental interactions. Our single-cell approach addresses these limitations and provides novel insights into epithelial heterogeneity, differentiation states, and tumor-immune crosstalk in AoV carcinoma. Among the four molecular subtypes identified, our data demonstrate that the intestinal subtype itself is not homogeneous but comprises at least two molecularly distinct programs: one characterized by active WNT/β-catenin signaling (Int-Wnt) and another driven by hypoxia-associated pathways (Int-Hypoxia). The Int-Wnt subtype was defined by robust expression of WNT target genes and selective activation of the MSX1 regulon. MSX1 is known to function downstream of WNT/β-catenin signaling, playing a key role in promoting intestinal tumorigenesis. Its loss suppresses ectopic crypt formation in Apc-deficient models, suggesting that MSX1 is a critical mediator of WNT-driven epithelial transformation [ 26 ]. These features suggest that the Int-Wnt subtype retains a proliferative, WNT-responsive phenotype reminiscent of early intestinal neoplasia. In contrast, the Int-Hypoxia subtype displayed prominent enrichment of hypoxia-related gene sets and strong activation of the SIRT6 regulon. This suggests a mechanism involving SIRT6-enhanced stability of HIF-1α, which is known to promote the expression of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-related transcription factors like SNAIL and TWIST [ 28 ]. The resultant overexpression of SNAIL and TWIST leads to suppression of E-cadherin and induction of Vimentin, hallmark events of EMT [ 28 ]. This molecular cascade facilitates increased cellular plasticity and motility, thereby promoting invasive behavior. EMT has been associated with enhanced metastatic potential and poor recurrence-free survival in several cancers, including papillary thyroid carcinoma, and may similarly portend aggressive clinical behavior in the Int-Hypoxia subtype of AoV carcinoma. By uncovering both a WNT-driven and a hypoxia-induced EMT program within the intestinal group, our analysis emphasizes the subtype’s underlying complexity and suggests that these distinctions may carry prognostic or therapeutic significance. The PB-KRAS subtype emerged as a particularly notable finding in our comprehensive epithelial subtyping. This subtype is defined by elevated KRAS expression and a transcriptional program robustly enriched for KRAS signaling. The PB-KRAS subtype exhibited a pronounced degree of genomic instability, carrying the highest CNV burden among all identified epithelial subtypes. Reflecting these substantial genomic aberrations, which are often associated with aggressive and self-renewal-enhancing phenotypes, we were guided to investigate its developmental hierarchy and specifically focused on evaluating its stem-like properties. Strikingly, the PB-KRAS subtype paradoxically exhibited high developmental potential and stemness scores, comparable to the canonical progenitor-like Cycling subtype. This unique combination of an apparent differentiated PB lineage state possessing high developmental potential defines a non-canonical stem-like epithelial state. Unlike the Cycling subtype, which represents a classical progenitor state, PB-KRAS cells achieve stemness through oncogenic signaling. Specifically, we found that the stemness signature was driven by the transcriptional upregulation of KRAS expression, independent of differential CNV at the KRAS locus. This suggests that elevated KRAS expression forces an aberrant, de-differentiated potential within a seemingly mature lineage. This is consistent with prior findings implicating KRAS signaling in the maintenance of stem-like features in pancreatic cancer cells [ 30 ]. Supporting this stem-like phenotype, HNF1B regulon activity was also selectively enriched in the PB-KRAS subtype. As HNF1B overexpression has been shown to enhance the expression of liver progenitor cell markers and stemness in liver cancer cells [ 27 ], this activation suggests a conserved role in supporting KRAS-associated epithelial states. Clinically, the PB-KRAS subtype was associated with significantly worse OS and DFS, as well as a higher incidence of recurrence. These findings collectively suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype program, defined by unique genomic instability and a KRAS-driven non-canonical stemness, represents the most clinically aggressive AoV subtype identified in this study, associated with poor outcomes and inherent therapeutic resistance. In addition to epithelial heterogeneity, our analysis revealed striking differences in the immune landscape across subtypes. PB-KRAS subtype were enriched for a distinct immune microenvironment characterized by abundant GZMK + CD8 + T cells (Tc-GZMK cells) and SPP1 + macrophages. GZMK enriched cytotoxic T cells, recently described as pre-dysfunctional T cells, represent an intermediate state preceding terminal T cell exhaustion [ 31 ]. Their accumulation within the PB-KRAS tumor microenvironment, coupled with spatial proximity to tumor epithelium and signaling through immunosuppressive ligand-receptor pairs (such as TGFB2 , FGF2 , and SPP1 ), strongly suggests active immune remodeling by tumor cells. These specific axes are known mediators of immunosuppressive signaling. For instance, TGF-β is known to suppress CD8 + T cell cytotoxicity by repressing a distinct program of cytotoxic gene responses, thereby limiting the antitumor immune response [ 35 ]. Similarly, FGF2 has been implicated in promoting T-cell exhaustion by regulating the expression of SPRY1 in esophageal tumor-infiltrating T cells, further impairing T cell function [ 36 ]. SPP1 directly suppresses CD8 + T cell proliferation and interferon-γ production, contributing to immune evasion by the tumor [ 37 ]. The co-enrichment of SPP1 + macrophages, previously implicated in promoting immune evasion and supporting tumor progression, further supports the presence of an immunosuppressive TME in PB-KRAS subtype. Importantly, high abundance of Tc-GZMK cells was associated with poor clinical outcomes, reinforcing the relevance of the immune milieu in disease progression. Taken together, our findings suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype defines a biologically aggressive, stem-like epithelial population that may either arise within or actively sculpt an immunosuppressive TME enriched for dysfunctional immune cell states. This epithelial-immune crosstalk may contribute to tumor recurrence and resistance to therapy. In contrast, the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtypes are characterized by alternative oncogenic programs and immune environments, with divergent prognostic implications. A key limitation of this study is that the observed association between the PB-KRAS subtype and the immunosuppressive TME is based on correlational multi-omics analysis rather than direct functional validation. It is well established that activating KRAS mutations can actively modulate the immune microenvironment by promoting pro-tumorigenic macrophage polarization, inhibiting T-cell cytotoxicity, and accelerating T-cell exhaustion. Moreover, KRAS-mediated metabolic reprogramming may create a feedback loop where metabolite accumulation induces further genomic instability and mutational burden [ 38 ]. Although our findings regarding the PB-KRAS subtype are highly consistent with these known roles of KRAS signaling, further in vivo studies—such as orthotopic or syngeneic mouse models—and co-culture experiments are necessary to definitively prove the causal role of PB-KRAS cells in shaping this specific immunosuppressive niche. Moreover, while the specific ligand-receptor axes identified in this study, such as TGFB2 and SPP1, represent highly promising therapeutic targets, we acknowledge that their functional significance requires further validation in follow-up translational models utilizing functional blocking with neutralizing antibodies or small molecule inhibitors in patient-derived organoid-immune co-culture systems. These insights have potential therapeutic implications. Targeting the KRAS-HNF1B axis or the immunosuppressive mediators enriched in PB-KRAS subtype may offer novel avenues for treatment. Moreover, immunotherapeutic strategies aiming to restore CD8 + T cell functionality or reprogram tumor-associated macrophages may be particularly effective in this context. Future studies should focus on elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying epithelial-immune interactions in AoV carcinoma and evaluating their druggability in preclinical models. Additionally, although the multivariate analysis yielded an inflated hazard ratio due to complete separation in our small cohort ( n  = 62), Bootstrap validation (1,000 resamples) confirmed the statistical stability and robust prognostic value of the PB-KRAS subtype. Given the limited number of patients included in the single-cell analysis, validation in larger multi-institutional cohorts will be important to further establish the generalizability and potential clinical utility of the PB-KRAS subtype classification. Conclusions Our single-cell atlas of AoV carcinoma reveals profound epithelial and immune heterogeneity and identifies a clinically relevant PB-KRAS subtype defined by KRAS-driven non-canonical stem-like features and an immunosuppressive microenvironment. These findings provide a foundation for precision classification of AoV carcinoma and suggest novel therapeutic vulnerabilities for high-risk patients. evidence_text:
Artificial intelligence in thoracic surgery: a narrative review of clinical advances and applications in 2025.

Background and objective

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into thoracic surgery accelerated notably over the course of 2025, transitioning from isolated diagnostic aids toward comprehensive clinical pathway integration. The objective of this narrative review is to synthesize the latest evidence on AI applications across the entire thoracic surgical workflow, organized along the patient care continuum from preoperative assessment through intraoperative execution to postoperative management.

Methods

A PubMed/MEDLINE search was performed on March 6, 2026, and retrieved 378 English-language records published between January 1, 2025 and March 6, 2026. After title and abstract screening, potentially relevant articles underwent full-text review, and studies addressing the clinical applications of AI and related digital technologies across the thoracic surgical pathway were included in this narrative review.

Key content and findings

In the preoperative domain, large-scale foundation models and computational pathology systems have demonstrated strong performance in nodule risk stratification and noninvasive genomic prediction [area under the curve (AUC) >0.900]. Notably, dual-phase computed tomography (CT) systems such as NeoPred have achieved validation for predicting pathological response to neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy. Intraoperatively, augmented reality (AR) navigation has achieved randomized controlled trial (RCT)-level evidence outperforming conventional localization, while generative AI systems have attained expert-level anatomical recognition for surgical video analytics. Postoperatively, wearable continuous monitoring systems and digital therapeutics (DTx) entered prospective clinical validation. Furthermore, large language models (LLMs) emerged as increasingly important tools for automated surgical documentation. Despite these advances, most studies remain retrospective, and domain shift across institutions limits generalizability.

Conclusions

While AI has substantially affected thoracic surgery, important gaps persist regarding prospective validation and regulatory governance. Future priorities must focus on prospective multicenter interventional trials linking AI predictions to standardized clinical action protocols, federated learning architectures to overcome data silos, and the development of specialty-specific guidelines building upon the Artificial Intelligence Organization for Next Generation Surgeons (AIONS) 2025 consensus.

evidence_text: AI-augmented intraoperative decision-making workflows in diffuse midline glioma biopsy using cryosection pathology. Cryosection pathology is essential for intraoperative diagnosis of diffuse midline gliomas, yet it often leads to diagnostic errors and may prompt unnecessary re-biopsies before completion of the formal molecular assessment. In this study, we propose an AI-augmented framework, CryoAID, for rapid molecular outcome prediction during surgery for patients with diffuse midline glioma. CryoAID integrates a generative model to correct cryosection artefacts and a pathology foundation model to predict molecular statuses directly from cryosection images. We validate CryoAID across multiple cohorts to predict tumoural molecular statuses in the internal (n = 326), external multi-centre (n = 52), and consecutive (n = 68) datasets. In particular, CryoAID accurately predicts major molecular statuses (e.g., ATRX, H3K27M, and TP53) using cryosection images that were previously deemed disqualified for molecular examinations. Beyond tumour cells, CryoAID reveals highly differential clinical features, including glial cell proliferation, abundant cytoplasm, and localised endothelial proliferation. In the retrospective analyses, CryoAID reduces re-biopsy rates by 26.4% and 26.6% in the internal and consecutive datasets, respectively. Our findings demonstrate that the AI-augmented pathology workflow can extract diagnostic value from specimens previously considered non-viable by traditional histopathology. This approach represents a shift towards real-time molecular pathology, potentially reducing re-biopsies and improving diagnostic precision for patients with diffuse midline glioma.

evidence_text: DeepLNM: A Multimodal Model for Predicting Lymph Node Metastasis in Colorectal Cancer. Accurate assessment of lymph node metastasis (LNM) is critical for prognostic stratification and treatment selection in colorectal cancer (CRC), yet imaging and routine pathology can yield false-negative/false-positive results. We propose DeepLNM, a multi-center foundation model for LNM prediction in CRC, evaluated with retrospective, external, prospective, and user study evidence. A multimodal dataset was assembled from three hospitals, with matched hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained whole-slide images (WSI), CT scans, and text. DeepLNM achieved a mean AUC of 0.922 in the internal cohort and AUCs of 0.872 and 0.848 in two external cohorts. In a prospective cohort from a registered clinical trial (NCT07239063), DeepLNM remained robust (AUC = 0.845). In a user study, DeepLNM improved diagnostic accuracy, especially for junior pathologists (95.0%-97.3%), while reducing diagnostic time and increasing confidence. To explore the model's generalizability, it was further validated in a gastric cancer cohort, achieving an AUC of 0.793. Finally, DeepLNM identified histopathological features associated with LNM, addressing the "black-box" concern of deep learning. Together, these results position DeepLNM as a clinically preliminarily validated multimodal model for predicting LNM status in CRC, potentially facilitating the clinical translation of AI pathology.

evidence_text:
Performance of an Artificial Intelligence Foundation Model for Prostate Radiotherapy Segmentation.

Purpose

Radiation therapy is a major treatment modality for localized prostate cancer, and accurate target segmentation is a critical aspect of radiation delivery that can directly affect patient outcomes. We evaluated the performance of an artificial intelligence (AI) foundation model in target segmentation tasks for prostate radiotherapy planning.

Methods

AI segmentation using Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM 2) was evaluated from computed tomography images with varying levels of human intervention, ranging from intervals of every 2nd to every 10th ground truth slice provided as input. Segmentation accuracy was measured using dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) for intact and postoperative prostate target delineation.

Results

SAM 2 achieved performance similar to and, in some cases, worse than interpolation in DSC and HD95 for both intact and postoperative prostate cancer patient cases, and the AI segmentation accuracy was significantly better in the intact preoperative patient cases where anatomic boundaries were better defined than postoperative patient cases (P < .01† for intervals 5-10). evidence_text: Learning Discrete Cell and Niche Codes from Spatial Transcriptomics Using Dual Residual Vector Quantization Spatially-resolved transcriptomics (SRT) measures gene expression at single-cell resolution while preserving each cell’s spatial location, enabling the joint study of  cell identity and cellular  niche , the recurring microenvironment that organises tissue function. Existing representation-learning methods typically capture only one of these axes at a time. We present SQUINT, a graph vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) that learns  two disjoint codebooks per cell from a shared architecture: a  cell codebook quantising the per-cell embedding before neighbourhood aggregation, biased toward cell-intrinsic identity, and a  niche codebook quantising the embedding after graph neural network (GNN) aggregation, biased toward spatial context. Both use residual vector quantization, giving a coarse-to-fine discrete-token hierarchy. SQUINT is trained with per-branch negative-binomial reconstruction objectives and three domain-motivated components that we show are crucial: a within-section cosine adjacency loss that anchors the niche codes in the spatial graph, a cross-section contrastive loss on the cell latents that aligns transcriptomically matched cells, and a decoder section covariate that absorbs batch effects. Across three datasets spanning four spatial assays (STARmap, MERFISH, CosMx, Xenium) and four tasks – niche identification, cell-type identification, cross-section integration, and spatial gene-expression imputation in held-out regions – SQUINT outperforms or is competitive with strong baselines on identification and achieves the most faithful cross-section integration. The resulting discrete vocabulary makes tissues directly consumable by transformer-style foundation models and enables one-step query-to-reference atlas mapping via code-distribution similarity, which we demonstrate on a CosMx human non-small-cell lung cancer cohort.

evidence_text: Cellular senescence in human liver under normal aging and cancer. Cellular senescence, a stress-induced program causing stable cell-cycle arrest, is a hallmark of liver aging, fibrosis, and cancer. However, the cell-type-specific mechanisms, spatial organization, and cancer-associated alterations in the liver remain unclear. We profiled 43 normal human livers spanning ages and fibrosis stages using a single-cell multiome, Xenium spatial transcriptomics, and CODEX, complemented by fibrotic mouse models and 24 colorectal cancer liver metastases. We found CDKN1A+ senescent hepatocytes, fibroblasts, cholangiocytes, and endothelial cells associated with age, liver disease, or cancer. Senescence differed between aged and fibrotic livers, with similar patterns in mice. Spatially, CDKN1A+ hepatocytes localized periportally, while SERPINE1+ aging-associated hepatocytes formed spatial clusters, potentially mediated by Claudins and THBS1. Fibrotic regions contained CXCL12+ senescent fibroblasts interacting with CXCR4+ immune cells. Chemotherapy intensified senescence in hepatocytes by 5-fold relative to aging and led to unique CDKN2A+ populations. Across conditions, senescent cells shared AP-1 activation, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and apoptosis resistance, suggesting therapeutic opportunities.

Spatial transcriptomics and single-cell methods are changing the questions we can ask about the human cardiovascular system. In this review, we share lessons learned from applying spatial profiling to human cardiovascular samples. We walk through experimental considerations, sampling, fixation, and ribonucleic acid quality control, then compare sequencing-based and imaging-based platforms within a 2-stage "discovery then validation" framework. We propose a heart-aware analytical pipeline: spatially informed quality control, normalization respecting the outsized transcriptome of cardiomyocytes, thoughtful segmentation, and honest assessment of reproducibility. We consider how spatial data can be woven together with single-cell, epigenomic, and proteomic layers, and look ahead to emerging frontiers including integration with cardiac imaging foundation models. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patient management relies on molecular analysis to determine eligibility for targeted therapy. Furthermore, neoadjuvant immunotherapy is primarily suitable in the absence of specific genomic alterations. However, significant challenges remain, including suboptimal molecular testing and patients being assigned to non-optimal treatment strategies. Here, we present AI classifiers for the identification of EGFR, ALK, BRAF and MET alterations directly from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained tissue using CanvOI 1.1, a digital pathology foundation model. Their performance was evaluated on an independent validation dataset of 968 NSCLC samples. The classifiers achieved AUCs of 0.87 for EGFR, 0.96 for ALK, 0.88 for BRAF and 0.83 for MET. Moreover, they demonstrated high accuracy in identifying cases lacking alterations. Our results highlight the potential of deep-learning tools for the detection of NSCLC biomarkers and specifically the identification of tumors without EGFR or ALK driver alterations, supporting more informed clinical decision-making.

A pre-trained foundation model framework for multiplanar MRI classification of extramural vascular invasion and mesorectal fascia invasion in rectal cancer.

Objectives

Accurate MRI-based identification of extramural vascular invasion (EVI) and mesorectal fascia invasion (MFI) is crucial for risk-stratified rectal cancer treatment. However, subjective visual assessment and inter-institutional variability limit diagnostic consistency. This study developed and evaluated a multi-center, foundation model-driven framework that automatically classifies EVI and MFI on axial and sagittal MRI.

Materials and methods

A total of 331 pre-treatment rectal cancer T2-weighted MRI scans from three European hospitals were retrospectively recruited. A self-supervised frequency domain harmonization strategy was applied to reduce scanner variability. Three classifiers, SeResNet, the universal biomedical pretrained model (UMedPT) with a multilayer perceptron head, and a logistic-regression variant using frozen UMedPT features (UMedPT_LR), were trained (n = 265) and tested (n = 66). Gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) visualized model predictions.

Results

UMedPT_LR achieved the best EVI performance with multiplanar fusion (AUC = 0.82, test set). For MFI, UMedPT trained on axial harmonized images yielded the highest performance (AUC = 0.77). Both tasks outperformed the CHAIMELEON 2024 benchmark (EVI: 0.82 vs 0.74; MFI: 0.77 vs 0.75). Harmonization enhanced MFI classification, and multiplanar fusion further boosted EVI performance. Grad-CAM confirmed biologically plausible attention on peritumoral regions (EVI) and mesorectal fascia margins (MFI).

Conclusion

The proposed foundation model-driven framework, leveraging frequency domain harmonization and multiplanar fusion, achieves state-of-the-art performance for automated EVI and MFI classification on MRI, demonstrating strong generalizability across multiple centers.

Critical relevance statement

Addressing inter-center inconsistencies in rectal cancer MRI, a multiplanar foundation model with cross-scanner harmonization significantly improves the detection of EVI and MFI, potentially standardizing staging and guiding therapy.

Key points

Among the first studies to investigate automated classification of both EVI and MFI using axial and sagittal T2-weighted MRI. Foundation model-derived features outperform conventional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for EVI and MFI classification. Frequency domain harmonization and multiplanar fusion selectively enhance diagnostic performance. Automated prediction of EVI and MFI may support more consistent staging and clinical decision-making across institutions.

evidence_text: A CT Lesion Foundation Model for Non-Invasive Assessment of Hepatocellular Carcinoma Aggressiveness and Prediction of Recurrence Risk.  Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with high recurrence rates following curative resection. Accurate non-invasive assessment of tumor aggressiveness and recurrence risk is critical for surgical decision-making and postoperative surveillance, yet remains challenging with conventional imaging modalities. Here, we developed a CT lesion foundation model (LFM), trained via self-supervised learning on 32,120 generic lesion and 6,387 HCC-specific CT patches to capture transferable intra-lesional imaging phenotypes. Across one internal and two external validation cohorts, the sequentially pretrained LFM (LFM-Seq) achieved area under the curve values of 0.916, 0.846, and 0.920 for microvascular invasion (MVI) assessment, and 0.833, 0.885 and 0.795 for pathological grade assessment. The model remained robust under scenarios of limited training data and tumor localization perturbations. Furthermore, LFM-Seq-derived risk scores stratified recurrence-free survival (RFS), yielding an externally validated C-index of 0.701, and remained independently associated with RFS after adjusting for clinicopathological factors. Exploratory biological interpretability analyses showed that LFM-Seq-derived risk phenotypes were associated with suppressed lymphocyte-related immune programs. These results suggest that CT lesion foundation models can support non-invasive and robust characterization of HCC aggressiveness, recurrence risk stratification and discovery of interpretable prognostic imaging biomarkers.
